UCOS Ω∞ — UNIVERSAL MARKETPLACE MASTER SPECIFICATION
===============================================================================

DOCUMENT ID:
UCOS-MKT-MASTER-SPECIFICATION-001

DOCUMENT TITLE:
UNIVERSAL MARKETPLACE
MASTER PRODUCT, BUSINESS, ARCHITECTURE, CAPABILITY, APPLICATION,
UI/UX, DATA, API, INTEGRATION, SECURITY, GOVERNANCE,
MULTI-COUNTRY, MALL, FINANCIAL COMMERCE AND VERIFICATION SPECIFICATION

DOCUMENT VERSION:
1.0 — CONSOLIDATED MASTER BASELINE

DOCUMENT STATUS:
PROPOSED — PENDING CONTEXT ASSIMILATION, CANONICAL OWNERSHIP
RECONCILIATION, REQUIREMENTS VALIDATION AND EXPLICIT APPROVAL

ARCHITECTURAL AUTHORITY:
UCOS Ω∞ — Universal Commerce and Marketplace Context

SPECIFICATION TYPE:
Product + Business + Logical Architecture + Capability Architecture
+ Application Architecture + UX Architecture + Data Architecture
+ Integration Architecture + Security Architecture + Governance
+ Verification + Operational Readiness

SCOPE:
A globally extensible, multi-country, multi-market, multi-currency,
multi-language, multi-merchant, multi-brand, multi-store,
multi-mall, multi-channel, multi-business-model commerce ecosystem.

PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:
Define the complete, extensible, reusable and verifiable requirements
for a universal marketplace platform capable of supporting consumer
commerce, business commerce, seller ecosystems, brand storefronts,
digital malls, physical malls, hybrid commerce, payments, financial
operations, fulfillment, loyalty, promotions, customer support,
trust, safety, AI-assisted commerce and future commercial models.

IMPORTANT STATUS QUALIFICATION:
This document defines the intended scope and architectural requirements.
It does not certify that all requirements have been implemented, that
every existing UCOS capability has been discovered, or that the platform
has achieved feature parity with Amazon or any other marketplace.

Completeness must be established through evidence-based requirements
assessment, canonical ownership reconciliation, implementation evidence,
independent verification and formal acceptance.

===============================================================================
00. GOVERNING ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
===============================================================================

00.1. UCOS ARCHITECTURAL PHILOSOPHY

The platform SHALL be designed according to these principles:

1. No unnecessary architectural compromises.
2. No avoidable technical debt.
3. No shortcuts that undermine correctness, security or extensibility.
4. No duplicate canonical knowledge.
5. No duplicate capability ownership.
6. No ambiguous domain boundaries.
7. No uncontrolled proliferation of universes, services or registries.
8. No hardcoded country, currency, language, provider or business model.
9. No unnecessary vendor lock-in.
10. No technology-specific assumptions in canonical business semantics.
11. No infrastructure-specific assumptions in domain architecture.
12. No orphaned artifacts, capabilities, interfaces or data definitions.
13. No circular dependencies.
14. No hidden business rules.
15. No undocumented state transitions.
16. No untraceable requirements.
17. No unsupported completeness claims.
18. No implementation before the applicable governance approvals.
19. No creation of a new canonical concept before reuse assessment.
20. No silent changes to financial, legal, security or governance rules.

00.2. REUSE-FIRST CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Before defining or implementing any capability:

A. Discover relevant existing UCOS constitutions.
B. Discover relevant universes and canonical concepts.
C. Discover existing capabilities and their owners.
D. Discover applicable laws, policies and contracts.
E. Discover schemas, APIs, events and registries.
F. Discover existing lifecycle models and state machines.
G. Discover existing UI patterns and application surfaces.
H. Discover verification, certification and evidence mechanisms.
I. Discover existing implementation and tests where available.
J. Map the requested requirement to the existing architecture.
K. Identify gaps, overlaps, conflicts and missing evidence.
L. Reuse existing canonical ownership whenever possible.
M. Extend an existing capability when that is architecturally correct.
N. Introduce a new canonical artifact only when justified.
O. Record the decision and its supporting evidence.

A concept being absent from a document does not automatically mean
that the concept is absent from the UCOS architecture.

An artifact being present does not automatically mean that its
capability is complete or correctly implemented.

00.3. CANONICAL OWNERSHIP

Every canonical concept SHALL have:

- One authoritative definition.
- One canonical owner.
- A defined lifecycle.
- A defined identity model.
- Defined relationships.
- Defined invariants.
- Defined permissions.
- Defined data classification.
- Defined interfaces.
- Defined change authority.
- Defined evidence requirements.
- Defined validation and certification criteria.

Multiple systems may maintain projections, indexes, caches or local
representations, but these must not become competing authorities.

00.4. KNOWLEDGE ONCE PRINCIPLE

Canonical knowledge SHALL be authored once and reused.

Derived representations may include:

- User interfaces.
- API schemas.
- Documentation.
- Registry projections.
- Analytics models.
- Search indexes.
- Operational dashboards.
- Test cases.
- Generated configuration.
- Developer documentation.

Derived representations SHALL remain traceable to their authoritative
sources and SHALL NOT independently redefine canonical semantics.

00.5. CONFIGURATION-DRIVEN EXTENSIBILITY

Where a capability is genuinely variable, the architecture SHALL
represent the variation through governed configuration, policies,
schemas, capabilities, contracts or extension points.

Examples include:

- Countries and markets.
- Currencies.
- Languages.
- Product categories.
- Business models.
- Seller types.
- Mall types.
- Payment providers.
- Fulfillment providers.
- Verification providers.
- Promotion types.
- Customer eligibility.
- Tax rules.
- Storefront layouts.
- Approval workflows.
- Jurisdictional requirements.

Configuration SHALL be validated, versioned, authorized and auditable.

Configuration must not be used to bypass required legal, security,
financial integrity or governance constraints.

00.6. ARCHITECTURAL NEUTRALITY

The logical architecture SHALL remain independent of specific:

- Cloud providers.
- Database vendors.
- Programming languages.
- Web frameworks.
- Mobile frameworks.
- Payment gateways.
- Search engines.
- AI providers.
- KYC/KYB providers.
- Logistics providers.
- Identity providers.
- Messaging platforms.
- Infrastructure topologies.

Technology decisions may be made during an approved implementation
phase through explicit evaluation and documented trade-offs.

00.7. NO PREMATURE IMPLEMENTATION

This specification does not authorize:

- Repository modifications.
- New production services.
- New universes or registries.
- Database migrations.
- Financial transaction processing.
- Production configuration changes.
- External provider onboarding.
- Deployment.
- Market activation.
- Unapproved implementation work.

These actions require the applicable context assessment, design
approval, implementation authority and release controls.

===============================================================================
01. PRODUCT VISION AND BUSINESS OBJECTIVES
===============================================================================

01.1. PRODUCT VISION

Create a universal commerce ecosystem that supports the complete
lifecycle of discovery, evaluation, purchase, payment, fulfillment,
service delivery, post-purchase support, loyalty, reputation and
merchant growth across digital and physical commerce environments.

The ecosystem SHALL support:

- Customers.
- Businesses and organizations.
- Sellers and merchants.
- Manufacturers.
- Brands.
- Authorized distributors.
- Affiliates and creators.
- Advertisers.
- Service providers.
- Mall operators.
- Physical store operators.
- Marketplace administrators.
- Customer-support agents.
- Financial and reconciliation operators.
- Risk and trust investigators.
- Developers and integration partners.

01.2. BUSINESS MODELS

The platform SHALL be architecturally capable of supporting applicable
combinations of:

- Business-to-consumer commerce.
- Business-to-business commerce.
- Consumer-to-consumer commerce.
- Direct-to-consumer commerce.
- Business-to-business-to-consumer commerce.
- Consumer-to-business commerce.
- Wholesale commerce.
- Retail commerce.
- Marketplace commerce.
- Distributor and reseller commerce.
- Dropshipping.
- Subscription commerce.
- Membership commerce.
- Digital goods.
- Physical goods.
- Services.
- Rentals and leasing.
- Appointments and bookings.
- Reservations.
- Auctions and bidding.
- Procurement.
- Replenishment.
- Pre-orders.
- Made-to-order products.
- Configurable and personalized products.
- Recurring orders.
- Local commerce.
- Cross-border commerce.
- Social and creator commerce.
- Live commerce.
- Physical, digital and hybrid mall commerce.

Not every business model must be activated in every market.

01.3. BUSINESS OUTCOMES

The platform should enable:

- Global reach with local compliance.
- Merchant and brand onboarding.
- Accurate product discovery.
- Transparent pricing.
- Reliable order processing.
- Secure payments.
- Correct financial settlement.
- Efficient fulfillment.
- Effective returns and refunds.
- Customer trust.
- Seller success.
- Brand protection.
- Mall and marketplace growth.
- Measurable marketing performance.
- Fraud reduction.
- Operational automation.
- Extensibility without architectural duplication.

02.2. SYSTEM BOUNDARIES

The architecture SHALL distinguish:

- Marketplace-owned responsibilities.
- Merchant-owned responsibilities.
- Brand-owned responsibilities.
- Mall-operator responsibilities.
- Customer responsibilities.
- External provider responsibilities.
- Jurisdictional and regulatory responsibilities.

External services may provide capabilities, but their use SHALL NOT
transfer canonical business ownership or eliminate the marketplace's
obligations for correctness, auditability and controlled integration.

02.3. SEPARATION OF CONCEPTS

The following concepts must not be conflated:

- Product != Listing.
- Listing != Offer.
- Offer != Price.
- Price != Discount.
- Discount != Payment.
- Payment != Order.
- Order != Shipment.
- Shipment != Delivery.
- Refund != Payment reversal in every possible payment model.
- Wallet != Payment instrument.
- Wallet balance != Loyalty points.
- Gift card != Coupon.
- Coupon != Store credit.
- Seller != Brand.
- Brand != Brand shop.
- Seller != Seller shop.
- Shop != Physical store.
- Mall != Marketplace.
- Mall != Legal entity.
- Country != Commercial market.
- Geographic territory != Jurisdiction.
- Currency != Locale.
- Identity authentication != KYC.
- KYC != KYB.
- Verification != Authorization.
- Verification status != Risk score.
- Rating != Review.
- Affiliate attribution != Seller attribution.
- Advertising spend != Sales commission.
- Catalog product != Market-specific listing.
- Customer account != Organization account.
- Available balance != Pending balance.
- Order cancellation != Return.
- Return != Refund.
- Inventory quantity != Sellable availability.

Every additional distinction discovered during context assimilation
must be recorded and resolved through canonical ownership rules.

03.1. ACTOR TYPES

Support configurable actor types, including:

- Individual customer.
- Business customer.

- Seller.

- Brand owner.
- Authorized representative.
- Affiliate.
- Creator.
- Advertiser.
- Mall operator.
- Store operator.
- Service provider.
- Support agent.
- Administrator.
- Financial operator.
- Risk investigator.
- Developer.
- Integration partner.

03.2. IDENTITY CAPABILITIES

The architecture SHALL support:

- Account registration.
- Authentication.
- Multi-factor authentication.
- Passwordless authentication where appropriate.
- Credential recovery.
- Session management.
- Device and session security.
- Account linking.
- Organization membership.
- Delegated access.
- Role-based authorization.
- Attribute-based authorization where appropriate.
- Scoped permissions.
- Consent and preference management.
- Account suspension and restoration.
- Account closure.

- Account takeover detection.

03.3. AUTHORIZATION

Authorization must consider the relevant context, including:

- Actor.
- Organization.
- Resource.
- Action.
- Relationship.
- Role.
- Market.
- Jurisdiction.
- Risk.
- Resource state.
- Applicable policy.
- Time and expiry.
- Delegation authority.

Permissions SHALL follow least privilege.

Administrative privileges SHALL be scoped and auditable.

Sensitive actions SHALL require stronger authorization where warranted.

===============================================================================
04. UNIVERSAL GEOGRAPHY, COUNTRIES AND DYNAMIC MARKETS
===============================================================================

04.1. OBJECTIVE

Support dynamic geographic and commercial configuration without
hardcoding a fixed country list or a single universal hierarchy.

04.2. GEOGRAPHIC CONCEPTS

The canonical model should be capable of representing:

- Geographic territories.
- Countries.
- Jurisdictions.
- Administrative regions.
- States and provinces.
- Districts.
- Municipalities.
- Cities.
- Localities.
- Postal regions.
- Delivery areas.
- Commercial zones.
- Economic zones.
- Customs territories.
- Special administrative areas.
- Physical service territories.
- Custom geographic boundaries.
- Overlapping territories.
- Non-territorial commercial markets.

Not every jurisdiction has the same hierarchy.

The model must support alternative parent-child relationships and
overlapping membership where justified.

04.3. COUNTRY CONTEXT

Country-specific configuration may include:

- Legal and regulatory rules.
- Languages and locales.
- Currency support.
- Tax requirements.
- Invoice requirements.
- Payment methods.
- Settlement methods.
- KYC/KYB requirements.
- Consumer protection.
- Product restrictions.
- Import and export requirements.
- Customs and duties.
- Shipping and delivery.
- Returns and refunds.
- Data protection.
- Data residency.
- Record retention.
- Seller eligibility.
- Marketplace terms.
- Support languages.
- Customer communication rules.

04.4. COMMERCIAL MARKET

A market is a commercial operating context and is not necessarily
identical to a country.

A market may be associated with:

- One country.
- A region within a country.
- Multiple territories where permitted.
- A customer segment.
- A commercial channel.
- A business model.
- A mall.
- A seller group.
- A brand.
- A defined operating model.

All associations must be governed and validated.

04.5. DYNAMIC MARKET ONBOARDING

The market lifecycle SHALL support:

1. Proposed.
2. Context discovery.
3. Requirements assessment.
4. Configuration.
5. Integration setup.
6. Security and compliance review.
7. Testing.
8. Certification.
9. Approval.
10. Activation.
11. Monitoring.
12. Restriction or suspension.
13. Reactivation.
14. Retirement.

A configured market is not necessarily a validated market.

A validated market is not necessarily an approved market.

An approved market is not necessarily an active market.

04.6. MARKET READINESS

Before activation, verify:

- Required legal and regulatory configuration.
- Seller eligibility.
- Product eligibility.
- Catalog publication.
- Pricing and currency rules.
- Taxes and invoices.
- Payment processing.
- Refund handling.
- Settlement.
- Shipping and fulfillment.
- Customer support.
- Privacy and security.
- Identity and verification workflows.
- Reconciliation.
- Operational monitoring.
- Failure recovery.
- End-to-end certification.

04.7. CUSTOMER MARKET SELECTION

Support:

- Explicit market selection.
- Market switching.
- Locale preferences.
- Currency preferences.
- Language preferences.
- Address-based availability.
- Delivery-area validation.
- Market-specific catalog views.
- Market-specific terms.
- Market-specific prices and taxes.

Automatic market suggestions must not silently override a customer's
explicit selection or misrepresent applicable prices or terms.

04.8. MARKET-SPECIFIC CATALOG

The platform must distinguish:

- Global product identity.
- Market availability.
- Market listing.
- Market-specific content.
- Market-specific pricing.
- Market-specific offers.
- Market-specific restrictions.
- Market-specific inventory.
- Market-specific fulfillment.
- Market-specific regulatory eligibility.

A global product's existence does not imply that it may be sold
in every market.

===============================================================================
05. MULTI-COUNTRY AND CROSS-BORDER COMMERCE
===============================================================================

05.1. REQUIRED SCENARIOS

Support applicable scenarios such as:

- Customer and seller in the same country.
- Customer and seller in different countries.
- Brand operating in multiple markets.
- Seller operating in multiple markets.
- Regional fulfillment.
- International fulfillment.
- Cross-border returns.
- Cross-border refunds.
- Cross-border seller settlement.
- Different catalog assortments by market.
- Different pricing by market.
- Different tax treatment.
- Different payment methods.
- Different legal terms.

05.2. CURRENCY MODEL

Distinguish:

- Product reference currency.
- Display currency.
- Order transaction currency.
- Payment processing currency.
- Refund currency.
- Seller settlement currency.
- Accounting or reporting currency.

These currencies may be identical or different.

Define:

- Exchange-rate source.
- Rate timestamp.
- Conversion direction.
- Rate precision.
- Rounding policy.
- FX fee treatment.
- Rate-lock policy where applicable.
- Refund conversion policy.
- Settlement conversion policy.
- Reconciliation rules.

Never silently change the financial meaning of a transaction because
a user changes their display-currency preference.

05.3. TAX AND CUSTOMS

Support configurable integration and calculation contracts for:

- Sales tax.
- VAT.
- GST.
- Other applicable indirect taxes.
- Tax exemptions.
- Tax-inclusive and tax-exclusive pricing.
- Invoice and credit-note requirements.
- Import duties.
- Customs declarations.
- Product origin.
- Import restrictions.
- Applicable seller tax information.

Actual legal treatment must be determined from the applicable
jurisdiction and approved tax rules, not generic assumptions.

05.4. CROSS-BORDER CONTROLS

Define controls for:

- Seller eligibility.
- Customer eligibility.
- Product restrictions.
- Restricted destinations.
- Import/export requirements.
- Payment and settlement restrictions.
- Identity verification.
- Sanctions screening where applicable.
- Privacy and data transfers.
- Delivery commitments.
- Returns.
- Dispute handling.
- Record retention.

10. UNIVERSAL MALL AND MALL OPERATING SYSTEM
===============================================================================

10.1. OBJECTIVE

Provide a configurable commercial mall capability supporting digital,
physical and hybrid shopping environments.

A mall is a commercial destination and governance context. It is not
synonymous with a marketplace, brand, seller, shop or legal entity.

10.2. MALL TYPES

Support configurable profiles such as:

- General digital mall.
- Brand mall.
- Luxury mall.
- Fashion mall.
- Electronics mall.
- B2B mall.
- Services mall.
- Local mall.
- Regional mall.
- Country-specific mall.
- Virtual mall.
- Physical shopping-center integration.
- Hybrid mall.
- Curated mall.
- Specialized mall.
- Event-based mall.
- Other approved commercial configurations.

These must be configurable profiles rather than separate hardcoded
applications.

10.3. MALL IDENTITY

A mall may have:

- Canonical mall identity.
- Commercial owner.
- Operator.
- Branding.
- Domain or URL.

- Participation policies.
- Categories.
- Zones.

- Store directory.

- Malls.
- Mall groups.
- Regions.

- Floors where applicable.
- Categories.
- Collections.
- Brand shops.
- Seller shops.
- Physical stores.
- Service locations.
- Pickup points.
- Events.
- Promotional areas.

The architecture must not assume that every store belongs to exactly
one mall or that every mall has a physical floor structure.

10.5. MALL STORE ADMISSION

10.10. MALL RELATIONSHIPS

The architecture must allow:

- One brand to operate multiple brand shops.
- One seller to operate multiple seller shops.
- One shop to participate in multiple authorized malls.
- One mall to contain many shops.
- One physical store to participate in digital and physical experiences.
- One marketplace to contain multiple malls.
- One market to contain multiple malls.
- One mall to serve multiple approved markets where permitted.

These relationships must be explicit, permission-controlled and
consistent with legal ownership and commercial agreements.

16.4. REDEMPTION INVARIANTS

- The same entitlement must not be consumed twice.
- Retries must not create duplicate redemption.
- Failed transactions must not leave unintended permanent consumption.
- Reversal must follow defined rules.
- Redemption must be traceable to an authoritative record.
- Expired or revoked instruments must not be accepted.
- Discounts must not silently become cash balances.
- Financial and promotional instruments must retain distinct semantics.
- Every material decision must be auditable.

- Projection refresh.
- Display rules.
- Dispute handling.

The platform must not silently manipulate ratings.

Verified-purchase status is evidence of a purchase relationship,
not proof that every statement in a review is truthful.

26.5. INTERFACES

- Submit review.
- Review history.
- Product review listing.
- Seller ratings.
- Brand ratings.
- Shop ratings.
- Mall ratings.
- Media gallery.
- Helpful-review interaction.
- Report review.
- Moderation queue.
- Appeals.
- Reputation analytics.
- Manipulation monitoring.

===============================================================================
27. KYC, KYB, VERIFICATION AND TRUST
===============================================================================

27.1. DISTINCTIONS

KYC:
Identity-related checks for individuals where applicable.

KYB:
Business and legal-entity verification where applicable.

Authentication:
Establishing that an actor controls an authenticated identity or
credential.

Authorization:
Determining whether an actor may perform an action.

Verification:
Checking a specific claim against defined evidence or an authoritative
source.

Risk assessment:
Evaluating indicators to support a governed decision.

These concepts must not be treated as interchangeable.

27.2. VERIFICATION TYPES

Support applicable verification for:

- Customer identity.
- Seller identity.
- Business identity.
- Legal entity.
- Beneficial owner.
- Authorized representative.
- Address.
- Tax registration.
- Bank-account ownership.
- Brand ownership.
- Trademark or rights evidence.
- Authorized reseller.
- Distributor authorization.
- Product authenticity.
- Product provenance.
- Affiliate identity.
- Advertiser identity.
- Service-provider eligibility.
- Other approved verification requirements.

27.3. VERIFICATION LIFECYCLE

Support:

1. Requirement determination.
2. Notice and consent where required.
3. Evidence collection.
4. Secure submission.
5. Completeness validation.
6. Authenticity and consistency checks.
7. Authoritative-source or provider checks.
8. Risk-based review.
9. Manual review where necessary.
10. Decision.
11. Reason codes.
12. Approval.
13. Rejection.
14. Pending review.
15. Remediation.
16. Resubmission.
17. Appeal.
18. Expiry.
19. Re-verification.
20. Suspension or revocation.
21. Audit and retention.

27.4. VERIFICATION STATES

Define applicable states such as:

- Not required.
- Not started.
- Required.
- In progress.
- Pending review.
- Additional information required.
- Approved.
- Rejected.
- Expired.
- Suspended.
- Revoked.
- Under appeal.

State transitions must be governed and auditable.

27.5. EVIDENCE SECURITY

- Minimize sensitive data collection.
- Encrypt protected evidence.
- Restrict access.
- Record access to sensitive evidence.
- Apply retention and deletion rules.
- Protect provider credentials.
- Avoid exposing sensitive evidence in general logs.
- Separate verification results from raw evidence.
- Preserve decision provenance.
- Apply applicable privacy and legal requirements.

27.6. VERIFICATION PROVIDER ABSTRACTION

Support provider-independent contracts for:

- Identity verification.
- Business verification.
- Document verification.
- Bank verification.
- Tax validation.
- Risk screening.
- Other approved checks.

Provider replacement must not require rewriting canonical business
semantics.

27.7. TRUST AND SAFETY

Detect and manage:

- Account takeover.
- Fake sellers.
- Fake brands.
- Counterfeit products.
- Fake reviews.
- Coupon abuse.
- Referral abuse.
- Payment fraud.
- Refund abuse.
- Return abuse.
- Affiliate fraud.
- Payout diversion.
- Suspicious account relationships.
- Policy violations.
- Impersonation.
- Prohibited products.
- Other applicable marketplace abuse.

27.8. CASE MANAGEMENT

Support:

- Alert creation.
- Case creation.
- Evidence collection.
- Investigation.
- Reviewer assignment.
- Decision.
- Reason codes.
- Corrective action.
- Restriction.
- Appeal.
- Reinstatement.
- Audit.
- Reporting.

Enforcement must be proportionate, authorized, and reviewable.

41. NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

41.1. SCALABILITY

where appropriate for:

- Catalog growth.
- Search traffic.
- Order volume.
- Seller growth.
- Country expansion.
- Mall expansion.
- Event volume.
- Financial transaction volume.
- Analytics workloads.

- Service-level objectives.
- Service-level indicators.
- Recovery time objectives.
- Recovery point objectives.
- Failure isolation.
- Backpressure.
- Retry policies.
- Circuit breaking where appropriate.
- Graceful degradation.
- Disaster recovery.
- Backup and restore.
- Dependency failure behavior.

41.3. PERFORMANCE

Performance targets must be measured, workload-specific and approved.

Potential initial targets for assessment—not accepted commitments—include:

- Search response p95 around 300 ms for defined workloads.
- Platform-controlled checkout processing p95 around 500 ms for
  defined workloads, excluding external provider latency.
- Critical event processing within a defined service-level objective.
- Explicit targets for product pages, cart operations, API latency,
  financial operations and operational dashboards.

Actual targets must be validated against expected load, infrastructure,
consistency requirements, business criticality and cost.

41.4. CONSISTENCY

Define consistency requirements separately for:

- Financial ledgers.
- Inventory reservations.
- Order state.
- Payment state.
- Promotion redemption.
- Gift-card balances.
- Loyalty balances.
- Search indexes.
- Analytics projections.
- Notifications.

Strong consistency, eventual consistency and reconciliation must be
chosen according to the correctness requirements of each domain.

41.5. OPERABILITY

The platform must support:

- Observability.
- Alerting.
- Runbooks.
- Incident management.
- Deployment safety.
- Rollback.
- Feature controls.
- Configuration validation.
- Capacity planning.
- Operational ownership.
- Change management.
- Disaster recovery testing.

===============================================================================
42. WORKFLOWS, STATE MACHINES AND INVARIANTS
===============================================================================

42.1. REQUIRED WORKFLOWS

Define complete workflows for:

- Customer registration.
- Seller onboarding.
- Brand onboarding.
- Brand verification.
- Seller verification.
- Country onboarding.
- Market activation.
- Mall creation.
- Mall activation.
- Store admission.
- Product publication.
- Listing publication.
- Promotion creation.
- Coupon redemption.
- Wallet transaction.
- Gift-card issuance.
- Gift-card redemption.
- Loyalty accrual.
- Checkout.
- Payment.
- Order confirmation.
- Fulfillment.
- Delivery.
- Cancellation.
- Return.
- Refund.
- Seller settlement.
- Payout.
- Review moderation.
- Fraud investigation.
- Verification appeal.
- Account suspension.
- Reinstatement.

42.2. STATE MACHINE REQUIREMENTS

Every state machine must define:

- Initial state.
- Allowed states.
- Allowed transitions.
- Transition authority.
- Preconditions.
- Side effects.
- Failure behavior.
- Retry behavior.
- Compensation.
- Audit.
- Terminal states.
- Recovery.

42.3. GLOBAL INVARIANTS

At minimum:

1. Every canonical entity has an authoritative owner.
2. No financial transaction is posted twice unintentionally.
3. No redemption is committed twice unintentionally.
4. Financial records are not silently overwritten.
5. Unauthorized actors cannot perform protected actions.
6. Restricted products cannot bypass applicable eligibility rules.
7. Unapproved sellers cannot access restricted selling capabilities.
8. Unverified claims are not represented as verified facts.
9. Country activation requires required readiness gates.
10. Mall activation requires required readiness gates.
11. Price and order calculations are reproducible under their rules.
12. Payment and order states are reconciled.
13. Refunds reference applicable original financial transactions.
14. Seller settlements reconcile with applicable financial records.
15. Review aggregates derive from authoritative review records.
16. Market-specific policies are explicitly resolved.
17. Conflicting policies cannot be silently ignored.
18. Derived projections remain traceable to their sources.
19. Administrative actions are authorized and auditable.
20. Every critical requirement has defined verification evidence.

===============================================================================
43. TRACEABILITY, TESTING AND CERTIFICATION
===============================================================================

43.1. REQUIREMENT TRACEABILITY

Every requirement must be traceable through:

Requirement
    -> Business outcome
    -> Canonical concept
    -> Capability
    -> Canonical owner
    -> Architecture component
    -> Data contract
    -> API or event
    -> UI screen
    -> Workflow
    -> State machine
    -> Implementation artifact
    -> Test case
    -> Test result
    -> Evidence
    -> Certification
    -> Deployment
    -> Operational monitoring

43.2. TESTING TYPES

Assess:

- Unit tests.
- Schema tests.
- Contract tests.
- Integration tests.
- End-to-end tests.
- Workflow tests.
- State-transition tests.
- Security tests.
- Privacy tests.
- Performance tests.
- Load tests.
- Resilience tests.
- Disaster recovery tests.
- Accessibility tests.
- Localization tests.
- Financial reconciliation tests.
- Cross-market tests.
- UI regression tests.
- Migration tests.
- Compatibility tests.
- Abuse and fraud tests.

43.3. CRITICAL FINANCIAL TESTS

Verify:

- Duplicate payment prevention.
- Duplicate wallet posting prevention.
- Duplicate redemption prevention.
- Refund correctness.
- Partial refund correctness.
- Currency conversion correctness.
- Rounding.
- Tax calculations.
- Seller fee calculations.
- Affiliate commission calculations.
- Settlement reconciliation.
- Payout failure handling.
- Chargeback treatment.
- Ledger correction.
- Concurrency.
- Retry and timeout behavior.

43.4. COUNTRY AND MARKET TESTS

Verify:

- Market configuration.
- Country-specific catalog.
- Currency.
- Tax.
- Payment methods.
- Seller eligibility.
- KYC/KYB.
- Delivery.
- Returns.
- Customer support.
- Localization.
- Privacy.
- Cross-border restrictions.
- Market activation and suspension.

43.5. MALL TESTS

Verify:

- Mall creation.
- Mall lifecycle.
- Store admission.
- Brand and seller shop relationships.
- Store removal.
- Permissions.
- Mall promotions.
- Market-specific content.
- Search and navigation.
- Commercial terms.
- Analytics.
- Suspension and reinstatement.

43.6. COMPLETENESS EVIDENCE

A feature must not be marked complete merely because:

- It appears in a menu.
- A database table exists.
- An API endpoint exists.
- A document mentions it.
- A mockup exists.
- A test has been written.
- A component compiles.
- A demonstration succeeds.

Completion requires evidence that the required behavior works across
the defined lifecycle and integration boundaries.

===============================================================================
44. MASTER REQUIREMENTS INVENTORY AND GAP REGISTER
===============================================================================

44.1. REQUIREMENT RECORD

Every requirement should have a governed record containing:

- Requirement identifier.
- Title.
- Description.
- Business justification.
- Scope.
- Actor.
- Preconditions.
- Expected behavior.
- Business rules.
- Canonical owner.
- Dependencies.
- Data requirements.
- API requirements.
- Event requirements.
- UI requirements.
- Security requirements.
- Compliance requirements.
- Failure behavior.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Test references.
- Evidence references.
- Priority.
- Status.
- Approval.
- Version.

44.2. GAP STATUSES

Use explicit statuses such as:

- Complete — verified by evidence.
- Partial — some required behavior exists.
- Missing — required behavior is absent.
- Duplicate — overlapping or duplicate capability exists.
- Conflicting — incompatible definitions or rules exist.
- Unverified — implementation or completeness is not evidenced.
- Blocked — dependency or authority prevents progress.
- Deferred — explicitly excluded from the current approved scope.
- Not Applicable — justified and approved as outside the applicable scope.

Do not use "complete" to mean merely documented.

44.3. GAP REGISTER FIELDS

Each gap must include:

- Gap identifier.
- Requirement identifier.
- Observed state.
- Expected state.
- Evidence.
- Canonical owner.
- Existing artifact references.
- Dependencies.
- Risk.
- Impact.
- Resolution proposal.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Verification plan.
- Approval status.

44.4. REUSE DECISION

For every identified gap, decide whether to:

1. Reuse an existing capability.
2. Extend an existing capability.
3. Correct an existing implementation.
4. Resolve conflicting ownership.
5. Consolidate duplicate artifacts.
6. Introduce a new canonical artifact when justified.
7. Defer with explicit approval.
8. Mark not applicable with evidence.

Creating a new service, universe, registry or database is not the
default response to a gap.

46. IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP
===============================================================================

Implementation is prohibited until the relevant requirements have
passed the required context and authorization gates.

PHASE 0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

- Discover existing UCOS architecture.
- Discover applicable constitutions.
- Discover canonical concepts.
- Discover capabilities and ownership.
- Discover APIs and data contracts.
- Discover registries and evidence.
- Discover relevant implementation.
- Discover existing verification.
- Establish the evidence baseline.

EXIT CRITERIA:
The relevant existing architecture is sufficiently understood to
avoid unnecessary duplication and incorrect ownership decisions.

PHASE 1 — CANONICAL OWNERSHIP RECONCILIATION

- Map requirements to existing canonical owners.
- Resolve overlapping concepts.
- Identify conflicting definitions.
- Identify missing ownership.
- Reuse existing contracts.
- Define only justified extensions.
- Reconcile proposed identifiers.

EXIT CRITERIA:
Every in-scope canonical concept has a clear owner or an explicitly
approved plan to establish one.

PHASE 2 — REQUIREMENTS AND GAP ASSESSMENT

- Evaluate every in-scope requirement.
- Record evidence.
- Assign a status.
- Identify missing behavior.
- Identify incomplete workflows.
- Identify missing screens.
- Identify missing integrations.
- Identify missing tests.
- Prioritize risks.

EXIT CRITERIA:
The approved scope has an evidence-backed gap register.

PHASE 3 — TARGET ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION BLUEPRINT

- Define approved architecture changes.
- Define component boundaries.
- Define data contracts.
- Define APIs and events.
- Define state machines.
- Define UI workflows.
- Define security and privacy controls.
- Define operational requirements.
- Define testing and certification.
- Define migration and recovery.

EXIT CRITERIA:
The target architecture is sufficiently specified for the approved
implementation scope and has received the required approval.

PHASE 4 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

- Approve scope.
- Approve priorities.
- Approve dependencies.
- Approve technology decisions where necessary.
- Approve migration plans.
- Approve risk controls.
- Approve verification criteria.
- Authorize implementation work.

EXIT CRITERIA:
Formal implementation authority exists.

PHASE 5 — IMPLEMENTATION

- Implement approved requirements.
- Reuse existing capabilities.
- Maintain canonical ownership.
- Generate derived artifacts where appropriate.
- Implement APIs and integrations.
- Implement UI workflows.
- Implement security controls.
- Implement observability.
- Maintain traceability.

EXIT CRITERIA:
The approved implementation scope is complete and ready for verification.

PHASE 6 — INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION

- Run required tests.
- Validate invariants.
- Verify financial correctness.
- Verify market behavior.
- Verify mall behavior.
- Verify security.
- Verify privacy.
- Verify resilience.
- Verify integrations.
- Verify UI/UX.
- Validate evidence.

EXIT CRITERIA:
Required acceptance criteria pass with traceable evidence.

PHASE 7 — CERTIFICATION AND RELEASE

- Complete operational readiness.
- Complete applicable compliance approvals.
- Complete migration validation.
- Verify recovery procedures.
- Verify monitoring.
- Approve release.
- Deploy through governed procedures.
- Monitor outcomes.

EXIT CRITERIA:
The approved release meets its defined certification and operational
readiness requirements.

PHASE 8 — GOVERNED EVOLUTION

- Monitor real-world behavior.
- Identify new requirements.
- Evaluate new markets.
- Assess new business models.
- Review performance.
- Review incidents.
- Reconcile new capabilities.
- Preserve backward compatibility.
- Update evidence and certification.

EXIT CRITERIA:
Changes continue through the same reuse-first, traceable and governed
evolution model.

===============================================================================
47. GOVERNANCE AND APPROVAL GATES
===============================================================================

G0 — DOCUMENT BASELINE
The master specification is recognized as a proposed requirements
baseline, not as proof of implementation.

G1 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION
Existing UCOS architecture and relevant artifacts have been examined.

G2 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION
Canonical ownership, reuse and conflict resolution are documented.

G3 — REQUIREMENTS APPROVAL
The in-scope requirements and acceptance criteria are approved.

G4 — ARCHITECTURE APPROVAL
Target architecture and integration boundaries are approved.

G5 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION
Implementation is explicitly authorized.

G6 — VERIFICATION APPROVAL
Required tests and evidence satisfy acceptance criteria.

G7 — COMPLIANCE AND OPERATIONAL READINESS
Applicable compliance, support, monitoring and recovery requirements
are satisfied.

G8 — RELEASE APPROVAL
The approved release is authorized.

G9 — POST-RELEASE CERTIFICATION
Production behavior, reconciliation, monitoring and ongoing obligations
are verified.

No gate may be treated as passed without the required evidence and
authorization.

48. MASTER ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
===============================================================================

The marketplace specification may be considered complete for an
approved scope only when:

1. The scope is explicitly defined.
2. Existing UCOS capabilities have been assessed.
3. Canonical ownership is reconciled.
4. Reuse decisions are documented.
5. Duplicate concepts are resolved.
6. Conflicting definitions are resolved.
7. All in-scope business workflows are specified.
8. All required state machines are specified.
9. All required user roles are defined.
10. All required permissions are defined.
11. All required data contracts are specified.
12. All required APIs and events are specified.
13. All required application surfaces are identified.
14. All applicable UI states are specified.
15. Country and market behavior is defined.
16. Cross-border behavior is defined where applicable.
17. Mall lifecycle and governance are defined.
18. Brand and seller shop behavior is defined.
19. Wallet and financial semantics are defined.
20. Redemption and reward semantics are defined.
21. Payment, refund and settlement behavior is defined.
22. Ratings and reviews are governed.
23. KYC/KYB and verification are evidence-backed.
24. Security and privacy controls are specified.
25. Legal and jurisdictional requirements are addressed.
26. Failure and recovery paths are specified.
27. Observability and operations are specified.
28. Requirements map to tests.
29. Tests produce traceable evidence.
30. Critical financial invariants are verified.
31. Market activation criteria are verified.
32. Mall activation criteria are verified.
33. Required compliance approvals exist.
34. Required documentation is available.
35. Required operational ownership is assigned.
36. No unresolved critical gap is hidden by a completeness claim.
37. Release authority exists before production activation.

===============================================================================
49. EXPLICIT COMPLETENESS AND CLAIMS POLICY
===============================================================================

The platform must distinguish among these maturity levels:

LEVEL 1 — IDENTIFIED
A capability is named and included in the requirements inventory.

LEVEL 2 — SPECIFIED
The capability has defined behavior, ownership, interfaces and
acceptance criteria.

LEVEL 3 — ARCHITECTED
The approved logical and implementation architecture is documented.

LEVEL 4 — IMPLEMENTED
The approved implementation exists.

LEVEL 5 — VERIFIED
The implementation has passed its required tests with evidence.

LEVEL 6 — CERTIFIED
Required independent, compliance and operational approvals exist.

LEVEL 7 — OPERATIONALLY VALIDATED
Production behavior and ongoing obligations have been validated.

A capability must not be described as implemented, verified, certified
or production-ready when it has only reached an earlier level.

"100% complete" may be claimed only relative to a clearly defined,
approved scope and explicit acceptance criteria.

No finite specification can guarantee every future business model,
jurisdiction, integration, screen or emerging technology without
continued governed evolution.

===============================================================================
50. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL DECLARATION
===============================================================================

UCOS-MKT-MASTER-SPECIFICATION-001 defines the proposed master
requirements baseline for a universal, extensible marketplace ecosystem.

Its intended scope includes:

- Global and local commerce.
- Dynamic countries and markets.
- Cross-border transactions.
- Global product catalog.
- Market-specific listings and offers.
- Brands and verified brand ownership.
- Brand shops.
- Sellers and seller shops.
- Digital malls.
- Physical mall integration.
- Hybrid commerce.
- Customer applications.
- Seller and brand portals.
- Mall administration.
- Search and recommendations.
- Pricing and promotions.
- Coupons and vouchers.
- Wallets and financial accounts.
- Gift cards and gifting.
- Redemption.
- Loyalty and rewards.
- Memberships and subscriptions.
- Cart and checkout.
- Orders.
- Payments.
- Financial ledger.
- Refunds.
- Settlements and payouts.
- Affiliate and creator commerce.
- Advertising.
- Fulfillment and logistics.
- Returns and warranties.
- Ratings and reviews.
- Customer support.
- KYC/KYB.
- Identity and business verification.
- Brand and product authenticity.
- Trust and safety.
- Fraud prevention.
- Analytics.
- Developer and partner integrations.
- AI-assisted commerce.
- Security and privacy.
- Governance and certification.
- Traceability and evidence.
- Operational readiness.
- Future extensibility.

MANDATORY GOVERNING RULES:

A. Reuse existing UCOS capabilities before extending the architecture.

B. Assign one canonical owner to each canonical concept.

C. Do not create duplicate universes, registries, services or
   control planes without a documented and approved justification.

D. Keep canonical knowledge authoritative and derived representations
   traceable.

E. Make applicable variability configurable, governed and validated.

F. Preserve technology, vendor, infrastructure and database neutrality
   in the logical architecture.

G. Define financial integrity, security and privacy as architectural
   requirements rather than optional enhancements.

H. Treat country, market and mall activation as governed lifecycle
   transitions.

I. Require evidence for implementation and completeness claims.

J. Do not begin implementation or modify repository truth until the
   required context reconciliation, approvals and implementation
   authorization are complete.

K. Maintain traceability from business requirement through canonical
   ownership, implementation, testing, evidence and certification.

L. Continue evolving the platform through governed, backward-compatible
   and evidence-based changes.

FINAL STATUS:

PROPOSED MASTER SPECIFICATION — CONSOLIDATED.

NOT YET PROVEN:
- Complete alignment with every existing UCOS artifact.
- Absence of all canonical duplication.
- Complete one-to-one parity with Amazon or another marketplace.
- Implementation of every listed capability.
- Production certification.
- Universal legal compliance across all possible jurisdictions.

NEXT GOVERNED ACTIVITY:

Reconcile this master specification against the actual UCOS canonical
architecture and existing implementation. Produce an evidence-backed
requirements and gap matrix, resolve ownership and overlap, and obtain
the applicable approval before authorizing implementation.

    remain implementation decisions governed by approved architecture.

    duplication or fragmentation.

- Geographic coverage.
- Eligible participants.

- Locale rules.

- Active.
- Restricted.
- Suspended.
- Retiring.
- Retired.

03.4. MARKET ACTIVATION CONTRACT

Market activation must be blocked until the required checks pass.

Checks may include:

- Applicable legal review.
- Catalog validation.
- Pricing validation.
- Tax configuration.
- Payment testing.
- Refund testing.
- Settlement testing.
- Seller verification.
- Delivery validation.
- Customer-support readiness.
- Security assessment.
- Privacy assessment.
- Operational monitoring.
- Reconciliation.
- End-to-end certification.

03.5. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

A market is ready for activation only when:

1. Its geographic and commercial scope is defined.
2. Required policies are configured and approved.
3. Applicable integrations are validated.
4. Restricted activities are controlled.
5. Required workflows pass.
6. Financial transactions reconcile.
7. Failure and recovery paths pass.
8. Operational owners are assigned.
9. Evidence is recorded.
10. Required approvals exist.

SECTION 04 — MULTI-COUNTRY AND CROSS-BORDER TRANSACTIONS
===============================================================================

04.1. REQUIRED SCENARIOS

- Reference currency.
- Display currency.

- Refund currency.

- Reporting currency.

- Rounding.

- Rate locking.
- Refund conversion.

- Reconciliation.

04.3. TAX CONTRACT

- Applicable transaction context.
- Relevant jurisdiction.
- Taxable items.
- Exemptions.
- Tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive treatment.
- Calculation basis.
- Rounding.
- Invoice requirements.
- Credit-note requirements.
- Refund treatment.
- Audit evidence.

The actual tax rules must come from approved jurisdiction-specific
configuration and authoritative legal interpretation.

04.4. CROSS-BORDER ACCEPTANCE

Verify that:

- Ineligible transactions are rejected.
- Applicable taxes are calculated correctly.
- Currency calculations are reproducible.
- Restricted products cannot bypass controls.
- Payment and settlement remain traceable.
- Refunds follow the defined currency and tax rules.
- Delivery and customs restrictions are enforced.
- Required evidence is retained.

- Restricted products cannot bypass market controls.
- Unverified claims are not represented as verified.
- Market activation follows required gates.
- Mall activation follows required gates.
- Review aggregates derive from authoritative records.
- Derived data remains traceable.
- Audit records exist for required actions.

23.3. EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS

For each verified requirement, retain appropriate evidence such as:

- Test identifiers.
- Test results.
- Logs.
- Traces.
- Reconciliation reports.
- Security findings.
- Approval records.
- Configuration versions.
- Build identifiers.
- Deployment references.
- Certification results.

Sensitive evidence must be protected according to its data classification.

===============================================================================
SECTION 24 — TRACEABILITY AND GAP MANAGEMENT
===============================================================================

24.1. TRACEABILITY CHAIN

Every requirement must trace through:

Requirement
    -> Business outcome
    -> Canonical concept
    -> Canonical owner
    -> Existing capability
    -> Gap decision
    -> Architecture contract
    -> Data contract
    -> API or event
    -> UI workflow
    -> Implementation
    -> Test
    -> Evidence
    -> Certification
    -> Release
    -> Operational monitoring

24.2. GAP STATUSES

Use:

- Complete.
- Partial.
- Missing.
- Duplicate.
- Conflicting.
- Unverified.
- Blocked.
- Deferred.
- Not Applicable.

24.3. GAP DECISIONS

For each gap, choose the justified action:

- Reuse.
- Extend.
- Correct.
- Consolidate.
- Resolve ownership.
- Introduce a justified new artifact.
- Defer with approval.
- Exclude with documented rationale.

24.4. ACCEPTANCE

No critical requirement may be hidden behind an aggregate completion
percentage.

Completeness must be reported at the requirement level and then
summarized using explicit rules.

===============================================================================
SECTION 25 — IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP AND APPROVAL
===============================================================================

PHASE 0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Discover relevant existing UCOS architecture and evidence.

PHASE 1 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

Resolve ownership, reuse, duplication and conflicting definitions.

PHASE 2 — REQUIREMENTS BASELINE

Approve in-scope requirements, exclusions and acceptance criteria.

PHASE 3 — TARGET ARCHITECTURE

Approve the architecture and integration contracts needed for the scope.

PHASE 4 — IMPLEMENTATION BLUEPRINT

Define approved technical decisions, work packages, migrations,
dependencies and verification plans.

PHASE 5 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

Obtain explicit authority to execute the approved work.

PHASE 6 — IMPLEMENTATION

Implement only the approved scope while maintaining traceability.

PHASE 7 — VERIFICATION

Run the required tests and validate evidence.

PHASE 8 — CERTIFICATION AND RELEASE

Complete required approvals and operational readiness.

PHASE 9 — GOVERNED EVOLUTION

Maintain compatibility, assess new requirements and preserve canonical
ownership as the platform evolves.

No phase may be marked complete solely because its documentation exists.

SECTION 26 — MASTER ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
===============================================================================

The approved scope is ready for implementation only when:

1. Existing UCOS architecture has been assessed.
2. Canonical ownership has been reconciled.
3. Required reuse decisions are documented.
4. Requirements have stable identifiers.
5. Scope and exclusions are explicit.
6. Functional behavior is specified.
7. Business rules are specified.
8. State transitions are specified.
9. Required data contracts are specified.
10. Required API and event contracts are specified.
11. Application and UI requirements are specified.
12. Security requirements are specified.
13. Privacy requirements are specified.
14. Applicable compliance requirements are identified.
15. Failure behavior is specified.
16. Recovery behavior is specified.
17. Acceptance criteria are measurable.
18. Tests are mapped to requirements.
19. Evidence requirements are defined.
20. Dependencies are resolved or explicitly managed.
21. Risks are documented.
22. Required approvals exist.

The approved implementation is complete only when:

1. Approved requirements are implemented.
2. Required tests pass.
3. Critical invariants are verified.
4. Integration behavior is validated.
5. Security findings are resolved or formally accepted.
6. Financial reconciliation passes.
7. Required operational controls exist.
8. Evidence is traceable.
9. Certification gates pass.
10. Release authority exists.

00. PURPOSE, SCOPE AND RELATIONSHIP
===============================================================================

00.1. PURPOSE

Specification-001 establishes the broad Universal Marketplace scope.

Specification-002 decomposes that scope into structured requirements,
engineering contracts, workflows, security controls and acceptance gates.

Specification-003 adds a more explicit domain-by-domain inventory of:

- Canonical concepts.
- Capability boundaries.
- Business operations.
- Actors and permissions.
- Lifecycle requirements.
- Data ownership.
- Cross-domain relationships.
- Integration contracts.
- Application coverage.
- Functional acceptance criteria.
- Negative-path behavior.
- Verification evidence.
- Traceability and completeness controls.

00.2. SCOPE

The specification covers the logical requirements for a universal
marketplace supporting:

- Global and local commerce.
- Dynamic countries and markets.
- Cross-border transactions.
- Global product catalog.
- Multi-brand and multi-seller commerce.
- Brand shops.
- Seller shops.
- Digital malls.
- Physical mall integration.
- Hybrid commerce.
- Customer commerce.
- Business procurement.
- Search and recommendations.
- Pricing and promotions.
- Wallets and financial accounts.
- Gift cards and gifting.
- Loyalty and redemption.
- Payments and settlement.
- Orders and fulfillment.
- Returns and refunds.
- Ratings and reviews.
- KYC/KYB and verification.
- Trust and safety.
- Affiliate and creator commerce.
- Advertising.
- Customer support.
- AI-assisted commerce.
- APIs and integrations.
- Security and privacy.
- Analytics and operations.
- Governance and certification.

00.3. DOCUMENT AUTHORITY

This document does not supersede existing UCOS constitutions,
canonical definitions, registries, ownership assignments or
approved implementation contracts.

Where a proposed concept conflicts with an existing canonical
definition, the conflict must be resolved through UCOS governance.

00.4. NON-GOALS

This document does not independently:

- Select a production technology stack.
- Mandate a particular microservice architecture.
- Mandate a new universe for each domain.
- Mandate a new database for each capability.
- Create new canonical registries.
- Authorize repository changes.
- Authorize production deployment.
- Certify legal compliance.
- Certify feature parity with another marketplace.

===============================================================================
01. CONSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENTS
===============================================================================

01.1. REUSE-FIRST

Before adding or modifying any artifact:

1. Discover the existing canonical concept.
2. Identify its authoritative owner.
3. Identify existing capabilities.
4. Identify existing contracts and interfaces.
5. Identify existing policies and state machines.
6. Identify applicable registries.
7. Identify implementation and verification evidence.
8. Determine whether the requirement is already satisfied.
9. Determine whether a genuine gap exists.
10. Select the smallest correct architectural change.
11. Record evidence and approval.

01.2. CANONICAL OWNERSHIP

Every canonical concept must have:

- One authoritative definition.
- One canonical owner.
- Explicit identity.
- Explicit relationships.
- Defined lifecycle.
- Defined invariants.
- Defined permissions.
- Defined data classification.
- Defined interfaces.
- Defined change authority.
- Defined evidence requirements.

Multiple systems may maintain projections or caches without
becoming competing canonical authorities.

01.3. KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Canonical knowledge must be authored once.

Documentation, APIs, schemas, UI metadata, reports, registries
and test definitions should reuse authoritative definitions
where technically and architecturally appropriate.

Generated artifacts must remain traceable to their sources.

01.4. CONFIGURATION OVER HARDCODING

Where appropriate, represent variability through governed configuration:

- Countries.
- Jurisdictions.
- Markets.
- Languages.
- Currencies.
- Business models.
- Product categories.
- Seller types.
- Mall types.
- Payment methods.
- Verification requirements.
- Fulfillment methods.
- Promotion types.
- Commercial agreements.
- Approval workflows.

Configuration must be validated and must not bypass legal,
financial, security or governance constraints.

01.5. TECHNOLOGY NEUTRALITY

Canonical business models must not depend on a particular:

- Programming language.
- Database.
- Cloud provider.
- Payment provider.
- Search engine.
- AI model.
- Identity provider.
- Logistics provider.
- Messaging provider.
- Infrastructure topology.

Implementation decisions require a separate approved engineering
decision with documented trade-offs.

01.6. NO UNCONTROLLED ARCHITECTURAL GROWTH

A capability category does not automatically justify a new:

- Universe.
- Service.
- Registry.
- Database.
- API gateway.
- Control plane.
- Event bus.
- Administrative application.

Architectural separation must be justified by ownership, lifecycle,
security, scalability, deployment, operational or governance needs.

03. FOUNDATIONAL DOMAIN CONTRACTS
===============================================================================

03.1. IDENTITY AND ACCESS

Required capabilities:

- Identity association.
- Authentication.
- Session management.
- Multi-factor authentication where appropriate.
- Account recovery.
- Authorization.
- Delegated access.
- Role assignment.
- Permission evaluation.
- Account suspension.
- Account recovery and reinstatement.
- Security audit.

Acceptance criteria:

- Protected operations require authorization.
- Delegated access has explicit scope.
- Revoked access is enforced.
- Sensitive actions produce required audit evidence.
- Identity records are not duplicated by domain-specific systems
  without an approved reason.

03.2. ACTORS AND ORGANIZATIONS

Required capabilities:

- Individual actors.
- Business organizations.
- Legal-entity associations.
- Organization membership.
- Authorized representatives.
- Organization roles.
- Ownership relationships.
- Delegation.
- Membership revocation.

Acceptance criteria:

- Organization membership does not imply unrestricted access.
- Legal identity and storefront identity remain distinct.
- Organization-level access is auditable.

03.3. RELATIONSHIPS

The platform must represent relationships such as:

- Brand owns or controls a brand shop.
- Seller operates a seller shop.
- Seller is authorized to sell a brand's products.
- Mall contains or admits a shop.
- Store belongs to an operating organization.
- Product belongs to a category.
- Listing references a product.
- Order contains order lines.
- Payment is associated with a transaction.
- Refund references applicable original transactions.

These relationships must use authoritative UCOS relationship semantics.

03.4. POLICY AND ELIGIBILITY

Policies must support:

- Eligibility.
- Preconditions.
- Scope.
- Priority.
- Applicability.
- Effective period.
- Exceptions.
- Approval.
- Versioning.
- Evaluation evidence.
- Conflict resolution.

Policy evaluation must be deterministic where the underlying rules
and context are identical.

03.5. EVIDENCE AND AUDIT

Evidence must be associated with:

- Requirement.
- Decision.
- Actor or system.
- Timestamp.
- Applicable policy version.
- Relevant resource.
- Outcome.
- Reason.
- Verification reference.

Sensitive evidence must have appropriate access restrictions and
retention rules.

10.5. ACCEPTANCE

External provider retries must not produce unintended duplicate

20. FINAL DECLARATION
===============================================================================

UCOS-MKT-MASTER-SPECIFICATION-003 provides a further decomposition
of the proposed Universal Marketplace requirements into foundational
domains, commerce capabilities, storefronts, malls, financial operations,
trust, interfaces, integrations and verification requirements.

It is designed to support the next stage of evidence-based architecture
reconciliation and implementation planning.

It does not establish that:

- All UCOS artifacts have been inspected.
- All canonical ownership conflicts have been resolved.
- All requirements are approved.
- Every listed capability is implemented.
- Every market is legally ready.
- All integrations are operational.
- Amazon-class feature parity has been proven.
- Production certification has been achieved.

The next governed action is to reconcile this specification with the
actual UCOS architecture and implementation, establish the requirement
and artifact crosswalk, identify genuine gaps, and obtain approval
before implementation.
