======================================================================

0. DOCUMENT PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY
======================================================================

0.1 PURPOSE

Define the comprehensive intelligence and analytical architecture
for the UCOS Ω∞ Universal Marketplace.

The architecture must transform authorized canonical business facts
into reliable, explainable, privacy-aware, operationally useful
intelligence without duplicating domain authority.

It must support:

- Marketplace performance intelligence.
- Commerce funnel analytics.
- Customer behavior analytics.
- Seller performance intelligence.
- Product and catalog intelligence.
- Search and discovery analytics.
- Pricing and promotion analytics.
- Inventory intelligence.
- Fulfillment and delivery intelligence.
- Payment and financial analytics.
- Return, refund, and dispute analytics.
- Trust, safety, fraud, and abuse analytics.
- Customer experience analytics.
- Operational control tower analytics.
- Marketplace growth intelligence.
- Revenue and profitability analysis.
- Demand forecasting.
- Inventory forecasting.
- Supply and fulfillment forecasting.
- Capacity forecasting.
- Customer and seller segmentation.
- Experimentation and causal analysis.
- Recommendation intelligence.
- Anomaly detection.
- Predictive analytics.
- Governed AI-assisted decision support.
- Executive reporting.
- Seller-facing analytics.
- Customer-facing personalization where permitted.
- Regulatory and compliance reporting.
- Data quality and lineage intelligence.
- Model evaluation and lifecycle governance.

0.2 ARCHITECTURAL OBJECTIVE

Establish a reusable, extensible, domain-agnostic intelligence
architecture that can operate across different marketplace business
models, industries, geographies, currencies, product types,
organizations, and deployment environments.

0.3 AUTHORITY BOUNDARY

This specification defines proposed marketplace intelligence
requirements.

It does not supersede existing UCOS authority for:

- Canonical knowledge.
- Identity.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Consent.
- Governance.
- Product.
- Commerce.
- Orders.
- Inventory.
- Payments.
- Finance.
- Workflow.
- Events.
- AI governance.
- Observability.
- Data management.
- Certification.

Existing canonical authorities must be reused wherever applicable.

0.4 IMPLEMENTATION BOUNDARY

This specification does not establish that a capability is absent
from UCOS.

It does not authorize new services, databases, dashboards, models,
registries, APIs, repository modifications, or production deployment.

All proposed capabilities must first pass context assimilation,
canonical reconciliation, impact analysis, and applicable approval.

0.5 FOUNDATIONAL PRINCIPLE

CANONICAL BUSINESS FACTS ARE AUTHORITATIVE.
ANALYTICAL PROJECTIONS ARE DERIVED.
PREDICTIONS ARE ESTIMATES.
RECOMMENDATIONS ARE ADVISORY UNLESS EXPLICITLY AUTHORIZED.
EXECUTED BUSINESS ACTIONS MUST BE RECORDED BY THEIR AUTHORITATIVE
DOMAINS.

======================================================================
1. ARCHITECTURAL PHILOSOPHY
======================================================================

1.1 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

A canonical business fact must be authored once by its authoritative
domain.

Analytics must reference, transform, aggregate, or derive information
from that fact without creating a competing business authority.

1.2 REUSE BEFORE CREATION

Before introducing any analytical capability:

1. Discover existing UCOS capabilities.
2. Identify the canonical owner.
3. Identify existing contracts and artifacts.
4. Determine whether the capability is reusable.
5. Determine whether an extension is sufficient.
6. Create a new artifact only when a justified gap remains.
7. Register dependencies and lineage.
8. Verify the resulting architecture.

1.3 SEPARATION OF FACT, DERIVATION, PREDICTION, AND DECISION

Every analytical output must be classifiable as one or more of:

A. CANONICAL FACT
   A fact recorded by its authoritative domain.

B. OBSERVED EVENT
   An event representing an occurrence or state transition.

C. DERIVED MEASURE
   A result calculated from canonical facts or approved observations.

D. ESTIMATE
   An approximation of an unobserved or incompletely observed value.

E. FORECAST
   A prediction about a future condition.

F. RECOMMENDATION
   A proposed action based on facts, policies, and analytical results.

G. DECISION
   An outcome produced by an authorized decision-making process.

H. EXECUTED ACTION
   A business operation completed by the relevant authoritative
   domain.

I. OUTCOME
   The observed consequence of an action.

These categories must not be conflated.

1.4 EXPLAINABILITY

Material analytical results must have sufficient provenance to
explain their source, definition, calculation, time context,
limitations, and intended interpretation.

1.5 TECHNOLOGY AGNOSTICISM

The logical architecture must not require a particular:

- Programming language.
- Database.
- Warehouse.
- Lakehouse.
- Search engine.
- Stream processor.
- Message broker.
- Cloud provider.
- BI platform.
- AI model.
- Model provider.
- Visualization framework.
- Deployment topology.

1.6 VENDOR NEUTRALITY

Provider-specific integrations must be isolated behind governed
contracts where abstraction is practical.

1.7 NO HIDDEN AUTHORITY

An analytics dashboard, model, feature store, cache, data mart,
semantic model, or report must not silently become authoritative
for a business fact.

1.8 AUDITABILITY

Material reports, model outputs, recommendations, and analytical
decisions must retain appropriate provenance and version information.

1.9 PRIVACY BY DESIGN

Personal data must not be collected, transformed, exposed, or retained
merely because an analytical use case could benefit from it.

1.10 MEASURABLE QUALITY

Analytical quality must be verified through defined tests, data
quality controls, semantic validation, lineage checks, and
decision-outcome evaluation.

======================================================================
2. SCOPE AND CAPABILITY BOUNDARIES
======================================================================

2.1 IN SCOPE

The specification covers the logical architecture for:

- Analytical ingestion.
- Data contracts.
- Event-derived analytics.
- Canonical metric definitions.
- Semantic modeling.
- Analytical projections.
- Data quality.
- Data lineage.
- Data freshness.
- Aggregation.
- Reporting.
- Dashboards.
- Exploratory analysis.
- Forecasting.
- Experimentation.
- Recommendation systems.
- Anomaly detection.
- AI-assisted analytics.
- Decision intelligence.
- Analytical access control.
- Privacy controls.
- Model governance.
- Analytical observability.
- Analytical certification.

2.2 OUT OF SCOPE AS AN AUTHORITY

This specification does not redefine the authoritative behavior of
the underlying transactional domains.

2.3 SEPARATE RESPONSIBILITIES

Transactional processing determines and records business outcomes.

Analytics interprets available business evidence.

Decision systems evaluate whether an action should be proposed or
authorized.

Execution systems perform authorized actions.

Outcome measurement determines what happened after execution.

2.4 SHARED CAPABILITIES

Where UCOS already provides general-purpose capabilities for data,
knowledge, AI, events, identity, security, governance, or reporting,
the marketplace must reuse those capabilities rather than create
parallel infrastructure without justification.

======================================================================
4. ANALYTICAL DOMAIN OWNERSHIP
======================================================================

4.1 CANONICAL FACT OWNERSHIP

The domain that owns a canonical business fact remains authoritative
for that fact.

4.2 METRIC DEFINITION OWNERSHIP

Every governed metric must have a designated semantic owner.

That owner is responsible for:
- Definition.
- Business interpretation.
- Calculation rules.
- Scope.
- Dimensional behavior.
- Versioning.
- Approval.
- Deprecation.
- Quality expectations.

4.3 SOURCE DATA OWNERSHIP

The analytical platform must preserve source ownership and lineage.

It must not assume that ingestion transfers business authority.

4.4 DERIVED DATA OWNERSHIP

Every derived dataset must have:
- A defined purpose.
- A source set.
- A transformation contract.
- An owner.
- A refresh policy.
- A quality contract.
- A retention policy.
- An access policy.

4.5 MODEL OWNERSHIP

Each production model must have an accountable owner for:
- Intended use.
- Training and evaluation methodology.
- Versioning.
- Performance.
- Limitations.
- Drift.
- Safety.
- Approval.
- Retirement.

4.6 DECISION OWNERSHIP

The authority to make a business decision must be distinct from
the ability to calculate a recommendation.

4.7 METRIC CONFLICTS

If two reports show different values for what appears to be the same
metric, the system must determine whether the difference arises from:
- Different definitions.
- Different filters.
- Different populations.
- Different time windows.
- Different attribution methods.
- Different data freshness.
- Different source versions.
- A genuine data quality defect.

The architecture must not resolve semantic conflicts by silently
choosing whichever value is most convenient.

======================================================================
5. CANONICAL ANALYTICAL CONCEPTS
======================================================================

5.1 ANALYTICAL OBSERVATION

An analytical observation is a governed representation of a fact,
event, measurement, or external input used for analysis.

5.2 METRIC

A metric is a defined measurement with explicit semantic rules.

5.3 MEASURE

A measure is a numerical or categorical value that may be aggregated
under defined rules.

5.4 DIMENSION

A dimension provides a governed context for grouping, filtering,
or interpreting measures.

5.5 SEGMENT

A segment defines a governed subset of an eligible population.

5.6 COHORT

A cohort defines a population grouped by a specified event,
attribute, or time-based eligibility rule.

5.7 ATTRIBUTION

Attribution assigns credit, contribution, or association according
to an explicit method.

Attribution must not automatically be interpreted as causation.

5.8 FORECAST

A forecast estimates a future value or condition under stated
assumptions and a defined forecast horizon.

5.9 ANOMALY

An anomaly is a result that differs materially from a defined
baseline or expected behavior.

An anomaly is not automatically proof of fraud, abuse, or error.

5.10 RECOMMENDATION

A recommendation is a proposed action or choice derived from
specified evidence, objectives, constraints, and methods.

5.11 DECISION

A decision is an authorized selection or determination under the
applicable governance model.

5.12 OUTCOME

An outcome is an observed consequence of a decision or action.

5.13 FEATURE

A feature is a defined input representation used by an analytical
or machine-learning model.

5.14 MODEL

A model is a governed computational representation used to estimate,
classify, rank, predict, or otherwise derive outputs from inputs.

5.15 SEMANTIC CONTRACT

A semantic contract defines the meaning of a metric, dimension,
measure, dataset, or analytical output.

5.16 DATA PRODUCT

A data product is a governed analytical asset with an explicit
consumer purpose, owner, contract, quality expectations, and
lifecycle.

These concepts must be reconciled with canonical UCOS terminology
before new definitions are registered.

======================================================================
6. ANALYTICAL DATA LIFECYCLE
======================================================================

6.1 LIFECYCLE

A governed analytical asset may pass through:

1. Proposed.
2. Context reviewed.
3. Source authority identified.
4. Contract defined.
5. Privacy reviewed.
6. Ingestion approved.
7. Quality validated.
8. Transformation approved.
9. Semantic definition validated.
10. Published.
11. Monitored.
12. Revised.
13. Deprecated.
14. Retired.

Not every asset requires a separate approval stage for every item.
The lifecycle must follow the applicable UCOS governance rules.

6.2 SOURCE DISCOVERY

Source discovery must identify:
- Canonical source.
- Owner.
- Supported access method.
- Contract.
- Version.
- Data classification.
- Refresh behavior.
- Known limitations.
- Permitted uses.

6.3 INGESTION

Ingestion must be authorized and contract-driven.

It must define:
- Source scope.
- Selection criteria.
- Incremental boundaries.
- Duplicate handling.
- Failure handling.
- Retry behavior.
- Checkpointing.
- Audit.
- Data quality requirements.

6.4 TRANSFORMATION

Every material transformation must be:
- Documented.
- Versioned.
- Traceable.
- Reproducible where required.
- Testable.
- Governed for sensitive data.
- Subject to appropriate review.

6.5 PUBLICATION

Publishing an analytical asset must establish:
- Consumer contract.
- Semantic definition.
- Quality status.
- Data freshness.
- Access controls.
- Owner.
- Change policy.

6.6 RETIREMENT

Retirement must identify:
- Consumers.
- Dependencies.
- Replacement options.
- Retention obligations.
- Historical report requirements.
- Migration requirements.

6.7 NO ORPHAN ANALYTICAL ASSETS

Material datasets, metrics, models, dashboards, and pipelines must
have owners, purposes, dependencies, and lifecycle status.

======================================================================
7. ANALYTICAL INGESTION AND SOURCE CONTRACTS
======================================================================

7.1 SOURCE TYPES

Potential source types include:
- Canonical transactional records.
- Domain events.
- Approved change streams.
- External provider records.
- Operational telemetry.
- Customer feedback.
- Seller-provided data.
- Market data.
- Experiment observations.
- Approved model outputs.

7.2 SOURCE ELIGIBILITY

A source may be ingested only when:
- The source is identified.
- Access is authorized.
- The intended use is permitted.
- Data classification is known.
- The contract is defined.
- The retention and privacy requirements are satisfied.

7.3 BATCH INGESTION

Batch ingestion must define:
- Extraction window.
- Watermark.
- Late-arriving record behavior.
- Duplicate handling.
- Retry behavior.
- Partial batch behavior.
- Completion evidence.

7.4 INCREMENTAL INGESTION

Incremental ingestion must define:
- Change detection.
- Cursor or checkpoint.
- Replay behavior.
- Deletion or correction handling.
- Ordering assumptions.
- Recovery after interruption.

7.5 EVENT INGESTION

Event ingestion must follow the canonical UCOS event contract.

The analytical consumer must not assume that:
- Every event arrives once.
- Events arrive in global order.
- Events are never delayed.
- Event delivery proves business completion.

7.6 EXTERNAL SOURCES

External analytical data must preserve:
- Provider.
- Retrieval time.
- Source timestamp where available.
- Contract version.
- Data rights.
- Known limitations.
- Validation status.

7.7 SCHEMA EVOLUTION

Schema changes must be evaluated for:
- Compatibility.
- Semantic changes.
- Data quality.
- Consumer impact.
- Historical interpretation.
- Migration requirements.

7.8 SOURCE UNAVAILABILITY

When a source is unavailable, the system must report freshness and
completeness limitations rather than silently presenting stale
information as current.

======================================================================
8. DATA QUALITY AND VALIDATION
======================================================================

8.1 QUALITY DIMENSIONS

The quality model may include:
- Completeness.
- Accuracy.
- Validity.
- Consistency.
- Uniqueness.
- Timeliness.
- Referential integrity.
- Provenance.
- Conformance.
- Freshness.
- Reproducibility.

8.2 QUALITY CONTRACT

Every material analytical asset must define the quality checks
relevant to its intended use.

8.3 STRUCTURAL VALIDATION

Validate:
- Schema.
- Data types.
- Required fields.
- Permitted values.
- Structural constraints.
- Identifier format where governed.

8.4 SEMANTIC VALIDATION

Validate:
- Metric meaning.
- Currency consistency.
- Unit consistency.
- Time interpretation.
- State-transition compatibility.
- Business rule conformance.

8.5 REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY

Analytical references must be checked against the applicable
canonical identifier and relationship contracts.

8.6 DUPLICATE DETECTION

Duplicate detection must distinguish:
- Duplicate ingestion.
- Legitimate repeated events.
- Repeated business transactions.
- Multiple observations of the same fact.
- Duplicate entities.

These cases must not be treated as equivalent.

8.7 LATE-ARRIVING DATA

The system must define how late-arriving records affect:
- Historical aggregates.
- Previously published reports.
- Forecasts.
- Experiment results.
- Financial analysis.
- Certified metrics.

8.8 CORRECTIONS

Corrected source records must be reflected according to the
approved source and analytical correction policies.

Historical outputs must remain explainable where required.

8.9 QUALITY FAILURE

When quality thresholds are violated, the system must determine
whether to:
- Reject the data.
- Quarantine the affected records.
- Publish with an explicit warning.
- Delay publication.
- Escalate.
- Trigger source remediation.

The choice must depend on risk and intended use.

8.10 NO FABRICATED COMPLETENESS

A missing observation must not silently become zero unless the
metric definition explicitly establishes that treatment.

======================================================================
9. DATA LINEAGE AND PROVENANCE
======================================================================

9.1 LINEAGE PURPOSE

Lineage must make it possible to understand where analytical outputs
originated and how they were transformed.

9.2 LINEAGE RELATIONSHIPS

Where applicable, record relationships between:
- Source.
- Source contract.
- Ingestion job.
- Raw observation.
- Transformation.
- Curated dataset.
- Metric.
- Model.
- Report.
- Recommendation.
- Decision.
- Executed action.
- Measured outcome.

9.3 LINEAGE METADATA

Relevant metadata may include:
- Artifact identity.
- Owner.
- Version.
- Source references.
- Transformation version.
- Execution time.
- Input range.
- Output range.
- Quality result.
- Policy version.
- Model version.
- Publication status.

9.4 IMPACT ANALYSIS

Before changing a material source, metric, or transformation,
identify downstream consumers and dependencies.

9.5 REPRODUCIBILITY

For material analytical results, retain sufficient version and
execution context to reproduce or explain the result to the degree
required by its risk and use.

9.6 LINEAGE LIMITATIONS

The system must disclose when complete lineage is unavailable.

A report must not claim full traceability without supporting evidence.

======================================================================
10. SEMANTIC LAYER AND METRIC GOVERNANCE
======================================================================

10.1 SINGLE GOVERNED MEANING

A metric must have one canonical semantic definition within its
approved scope.

Different valid business interpretations may exist, but they must
be represented as explicitly distinct definitions.

10.2 METRIC DEFINITION

A governed metric must define:

- Canonical identity.
- Name.
- Description.
- Business purpose.
- Owner.
- Calculation.
- Unit.
- Currency where applicable.
- Population.
- Inclusion criteria.
- Exclusion criteria.
- Time basis.
- Aggregation behavior.
- Dimensions.
- Source dependencies.
- Data freshness.
- Quality requirements.
- Version.
- Approval status.
- Known limitations.

10.3 METRIC TYPES

Potential types include:
- Count.
- Distinct count.
- Sum.
- Average.
- Ratio.
- Rate.
- Percentage.
- Monetary amount.
- Duration.
- Distribution.
- Quantile.
- Forecast.
- Composite index.

10.4 ADDITIVE AND NON-ADDITIVE METRICS

Metric definitions must identify whether values can be summed across
dimensions or time.

For example, a conversion rate generally cannot be aggregated by
simply summing the individual rates.

10.5 DENOMINATORS

Rates and ratios must define their denominator and treatment of
empty or ineligible populations.

10.6 CURRENCY CONVERSION

Cross-currency aggregation must follow an approved conversion
contract, including rate source, effective time, and rounding policy.

10.7 TIME SEMANTICS

Metrics must distinguish relevant time concepts, such as:
- Event occurrence time.
- Recording time.
- Processing time.
- Business-effective time.
- Reporting period.
- Forecast horizon.

10.8 METRIC VERSIONING

Semantic changes must be versioned and communicated to consumers.

10.9 METRIC DEPRECATION

Deprecation must identify replacement definitions and the effects
on historical reporting.

10.10 METRIC CERTIFICATION

Certification must verify definition, lineage, quality, ownership,
and intended-use constraints.

======================================================================
11. UNIVERSAL MARKETPLACE KPI CATALOG
======================================================================

11.1 CATALOG STATUS

The following catalog is a proposed discovery and design inventory.

It does not declare that every metric must be implemented or that
the definitions are already registered in UCOS.

Each metric must be reconciled with canonical UCOS semantics before
publication.

11.2 EXECUTIVE MARKETPLACE METRICS

Potential measures:
- Gross merchandise value.
- Net merchandise value.
- Recognized revenue.
- Net revenue.
- Contribution margin.
- Order count.
- Completed order count.
- Active customer count.
- Active seller count.
- Active listing count.
- Purchase conversion.
- Customer retention.
- Seller retention.
- Average order value.
- Refund rate.
- Cancellation rate.
- Repeat purchase rate.
- Marketplace growth.
- Customer acquisition cost.
- Customer lifetime value estimate.

These measures require explicit financial, population, and time
definitions.

11.3 COMMERCE FUNNEL METRICS

Potential stages:
- Eligible visit.
- Product impression.
- Product detail view.
- Search interaction.
- Add to cart.
- Checkout initiation.
- Checkout completion.
- Order commitment.
- Payment confirmation.
- Fulfillment.
- Delivery.
- Repeat purchase.

Each stage must define eligibility, identity resolution, attribution,
and event semantics.

11.4 CUSTOMER METRICS

Potential measures:
- New customers.
- Returning customers.
- Purchase frequency.
- Retention by cohort.
- Time to first purchase.
- Basket composition.
- Customer support contact rate.
- Customer satisfaction.
- Return behavior.
- Refund experience.
- Customer lifetime value estimate.

Customer analytics must follow privacy and consent requirements.

11.5 SELLER METRICS

Potential measures:
- Seller activation.
- Seller retention.
- Listing quality.
- Listing availability.
- Order acceptance.
- Fulfillment cycle time.
- Cancellation rate.
- Return rate.
- Delivery performance.
- Dispute rate.
- Settlement timeliness.
- Seller revenue.
- Seller contribution.
- Customer feedback.

Seller scorecards must disclose relevant calculation methods and
avoid misleading comparisons between materially different seller
contexts.

11.6 PRODUCT AND CATALOG METRICS

Potential measures:
- Catalog coverage.
- Attribute completeness.
- Listing quality.
- Product discovery.
- Product conversion.
- Product availability.
- Product return rate.
- Product defect rate.
- Product content quality.
- Duplicate listing rate.
- Catalog correction rate.

11.7 SEARCH AND DISCOVERY METRICS

Potential measures:
- Search success rate.
- Search-to-product-view rate.
- Search-to-purchase conversion.
- Zero-result rate.
- Search refinement rate.
- Result relevance.
- Ranking stability.
- Discovery latency.
- Recommendation engagement.

11.8 PROMOTION AND OFFER METRICS

Potential measures:
- Offer exposure.
- Offer redemption.
- Incremental conversion estimate.
- Promotion cost.
- Discount amount.
- Margin impact.
- Promotion abuse indicators.
- Promotion cannibalization estimate.
- Post-promotion retention.

Observed redemption must not automatically be interpreted as
incremental sales caused by a promotion.

11.9 INVENTORY METRICS

Potential measures:
- Availability rate.
- Stockout rate.
- Reservation failure rate.
- Inventory accuracy.
- Inventory aging.
- Turnover.
- Sell-through.
- Overstock indicators.
- Lost-sales estimate.
- Replenishment lead time.

11.10 FULFILLMENT AND DELIVERY METRICS

Potential measures:
- Fulfillment cycle time.
- Dispatch latency.
- On-time dispatch.
- On-time delivery.
- Delivery failure.
- Shipment damage.
- Lost shipment.
- Partial fulfillment.
- Delivery cost.
- Exception resolution time.

11.11 PAYMENT AND FINANCIAL METRICS

Potential measures:
- Payment authorization rate.
- Capture success rate.
- Payment failure rate.
- Payment latency.
- Refund completion time.
- Refund failure rate.
- Chargeback rate.
- Financial discrepancy rate.
- Settlement completion time.
- Unreconciled amount.
- Seller payable aging.

Financial definitions must reconcile with the authoritative ledger,
payment, tax, and settlement contracts.

11.12 TRUST AND SAFETY METRICS

Potential measures:
- Suspected fraud rate.
- Confirmed fraud rate.
- False-positive rate.
- Review completion time.
- Abuse report rate.
- Policy violation rate.
- Account compromise indicators.
- Dispute loss.
- Recovery rate.

Suspected and confirmed cases must remain distinct.

11.13 CUSTOMER SUPPORT METRICS

Potential measures:
- First response time.
- Resolution time.
- Reopen rate.
- Escalation rate.
- Contact rate per eligible transaction.
- Customer satisfaction.
- Repeat contact rate.

11.14 DATA QUALITY METRICS

Potential measures:
- Source freshness.
- Ingestion failure rate.
- Schema rejection rate.
- Missing data rate.
- Duplicate ingestion rate.
- Referential integrity failures.
- Metric certification coverage.
- Lineage coverage.
- Data correction rate.

11.15 METRIC APPROVAL REQUIREMENT

No KPI is authoritative merely because it appears in this catalog.

Each metric must have a canonical definition and owner.

======================================================================
12. MARKETPLACE ANALYTICS DOMAINS
======================================================================

12.1 CUSTOMER ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Understand customer behavior and experience within permitted
privacy and governance boundaries.

Capabilities:
- Customer journey analysis.
- Cohort analysis.
- Retention analysis.
- Purchase frequency.
- Basket analysis.
- Customer service analysis.
- Churn-risk estimation.
- Customer lifetime value estimation.
- Personalization evaluation.

Constraints:
- No unauthorized identity linkage.
- No unsupported claims about individual behavior.
- No prohibited sensitive-data inference.
- No ungoverned customer scoring.

12.2 SELLER ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Help authorized sellers understand their business performance.

Capabilities:
- Sales performance.
- Listing performance.
- Inventory performance.
- Fulfillment performance.
- Customer experience.
- Returns and refunds.
- Promotion performance.
- Settlement reporting.

Constraints:
- Seller-level isolation.
- Authorized access only.
- No leakage of other sellers' confidential data.
- Clear distinction between marketplace-wide benchmarks and
  confidential competitor information.

12.3 PRODUCT ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Understand product performance and catalog quality.

Capabilities:
- Product demand.
- Search exposure.
- Conversion.
- Availability.
- Pricing response.
- Return patterns.
- Product quality signals.

12.4 COMMERCIAL ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Evaluate offers, prices, campaigns, promotions, and commercial
strategies.

Capabilities:
- Promotion performance.
- Price elasticity estimates.
- Campaign attribution.
- Discount analysis.
- Incrementality analysis.
- Margin analysis.

12.5 OPERATIONS ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Understand order flow, fulfillment, logistics, returns, refunds,
settlement, and operational exceptions.

12.6 FINANCIAL ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Provide governed financial analysis derived from authoritative
financial records.

Financial analytics must distinguish:
- Gross transaction value.
- Net transaction value.
- Revenue.
- Cash flow.
- Payables.
- Receivables.
- Refund obligations.
- Refund execution.
- Settlement obligations.
- Settled amounts.
- Accounting profit.
- Contribution margin.

These concepts are not interchangeable.

12.7 TRUST AND RISK ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Identify suspicious patterns, measure control effectiveness, and
support governed investigations.

12.8 MARKETPLACE GROWTH ANALYTICS

Purpose:
Measure acquisition, activation, engagement, retention, and
marketplace liquidity.

12.9 ANALYTICS CROSS-DOMAIN RULE

Cross-domain analytics may combine authorized facts from multiple
domains, but it must preserve source ownership, semantic definitions,
access controls, and lineage.

======================================================================
13. REPORTING AND DASHBOARD ARCHITECTURE
======================================================================

13.1 REPORT TYPES

Potential report classes include:
- Executive.
- Operational.
- Financial.
- Seller.
- Product.
- Marketing.
- Customer experience.
- Risk and trust.
- Compliance.
- Data quality.
- Model performance.
- Experimentation.

13.2 REPORT CONTRACT

Every governed report should define:
- Identity.
- Purpose.
- Audience.
- Owner.
- Metrics.
- Dimensions.
- Filters.
- Time semantics.
- Refresh expectation.
- Data freshness display.
- Access policy.
- Lineage.
- Version.
- Known limitations.

13.3 DASHBOARD REQUIREMENTS

Dashboards must:
- Use governed metrics.
- Identify the reporting period.
- Display relevant freshness information.
- Preserve currency and unit context.
- Avoid ambiguous labels.
- Distinguish actuals from forecasts.
- Distinguish estimates from confirmed facts.
- Show relevant quality warnings.
- Enforce authorization.
- Support appropriate drill-down.
- Preserve data provenance.

13.4 FILTER SEMANTICS

Filters must have defined behavior.

For example, a seller filter must not silently change the meaning
of a marketplace-wide metric.

13.5 DRILL-DOWN

Drill-down must respect data authorization and disclosure limits.

13.6 EXPORTS

Exported reports must retain relevant:
- Metric definitions.
- Reporting period.
- Data freshness.
- Classification.
- Generation time.
- Access restrictions where supported.

13.7 SCHEDULED REPORTS

Scheduled reports must define:
- Recipients.
- Authorization.
- Frequency.
- Data cutoff.
- Failure handling.
- Retention.
- Delivery audit.

13.8 REPORT REPRODUCIBILITY

Material reports should be reproducible under their applicable
data, metric, and transformation versions.

13.9 REPORT ACCESS

Access to a dashboard must not imply unrestricted access to all
underlying records.

======================================================================
14. TIME, TEMPORAL SEMANTICS, AND HISTORICAL ANALYSIS
======================================================================

14.1 TIME AUTHORITY

Reuse the canonical UCOS temporal architecture.

Do not create a competing time ontology or timestamp authority.

14.2 TIME DIMENSIONS

Analytics may need to distinguish:
- Event time.
- Processing time.
- Recording time.
- Business-effective time.
- Transaction time.
- Reporting time.
- Forecast horizon.
- Policy-effective time.

14.3 TIME ZONES

Reporting must define the applicable time zone or temporal context.

Time-zone conversion must not be silently applied when it changes
the business interpretation.

14.4 HISTORICAL SNAPSHOTS

Historical analysis must specify whether it uses:
- Current corrected facts.
- Facts as originally recorded.
- Facts effective at the historical time.
- Facts known to the system at the historical time.

These are different analytical questions.

14.5 LATE CORRECTIONS

When source data changes after publication, the system must follow
the approved restatement and versioning policy.

14.6 COMPARISON PERIODS

Period-over-period comparisons must define equivalent periods,
eligibility, missing-data treatment, and relevant calendar effects.

14.7 TEMPORAL LINEAGE

Time-dependent analytical results must preserve the relevant
observation windows and temporal assumptions.

======================================================================
15. ATTRIBUTION AND CAUSAL ANALYSIS
======================================================================

15.1 ATTRIBUTION PURPOSE

Attribution allocates credit or contribution under a specified
method.

15.2 ATTRIBUTION METHODS

Potential methods include:
- First interaction.
- Last interaction.
- Rule-based allocation.
- Position-based allocation.
- Time-decay allocation.
- Multi-touch allocation.
- Experimental incrementality.
- Other approved methods.

15.3 METHOD TRANSPARENCY

Every attribution result must identify its method and version.

15.4 ATTRIBUTION IS NOT CAUSATION

An attribution model may describe how credit is assigned without
establishing that an interaction caused the outcome.

15.5 CAUSAL CLAIMS

Causal claims require an appropriate experimental or causal
inference methodology and explicit assumptions.

15.6 SELECTION BIAS

Analysis must consider whether the observed population differs
materially from the population to which the result is applied.

15.7 CONFOUNDING

Potential confounding factors must be considered when interpreting
observational results.

15.8 INCREMENTALITY

Incremental impact must be evaluated against a suitable counterfactual
or approved experimental design.

15.9 REPORTING

Reports must distinguish:
- Observed association.
- Model-based attribution.
- Experimental estimate.
- Causal estimate.
- Unverified hypothesis.

======================================================================
16. CUSTOMER AND SELLER SEGMENTATION
======================================================================

16.1 SEGMENT PURPOSE

Segmentation groups eligible entities according to governed rules
for analysis or authorized actions.

16.2 SEGMENT CONTRACT

A segment definition must specify:
- Segment identity.
- Intended purpose.
- Eligible population.
- Inclusion rules.
- Exclusion rules.
- Data sources.
- Refresh behavior.
- Version.
- Owner.
- Access policy.
- Retention.
- Evaluation criteria.

16.3 DYNAMIC SEGMENTS

Dynamic membership must define when membership is recalculated
and how historical membership is interpreted.

16.4 HISTORICAL MEMBERSHIP

Historical reporting must distinguish current membership from
membership at the time of the original observation.

16.5 SENSITIVE SEGMENTATION

Segmentation must not infer or use prohibited sensitive attributes
without a lawful, approved, and explicitly governed basis.

16.6 SELLER SEGMENTS

Seller segmentation may support:
- Operational support.
- Seller onboarding.
- Performance analysis.
- Service eligibility.
- Training.
- Risk review.

Seller segments must not silently become punitive decisions without
the applicable policy and due-process controls.

16.7 CUSTOMER SEGMENTS

Customer segmentation may support permitted analysis and
personalization.

It must follow consent, privacy, fairness, and disclosure rules.

16.8 SEGMENT DRIFT

Segment composition and behavior must be monitored where material.

======================================================================
17. FORECASTING AND PREDICTIVE INTELLIGENCE
======================================================================

17.1 FORECASTING PURPOSE

Forecasting estimates future conditions to support planning and
decision-making.

17.2 FORECAST DOMAINS

Potential applications include:
- Demand.
- Sales.
- Inventory.
- Stockouts.
- Fulfillment capacity.
- Delivery volume.
- Returns.
- Refund volume.
- Customer support demand.
- Seller activity.
- Cash-flow scenarios.
- Marketplace growth.

17.3 FORECAST CONTRACT

A forecast must define:
- Forecast identity.
- Target variable.
- Eligible population.
- Horizon.
- Granularity.
- Input sources.
- Model version.
- Training window.
- Generation time.
- Assumptions.
- Uncertainty representation.
- Evaluation method.
- Known limitations.

17.4 UNCERTAINTY

Forecasts should provide an appropriate uncertainty representation
where supported by the method and intended use.

17.5 FORECAST VS ACTUAL

Forecasted values must remain distinguishable from observed values.

17.6 FORECAST EVALUATION

Evaluation must use a suitable methodology and avoid inappropriate
data leakage.

17.7 BASELINES

Complex models must be compared with relevant simple baselines
where appropriate.

17.8 DRIFT

Forecasting systems must detect material changes in:
- Input distributions.
- Relationships.
- Error patterns.
- Operational conditions.
- Business policies.

17.9 FALLBACK

When a model is unavailable or outside its approved operating
conditions, the system must follow a defined fallback strategy.

17.10 HIGH-IMPACT USE

Forecasts that influence material financial, customer, or operational
decisions require proportionate validation and approval.

======================================================================
18. RECOMMENDATION AND RANKING INTELLIGENCE
======================================================================

18.1 RECOMMENDATION PURPOSE

Recommendations may help users discover products, help sellers
understand opportunities, or help operators prioritize work.

18.2 RECOMMENDATION CONTRACT

A recommendation must define:
- Recommendation identity.
- Intended recipient.
- Intended action.
- Eligible population.
- Input sources.
- Ranking or selection method.
- Policy constraints.
- Model version where applicable.
- Generation time.
- Expiration or validity.
- Explanation.
- Confidence or uncertainty where meaningful.
- Feedback mechanism.
- Evaluation method.

18.3 PRODUCT RECOMMENDATIONS

Potential signals may include:
- Product relevance.
- User-stated preferences.
- Context.
- Availability.
- Price.
- Eligibility.
- Quality.
- Delivery constraints.

The system must apply applicable privacy, seller fairness, product
eligibility, and commercial rules.

18.4 SEARCH RANKING

Ranking must respect:
- Query relevance.
- Product eligibility.
- Availability.
- Policy restrictions.
- Sponsored-placement disclosure where applicable.
- Marketplace governance.
- Applicable fairness requirements.

18.5 SELLER RECOMMENDATIONS

Potential recommendations include:
- Improve listing quality.
- Resolve inventory discrepancies.
- Improve fulfillment performance.
- Review pricing.
- Improve product content.

Recommendations must distinguish evidence from inference.

18.6 OPERATIONAL RECOMMENDATIONS

Potential recommendations include:
- Investigate delayed shipments.
- Reconcile payment discrepancies.
- Prioritize unresolved exceptions.
- Rebalance fulfillment workload.
- Review unusual inventory changes.

18.7 RECOMMENDATION VALIDITY

A recommendation must be re-evaluated when material inputs change
or the recommendation expires.

18.8 NO AUTOMATIC EXECUTION BY DEFAULT

A recommendation must not automatically mutate authoritative
business records unless an explicitly approved policy authorizes
the action and defines all necessary controls.

======================================================================
19. ANOMALY DETECTION AND RISK INTELLIGENCE
======================================================================

19.1 ANOMALY DETECTION

Anomaly detection identifies unusual patterns relative to a defined
baseline, distribution, rule, or model.

19.2 POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS

- Sudden payment failure increases.
- Unusual refund patterns.
- Inventory discrepancies.
- Abnormal seller cancellation patterns.
- Unexpected traffic spikes.
- Search-quality regressions.
- Settlement discrepancies.
- Data pipeline failures.
- Operational latency increases.

19.3 ANOMALY CONTRACT

An anomaly result must define:
- Detection identity.
- Detection method.
- Affected population.
- Observation window.
- Baseline.
- Severity.
- Evidence.
- Confidence or score semantics.
- Owner.
- Recommended investigation.
- Resolution status.

19.4 ANOMALY IS NOT PROOF

An anomaly must not automatically be treated as:
- Fraud.
- Malicious behavior.
- Policy violation.
- Employee misconduct.
- Seller wrongdoing.
- Customer abuse.

19.5 FALSE POSITIVES

Detection systems must be evaluated for false positives and
false negatives where appropriate.

19.6 HUMAN REVIEW

Material adverse actions must follow the approved decision and
review policies.

19.7 FEEDBACK

Investigation outcomes may inform future detection models, subject
to data quality, privacy, governance, and model lifecycle controls.

======================================================================
20. EXPERIMENTATION PLATFORM
======================================================================

20.1 PURPOSE

Enable controlled evaluation of changes to marketplace experiences,
ranking, pricing, promotions, fulfillment, and operational processes.

20.2 EXPERIMENT TYPES

Potential experiment types include:
- A/B testing.
- Multi-arm testing.
- Factorial designs.
- Controlled rollout.
- Holdout groups.
- Quasi-experimental evaluation.
- Other approved designs.

20.3 EXPERIMENT CONTRACT

Every experiment must define:
- Experiment identity.
- Business question.
- Hypothesis.
- Owner.
- Treatment.
- Control or comparator.
- Eligible population.
- Assignment method.
- Primary metric.
- Secondary metrics.
- Guardrail metrics.
- Observation window.
- Analysis method.
- Sample-size rationale where applicable.
- Stopping rules.
- Risk assessment.
- Approval.
- Final outcome.

20.4 RANDOMIZATION

Where randomization is used, assignment must follow the approved
experimental design and avoid unintended assignment changes.

20.5 UNIT OF ASSIGNMENT

The unit may be a user, seller, store, product, geography, session,
or another appropriate entity.

The chosen unit must match the experimental question and interference
risks.

20.6 CONTAMINATION

The design must evaluate whether control and treatment groups
influence one another.

20.7 METRIC PRE-SELECTION

Primary metrics and analysis rules should be specified before
results are evaluated to reduce selective interpretation.

20.8 GUARDRAILS

Experiments must define relevant safety and business guardrails,
such as:
- Customer harm.
- Seller impact.
- Financial loss.
- Fraud exposure.
- Fulfillment degradation.
- Privacy risk.
- Reliability.

20.9 STOPPING

Experiments must define conditions for:
- Planned completion.
- Early success declaration.
- Early termination.
- Safety stop.
- Invalid experiment classification.

20.10 RESULT INTERPRETATION

Results must communicate:
- Effect estimate.
- Uncertainty.
- Method.
- Sample limitations.
- Population.
- Duration.
- Guardrail outcomes.
- Generalization limitations.

20.11 EXPERIMENT AUDIT

Material experiments must preserve their configuration, assignment
rules, metric definitions, analysis version, and final interpretation.

======================================================================
21. GOVERNED AI-ASSISTED ANALYTICS
======================================================================

21.1 AI AUTHORITY

This specification does not establish a separate AI authority.

All AI functionality must reuse and comply with the canonical UCOS
AI, model governance, security, identity, privacy, and policy
architecture.

21.2 PERMITTED USE CASES

Subject to approval, AI may assist with:
- Natural-language analytics.
- Report explanation.
- Metric discovery.
- Trend summarization.
- Anomaly investigation.
- Forecast interpretation.
- Root-cause hypothesis generation.
- Seller performance explanations.
- Operational recommendations.
- Data quality diagnosis.
- Experiment analysis.
- Query generation.
- Analytical documentation.

21.3 NATURAL-LANGUAGE ANALYTICS

Natural-language interfaces must map user requests to approved
metrics, dimensions, filters, and data sources.

They must not invent metric definitions when a canonical definition
exists.

21.4 QUERY SAFETY

Generated analytical queries must:
- Follow authorization.
- Respect data classification.
- Enforce query limits.
- Avoid unauthorized cross-tenant access.
- Avoid destructive operations.
- Use approved data interfaces.
- Preserve query provenance where required.

21.5 ANSWER PROVENANCE

Material analytical answers should identify relevant:
- Metrics.
- Time periods.
- Data sources.
- Definitions.
- Filters.
- Data freshness.
- Assumptions.
- Limitations.

21.6 HALLUCINATION CONTROL

The system must distinguish:
- Data-backed statements.
- Model-generated interpretations.
- Hypotheses.
- Missing evidence.
- Unknown results.

22.7 AI-GENERATED RECOMMENDATIONS

AI-generated recommendations must follow the same authorization
and policy controls as other recommendations.

An AI model must not acquire execution authority merely because it
produced a recommendation.

21.8 HUMAN OVERSIGHT

High-impact recommendations require the appropriate human or
policy-based approval.

21.9 MODEL OUTPUT VALIDATION

Outputs must be checked for:
- Schema conformance.
- Type validity.
- Permitted values.
- Policy violations.
- Unsupported claims.
- Sensitive-data exposure.
- Action eligibility.

21.10 PROMPT AND CONTEXT GOVERNANCE

Where generative models are used, govern:
- Instructions.
- Context sources.
- Data permissions.
- Model version.
- Output validation.
- Logging.
- Retention.
- Injection resistance.
- External data handling.

21.11 PROVIDER NEUTRALITY

Model-provider integration must not force business analytics
contracts to depend on one provider.

21.12 MODEL FAILURE

If AI output is unavailable, invalid, unsafe, or outside its approved
scope, the system must use an approved fallback or return an explicit
unavailable result.

21.13 NO UNAUTHORIZED TRAINING

Analytical data must not be used to train or improve external models
unless the use is explicitly authorized under the applicable data,
privacy, contractual, and AI governance policies.

======================================================================
22. DECISION INTELLIGENCE AND CLOSED-LOOP CONTROL
======================================================================

22.1 PURPOSE

Connect analytical evidence to governed business decisions and
measure the resulting outcomes.

22.2 DECISION LOOP

OBSERVE
  -> VALIDATE
    -> ANALYZE
      -> ESTIMATE
        -> RECOMMEND
          -> EVALUATE POLICY
            -> APPROVE WHERE REQUIRED
              -> EXECUTE THROUGH AUTHORITY
                -> OBSERVE OUTCOME
                  -> EVALUATE RESULT
                    -> UPDATE APPROVED KNOWLEDGE

22.3 DECISION CONTRACT

A material decision record should identify:
- Decision identity.
- Business objective.
- Decision owner.
- Inputs.
- Relevant metrics.
- Policy version.
- Recommendation.
- Alternatives considered where required.
- Approval.
- Selected action.
- Execution reference.
- Outcome evaluation.
- Audit.

22.4 DECISION SEPARATION

A recommendation is not a decision.

A decision is not an executed action.

An accepted command is not proof of successful execution.

Execution is not proof that the desired outcome occurred.

22.5 AUTHORIZED AUTOMATION

Automation may execute actions only when:
- The action is permitted.
- The responsible authority is identified.
- Preconditions are satisfied.
- Required approvals exist.
- Safety limits are defined.
- Idempotency is handled.
- Audit is preserved.
- Failure recovery is defined.
- Outcomes can be evaluated.

22.6 HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP

Human approval must be used when required by:
- Policy.
- Financial materiality.
- Customer impact.
- Security.
- Legal obligation.
- Uncertainty.
- Operational risk.

22.7 FEEDBACK LOOP

Feedback may improve models or policies only through approved
evaluation and governance.

An observed outcome must not automatically rewrite canonical
business rules.

======================================================================
23. PRIVACY, CONSENT, AND ANALYTICAL ACCESS CONTROL
======================================================================

23.1 PRIVACY AUTHORITY

Reuse the canonical UCOS privacy and consent architecture.

23.2 PURPOSE LIMITATION

Every analytical use must have a defined purpose and permitted
data scope.

23.3 DATA MINIMIZATION

Collect and process only the information necessary for the approved
analytical purpose.

23.4 ACCESS CONTROL

Apply:
- Identity verification.
- Role-based controls where appropriate.
- Attribute-based controls where appropriate.
- Resource-level authorization.
- Tenant isolation.
- Field-level restrictions where required.
- Purpose-specific access.
- Audit.

23.5 SELLER ISOLATION

A seller must not gain access to another seller's confidential
records through:
- Dashboards.
- Exports.
- Drill-down.
- Generated queries.
- AI explanations.
- Shared analytical datasets.

23.6 CUSTOMER PRIVACY

Customer-level analytics must follow applicable privacy, consent,
retention, and access rules.

23.7 AGGREGATION

Aggregated results must be evaluated for re-identification risk
where relevant.

23.8 SMALL GROUPS

Small-population reports may require suppression, aggregation,
or other disclosure controls.

23.9 EXPORT GOVERNANCE

Exports must follow the applicable data classification and access
policy.

23.10 RETENTION

Analytical data must have a governed retention policy.

23.11 DELETION AND CORRECTION

The architecture must define how deletion, anonymization, correction,
and access restrictions propagate to derived data and model artifacts.

23.12 PRIVACY-PRESERVING ANALYTICS

Where appropriate, evaluate:
- Aggregation.
- Pseudonymization.
- Anonymization.
- Access-controlled computation.
- Differential privacy.
- Other approved privacy-preserving methods.

No method must be claimed effective without appropriate evaluation.

======================================================================
24. FAIRNESS AND RESPONSIBLE ANALYTICS
======================================================================

24.1 RISK-BASED APPLICATION

Fairness and impact evaluation must be proportionate to the
analytical system's intended use and affected population.

24.2 EVALUATION QUESTIONS

Where relevant, assess:
- Unequal error rates.
- Disparate impact.
- Proxy variables.
- Data representativeness.
- Selection bias.
- Feedback loops.
- Exclusion effects.
- Explainability.
- Contestability.
- Customer and seller harm.

24.3 SELLER FAIRNESS

Seller ranking, performance scoring, and recommendations must
consider the consequences of:
- Unequal exposure.
- Historical data imbalance.
- Marketplace-controlled variables.
- Product category differences.
- Geography and logistics constraints.
- New-seller cold starts.

24.4 CUSTOMER FAIRNESS

Customer segmentation and recommendations must follow applicable
fairness, privacy, and consumer protection policies.

24.5 HUMAN REVIEW

Where adverse decisions materially affect customers or sellers,
provide the review or appeal mechanisms required by policy or law.

24.6 LIMITATIONS

Fairness evaluation does not guarantee the absence of all harm.
Known limitations must be documented and managed.

======================================================================
25. MODEL LIFECYCLE GOVERNANCE
======================================================================

25.1 MODEL LIFECYCLE

A governed model may progress through:
- Proposed.
- Intended use defined.
- Data approved.
- Development.
- Evaluation.
- Risk review.
- Approval.
- Deployment.
- Monitoring.
- Revalidation.
- Rollback.
- Retirement.

25.2 MODEL CARD

A production model should have a governed record covering:
- Model identity.
- Version.
- Owner.
- Purpose.
- Intended users.
- Input features.
- Output semantics.
- Training data references.
- Evaluation data.
- Evaluation results.
- Known limitations.
- Risks.
- Approval.
- Deployment scope.
- Monitoring.
- Retirement criteria.

25.3 DATA LEAKAGE

Training and evaluation procedures must prevent inappropriate
information leakage.

25.4 TRAINING DATA GOVERNANCE

Training data must have:
- Provenance.
- Permitted use.
- Quality checks.
- Version.
- Retention policy.
- Sensitive-data controls.

25.5 EVALUATION

Evaluation must match the intended use and risk.

5.6 MODEL VERSIONING

Changes to model parameters, training data, features, or serving
logic must be traceable.

25.7 MODEL ROLLBACK

Production models must have an approved fallback or rollback
procedure proportionate to their operational impact.

25.8 DRIFT

Monitor relevant:
- Input drift.
- Prediction drift.
- Outcome drift.
- Concept drift.
- Quality degradation.
- Latency.
- Cost.
- Safety violations.

25.9 RETIREMENT

Retirement must identify downstream consumers and the required
replacement or fallback behavior.

======================================================================
26. EXPERIMENTAL AND ANALYTICAL REPRODUCIBILITY
======================================================================

26.1 REPRODUCIBILITY OBJECTIVE

Material analytical results must retain sufficient information
to explain or reproduce their derivation where required.

26.2 REPRODUCIBILITY CONTEXT

Relevant context may include:
- Source versions.
- Data window.
- Query or transformation version.
- Metric version.
- Model version.
- Experiment configuration.
- Randomization seed where applicable.
- Parameters.
- Execution time.
- Software environment.
- Quality status.

26.3 DETERMINISTIC ANALYSIS

Where deterministic output is required, define the conditions
necessary to reproduce it.

26.4 NON-DETERMINISTIC MODELS

Where exact reproducibility is not practical, preserve sufficient
context to explain the result and characterize expected variability.

26.5 HISTORICAL REPORTS

Historical report interpretation must account for:
- Data corrections.
- Metric revisions.
- Model changes.
- Attribution changes.
- Policy changes.

26.6 RESULT VERSIONING

Material changes to an analytical result must be traceable.

======================================================================
27. ANALYTICAL APIs AND DATA PRODUCTS
======================================================================

27.1 API PURPOSE

Analytical APIs expose governed metrics, reports, datasets,
recommendations, and analytical operations.

27.2 API CONTRACT

An API must define:
- Identity.
- Purpose.
- Inputs.
- Outputs.
- Metric semantics.
- Filters.
- Pagination.
- Time semantics.
- Authorization.
- Rate limits.
- Errors.
- Versioning.
- Freshness.
- Provenance.

27.3 QUERY SAFETY

Analytical query interfaces must enforce resource limits and
authorization boundaries.

27.4 API CONSISTENCY

APIs must distinguish:
- Actual values.
- Estimated values.
- Forecast values.
- Stale values.
- Unavailable values.
- Suppressed values.

27.5 DATA PRODUCTS

A governed data product must define:
- Owner.
- Consumer.
- Purpose.
- Contract.
- Dependencies.
- Quality.
- Freshness.
- Privacy.
- Access.
- Support.
- Lifecycle.

27.6 VERSIONING

Breaking changes must follow the applicable contract versioning
and migration rules.

27.7 EXTERNAL EXPOSURE

External analytical interfaces must follow security, privacy,
commercial confidentiality, and data licensing rules.

======================================================================
28. ANALYTICAL PERFORMANCE AND COST GOVERNANCE
======================================================================

28.1 PERFORMANCE DIMENSIONS

Measure:
- Ingestion latency.
- Data freshness.
- Transformation duration.
- Query latency.
- Report generation time.
- Forecast generation time.
- Model inference latency.
- API availability.
- Resource consumption.
- Cost per analytical operation where useful.

28.2 WORKLOAD ISOLATION

Workloads with materially different resource or risk characteristics
may require separate execution controls.

28.3 RESOURCE LIMITS

Define limits for:
- Query size.
- Execution time.
- Concurrent workloads.
- Data export.
- Model inference.
- Scheduled jobs.
- Expensive ad hoc analysis.

28.4 COST ATTRIBUTION

Where appropriate, attribute costs to:
- Business domain.
- Data product.
- Model.
- Report.
- Consumer.
- Workload.

28.5 COST OPTIMIZATION

Optimization must preserve correctness, security, lineage, and
the approved freshness requirements.

28.6 NO FALSE ECONOMY

A cheaper design must not be accepted if it violates required
financial integrity, privacy, reliability, or correctness controls.

======================================================================
29. ANALYTICAL RELIABILITY AND RECOVERY
======================================================================

29.1 FAILURE TYPES

Potential failures include:
- Source outage.
- Ingestion interruption.
- Schema incompatibility.
- Transformation failure.
- Data corruption.
- Semantic defect.
- Query overload.
- Model outage.
- Provider outage.
- Authorization failure.
- Stale data.
- Lineage loss.
- Incorrect publication.

29.2 FAILURE HANDLING

Every material pipeline must define:
- Detection.
- Classification.
- Retry.
- Recovery.
- Checkpointing.
- Duplicate handling.
- Data validation.
- Alerting.
- Escalation.
- Reprocessing.
- Publication policy.

29.3 BACKFILL

Backfills must define:
- Scope.
- Source version.
- Time range.
- Resource limits.
- Duplicate prevention.
- Historical restatement.
- Downstream impact.
- Audit.

29.4 RECOVERY OBJECTIVES

Recovery time and recovery point objectives must be determined
from approved business requirements.

No universal numeric objective is established here.

29.5 PARTIAL PUBLICATION

If a pipeline partially succeeds, consumers must not be misled
about completeness.

29.6 MODEL FALLBACK

Model-dependent systems must define behavior when a model is
unavailable or fails validation.

29.7 RECOVERY VERIFICATION

Recovery must verify the resulting data and outputs before
declaring the analytical workflow restored.

======================================================================
30. ANALYTICAL OBSERVABILITY
======================================================================

30.1 OBSERVABILITY OBJECTIVE

Provide visibility into the correctness, timeliness, reliability,
cost, and governance of analytical workloads.

30.2 MONITORING DOMAINS

Monitor:
- Source health.
- Ingestion.
- Data quality.
- Transformation.
- Metric freshness.
- Semantic failures.
- Report generation.
- Query performance.
- Model performance.
- Experiment integrity.
- Access violations.
- Privacy controls.
- Cost.
- Lineage.
- Certification status.

30.3 ALERT CONTRACT

An alert should define:
- Condition.
- Severity.
- Affected asset.
- Detection time.
- Owner.
- Evidence.
- Expected response.
- Escalation.
- Resolution criteria.

30.4 FALSE ALERTS

Alerting must be evaluated for false positives, missed failures,
and alert fatigue.

30.5 ANALYTICAL INCIDENT

An analytical incident may involve:
- Incorrect metric.
- Misleading report.
- Corrupted dataset.
- Unauthorized data exposure.
- Defective model.
- Invalid experiment.
- Failed regulatory report.

30.6 INCIDENT RESPONSE

Material analytical incidents must follow the applicable UCOS
incident, security, privacy, and governance procedures.

30.7 HISTORICAL IMPACT

Incident resolution must identify whether previously published
outputs require correction, withdrawal, or notification.

======================================================================
31. REGULATORY AND COMPLIANCE REPORTING
======================================================================

31.1 AUTHORITY

Compliance reporting must follow the canonical UCOS regulatory,
legal, privacy, and records-management architecture.

31.2 REPORT REQUIREMENTS

Each regulated report must define:
- Applicable obligation.
- Jurisdiction.
- Reporting entity.
- Reporting period.
- Required fields.
- Authoritative sources.
- Calculation method.
- Validation rules.
- Approval.
- Submission evidence.
- Retention.

31.3 REPRODUCIBILITY

The organization must retain the evidence necessary to explain
material reported values according to applicable requirements.

31.4 CORRECTIONS

Corrections and resubmissions must follow the relevant authority's
rules and preserve the applicable audit history.

31.5 LEGAL INTERPRETATION

This specification does not establish legal compliance or replace
qualified jurisdiction-specific review.

32. VERIFICATION AND CERTIFICATION
======================================================================

32.1 CERTIFICATION PRINCIPLE

Certification must be evidence-based.

A capability must not be described as certified solely because
its specification is complete.

32.2 VERIFICATION CATEGORIES

VERIFY-001 — Source authority verification.

VERIFY-002 — Schema contract verification.

VERIFY-003 — Semantic definition verification.

VERIFY-004 — Data quality verification.

VERIFY-005 — Referential integrity verification.

VERIFY-006 — Lineage verification.

VERIFY-007 — Freshness verification.

VERIFY-008 — Metric calculation verification.

VERIFY-009 — Currency and unit consistency verification.

VERIFY-010 — Time semantics verification.

VERIFY-011 — Access-control verification.

VERIFY-012 — Tenant-isolation verification.

VERIFY-013 — Privacy and consent verification.

VERIFY-014 — Data retention verification.

VERIFY-015 — Report reproducibility verification.

VERIFY-016 — Forecast evaluation verification.

VERIFY-017 — Model governance verification.

VERIFY-018 — Experiment integrity verification.

VERIFY-019 — Recommendation policy verification.

VERIFY-020 — AI output validation verification.

VERIFY-021 — Decision audit verification.

VERIFY-022 — Analytical API contract verification.

VERIFY-023 — Pipeline recovery verification.

VERIFY-024 — Backfill and restatement verification.

VERIFY-025 — Cost and resource-control verification.

VERIFY-026 — Regulatory report verification where applicable.

VERIFY-027 — Historical correction verification.

VERIFY-028 — Anomaly detection evaluation.

VERIFY-029 — Model drift and fallback verification.

VERIFY-030 — End-to-end analytical traceability verification.

32.3 CERTIFICATION EVIDENCE

Evidence may include:
- Approved contract.
- Source mapping.
- Metric definition.
- Test result.
- Data quality report.
- Lineage record.
- Access-control test.
- Privacy review.
- Model evaluation.
- Experiment analysis.
- Recovery test.
- Audit record.
- Approval record.

32.4 CERTIFICATION SCOPE

Certification must identify the exact:
- Artifact.
- Version.
- Environment.
- Test scope.
- Evidence.
- Known limitations.
- Approval status.

32.5 CERTIFICATION EXPIRATION OR REVALIDATION

Where required, define conditions that trigger revalidation:
- Schema changes.
- Metric changes.
- Model changes.
- Policy changes.
- Source changes.
- Material data drift.
- Security changes.
- Regulatory changes.

======================================================================
33. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
======================================================================

AC-001
Every material analytical asset has an identified owner and purpose.

AC-002
Every canonical source has a traceable authority reference.

AC-003
Every governed metric has an explicit semantic definition.

AC-004
Metrics with the same canonical meaning do not silently diverge
across reports.

AC-005
Analytical projections are distinguishable from canonical facts.

AC-006
Predictions are distinguishable from observed outcomes.

AC-007
Data freshness is visible where it materially affects interpretation.

AC-008
Data quality failures are detectable and governed.

AC-009
Material transformations preserve lineage.

AC-010
Schema changes are evaluated for downstream impact.

AC-011
Currency aggregation follows approved financial semantics.

AC-012
Temporal semantics are explicit.

AC-013
Seller analytical access respects seller-level authorization.

AC-014
Customer analytics follows applicable privacy and consent rules.

AC-015
Exports follow the relevant classification and authorization rules.

AC-016
Reports identify their definitions, periods, and material limitations.

AC-017
Forecasts identify their horizons and evaluation methodology.

AC-018
Material model outputs have governed ownership and lifecycle status.

AC-019
Experiments preserve assignment, metric, and analysis context.

AC-020
Attribution is not represented as causation without appropriate
evidence.

AC-021
Anomalies are not automatically treated as proof of wrongdoing.

AC-022
Recommendations cannot bypass authoritative domain policies.

AC-023
AI-generated analytical answers distinguish evidence from inference.

AC-024
Material decisions are traceable to their inputs and authority.

AC-025
Executed actions are recorded by their authoritative domains.

AC-026
Outcome measurement is connected to relevant decisions where
the necessary evidence exists.

AC-027
Analytical failures have explicit recovery procedures.

AC-028
Backfills preserve the applicable historical and audit semantics.

AC-029
Model drift and degradation can be detected for governed production
models where applicable.

AC-030
Material analytical changes can be traced to affected consumers.

AC-031
Regulatory reports preserve required source and calculation evidence.

AC-032
Material analytical outputs can be verified against their contracts.

AC-033
Certification claims are supported by actual verification evidence.

AC-034
Existing UCOS capabilities are reused before duplicate capabilities
are proposed.

AC-035
No implementation or certification claim is made without evidence.

37. READINESS GATES
======================================================================

GATE G0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Review existing UCOS data, knowledge, analytics, metric, event,
AI, privacy, identity, security, governance, and certification
artifacts.

Exit condition:
Relevant authoritative context is identified and traceable.

GATE G1 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

Map every proposed concept to existing canonical capabilities.

Exit condition:
Reuse, extension, duplication, conflict, and justified gaps
are explicitly classified.

GATE G2 — SOURCE AUTHORITY

Identify authoritative source owners and approved analytical access.

Exit condition:
No material source is consumed without an identified authority
and permitted use.

GATE G3 — SEMANTIC GOVERNANCE

Validate metric definitions, dimensions, temporal semantics,
financial meanings, and aggregation rules.

Exit condition:
Material metrics have explicit and approved definitions.

GATE G4 — DATA QUALITY AND LINEAGE

Define quality contracts, lineage, freshness, and correction behavior.

Exit condition:
Material outputs can be validated and traced.

GATE G5 — PRIVACY AND SECURITY

Reconcile access controls, privacy, consent, retention, tenant
isolation, and disclosure controls.

Exit condition:
Applicable data access and privacy controls are approved.

GATE G6 — ANALYTICAL METHOD

Validate forecasting, attribution, experimentation, recommendation,
and model evaluation methods as applicable.

Exit condition:
Methods are suitable for their intended use and limitations
are documented.

GATE G7 — DECISION GOVERNANCE

Define recommendation authority, action permissions, approvals,
and outcome measurement.

Exit condition:
Analytical outputs cannot bypass the applicable decision authority.

GATE G8 — VERIFICATION

Map requirements to tests and collect relevant evidence.

Exit condition:
Required verification is complete for the approved scope.

GATE G9 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

Obtain the required governance approvals and explicit authorization.

Exit condition:
Only approved implementation work may begin.

======================================================================
38. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
======================================================================

Until the relevant readiness gates are satisfied, do not:

1. Create a competing UCOS analytics authority.
2. Create duplicate metric registries.
3. Duplicate existing source catalogs or lineage mechanisms.
4. Treat analytical projections as canonical business facts.
5. Treat predictions as confirmed outcomes.
6. Treat correlation as causation.
7. Publish an undefined metric as authoritative.
8. Aggregate incompatible currencies or units without approved rules.
9. Silently change metric semantics.
10. Hide material data freshness limitations.
11. Treat missing data as zero without an explicit rule.
12. Use unauthorized personal data.
13. Expose confidential seller data across seller boundaries.
14. Use sensitive attributes without an approved lawful basis.
15. Allow generated queries to bypass authorization.
16. Allow an AI model to create its own execution authority.
17. Execute recommendations without approved policy.
18. Interpret an anomaly as proof of misconduct.
19. Publish forecasts without appropriate limitations.
20. Declare experiments successful without appropriate evaluation.
21. Use outcome data for model training without approved governance.
22. Modify historical reports without governed correction semantics.
23. Backfill data without analyzing downstream impact.
24. Claim complete lineage without evidence.
25. Claim model certification without verification.
26. Create dashboards that conceal source or metric limitations.
27. Introduce a technology choice solely because it is convenient.
28. Introduce a new service for every logical capability by default.
29. Claim a capability is missing without context assimilation.
30. Claim repository changes or implementation that have not occurred.

======================================================================
40. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES
======================================================================

RULE 001 — CANONICAL FACTS REMAIN AUTHORITATIVE

Analytics must not replace the business domain that owns a fact.

RULE 002 — KNOWLEDGE IS AUTHORED ONCE

Reuse canonical facts rather than inventing competing definitions.

RULE 003 — SEMANTICS MUST BE EXPLICIT

Every material metric must have a governed meaning.

RULE 004 — PROJECTIONS ARE DERIVED

Derived data must retain lineage and must not silently become
authoritative.

RULE 005 — FACTS AND FORECASTS ARE DISTINCT

Predictions must never be presented as confirmed observations.

RULE 006 — ASSOCIATION IS NOT CAUSATION

Causal claims require appropriate evidence and methodology.

RULE 007 — METRICS MUST BE COMPARABLE

Comparisons require compatible definitions, populations, time
windows, and units.

RULE 008 — DATA QUALITY MUST BE VISIBLE

Material quality failures must not be concealed.

RULE 009 — LINEAGE MUST BE TRACEABLE

Material outputs must identify their relevant sources and derivation.

RULE 010 — PRIVACY IS A DESIGN REQUIREMENT

Analytical usefulness does not automatically justify data access.

RULE 011 — ACCESS MUST FOLLOW AUTHORITY

A report or model must not bypass domain authorization.

RULE 012 — SELLER DATA MUST REMAIN ISOLATED

Seller-facing analytics must respect contractual confidentiality
and access controls.

RULE 013 — AI IS NOT AN AUTHORITY BY DEFAULT

AI-generated output must follow the canonical UCOS AI governance.

RULE 014 — RECOMMENDATIONS ARE NOT EXECUTION

Authorized domain capabilities must execute approved actions.

RULE 015 — DECISIONS MUST BE TRACEABLE

Material decisions must retain their inputs, policy context,
authority, and outcome.

RULE 016 — MODELS REQUIRE LIFECYCLE GOVERNANCE

Production models require appropriate ownership, evaluation,
monitoring, and retirement controls.

RULE 017 — EXPERIMENTS REQUIRE METHOD INTEGRITY

Experimental conclusions must follow the approved design and
analysis methodology.

RULE 018 — HISTORICAL CORRECTIONS MUST BE GOVERNED

Changes to data and definitions must preserve explainability.

RULE 019 — AUTOMATION MUST BE CONTROLLED

Automated analytical actions require explicit permissions,
preconditions, limits, and recovery.

RULE 020 — ANALYTICAL RESULTS MUST BE EVALUATED

The system must measure whether material recommendations and
decisions produce the intended outcomes.

RULE 021 — COST OPTIMIZATION MUST PRESERVE CORRECTNESS

Lower cost must not undermine required accuracy, security, privacy,
or reliability.

RULE 022 — CERTIFICATION REQUIRES EVIDENCE

A complete specification is not proof of implementation or success.

RULE 023 — NO DUPLICATE AUTHORITY

Existing UCOS capabilities must be reused or extended when appropriate.

RULE 024 — NO UNVERIFIED COMPLETENESS CLAIMS

Claims of completeness must be supported by context reconciliation
and evidence.

RULE 025 — IMPLEMENTATION REQUIRES APPROVAL

This document does not authorize repository changes or production
implementation.
