# =====================================================================
# 0. DOCUMENT PURPOSE AND ARCHITECTURAL AUTHORITY
# =====================================================================

0.1 PURPOSE

Define the proposed end-to-end architecture for managing the
marketplace's business participants, including:

- Sellers.
- Merchants.
- Suppliers.
- Service providers.
- Brands.
- Distributors.
- Manufacturers.
- Franchisees.
- Resellers.
- Marketplace operators.
- Authorized commercial partners.
- Other configurable participant types.

The architecture must support participant discovery, application,
onboarding, identity verification, business verification, qualification,
contracting, capability assessment, catalog authorization, commercial
configuration, operational readiness, activation, ongoing monitoring,
suspension, remediation, termination, and offboarding.

The design must work across industries, jurisdictions, business models,
participant sizes, product categories, service categories, channels,
currencies, regulatory environments, and commercial relationships.

0.2 PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Establish a reusable participant-management architecture that enables
the marketplace to manage commercial relationships without creating
duplicate authorities for identity, legal entities, compliance,
catalog, pricing, contracts, financial accounts, orders, fulfillment,
settlement, risk, or trust.

0.3 CORE ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT

A marketplace participant is not necessarily a seller.

A seller is not necessarily a legal entity.

A legal entity may operate multiple seller accounts.

A seller account may represent multiple brands or commercial
relationships where policy permits.

A brand may be owned by one entity and distributed by another.

A supplier may provide products without directly selling to customers.

A service provider may offer services without maintaining physical
inventory.

A participant may have different roles in different contexts.

Therefore, the architecture MUST distinguish:

A. PARTICIPANT
   A governed actor participating in marketplace relationships.

B. PARTY
   A canonical representation of a person, organization, or other
   recognized party, as defined by the UCOS identity model.

C. LEGAL ENTITY
   A legally recognized entity governed by the canonical legal-entity
   or party authority.

D. SELLER
   A participant authorized to offer products or services for sale
   under defined marketplace conditions.

E. MERCHANT
   A participant associated with commercial selling or transaction
   processing according to the applicable business model.

F. SUPPLIER
   A participant that supplies goods, services, components, or other
   inputs to an authorized recipient.

G. BRAND
   A governed commercial identity associated with products or services.

H. SELLER ACCOUNT
   A marketplace-scoped account through which a participant performs
   authorized operations.

I. PARTICIPANT ROLE
   A governed assignment of responsibilities and permissions.

J. COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIP
   A governed relationship between participants and the marketplace
   or other authorized participants.

K. PARTICIPANT CAPABILITY
   A verified or declared ability to perform a specific operation.

L. PARTICIPANT STATUS
   The current lifecycle status of a participant, account, role,
   relationship, or authorization.

These concepts MUST NOT be collapsed into one generic seller record.

0.4 AUTHORITY BOUNDARY

This specification coordinates participant-facing and marketplace
operations. It does not independently redefine:

- Universal identity.
- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Legal entities.
- Geography.
- Jurisdiction.
- Product master.
- Product taxonomy.
- Brand authority.
- Catalog authority.
- Offer authority.
- Pricing.
- Inventory.
- Order management.
- Fulfillment.
- Logistics.
- Payment.
- Financial ledger.
- Settlement.
- Tax.
- Contracts.
- Regulatory compliance.
- Trust and safety.
- Fraud and risk.
- Document management.
- Workflow orchestration.
- Notification delivery.
- Analytics.
- Audit.
- Evidence management.

Where these capabilities already exist in UCOS, they MUST be reused.

0.5 NON-GOALS

This specification does not authorize:

- A second identity system.
- A second legal-entity registry.
- A second product catalog.
- A second contract repository.
- A second financial ledger.
- A second settlement authority.
- A second compliance authority.
- A parallel authentication system.
- A new vendor-specific architecture.
- A monolithic seller-management application.
- Implementation before canonical reconciliation.

# =====================================================================
# 1. ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
# =====================================================================

1.1 CANONICAL AUTHORITY

Each business fact has one designated authoritative owner.

1.2 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Participant, entity, brand, document, contract, qualification, and
capability facts must be authored once and reused through governed
references and projections.

1.3 REUSE FIRST

Before introducing a capability, discover existing UCOS artifacts,
contracts, registries, services, policies, and workflows.

1.4 PARTICIPANT-ROLE SEPARATION

Participant identity must be independent of the roles a participant
may perform.

1.5 RELATIONSHIP-CENTRIC MODEL

Marketplace participation is governed through explicit relationships,
not merely through a global participant status.

1.6 POLICY-DRIVEN BEHAVIOR

Eligibility, qualification, activation, restrictions, and offboarding
must be governed by versioned policies.

1.7 CONFIGURATION OVER HARDCODING

Industry, geography, product category, service type, participant type,
and commercial model must be represented through canonical references
and governed configuration.

1.8 EXPLICIT LIFECYCLE

Application, verification, approval, activation, suspension,
remediation, termination, and offboarding must be distinguishable.

1.9 EVIDENCE-BASED QUALIFICATION

A declared capability must not automatically be treated as a verified
capability.

1.10 LEAST PRIVILEGE

Participant access must be limited by role, resource, relationship,
scope, purpose, and applicable policy.

1.11 AUTOMATED DISCOVERY

The architecture must discover available participant capabilities
through self-describing, governed registries.

1.12 EXTENSIBILITY

New participant types and business models must not require redesigning
the entire participant-management domain.

1.13 AUDITABILITY

Material decisions, changes, approvals, and revocations must be
traceable.

1.14 REVERSIBILITY

Where legally and operationally permissible, changes to eligibility,
permissions, and configuration must have defined correction and
recovery procedures.

1.15 NO IMPLICIT TRUST

Registration, successful authentication, or document upload does not
automatically establish commercial authorization.

# =====================================================================
# 3. LOGICAL ARCHITECTURE
# =====================================================================

3.1 LOGICAL COMPONENTS

A. PARTICIPANT REGISTRY INTEGRATION
   Resolves canonical participant, party, organization, and entity
   references.

B. PARTICIPANT RELATIONSHIP MANAGER
   Coordinates marketplace-scoped relationships and their lifecycle.

C. ONBOARDING ORCHESTRATOR
   Coordinates application, evidence collection, verification,
   qualification, approvals, and activation readiness.

D. REQUIREMENTS AND POLICY RESOLVER
   Determines applicable requirements from participant type,
   jurisdiction, business model, role, category, and risk context.

E. EVIDENCE COORDINATOR
   References canonical documents and evidence records, their
   provenance, verification state, and expiration.

F. QUALIFICATION ENGINE
   Evaluates whether required conditions are satisfied.

G. APPROVAL WORKFLOW
   Coordinates authorized decisions and exception handling.

H. COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT INTEGRATION
   Uses canonical contract and agreement capabilities.

I. CAPABILITY REGISTRY INTEGRATION
   Discovers and references verified participant capabilities.

J. COMMERCIAL CONFIGURATION COORDINATOR
   Coordinates approved participant-specific commercial settings.

K. OPERATIONAL READINESS MANAGER
   Evaluates whether the participant is ready to perform authorized
   marketplace operations.

L. PARTICIPANT CONTROL PLANE
   Coordinates activation, restrictions, suspension, reinstatement,
   termination, and offboarding.

M. PERFORMANCE AND COMPLIANCE MONITOR
   Consumes governed operational, quality, risk, and compliance facts.

N. PARTICIPANT PORTAL EXPERIENCE
   Presents onboarding, status, settings, tasks, and operational
   information without becoming a canonical authority.

O. AUDIT AND TRACEABILITY INTEGRATION
   Connects material changes and decisions to canonical audit and
   evidence records.

3.3 DEPLOYMENT NEUTRALITY

The logical components do not prescribe separate microservices,
databases, clusters, or vendors.

Physical deployment must follow canonical UCOS architecture and
approved non-functional requirements.

# =====================================================================
# 4. PARTICIPANT ONTOLOGY
# =====================================================================

4.1 PARTICIPANT

A governed actor participating in one or more marketplace
relationships.

4.2 PARTICIPANT TYPE

A classification describing a participant's permitted business
context.

Examples are illustrative, not an exhaustive hardcoded enumeration:
seller, supplier, service provider, distributor, manufacturer,
reseller, marketplace operator, or commercial partner.

4.3 PARTICIPANT ROLE

A responsibility assigned to a participant within a defined scope.

4.4 PARTICIPANT ACCOUNT

An account through which an authorized participant interacts with
the marketplace.

4.5 PARTICIPANT RELATIONSHIP

A governed association between parties or participants, with defined
purpose, scope, status, and applicable terms.

4.6 SELLER PROFILE

A marketplace-facing projection of seller-related information.
It is not automatically a separate identity authority.

4.7 LEGAL ENTITY REFERENCE

A reference to the canonical representation of a legally recognized
entity.

4.8 BRAND RELATIONSHIP

A governed relationship associating a participant with a brand and
defining permitted activities.

4.9 PARTICIPANT CAPABILITY

A declared or verified ability to perform a specific operation.

4.10 QUALIFICATION

An evaluation of whether a participant satisfies specified conditions.

4.11 EVIDENCE

A governed reference to information used to support a claim or decision.

4.12 APPROVAL

An authorized decision that permits a defined action or relationship
under specified conditions.

4.13 COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT

A governed reference to an agreement defining commercial rights,
obligations, and conditions.

4.14 OPERATIONAL READINESS

An assessment that required capabilities and prerequisites are
satisfied for a defined scope.

4.15 RESTRICTION

A governed limitation on an activity, capability, role, or
relationship.

4.16 SUSPENSION

A governed temporary restriction on specified participation rights.

4.17 TERMINATION

The governed ending of a relationship or authorization.

4.18 OFFBOARDING

The controlled process of ending participation, resolving outstanding
obligations, revoking access, and preserving required records.

4.19 CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

All ontology terms must be compared with existing UCOS definitions
before new canonical terms are registered.

# =====================================================================
# 5. PARTICIPANT IDENTITY AND ACCOUNT MODEL
# =====================================================================

5.1 IDENTITY SEPARATION

Participant identity, user identity, legal-entity identity, and
seller-account identity must remain distinct.

5.2 MULTIPLE USERS

A participant may have multiple authorized users.

5.3 MULTIPLE ROLES

A user may hold multiple roles where policy permits.

5.4 MULTIPLE ENTITIES

A participant relationship may reference multiple legal entities
where the applicable business and legal model supports it.

5.5 MULTIPLE ACCOUNTS

A legal entity may have multiple marketplace accounts when permitted.

5.6 MULTI-TENANCY

All participant data access must respect tenant, organization,
relationship, and resource boundaries.

5.7 ACCOUNT OWNERSHIP

Account ownership and administrative authority must be explicit.

5.8 ACCOUNT TRANSFER

Transfer of account control must follow canonical identity,
authorization, legal, and audit policies.

5.9 ACCOUNT RECOVERY

Recovery must not bypass ownership verification or applicable
security controls.

5.10 ACCOUNT MERGER

Merging participant records must follow canonical identity and
entity-resolution rules. Duplicate accounts must not be merged
solely on similar names or contact details.

5.11 ACCOUNT SEPARATION

Separating previously associated accounts must preserve correct
ownership, transaction, financial, and audit references.

5.12 IDENTITY PROHIBITION

This architecture must not create its own authentication credential
store or duplicate legal-entity master.

# =====================================================================
# 6. PARTICIPANT RELATIONSHIPS
# =====================================================================

6.1 RELATIONSHIP PURPOSE

Represent the commercial relationship between the marketplace
and each participant, as well as supported relationships between
participants.

6.2 RELATIONSHIP ATTRIBUTES

A relationship may reference:

- Relationship identifier.
- Relationship type.
- Party or participant references.
- Marketplace or tenant scope.
- Business purpose.
- Geographic scope.
- Product or service scope.
- Channel scope.
- Effective period.
- Agreement reference.
- Approval references.
- Qualification status.
- Applicable policies.
- Restrictions.
- Relationship status.
- Version.
- Audit provenance.

6.3 RELATIONSHIP TYPES

Types must be extensible and governed by canonical taxonomy.

6.4 RELATIONSHIP SCOPE

A relationship may be restricted by:

- Product category.
- Service category.
- Brand.
- Territory.
- Jurisdiction.
- Channel.
- Customer segment where lawful.
- Fulfillment model.
- Commercial model.
- Contractual scope.
- Regulatory authorization.

6.5 RELATIONSHIP STATUS

Potential states include:

- Draft.
- Proposed.
- Pending review.
- Pending evidence.
- Pending agreement.
- Approved.
- Active.
- Restricted.
- Suspended.
- Termination pending.
- Terminated.
- Expired.
- Rejected.
- Withdrawn.

Applicable transitions must be governed by explicit policy.

6.6 RELATIONSHIP EFFECTIVE PERIOD

A relationship must not be treated as valid outside its authorized
effective period.

6.7 RELATIONSHIP TERMINATION

Ending one relationship must not automatically delete the participant
or terminate unrelated relationships.

6.8 RELATIONSHIP CONFLICT

Conflicting scopes or authorizations must be resolved through
canonical governance, not arbitrary precedence.

6.9 RELATIONSHIP HISTORY

Material relationship changes must be traceable.

# =====================================================================
# 7. ONBOARDING LIFECYCLE
# =====================================================================

7.1 ONBOARDING OBJECTIVE

Provide a controlled, resumable, auditable process for qualifying
participants for a defined marketplace relationship.

7.2 PROPOSED LIFECYCLE

DISCOVERY
  -> APPLICATION STARTED
  -> APPLICATION DRAFT
  -> APPLICATION SUBMITTED
  -> INITIAL VALIDATION
  -> REQUIREMENTS DETERMINED
  -> EVIDENCE COLLECTION
  -> IDENTITY AND ENTITY VERIFICATION
  -> QUALIFICATION ASSESSMENT
  -> RISK AND COMPLIANCE REVIEW
  -> COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT
  -> CAPABILITY ASSESSMENT
  -> APPROVAL
  -> OPERATIONAL READINESS
  -> ACTIVATION
  -> CONTINUOUS MONITORING

Alternative states may include:

- Awaiting applicant.
- Awaiting third-party verification.
- More information required.
- Remediation required.
- Review escalated.
- Rejected.
- Withdrawn.
- Expired.
- Suspended.
- Activation blocked.

7.3 STATE OWNERSHIP

The onboarding orchestrator may own the workflow state.

Identity, compliance, agreement, payment, and other domain states
remain owned by their respective authorities.

7.4 RESUMABILITY

An application must be resumable when permitted by its status,
security requirements, and data-retention policy.

7.5 DRAFT PERSISTENCE

Draft applications must have an explicit expiration and retention
policy.

7.6 SUBMISSION VALIDATION

Submission must validate required fields and evidence references
for the applicable application policy.

7.7 PARTIAL SUBMISSION

If partial submission is allowed, incomplete requirements must be
explicitly recorded.

7.8 WITHDRAWAL

Applicants may withdraw where permitted. Withdrawal must not erase
records that must be retained for legal, financial, fraud, or audit
reasons.

7.9 REAPPLICATION

Reapplication must reference relevant historical outcomes where
authorized and must not silently bypass prior restrictions.

7.10 ONBOARDING SLA

Processing expectations must be defined by the applicable workflow,
business context, and external dependencies.

7.11 THIRD-PARTY DELAYS

Pending external verification must be distinguished from applicant
failure.

7.12 ONBOARDING COMPLETION

Onboarding completion does not automatically authorize every
product, geography, channel, or commercial activity.

# =====================================================================
# 8. DYNAMIC REQUIREMENTS AND POLICY RESOLUTION
# =====================================================================

8.1 PURPOSE

Determine the requirements applicable to a participant and a
specific proposed relationship.

8.2 INPUT DIMENSIONS

Potential inputs include:

- Participant type.
- Legal-entity type.
- Jurisdiction.
- Geographic scope.
- Business model.
- Product or service category.
- Brand relationship.
- Intended activity.
- Channel.
- Fulfillment model.
- Risk classification.
- Regulatory obligations.
- Contractual requirements.
- Marketplace policy.
- Declared operational capabilities.

8.3 POLICY CONTRACT

A requirements policy must define:

- Policy identity.
- Purpose.
- Owner.
- Scope.
- Preconditions.
- Applicable conditions.
- Required information.
- Required evidence.
- Verification methods.
- Approval requirements.
- Validity period.
- Effective period.
- Version.
- Exceptions.
- Review schedule.
- Retirement conditions.

8.4 POLICY COMPOSITION

Multiple policies may apply to a relationship.

Composition rules must be explicit and must not silently discard
a stricter applicable obligation.

8.5 CONFLICT RESOLUTION

Where policies conflict, use the established UCOS policy and
governance hierarchy. Do not invent a precedence order locally.

8.6 POLICY VERSIONING

Every material qualification decision must identify the policy
versions used.

8.7 POLICY CHANGE

Policy changes must define their impact on:

- Existing participants.
- In-flight applications.
- Active relationships.
- Expiring evidence.
- Previously granted authorizations.
- Remediation obligations.

8.8 REQUIREMENT EXPLANATION

The participant experience should explain required information,
applicable evidence, and unresolved prerequisites at an appropriate
level of detail.

8.9 PROHIBITED HARDCODING

Do not embed jurisdiction-specific or industry-specific requirement
lists directly into workflow code when they belong in canonical
policy or regulatory capabilities.

# =====================================================================
# 9. DOCUMENTS, EVIDENCE, AND VERIFICATION
# =====================================================================

9.1 AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical document management, evidence, identity verification,
and compliance capabilities.

9.2 EVIDENCE TYPES

Evidence may relate to:

- Identity.
- Legal-entity registration.
- Ownership or control.
- Brand authorization.
- Distribution rights.
- Product compliance.
- Professional qualifications.
- Insurance.
- Tax registration.
- Financial account verification.
- Certifications.
- Licenses.
- Operational capabilities.
- Quality standards.
- Regulatory permissions.

This list is illustrative and not a universal legal requirement.

9.3 EVIDENCE CONTRACT

An evidence reference should identify:

- Evidence identifier.
- Canonical storage reference.
- Evidence type.
- Subject reference.
- Claim being supported.
- Issuer or source.
- Issue date where applicable.
- Expiration date where applicable.
- Verification method.
- Verification state.
- Provenance.
- Access classification.
- Retention requirements.
- Version.

9.4 EVIDENCE STATES

Potential states include:

- Expected.
- Submitted.
- Received.
- Under review.
- Verified.
- Rejected.
- Expired.
- Revoked.
- Superseded.
- Unable to verify.

9.5 SUBMISSION VS. VERIFICATION

Uploading a document does not establish its validity.

9.6 EXPIRATION

Expired evidence must trigger the applicable revalidation workflow.

9.7 REVOCATION

Revocation must propagate to affected qualifications and
authorizations according to policy.

9.8 PROVENANCE

Verification results must identify their source and method.

9.9 MANUAL REVIEW

Manual verification must record the responsible authority, decision,
reason, and applicable evidence.

9.10 AUTOMATED VERIFICATION

Automated verification must use approved providers or canonical
verification capabilities.

9.11 PROVIDER FAILURE

Provider unavailability must not automatically be interpreted as
verification success or applicant misconduct.

9.12 SENSITIVE DOCUMENTS

Access, storage, transfer, and retention must follow applicable
privacy and security requirements.

9.13 DUPLICATE EVIDENCE

Evidence reuse must follow source validity, subject matching,
purpose, scope, and policy requirements.

9.14 EVIDENCE CORRECTION

Corrections must preserve required historical traceability.

# =====================================================================
# 10. QUALIFICATION AND APPROVAL
# =====================================================================

10.1 QUALIFICATION OBJECTIVE

Determine whether a participant satisfies the requirements for a
specific relationship, role, capability, category, or scope.

10.2 QUALIFICATION DIMENSIONS

Potential dimensions include:

- Identity verification.
- Legal-entity verification.
- Agreement completion.
- Regulatory eligibility.
- Product-category eligibility.
- Geographic eligibility.
- Brand authorization.
- Operational capability.
- Fulfillment readiness.
- Financial onboarding.
- Security readiness.
- Quality standards.
- Support readiness.
- Required evidence validity.

10.3 QUALIFICATION CONTRACT

A qualification result must define:

- Qualification identifier.
- Subject.
- Requested scope.
- Applicable policy versions.
- Requirements evaluated.
- Evidence references.
- Passed conditions.
- Failed conditions.
- Pending conditions.
- Exceptions.
- Decision authority.
- Effective period.
- Review date.
- Outcome.
- Reason codes.
- Version.

10.4 OUTCOMES

Potential outcomes include:

- Qualified.
- Qualified with restrictions.
- Not qualified.
- Pending evidence.
- Pending review.
- Expired.
- Revoked.
- Reassessment required.

10.5 QUALIFICATION SCOPE

Qualification for one activity must not imply qualification for
all marketplace activities.

10.6 APPROVAL AUTHORITY

Approvals must follow canonical authorization and separation-of-duties
requirements.

10.7 APPROVAL EVIDENCE

Every material approval or rejection must have traceable evidence
and a decision record.

10.8 EXCEPTION APPROVAL

Exceptions must identify:

- Permitted scope.
- Approving authority.
- Rationale.
- Duration.
- Compensating controls.
- Review conditions.
- Revocation conditions.

10.9 NO IMPLICIT APPROVAL

Missing a deadline, completing a form, or receiving an automated
provider response must not imply approval unless an explicit
canonical policy establishes that behavior.

10.10 REASSESSMENT

Material changes to participant identity, ownership, geography,
capability, evidence, or policy must trigger reassessment where
required.

# =====================================================================
# 11. COMMERCIAL AGREEMENTS AND RELATIONSHIP TERMS
# =====================================================================

11.1 AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical contract, document, policy, and commercial
configuration capabilities.

11.2 AGREEMENT CATEGORIES

Potential agreements include:

- Marketplace participation.
- Seller terms.
- Supplier terms.
- Service-provider terms.
- Distribution agreements.
- Brand authorization.
- Fulfillment agreements.
- Data-processing agreements.
- Channel-specific agreements.
- Other approved commercial relationships.

11.3 AGREEMENT REFERENCE

An agreement reference should identify:

- Canonical agreement identifier.
- Parties.
- Agreement type.
- Version.
- Status.
- Effective date.
- Expiration date where applicable.
- Scope.
- Governing jurisdiction where applicable.
- Signature or acceptance evidence.
- Amendment history.
- Renewal conditions.

11.4 AGREEMENT STATE

Distinguish:
- Draft.
- Under review.
- Awaiting acceptance.
- Accepted or executed.
- Active.
- Expiring.
- Expired.
- Suspended where applicable.
- Terminated.
- Superseded.

11.5 ACCEPTANCE

Acceptance must follow the applicable legal and contractual process.

11.6 VERSION CONTROL

Material changes must preserve agreement lineage.

11.7 COMMERCIAL CONFIGURATION

Commission, fees, permitted categories, geographic coverage,
service levels, and other terms must be represented through
authorized commercial configuration.

11.8 NO DUPLICATE CONTRACT STORE

This specification must not create a competing legal contract
repository.

11.9 EXPIRATION

Agreement expiration must trigger the applicable review, renewal,
restriction, or suspension process.

11.10 CONFLICTS

Conflicting agreement terms must be resolved by the canonical
contract and governance authorities.

# =====================================================================
# 12. BRAND, DISTRIBUTION, AND CATALOG AUTHORIZATION
# =====================================================================

12.1 PURPOSE

Control whether a participant is authorized to offer specific
products, services, brands, or categories through a defined scope.

12.2 AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical brand, product, catalog, taxonomy, compliance,
and authorization capabilities.

12.3 AUTHORIZATION DIMENSIONS

Potential dimensions include:

- Brand.
- Product or service.
- Product category.
- Geographic scope.
- Sales channel.
- Distribution territory.
- Effective period.
- Contractual basis.
- Required evidence.
- Regulatory restrictions.

12.4 AUTHORIZATION CONTRACT

An authorization should identify:

- Authorization identifier.
- Authorized participant.
- Subject of authorization.
- Permitted activity.
- Scope.
- Evidence.
- Source agreement.
- Effective period.
- Status.
- Revocation conditions.
- Version.

12.5 AUTHORIZATION STATES

Potential states include:

- Requested.
- Pending evidence.
- Pending review.
- Approved.
- Active.
- Restricted.
- Expired.
- Revoked.
- Rejected.

12.6 AUTHORIZATION VS. CATALOG

Authorization to sell a product does not create or alter the
canonical product master.

12.7 CATALOG PUBLICATION

Catalog publication must follow the canonical catalog and listing
governance process.

12.8 BRAND OWNERSHIP

Brand ownership must not be inferred solely from a participant's
claim or account name.

12.9 DISTRIBUTION RIGHTS

Distribution authorization must follow the applicable agreement,
territory, product scope, and policy.

12.10 REVOCATION

Revoked authorization must propagate to applicable listing,
offer, and selling capabilities through canonical workflows.

12.11 NO SILENT REACTIVATION

Expired or revoked authorization must not become active without
the required reassessment and approval.

# =====================================================================
# 13. PARTICIPANT CAPABILITY REGISTRY
# =====================================================================

13.1 PURPOSE

Represent and discover the capabilities a participant may perform
within an approved scope.

13.2 CAPABILITY CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Product selling.
- Service delivery.
- Inventory provision.
- Warehousing.
- Fulfillment.
- Shipping.
- Installation.
- Repair.
- Returns handling.
- Customer support.
- Quality assurance.
- Regulatory compliance.
- Data exchange.
- Catalog synchronization.
- Order integration.
- Payment or settlement eligibility.
- Specialized service delivery.

13.3 CAPABILITY CONTRACT

A capability definition should include:

- Capability identifier.
- Capability type.
- Participant reference.
- Scope.
- Preconditions.
- Verification evidence.
- Capacity constraints where relevant.
- Geographic coverage.
- Service constraints.
- Effective period.
- Status.
- Version.
- Owner.

13.4 DECLARED VS. VERIFIED

Distinguish capabilities declared by a participant from those
verified through an approved process.

13.5 CAPABILITY DISCOVERY

Authorized systems should discover eligible capabilities through
governed registries rather than hardcoded participant lists.

13.6 CAPABILITY AVAILABILITY

A capability's existence does not guarantee current capacity,
availability, or service acceptance.

13.7 CAPABILITY EXPIRATION

Expired qualifications or evidence must invalidate or restrict
dependent capabilities according to policy.

13.8 CAPABILITY VERSIONING

Material capability changes must be versioned and traceable.

13.9 CAPABILITY COMPOSITION

Complex operations may require multiple capabilities.

The composition rules and failure handling must be explicit.

13.10 CAPABILITY PROHIBITION

The registry must not duplicate inventory, shipping, or fulfillment
state merely because a participant offers those capabilities.

Coordinate approved commercial settings for each participant
relationship.

14.2 POTENTIAL CONFIGURATION

- Commission arrangement.

- Payment eligibility.
- Settlement eligibility.
- Supported currencies.
- Tax configuration references.
- Payout schedule references.
- Permitted categories.
- Commercial territory.
- Service levels.
- Returns obligations.
- Fulfillment model.
- Contractual restrictions.

14.3 AUTHORITY

Financial, tax, payment, and settlement facts must remain in their
canonical domains.

14.4 CONFIGURATION CONTRACT

A configuration record should identify:

- Configuration identity.
- Participant relationship.
- Configuration type.
- Canonical source.
- Applicable scope.
- Effective period.
- Approval.
- Version.
- Status.
- Audit lineage.

14.5 COMMISSION

Commission calculations must use the canonical commercial pricing
and financial rules.

14.6 FEES

Fee definitions must have explicit calculation semantics and
effective periods.

14.7 TAX

Tax registration references and tax determinations must use
canonical tax capabilities.

14.8 PAYMENT ELIGIBILITY

Payment onboarding must not be interpreted as a guarantee of
payment acceptance or settlement.

14.9 SETTLEMENT

Settlement eligibility does not authorize the participant domain
to execute or record settlement independently.

14.10 BANKING INFORMATION

Sensitive financial information must be handled by the appropriate
canonical financial capability.

14.11 FINANCIAL HOLDS

Holds must be governed by authorized financial, compliance, or
risk policies.

14.12 RECONCILIATION

Participant-facing financial summaries must reconcile with
canonical financial records.

# =====================================================================
# 15. OPERATIONAL READINESS AND ACTIVATION
# =====================================================================

15.1 PURPOSE

Determine whether a participant is ready to perform a defined
marketplace activity.

15.2 READINESS DIMENSIONS

Potential dimensions include:

- Identity verified.
- Entity verified.
- Agreement active.
- Required evidence valid.
- Qualification satisfied.
- Brand authorization valid.
- Catalog setup complete.
- Required product information available.
- Pricing configuration valid.
- Inventory integration ready.
- Order integration ready.
- Fulfillment capability ready.
- Return handling configured.
- Customer support configured.
- Payment onboarding complete where required.
- Settlement eligibility established where required.
- Security requirements satisfied.
- Operational contacts configured.
- Applicable training completed.
- Required tests passed.

15.3 READINESS CONTRACT

A readiness assessment should identify:

- Participant relationship.
- Intended operation.
- Required prerequisites.
- Satisfied prerequisites.
- Failed prerequisites.
- Pending prerequisites.
- Evidence.
- Policy version.
- Assessment time.
- Decision.
- Validity period.

15.4 READINESS STATES

- Not assessed.
- Assessment in progress.
- Ready.
- Ready with restrictions.
- Not ready.
- Reassessment required.
- Expired.

15.5 ACTIVATION

Activation must occur only when the required conditions and approvals
are satisfied.

15.6 PARTIAL ACTIVATION

Where policy permits, activate a limited scope while retaining
explicit restrictions on other capabilities.

15.7 ACTIVATION VS. VISIBILITY

Participant account activation does not necessarily authorize
public visibility, product publication, offer publication, or
transaction acceptance.

15.8 ACTIVATION VS. SELLING

Selling authorization must be evaluated independently from
administrative account access.

15.9 ACTIVATION VERIFICATION

Verify the applicable canonical authorizations after activation.

15.10 ROLLBACK

If activation fails partially, reconcile each affected domain and
apply authorized compensating actions.

# =====================================================================
# 16. PARTICIPANT PORTAL AND SELF-SERVICE EXPERIENCE
# =====================================================================

16.1 PURPOSE

Provide an authorized interface for participants to manage their
marketplace relationship.

16.2 CAPABILITIES

Potential portal functions include:

- Application creation.
- Application progress.
- Missing-requirement display.
- Evidence submission.
- Verification status.
- Agreement review.
- Qualification status.
- Capability configuration.
- Catalog setup entry points.
- Operational readiness.
- Order and fulfillment entry points.
- Performance reporting.
- Compliance tasks.
- Support access.
- Account and user management.
- Security settings.
- Notifications.
- Suspension and remediation status.
- Offboarding requests where supported.

16.3 AUTHORITY

The portal is an experience layer, not a separate source of truth.

16.4 ACCESS CONTROL

Every operation must be authorized according to the participant,
user, role, relationship, resource, and applicable policy.

16.5 MULTI-USER PARTICIPANTS

Different users may receive different permissions according to
responsibility and separation-of-duties requirements.

16.6 SENSITIVE INFORMATION

The portal must not expose confidential financial, legal, personal,
or compliance information to unauthorized users.

16.7 SELF-SERVICE VALIDATION

Self-service operations must invoke canonical validation and
workflow contracts.

16.8 STATUS EXPLANATION

The portal should explain blockers, pending actions, and next steps
without revealing protected internal detection logic.

16.9 ACCESSIBILITY

Participant interfaces must follow the applicable accessibility
standards.

16.10 AUDIT

Material participant-initiated changes must be traceable.

# =====================================================================
# 17. PARTICIPANT PERFORMANCE AND QUALITY MANAGEMENT
# =====================================================================

17.1 PURPOSE

Measure participant performance using governed, interpretable
metrics and authorized source data.

17.2 POTENTIAL PERFORMANCE DIMENSIONS

- Order acceptance.
- Cancellation rate.
- Fulfillment performance.
- Delivery performance.
- Product quality.
- Return rate.
- Complaint rate.
- Support responsiveness.
- Refund cooperation.
- Inventory accuracy.
- Listing quality.
- Policy compliance.
- Customer feedback.
- Service availability.
- Data integration reliability.
- Regulatory compliance.

17.3 METRIC AUTHORITY

Metrics must use canonical definitions and approved source systems.

17.4 PERFORMANCE CONTRACT

Each metric must define:

- Metric identity.
- Meaning.
- Population.
- Calculation.
- Time window.
- Data sources.
- Exclusions.
- Freshness.
- Version.
- Owner.
- Limitations.

17.5 COMPARABILITY

Performance comparisons must account for meaningful differences
in scope, product type, geography, service model, and data quality.

17.6 SAMPLE SIZE

Small or biased samples must not be presented as definitive
evidence of overall performance.

17.7 PERFORMANCE VS. COMPLIANCE

A performance score must not replace a mandatory compliance decision.

17.8 PERFORMANCE VS. RISK

A performance metric must not silently replace the canonical risk
assessment.

17.9 IMPROVEMENT PLANS

Material deficiencies may trigger an approved corrective-action
workflow.

17.10 APPEALS

Where applicable, participants must have a defined mechanism to
challenge incorrect data or decisions.

17.11 METRIC CORRECTION

Corrections must preserve traceability and recalculate affected
derived results where required.

# =====================================================================
# 18. COMPLIANCE, RISK, AND TRUST INTEGRATION
# =====================================================================

18.1 PURPOSE

Integrate participant operations with canonical compliance, risk,
fraud, and trust capabilities.

18.2 AUTHORITY

This specification does not establish a competing risk engine
or compliance authority.

18.3 POTENTIAL INPUTS

Authorized inputs may include:

- Verification outcomes.
- Expired licenses.
- Regulatory restrictions.
- Confirmed policy violations.
- Material security incidents.
- Product-safety issues.
- Confirmed fraud findings.
- Sanctions or restricted-party screening outcomes where legally
  required and supported.
- Material contractual breaches.
- Risk-review decisions.

18.4 RISK CLASSIFICATION

Risk classifications must follow the canonical risk model.

18.5 DECISION TRACEABILITY

Material restrictions or adverse decisions must have authorized
decision records and appropriate supporting evidence.

18.6 FALSE POSITIVES

Unconfirmed risk indicators must not automatically be treated as
verified misconduct.

18.7 HUMAN REVIEW

Human review must be available where required by applicable policy
or law.

18.8 PROPORTIONALITY

Actions must be proportionate to the established issue, risk,
applicable policy, and legal requirements.

18.9 RESTRICTION SCOPE

Where possible and lawful, restrict only the affected activity
rather than unrelated legitimate operations.

18.10 PRIVACY

Risk and compliance information must be access-controlled and
retained according to applicable policy.

- Brand authorization.
- Required licenses.
- Certifications.
- Insurance.
- Contract status.
- Fulfillment capability.
- Technical integration.
- Financial eligibility.
- Compliance status.
- Contact and operational responsibility.

19.3 CHANGE CONTRACT

A material change should identify:

- Change reference.
- Subject.
- Previous state.
- Proposed state.
- Source.
- Evidence.
- Effective time.
- Required approvals.
- Affected capabilities.
- Impact assessment.
- Final outcome.

19.4 REASSESSMENT

19.5 EXPIRATION MONITORING

Expiring evidence and agreements must be monitored according to

19.6 CONTINUOUS MONITORING

Monitoring frequency must be determined by the applicable policy,

19.7 CHANGE PROPAGATION

19.8 STALE AUTHORIZATION

A participant must not continue performing an operation solely
because an old authorization remains cached.

19.9 CHANGE FAILURE

# =====================================================================
# 20. SUSPENSION, RESTRICTION, AND REINSTATEMENT
# =====================================================================

20.1 PURPOSE

Manage temporary or scoped limitations on participant activity.

20.2 RESTRICTION TYPES

Potential types include:

- Catalog restriction.
- Product-category restriction.
- Geographic restriction.
- Channel restriction.
- Fulfillment restriction.
- New-order restriction.
- Financial restriction.
- Administrative restriction.
- Full suspension.

The available types must follow canonical UCOS policy.

20.3 RESTRICTION CONTRACT

A restriction should define:

- Restriction identity.
- Subject.
- Scope.
- Reason category.
- Authorizing authority.
- Effective time.
- Review date.
- Expiration where applicable.
- Remediation conditions.
- Appeal process where applicable.
- Revocation conditions.

20.4 SUSPENSION TRIGGERS

Potential triggers include:
- Expired mandatory evidence.
- Agreement expiration.
- Verified compliance issue.
- Material security incident.
- Operational safety issue.
- Authorized risk decision.
- Regulatory instruction.
- Repeated verified policy violations.

20.5 NO AUTOMATIC GUILT

A failed external verification or unavailable provider must not
automatically be interpreted as misconduct.

20.6 CUSTOMER IMPACT

Where a restriction affects customers or open transactions,
the relevant canonical domains must coordinate appropriate handling.

20.7 OPEN OBLIGATIONS

Suspension must not erase existing orders, financial obligations,
support cases, return obligations, or required records.

20.8 REINSTATEMENT

Reinstatement must verify that required conditions are satisfied.

20.9 PARTIAL REINSTATEMENT

Where permitted, restore eligible capabilities independently.

20.10 AUDIT

Every material restriction and reinstatement must be traceable.

# =====================================================================
# 21. TERMINATION AND OFFBOARDING
# =====================================================================

21.1 PURPOSE

End a participant relationship safely while preserving legitimate
customer, financial, legal, and operational obligations.

21.2 TERMINATION TRIGGERS

Potential triggers include:

- Participant request.
- Agreement expiration.
- Contractual termination.
- Regulatory requirement.
- Verified policy violation.
- Business closure.
- Relationship no longer required.
- Authorized risk decision.

21.3 TERMINATION CONTRACT

A termination record should define:

- Relationship.
- Reason category.
- Authority.
- Effective time.
- Required notices.
- Open obligations.
- Required approvals.
- Customer impact.
- Financial impact.
- Data-retention requirements.
- Finalization conditions.

21.4 OFFBOARDING CHECKLIST

Evaluate:

- New transaction eligibility.
- Existing orders.
- Open shipments.
- Returns.
- Refunds.
- Support cases.
- Financial balances.
- Settlement obligations.
- Chargebacks or disputes.
- Contractual obligations.
- Catalog and offer authorization.
- API credentials and integrations.
- User access.
- Data retention.
- Legal holds.
- Required notices.
- Audit records.

21.5 OPEN TRANSACTIONS

Termination must not automatically cancel or delete open transactions.

Each transaction must be handled by its canonical domain and
applicable policy.

21.6 FINANCIAL FINALIZATION

Financial obligations must be reconciled through canonical
financial and settlement workflows.

21.7 ACCESS REVOCATION

Access revocation must follow the approved timing and security
policy.

21.8 CATALOG AND OFFERS

Affected listings and offers must be handled by canonical catalog
and offer capabilities.

21.9 DATA RETENTION

Required records must be preserved according to applicable policy.

21.10 REACTIVATION

Reactivation after termination requires an explicitly authorized
process and must not silently restore prior permissions.

- Correlation identifier.
- Causation reference.
- Provenance.
- Classification.
- Relevant policy version.

22.4 EVENT DELIVERY

Consumers must handle duplicate, delayed, missing, and out-of-order
delivery according to canonical event guarantees.

22.5 EVENT VS. AUTHORITY

Receiving an event does not grant a consumer authority to overwrite
the source domain's canonical state.

22.6 REPLAY

Event replay must not create duplicate approvals, financial
operations, activations, or notifications.

22.7 DEAD-LETTER AND FAILURE HANDLING

Failed processing must be observable, recoverable, and auditable.

# =====================================================================
# 23. WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION AND CONSISTENCY
# =====================================================================

23.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate multi-domain onboarding and participant lifecycle
workflows.

23.2 WORKFLOW CHARACTERISTICS

Every material workflow must define:

- Initiating event or command.
- Preconditions.
- Required authorities.
- Steps.
- State transitions.
- Timeout.
- Retry policy.
- Idempotency.
- Compensation.
- Escalation.
- Audit.
- Completion conditions.

23.3 PARTIAL FAILURE

A workflow must distinguish a failed step from a failed overall
business outcome.

23.4 COMPENSATING ACTIONS

Compensation must use authorized domain operations and must not
assume that all prior actions can be reversed.

23.5 UNKNOWN OUTCOME

When a domain command times out, reconcile its result before issuing
a potentially duplicative command.

23.6 HUMAN APPROVAL

Human decisions must be represented as explicit workflow outcomes
with traceable authority.

23.7 WORKFLOW VERSIONING

In-flight workflows must have a governed version migration policy.

23.8 CANCELLATION

Workflow cancellation must not automatically reverse completed
business actions.

23.9 RECOVERY

Recovery must resume from a reconciled state.

23.10 NO DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION ASSUMPTION

The architecture must not assume atomic transactions across
independent canonical domains.

# =====================================================================
# 24. API AND INTEGRATION CONTRACTS
# =====================================================================

24.1 API PRINCIPLES

APIs must be:

- Explicitly versioned.
- Authenticated.
- Authorized.
- Idempotent where appropriate.
- Observable.
- Documented.
- Backward-compatible where required.
- Vendor neutral.
- Governed by canonical API standards.

24.2 LOGICAL API GROUPS

A. APPLICATION INTERACTION
   Create, update, submit, withdraw, and retrieve applications.

B. REQUIREMENTS
   Retrieve applicable requirements and validation outcomes.

C. EVIDENCE COORDINATION
   Submit evidence references and retrieve verification outcomes.

D. QUALIFICATION
   Request and retrieve qualification assessments.

E. RELATIONSHIPS
   Retrieve and manage authorized participant relationships.

F. AGREEMENTS
   Retrieve agreement references and authorized lifecycle outcomes.

G. CAPABILITIES
   Declare, verify, discover, and retrieve participant capabilities.

H. READINESS
   Request and retrieve readiness assessments.

I. PARTICIPANT LIFECYCLE
   Request authorized activation, restriction, reinstatement,
   termination, or offboarding workflows.

J. PERFORMANCE
   Retrieve authorized participant metrics and assessments.

K. AUDIT AND STATUS
   Retrieve authorized decision and workflow status.

These are logical API groups, not finalized endpoint definitions.

24.3 COMMAND VS. QUERY

Commands request state changes.

Queries retrieve authorized representations.

24.4 IDEMPOTENCY

Material commands must support the applicable canonical
idempotency contract.

24.5 CONCURRENCY

Conflicting updates must be detected through canonical versioning,
optimistic concurrency, or equivalent approved mechanisms.

24.6 ERROR MODEL

Errors must distinguish:

- Invalid input.
- Unauthorized operation.
- Forbidden scope.
- Missing prerequisite.
- Conflict.
- Expired evidence.
- Policy rejection.
- External dependency failure.
- Timeout.
- Outcome unknown.
- Internal processing failure.

24.7 CONTRACT VERSIONING

Breaking changes must follow canonical API governance.

24.8 EXTERNAL INTEGRATION

External systems must be integrated through approved adapters or
canonical integration capabilities.

24.9 PROVIDER NEUTRALITY

The domain must not depend on one identity verification, document
processing, signing, or compliance vendor.

# =====================================================================
# 25. DATA MODEL AND RELATIONSHIP INTEGRITY
# =====================================================================

25.1 MODELING PRINCIPLE

The following are logical concepts to reconcile with the canonical
UCOS data model. They are not authorization to create duplicate
entities or tables.

25.2 LOGICAL CONCEPTS

- Participant Reference.
- Participant Role Assignment.
- Participant Account Reference.
- Participant Relationship.
- Application.
- Requirement Set Reference.
- Evidence Reference.
- Verification Result Reference.
- Qualification Assessment.
- Approval Decision.
- Agreement Reference.
- Brand Authorization Reference.
- Capability Declaration.
- Capability Verification.
- Readiness Assessment.
- Commercial Configuration Reference.
- Restriction.
- Suspension.
- Remediation Plan.
- Termination Record.
- Offboarding Record.
- Audit Reference.

25.3 IDENTIFIER REQUIREMENTS

Identifiers must follow canonical UCOS identifier governance.

They must not be generated by an unapproved local naming convention.

25.4 REFERENCE INTEGRITY

Every relationship reference must resolve to the appropriate
canonical authority.

25.5 TEMPORAL INTEGRITY

Relationships, qualifications, agreements, and authorizations
must preserve effective-time semantics.

25.6 VERSIONING

Material changes must be traceable to their applicable versions.

25.7 DERIVED PROJECTIONS

Portal summaries and operational views must be treated as derived
representations rather than independent canonical records.

25.8 DUPLICATE DETECTION

Duplicate participant detection must use governed entity-resolution
rules and appropriate evidence.

25.9 HISTORICAL PRESERVATION

Required historical records must remain traceable after a
participant changes status or relationship.

25.10 SCHEMA EVOLUTION

Schema changes must follow canonical UCOS schema governance.

# =====================================================================
# 26. SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND SEGREGATION OF DUTIES
# =====================================================================

26.1 SECURITY AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical UCOS identity, access control, and security
capabilities.

26.2 AUTHORIZATION DIMENSIONS

Authorization may depend on:

- User identity.
- Participant identity.
- Role.
- Relationship.
- Resource.
- Operation.
- Scope.
- Tenant.
- Purpose.
- Policy.
- Current status.

26.3 LEAST PRIVILEGE

Grant only the permissions required for an approved purpose.

26.4 SEGREGATION OF DUTIES

Where required, separate application submission, evidence review,
qualification, approval, and financial authorization.

26.5 PRIVILEGED OPERATIONS

Material actions require appropriate authorization and audit.

26.6 MULTI-TENANT ISOLATION

Cross-participant and cross-tenant access must be prevented unless
explicitly authorized.

26.7 DATA CLASSIFICATION

Participant records must follow canonical data classification.

26.8 PRIVACY

Collect only the information necessary for the defined purpose.

26.9 RETENTION

Retention must follow applicable legal, contractual, financial,
security, and privacy requirements.

26.10 EXTERNAL PROVIDERS

Third-party processing must follow approved security, privacy,
contractual, and data-processing controls.

26.11 INCIDENT RESPONSE

Relevant incidents must integrate with canonical security and
privacy incident management.

26.12 CREDENTIAL REVOCATION

Termination or suspension must trigger appropriate access and
credential review.

# =====================================================================
# 27. OBSERVABILITY AND OPERATIONAL CONTROL
# =====================================================================

27.1 PURPOSE

Provide visibility into onboarding, qualification, activation,
participant health, and lifecycle workflows.

27.2 OPERATIONAL MEASURES

Potential measures include:

- Application volume.
- Application completion rate.
- Incomplete application rate.
- Verification latency.
- External verification failure rate.
- Qualification latency.
- Approval latency.
- Readiness failure rate.
- Activation time.
- Evidence expiration rate.
- Agreement expiration rate.
- Capability revocation rate.
- Reassessment backlog.
- Suspension rate.
- Reinstatement time.
- Offboarding completion time.
- Integration reliability.
- Unresolved reconciliation cases.

27.3 METRIC GOVERNANCE

Each metric must have an explicit definition, source, owner,
time window, and limitation.

27.4 CORRELATION

Material workflows must carry canonical correlation identifiers.

27.5 LOGGING

Logs must not contain unnecessary sensitive participant data.

27.6 ALERTING

Alerts must identify affected workflows, severity, owner,
evidence, and expected response.

27.7 OPERATIONAL DASHBOARDS

Dashboards must consume governed data and must not become
independent business authorities.

27.8 INCIDENT MANAGEMENT

Operational incidents must integrate with canonical incident
management capabilities.

27.9 SERVICE LEVELS

Processing targets must be defined through approved business
and operational requirements.

27.10 MONITORING FAILURE

Failure of monitoring must not silently disable required
authorization or compliance controls.

# =====================================================================
# 28. RECONCILIATION AND EXCEPTION MANAGEMENT
# =====================================================================

28.1 PURPOSE

Detect and resolve discrepancies between participant workflow
state and canonical domain state.

28.2 RECONCILIATION SCENARIOS

- Application marked approved while a required qualification remains
  pending.
- Participant marked active while required agreement is expired.
- Capability remains enabled after its authorization is revoked.
- Expired evidence is still treated as valid.
- Financial onboarding is presented as settlement readiness.
- Seller account is active but required category authorization
  is absent.
- Participant is suspended but an unauthorized operation remains
  available.
- Offboarding is complete while unresolved obligations remain.
- Duplicate participant records reference the same legal entity
  incorrectly.
- Agreement scope conflicts with active commercial configuration.
- Brand authorization expires while affected offers remain active.
- External verification times out and is incorrectly treated as
  success.
- A qualification decision uses an obsolete policy version.
- A portal projection disagrees with canonical participant state.
- An event is replayed and creates duplicate lifecycle effects.

28.3 EXCEPTION RECORD

An exception record should identify:

- Exception identity.
- Affected participant or relationship.
- Expected state.
- Observed state.
- Canonical authority.
- Severity.
- Detection time.
- Root cause where known.
- Responsible owner.
- Remediation.
- Evidence.
- Resolution time.

28.4 SOURCE AUTHORITY

The designated canonical domain must resolve the authoritative
business fact.

28.5 NO SILENT REPAIR

Material discrepancies must not be concealed by editing a
projection alone.

28.6 AUTOMATED RECONCILIATION

Automated repair is permitted only where explicitly governed,
safe, idempotent, and auditable.

28.7 HUMAN ESCALATION

Ambiguous, legally material, or high-impact discrepancies must
be escalated to the appropriate authority.

# =====================================================================
# 29. FAILURE SCENARIO CATALOG
# =====================================================================

FS-001 — DUPLICATE APPLICATION

A participant submits the same application multiple times.

Expected control:
Idempotency and governed duplicate detection.

FS-002 — IDENTITY VERIFICATION UNAVAILABLE

An external identity provider is unavailable.

Expected control:
Pending verification; no implicit approval.

FS-003 — EXPIRED EVIDENCE

Required evidence expires.

Expected control:
Reassessment and policy-driven restriction where required.

FS-004 — AGREEMENT EXPIRED

A required agreement is no longer active.

Expected control:
Reevaluate the affected relationship and capabilities.

FS-005 — POLICY CHANGED

Requirements change while an application is in progress.

Expected control:
Apply governed policy-versioning and transition rules.

FS-006 — APPROVAL TIMEOUT

An approval request times out.

Expected control:
Reconcile the decision before resubmitting.

FS-007 — PARTIAL ACTIVATION

Some downstream capabilities activate while another fails.

Expected control:
Track each outcome and perform approved compensation or recovery.

FS-008 — DUPLICATE PARTICIPANT

Multiple records may represent the same participant.

Expected control:
Use canonical entity-resolution rules and preserve lineage.

FS-009 — INVALID BRAND AUTHORIZATION

A participant lacks required brand authorization.

Expected control:
Block or restrict the affected activity according to policy.

FS-010 — SETTLEMENT MISREPRESENTATION

The portal indicates settlement readiness without canonical
confirmation.

Expected control:
Use authoritative financial and settlement state.

FS-011 — SUSPENSION PROPAGATION FAILURE

A restriction does not reach an affected capability.

Expected control:
Detect the discrepancy and invoke the approved containment process.

FS-012 — OFFBOARDING WITH OPEN OBLIGATIONS

A relationship terminates while financial or customer obligations
remain.

Expected control:
Preserve obligations and coordinate domain-specific resolution.

FS-013 — STALE PORTAL PROJECTION

The portal presents outdated participant state.

Expected control:
Enforce freshness policy and reconcile with the source authority.

FS-014 — DUPLICATE EVENT

An event is delivered more than once.

Expected control:
Idempotent processing.

FS-015 — OUT-OF-ORDER EVENTS

Lifecycle events arrive in an unexpected order.

Expected control:
Validate version and current authoritative state.

FS-016 — UNAUTHORIZED ADMINISTRATIVE ACTION

A user attempts to alter a participant outside their authority.

Expected control:
Deny, record, and apply applicable security monitoring.

FS-017 — TENANT DATA LEAKAGE

One participant accesses another participant's information.

Expected control:
Prevent access and initiate applicable incident procedures.

FS-018 — FALSE POSITIVE COMPLIANCE SIGNAL

An unconfirmed indicator triggers a proposed restriction.

Expected control:
Apply the canonical review and decision policy.

FS-019 — CAPABILITY DECLARATION WITHOUT EVIDENCE

A participant declares a capability but verification is incomplete.

Expected control:
Keep the capability in an unverified state.

FS-020 — QUALIFICATION POLICY CONFLICT

Two applicable policies appear inconsistent.

Expected control:
Use canonical governance; do not silently choose a winner.

FS-021 — EXTERNAL PROVIDER DATA CORRUPTION

An external provider returns malformed or inconsistent data.

Expected control:
Validate provenance, schema, and permitted state transitions.

FS-022 — FAILED REVOCATION

A revoked authorization remains available in a downstream system.

Expected control:
Detect and reconcile the unauthorized residual capability.

FS-023 — INVALID ACCOUNT TRANSFER

Account control is transferred without required verification.

Expected control:
Block the transfer and preserve the existing authority state.

FS-024 — FINANCIAL INFORMATION EXPOSURE

Sensitive financial information becomes visible to an unauthorized
participant user.

Expected control:
Enforce access boundaries and applicable incident response.

FS-025 — REACTIVATION WITHOUT APPROVAL

A terminated participant is reactivated through stale state.

Expected control:
Require explicit reauthorization.

FS-026 — INVALID EVIDENCE REUSE

Evidence is reused outside its permitted scope or validity.

Expected control:
Revalidate scope, source, freshness, and policy.

FS-027 — INCOMPLETE OFFBOARDING

Access is revoked but required financial or operational tasks
remain unresolved.

Expected control:
Track outstanding tasks and retain the correct termination state.

FS-028 — METRIC SEMANTIC DRIFT

Participant performance metrics change meaning without governance.

Expected control:
Version definitions and preserve comparability information.

FS-029 — WORKFLOW REPLAY

A recovered workflow repeats a completed approval or activation.

Expected control:
Reconcile current state and enforce idempotency.

FS-030 — UNAUTHORIZED SCOPE EXPANSION

A participant qualified for one category performs activity in
another category.

Expected control:
Validate authorization against the requested operation and scope.

FS-031 — LEGAL-ENTITY CHANGE

The participant's legal-entity relationship changes.

Expected control:
Trigger the applicable identity, contract, compliance, and
qualification reassessment.

FS-032 — INCONSISTENT TERMINATION

The relationship is terminated in one system but remains active
in another.

Expected control:
Canonical reconciliation and authorized corrective action.

FS-033 — VERIFICATION RESULT REVOKED

A previously accepted verification result is revoked.

Expected control:
Reevaluate dependent qualifications and authorizations.

FS-034 — PARTIAL POLICY PROPAGATION

Some services apply a new policy version while others remain stale.

Expected control:
Version-aware rollout and governed consistency verification.

FS-035 — COMPENSATION FAILURE

A compensating action fails during a multi-domain workflow.

Expected control:
Preserve the unresolved state, escalate, and resume from reconciled
canonical state.

# 30. VERIFICATION AND ACCEPTANCE TEST CATALOG
# =====================================================================

CATEGORY A — IDENTITY AND PARTICIPANT MODEL

AT-001 Verify participant, party, legal entity, account, and role
       remain distinguishable.
AT-002 Verify multiple authorized users can access the same
       participant according to permissions.
AT-003 Verify tenant isolation.
AT-004 Verify duplicate detection does not merge records without
       sufficient governed evidence.
AT-005 Verify role revocation takes effect according to policy.

CATEGORY B — ONBOARDING

AT-006 Verify an application can be created and resumed.
AT-007 Verify submission rejects missing mandatory requirements.
AT-008 Verify external verification failure does not imply success.
AT-009 Verify an application can be withdrawn where permitted.
AT-010 Verify resubmission preserves required historical lineage.

CATEGORY C — REQUIREMENTS AND EVIDENCE

AT-011 Verify requirements change with applicable policy context.
AT-012 Verify policy versions are traceable.
AT-013 Verify expired evidence triggers the appropriate workflow.
AT-014 Verify evidence upload does not imply verification.
AT-015 Verify revoked evidence invalidates dependent authorization
        where required.

CATEGORY D — QUALIFICATION AND APPROVAL

AT-016 Verify qualification is scoped to the requested activity.
AT-017 Verify approval authority is enforced.
AT-018 Verify exceptions require authorized evidence.
AT-019 Verify conflicting policies follow canonical governance.
AT-020 Verify rejection records preserve required reasons and
        provenance.

CATEGORY E — AGREEMENTS AND AUTHORIZATION

AT-021 Verify agreement expiration is detected.
AT-022 Verify brand authorization is scope-aware.
AT-023 Verify revoked authorization cannot be silently reused.
AT-024 Verify catalog authority remains canonical.
AT-025 Verify agreement changes trigger applicable reassessment.

CATEGORY F — CAPABILITIES AND READINESS

AT-026 Verify declared and verified capabilities are distinguished.
AT-027 Verify readiness assessment identifies missing prerequisites.
AT-028 Verify partial activation remains explicitly scoped.
AT-029 Verify activation does not grant unrelated permissions.
AT-030 Verify readiness expires or is reassessed as required.

CATEGORY G — COMMERCIAL AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION

AT-031 Verify commission configuration uses canonical commercial
        authority.
AT-032 Verify financial account data is appropriately protected.
AT-033 Verify settlement eligibility is not misrepresented as
        completed settlement.
AT-034 Verify financial holds follow canonical authority.
AT-035 Verify participant financial summaries can be reconciled
        to canonical financial records.

CATEGORY H — LIFECYCLE

AT-036 Verify restrictions have explicit scope.
AT-037 Verify suspension preserves open obligations.
AT-038 Verify reinstatement requires required conditions.
AT-039 Verify termination does not erase required records.
AT-040 Verify offboarding detects unresolved obligations.

CATEGORY I — WORKFLOW AND EVENTS

AT-041 Verify commands are idempotent where required.
AT-042 Verify duplicate events do not duplicate business effects.
AT-043 Verify out-of-order events do not corrupt state.
AT-044 Verify timeouts trigger reconciliation.
AT-045 Verify workflow replay does not repeat completed approvals.
AT-046 Verify failed compensation remains observable and recoverable.

CATEGORY J — SECURITY AND PRIVACY

AT-047 Verify unauthorized access is denied.
AT-048 Verify participant-to-participant data isolation.
AT-049 Verify privileged actions are audited.
AT-050 Verify sensitive evidence follows retention and access policy.
AT-051 Verify terminated access is revoked according to policy.

CATEGORY K — OBSERVABILITY AND RECONCILIATION

AT-052 Verify lifecycle discrepancies are detected.
AT-053 Verify material exceptions have owners.
AT-054 Verify corrective actions preserve canonical authority.
AT-055 Verify metric definitions are versioned.
AT-056 Verify reconciliation does not silently alter authoritative
        business facts.

CATEGORY L — GOVERNANCE AND TRACEABILITY

AT-057 Verify every material decision has traceable provenance.
AT-058 Verify policies and contracts are versioned.
AT-059 Verify all requirements map to evidence or an approved
        disposition.
AT-060 Verify certification claims match actual test evidence.

Passing these proposed tests must be demonstrated before a claim of
implementation readiness or certification is made.

# =====================================================================
# 31. TRACEABILITY MODEL
# =====================================================================

31.1 PURPOSE

Connect requirements to architecture, policy, data, implementation,
tests, and evidence.

31.2 TRACEABILITY CHAIN

BUSINESS OBJECTIVE
  -> REQUIREMENT
    -> CANONICAL AUTHORITY
      -> ARCHITECTURAL COMPONENT
        -> CONTRACT
          -> POLICY
            -> IMPLEMENTATION ARTIFACT
              -> TEST
                -> EVIDENCE
                  -> APPROVAL
                    -> RELEASE

31.3 REQUIREMENT RECORD

A requirement record should identify:

- Requirement identifier.
- Requirement statement.
- Business rationale.
- Canonical authority.
- Scope.
- Risk.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Dependencies.
- Verification method.
- Evidence reference.
- Status.
- Owner.
- Version.

31.4 COVERAGE

Every approved requirement must be implemented, reused, explicitly
excluded, deferred, or otherwise dispositioned through governance.

31.5 ORPHAN DETECTION

Detect requirements without owners, contracts without consumers,
tests without requirements, and implementation artifacts without
approved scope.

31.6 CHANGE IMPACT

Changes to policies, schemas, agreements, and contracts must support
traceable impact analysis.

31.7 CERTIFICATION EVIDENCE

Certification must reference reproducible evidence and the
applicable version of the specification.

# =====================================================================
# 35. READINESS GATES
# =====================================================================

GATE G0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Review existing UCOS participant, identity, party, legal-entity,
relationship, policy, workflow, contract, evidence, catalog,
financial, compliance, and governance artifacts.

EXIT:
Relevant canonical authorities and contracts are identified.

GATE G1 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

Determine whether each proposed capability is reusable, extensible,
duplicated, conflicting, missing, or unnecessary.

EXIT:
Authority and reuse decisions are documented.

GATE G2 — ONTOLOGY AND DATA CONTRACTS

Reconcile participant concepts, identifiers, relationships,
effective-time semantics, and lifecycle states.

EXIT:
No unresolved canonical terminology or ownership conflict.

GATE G3 — POLICY AND QUALIFICATION

Define applicable requirements, evidence, verification, qualification,
approval, and exception semantics.

EXIT:
Material qualification decisions are reproducible and traceable.

GATE G4 — COMMERCIAL AND CAPABILITY INTEGRATION

Reconcile agreements, authorization, commercial configuration,
capabilities, and readiness.

EXIT:
No duplicate commercial or capability authority.

GATE G5 — SECURITY AND PRIVACY

Validate access controls, tenant isolation, data minimization,
evidence handling, and audit.

EXIT:
Required security and privacy approvals exist.

GATE G6 — LIFECYCLE AND RECOVERY

Validate activation, monitoring, restriction, suspension,
reinstatement, termination, and offboarding.

EXIT:
Open obligations and partial failures are handled explicitly.

GATE G7 — INTEGRATION AND CONSISTENCY

Validate API contracts, events, idempotency, versioning,
reconciliation, and failure recovery.

EXIT:
Material failure scenarios have verified controls.

GATE G8 — VERIFICATION

Execute the approved acceptance tests and retain evidence.

EXIT:
Required verification evidence exists.

GATE G9 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

Obtain the required approvals and explicit implementation
authorization.

EXIT:
Only the approved scope may proceed to implementation.

# =====================================================================
# 36. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
# =====================================================================

Until the applicable gates are satisfied:

1. Do not create a competing identity authority.
2. Do not create a duplicate legal-entity registry.
3. Do not collapse participant, party, account, and legal entity
   into one record.
4. Do not create a second contract repository.
5. Do not create a duplicate evidence store.
6. Do not treat submitted evidence as verified evidence.
7. Do not treat authentication as commercial authorization.
8. Do not treat onboarding completion as universal selling approval.
9. Do not hardcode jurisdiction-specific requirements without
   canonical governance.
10. Do not create a parallel compliance or risk engine.
11. Do not create a duplicate product or brand authority.
12. Do not create a competing financial ledger.
13. Do not create a parallel settlement authority.
14. Do not grant permissions based solely on participant status.
15. Do not allow account transfer without required verification.
16. Do not activate a participant with unresolved mandatory
    prerequisites.
17. Do not treat a declared capability as verified capability.
18. Do not treat readiness for one activity as readiness for all.
19. Do not allow expired or revoked authorization to remain
    effective without an approved policy basis.
20. Do not interpret provider failure as successful verification.
21. Do not bypass separation-of-duties requirements.
22. Do not automatically treat an unconfirmed risk signal as
    proven misconduct.
23. Do not silently change qualification outcomes after a policy
    update.
24. Do not revoke unrelated capabilities without appropriate scope
    analysis.
25. Do not erase open customer or financial obligations during
    suspension or termination.
26. Do not mark offboarding complete while required obligations
    remain unresolved.
27. Do not process duplicate lifecycle events as duplicate actions.
28. Do not trust stale portal projections for authorization decisions.
29. Do not expose sensitive participant data across tenants.
30. Do not introduce a vendor-specific dependency without approved
    architectural justification.
31. Do not claim that proposed APIs or events are already canonical.
32. Do not claim that proposed tests have passed without execution.
33. Do not claim certification without evidence.
34. Do not claim a capability is missing before context assimilation.
35. Do not modify the UCOS repository without explicit authorization.

# =====================================================================
# 38. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES
# =====================================================================

RULE 001 — CANONICAL PARTICIPANT AUTHORITY
Participant facts must have a designated canonical owner.

RULE 002 — IDENTITY SEPARATION
Participant, party, legal entity, user, and account are distinct
concepts unless canonical UCOS modeling explicitly establishes
a valid relationship between them.

RULE 003 — RELATIONSHIP-CENTRIC AUTHORIZATION
Authorization must be evaluated for a defined relationship and scope.

RULE 004 — KNOWLEDGE ONCE
Canonical participant knowledge must not be duplicated.

RULE 005 — REUSE FIRST
Existing UCOS capabilities must be reused before new capabilities
are proposed.

RULE 006 — EVIDENCE BEFORE QUALIFICATION
Claims must not be treated as verified facts without required evidence.

RULE 007 — QUALIFICATION IS SCOPED
Qualification for one activity does not grant universal permission.

RULE 008 — POLICY IS VERSIONED
Material qualification decisions must identify their applicable
policy versions.

RULE 009 — APPROVAL IS EXPLICIT
No implicit approval may be inferred unless an authorized canonical
policy explicitly permits it.

RULE 010 — AGREEMENTS ARE AUTHORITATIVE
Commercial relationship terms must use canonical agreement authority.

RULE 011 — BRAND AUTHORIZATION IS EXPLICIT
Brand or distribution claims must be validated through approved
authorization mechanisms.

RULE 012 — CAPABILITY IS NOT CAPACITY
A capability declaration does not guarantee current operational
availability.

RULE 013 — READINESS IS EVIDENCE-BASED
Activation must satisfy the prerequisites for the requested scope.

RULE 014 — ACCOUNT STATUS IS NOT SELLING AUTHORITY
Account access and commercial authorization are separate.

RULE 015 — FINANCIAL AUTHORITY IS PRESERVED
Payments, financial records, and settlement remain with their
canonical authorities.

RULE 016 — REASSESSMENT IS GOVERNED
Material changes must trigger the applicable reassessment.

RULE 017 — RESTRICTIONS ARE SCOPED
Restrictions must identify their affected activities and resources.

RULE 018 — OPEN OBLIGATIONS SURVIVE TERMINATION
Termination does not erase outstanding customer, financial, or
legal obligations.

RULE 019 — EVENTS DO NOT REPLACE AUTHORITY
Events communicate changes; they do not transfer canonical ownership.

RULE 020 — RETRIES MUST BE SAFE
Potentially duplicative operations require idempotency and
appropriate reconciliation.

RULE 021 — UNKNOWN IS NOT SUCCESS
Unresolved outcomes must remain explicitly unknown.

RULE 022 — SECURITY IS RELATIONSHIP-AWARE
Access must respect participant, role, relationship, tenant,
resource, and purpose boundaries.

RULE 023 — RISK DECISIONS REQUIRE GOVERNANCE
Material restrictions must follow canonical risk and compliance rules.

RULE 024 — METRICS REQUIRE SEMANTICS
Participant performance metrics require explicit definitions and
appropriate interpretation.

RULE 025 — RECONCILIATION MUST BE TRACEABLE
Corrections must preserve canonical authority and audit lineage.

RULE 026 — AUTOMATION MUST BE CONTROLLED
Automated decisions must follow approved policy, evidence, and
exception-handling requirements.

RULE 027 — VENDOR NEUTRALITY
External verification and integration providers must not define
the canonical domain model.

RULE 028 — NO ORPHAN ARTIFACTS
Every approved capability, contract, policy, and test must have
traceable ownership and dependencies.

RULE 029 — CERTIFICATION REQUIRES EVIDENCE
Specification completeness is not implementation certification.

RULE 030 — IMPLEMENTATION REQUIRES AUTHORIZATION
No repository or production changes are authorized by this
specification alone.
