# =============================================================================
# 0. PURPOSE, SCOPE, AND AUTHORITY
# =============================================================================

0.1 PURPOSE

Define a universal, extensible architecture for protecting a
marketplace against malicious activity, fraudulent transactions,
participant abuse, customer exploitation, counterfeit activity,
policy violations, account compromise, coordinated manipulation,
and other threats to marketplace integrity.

The architecture must coordinate detection, assessment, prevention,
investigation, enforcement, remediation, and recovery while preserving
the canonical authority of the UCOS domains responsible for identity,
authentication, authorization, payments, financial records, orders,
catalog, communications, legal compliance, customer support, and
other affected business capabilities.

The design must support multiple:

- Industries.
- Marketplace models.
- Participant types.
- Product and service categories.
- Jurisdictions.
- Currencies.
- Transaction models.
- Fulfillment models.
- Business relationships.
- Risk classes.
- Threat categories.
- Regulatory environments.
- Interaction channels.
- Deployment models.
- Evidence sources.
- Detection technologies.

No specific threat list is considered permanently exhaustive.

0.2 PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Establish a governed trust-and-safety architecture capable of
identifying and managing threats while minimizing false positives,
unjustified restrictions, privacy violations, operational disruption,
and adverse impact on legitimate customers and participants.

0.3 CORE RESPONSIBILITIES

The proposed domain coordinates:

A. TRUST CONTEXT
   Governed references to trust-related facts and evidence.

B. THREAT TAXONOMY
   Classification of threat types, abuse patterns, and risk scenarios.

C. SIGNAL INTAKE
   Controlled intake of signals from authorized sources.

D. RISK ASSESSMENT
   Evaluation of signals using approved policies and models.

E. DETECTION COORDINATION
   Coordination of deterministic rules, statistical methods,
   graph-based analysis, anomaly detection, and approved AI systems.

F. CASE MANAGEMENT
   Creation and management of investigation cases.

G. EVIDENCE MANAGEMENT INTEGRATION
   Reference, preserve, and evaluate relevant evidence.

H. DECISION GOVERNANCE
   Record authorized decisions, confidence, rationale, and scope.

I. ENFORCEMENT COORDINATION
   Request and coordinate actions through canonical authorities.

J. REVIEW AND APPEALS
   Support authorized human review, correction, and appeal.

K. CONTINUOUS MONITORING
   Evaluate changing risk conditions and expiring controls.

L. MARKETPLACE INTEGRITY
   Coordinate prevention, detection, investigation, and recovery.

M. RISK OBSERVABILITY
   Measure detection quality, false positives, operational impact,
   remediation effectiveness, and residual risk.

0.4 NON-GOALS

This specification does not create:

- A replacement identity provider.
- A replacement authentication service.
- A second authorization authority.
- A duplicate payment-fraud ledger.
- A parallel financial ledger.
- A second order authority.
- A duplicate product or catalog authority.
- A replacement regulatory compliance engine.
- An independent sanctions authority.
- A competing legal case-management authority where one exists.
- An independent law-enforcement decision system.
- A universal risk score that overrides all domain-specific policies.
- An unrestricted surveillance platform.
- An ungoverned customer or participant blacklist.
- An automatic punishment mechanism without authorized policy.
- A second customer-support or dispute authority.

0.5 AUTHORITY RULE

Trust and safety may evaluate risk and recommend or coordinate action.

It may not silently assume authority to change canonical state.

For example:

- Authentication decisions remain with the identity authority.
- Access grants and revocations remain with the authorization authority.
- Payment authorization and payment execution remain with payment
  authorities.
- Financial holds remain with the authorized financial or risk
  authority.
- Order state remains with the order authority.
- Listing and catalog state remain with catalog and listing authorities.
- Legal and regulatory determinations remain with their authorized
  authorities.
- Customer support case state remains with the support authority.
- Appeals and adjudication remain with their designated authorities.

The exact authority mapping must be established through UCOS
canonical reconciliation.

# =============================================================================
# 1. ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
# =============================================================================

1.1 CANONICAL AUTHORITY

Every material fact, decision, and state transition must have an
explicit authoritative owner.

1.2 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Threat signals, evidence, assessments, decisions, and enforcement
records must be reused through canonical references rather than
copied into competing sources of truth.

1.3 REUSE FIRST

Existing UCOS risk, security, fraud, compliance, identity, audit,
evidence, and investigation capabilities must be discovered before
new components are proposed.

1.4 SEPARATION OF CONCERNS

Signal generation, risk assessment, case investigation, decision
authorization, enforcement, and appeal must remain distinguishable.

1.5 PROPORTIONALITY

Actions must be proportionate to the established threat, evidence,
potential impact, applicable policy, and legal obligations.

1.6 EVIDENCE BEFORE ADVERSE CONCLUSION

A signal or model score must not automatically be treated as proof
of misconduct.

1.7 EXPLICIT UNCERTAINTY

Unknown, incomplete, conflicting, or low-confidence information
must remain distinguishable from verified facts.

1.8 LEAST PRIVILEGE

Trust-and-safety access must be limited by role, purpose, case,
resource, jurisdiction, and policy.

1.9 PRIVACY BY DESIGN

Risk processing must use only data that is necessary, permitted,
and appropriate for the defined purpose.

1.10 HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY

High-impact decisions must have the review, approval, and appeal
mechanisms required by applicable law and canonical policy.

1.11 DETERMINISTIC ENFORCEMENT

Once an authorized decision is made, its scope, effective time,
target, and intended outcome must be explicit.

1.12 SAFE AUTOMATION

Automation must have bounded authority, defined failure behavior,
monitoring, and appropriate human escalation.

1.13 REVERSIBILITY

Where legally and operationally permissible, erroneous restrictions
must be correctable through an authorized process.

1.14 AUDITABILITY

Material decisions and actions must preserve traceable provenance.

1.15 CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT

Detection effectiveness, false-positive rates, customer impact,
and operational outcomes must be evaluated through governed
measurement.

1.16 NO UNIVERSAL SCORE OVERRIDE

A generalized risk score must not override a domain-specific
mandatory rule unless canonical governance explicitly permits it.

1.17 NO PERMANENT ASSUMPTION

Threat models, signals, policies, and detection methods must be
versioned and periodically reviewed.

# =============================================================================
# 2. LOGICAL ARCHITECTURE
# =============================================================================

2.1 COMPONENTS

A. TRUST CONTEXT INTEGRATION
   Retrieves authorized identity, relationship, transaction,
   capability, and compliance references.

B. SIGNAL INTAKE GATEWAY
   Validates source, schema, provenance, permitted purpose, and
   data classification.

C. THREAT TAXONOMY REGISTRY
   Maintains governed threat categories and their relationships.

D. SIGNAL NORMALIZATION
   Converts source-specific observations into canonical signal
   representations without discarding provenance.

E. DETECTION COORDINATOR
   Coordinates approved rules, models, heuristics, and detection
   capabilities.

F. RISK ASSESSMENT COORDINATOR
   Combines authorized assessment results according to policy.

G. POLICY EVALUATION INTEGRATION
   Applies canonical policy and decision-governance contracts.

H. CASE ORCHESTRATOR
   Coordinates investigation cases, tasks, evidence, review, and
   resolution.

I. EVIDENCE INTEGRATION
   References canonical evidence and document-management systems.

J. DECISION RECORD COORDINATOR
   Records proposed and authorized decisions with provenance.

K. ENFORCEMENT ORCHESTRATOR
   Requests actions from the responsible canonical domains.

L. APPEAL AND REVIEW COORDINATOR
   Routes authorized challenges and independent reviews.

M. MONITORING AND REASSESSMENT
   Re-evaluates active risk conditions and control validity.

N. RISK INTELLIGENCE
   Provides governed analysis, trend detection, and aggregate insights.

O. CONTROL TOWER
   Presents operational status, queues, exceptions, and performance.

P. AUDIT AND RECONCILIATION
   Detects discrepancies between authorized decisions and actual
   canonical domain state.

2.3 DEPLOYMENT NEUTRALITY

This is a logical architecture.

It does not prescribe a specific programming language, database,

# =============================================================================
# 3. TRUST AND SAFETY ONTOLOGY
# =============================================================================

3.1 TRUST CONTEXT

A governed collection of authorized facts relevant to assessing
the trustworthiness or risk of an activity.

3.2 THREAT

A potential source of harm to customers, participants, the
marketplace, its infrastructure, or its legitimate operations.

3.3 RISK

A governed assessment of the likelihood, impact, and relevant
uncertainty associated with a defined event or activity.

3.4 SIGNAL

An observation that may be relevant to a risk assessment.

A signal is not necessarily accurate, complete, or independently
actionable.

3.5 INDICATOR

A defined characteristic that may contribute to detection or
assessment.

3.6 DETECTION

An evaluation that identifies a potential threat or policy concern.

3.7 RISK ASSESSMENT

A contextual evaluation using authorized evidence, indicators,
models, and policies.

3.8 CASE

A governed investigation object containing a defined question,
scope, evidence references, tasks, findings, and resolution.

3.9 EVIDENCE

Information collected or referenced to support or challenge a claim.

3.10 FINDING

A documented conclusion derived from evidence and an approved
assessment process.

3.11 DECISION

An authorized determination about an activity, relationship,
restriction, or case.

3.12 ENFORCEMENT ACTION

An authorized request or operation intended to implement a decision.

3.13 CONTROL

A mechanism intended to prevent, detect, contain, or remediate risk.

3.14 FALSE POSITIVE

A detection or adverse classification that incorrectly identifies
a legitimate activity as suspicious or noncompliant.

3.15 FALSE NEGATIVE

A threat that the detection process fails to identify.

3.16 RESIDUAL RISK

Risk remaining after applicable controls have been applied.

3.17 APPEAL

A governed request to review a decision or its factual basis.

3.18 REMEDIATION

An action intended to correct a verified issue or reduce risk.

3.19 TRUST STATUS

A context-specific, time-bounded representation of a governed
assessment or eligibility result.

3.20 CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

These definitions must be compared with existing UCOS ontology,
risk, security, compliance, and governance artifacts before adoption.

# =============================================================================
# 4. THREAT TAXONOMY AND CLASSIFICATION
# =============================================================================

4.1 PURPOSE

Provide a flexible taxonomy for classifying threats without
hardcoding the architecture around a fixed list of attack types.

4.2 TAXONOMY DIMENSIONS

A threat classification may include:

- Threat family.
- Threat subtype.
- Affected domain.
- Affected asset.
- Attack surface.
- Threat actor category.
- Entry vector.
- Target activity.
- Potential impact.
- Evidence class.
- Confidence category.
- Applicable jurisdiction.
- Relevant policy.
- Required response class.
- Review requirements.

4.3 ILLUSTRATIVE THREAT FAMILIES

A. IDENTITY AND ACCOUNT ABUSE
   Account takeover, impersonation, synthetic identity indicators,
   credential misuse, unauthorized account recovery.

B. TRANSACTION ABUSE
   Unauthorized transaction patterns, payment abuse indicators,
   duplicate transaction attempts, suspicious transaction sequences.

C. FINANCIAL ABUSE
   Refund abuse, chargeback abuse indicators, settlement manipulation,
   unauthorized payout changes, financial account compromise.

D. SELLER AND PARTICIPANT ABUSE
   Misrepresentation, unauthorized selling, repeated policy violations,
   coordinated seller abuse, deceptive business practices.

E. PRODUCT AND CATALOG ABUSE
   Counterfeit indicators, prohibited listings, misleading product
   claims, unauthorized brand usage, catalog manipulation.

F. CUSTOMER ABUSE
   Automated account creation, abusive interaction patterns,
   exploitation of marketplace workflows.

G. REVIEW AND REPUTATION MANIPULATION
   Coordinated fake reviews, rating manipulation, fabricated feedback,
   coercion, retaliatory review patterns.

H. PROMOTION AND LOYALTY ABUSE
   Coupon exploitation, unauthorized benefit reuse, loyalty manipulation,
   incentive abuse.

I. AUTOMATION AND BOT ABUSE
   Unapproved automated traffic, scraping, resource exhaustion,
   credential stuffing indicators, automated transaction attempts.

J. CONTENT AND COMMUNICATION ABUSE
   Phishing, spam, impersonation, malicious content, harassment,
   prohibited communications.

K. SUPPLY-CHAIN AND FULFILLMENT ABUSE
   False fulfillment signals, shipment manipulation, delivery evidence
   manipulation, inventory misrepresentation.

L. PLATFORM AND INTEGRATION ABUSE
   API misuse, authorization bypass attempts, integration compromise,
   suspicious service-to-service activity.

M. COLLUSION AND COORDINATED ABUSE
   Coordinated activity across accounts, entities, transactions,
   devices, or relationships where supported by lawful evidence.

N. POLICY AND REGULATORY VIOLATIONS
   Suspected or confirmed violations routed to the appropriate
   canonical compliance authority.

4.4 TAXONOMY EXTENSIBILITY

New threat categories must be registered through canonical governance.

4.5 TAXONOMY SEMANTICS

A category must define its meaning, scope, owner, applicable
evidence, decision constraints, and lifecycle.

4.6 CATEGORY VS. FINDING

Classifying a case under a threat category does not establish
that the threat occurred.

4.7 THREAT TAXONOMY VERSIONING

Taxonomy changes must preserve historical interpretability.

# =============================================================================
# 5. TRUST BOUNDARIES AND AUTHORITY MATRIX
# =============================================================================

5.1 AUTHORITY MATRIX

IDENTITY
  Authority: canonical identity domain.
  Trust-and-safety responsibility: consume authorized identity
  verification and identity-risk outcomes.

AUTHENTICATION
  Authority: canonical authentication domain.
  Responsibility: request governed protective actions when authorized.

AUTHORIZATION
  Authority: canonical access-control domain.
  Responsibility: submit scoped access restrictions or revocations.

PAYMENT
  Authority: canonical payment domain.
  Responsibility: supply risk assessments or request authorized
  controls through the payment authority.

FINANCE
  Authority: canonical financial domain.
  Responsibility: request authorized holds, adjustments, or reviews
  without directly mutating financial records.

ORDERS
  Authority: canonical order domain.
  Responsibility: request approved order-related controls.

CATALOG
  Authority: canonical product, catalog, and listing domains.
  Responsibility: request authorized listing review or restriction.

COMPLIANCE
  Authority: canonical compliance domain.
  Responsibility: route evidence and assessment requests.

LEGAL
  Authority: designated legal governance.
  Responsibility: preserve evidence and route matters requiring
  legal interpretation.

SUPPORT
  Authority: canonical customer-support domain.
  Responsibility: coordinate case references and customer communication.

COMMUNICATIONS
  Authority: canonical communication domain.
  Responsibility: request approved messaging or suppression actions.

AUDIT
  Authority: canonical audit domain.
  Responsibility: supply required provenance and decision records.

5.2 NO SHADOW AUTHORITY

A risk coordinator must not directly overwrite another domain's
authoritative state.

5.3 DECISION AUTHORITY

Every adverse action must identify the authority permitted to
make that decision.

5.4 POLICY CONFLICT

If two canonical policies conflict, route the conflict through
governance rather than inventing a local precedence rule.

5.5 EMERGENCY ACTIONS

Emergency containment must follow preapproved policies, narrowly
defined scopes, explicit time limits, and required review.

5.6 ACTION CONFIRMATION

A requested enforcement action is not complete until its authoritative
result is confirmed or explicitly classified as unknown or failed.

# =============================================================================
# 6. SIGNAL INTAKE AND NORMALIZATION
# =============================================================================

6.1 PURPOSE

Accept authorized risk signals from canonical systems and approved
external sources.

6.2 SIGNAL SOURCES

Potential sources include:

- Authentication events.
- Authorization events.
- Payment risk outcomes.
- Order anomalies.
- Catalog moderation outcomes.
- Participant verification.
- Customer reports.
- Seller reports.
- Support cases.
- Security telemetry.
- Compliance notifications.
- Device or network signals where lawful and authorized.
- External verification results.
- Approved threat-intelligence sources.
- Manual investigator observations.

6.3 SIGNAL CONTRACT

A normalized signal should identify:

- Signal identifier.
- Signal type.
- Source authority.
- Source record reference.
- Subject reference.
- Observed activity.
- Observation time.
- Recording time.
- Provenance.
- Data classification.
- Confidence or reliability information where available.
- Applicable purpose.
- Relevant policy.
- Expiration or freshness information.
- Correlation reference.

6.4 SOURCE TRUST

Signal reliability must be evaluated according to the source,
provenance, integrity, freshness, and known limitations.

6.5 SCHEMA VALIDATION

Malformed signals must be rejected, quarantined, or routed through
an approved correction process.

6.6 DUPLICATE SIGNALS

Repeated signals must be deduplicated where appropriate without
destroying legitimate evidence that the same behavior occurred
multiple times.

6.7 SIGNAL VS. EVIDENCE

A signal may trigger review but must not automatically become
verified evidence.

6.8 PURPOSE LIMITATION

Signals must be processed only for authorized purposes.

6.9 DATA MINIMIZATION

Do not collect or retain additional personal data solely because
it may help future investigations.

6.10 SIGNAL EXPIRATION

Signals must have governed freshness and retention semantics.

6.11 EXTERNAL SIGNALS

External intelligence must preserve source provenance and must
not be treated as authoritative without an approved validation process.

6.12 INTAKE FAILURE

Signal processing failures must be observable and recoverable.

# =============================================================================
# 7. DETECTION ENGINE AND RISK ASSESSMENT
# =============================================================================

7.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate approved detection methods while preserving their
distinct assumptions, confidence, and limitations.

7.2 DETECTION METHODS

Potential methods include:

- Deterministic rules.
- Threshold-based controls.
- Statistical anomaly detection.
- Time-series analysis.
- Graph-based relationship analysis.
- Behavioral pattern analysis.
- Sequence analysis.
- Approved machine-learning models.
- Approved AI-assisted analysis.
- External risk assessments.
- Human-generated findings.

7.3 METHOD GOVERNANCE

Each method must have an explicit owner, intended use, input
requirements, output contract, validation process, and limitations.

7.4 RISK ASSESSMENT CONTEXT

Assessment may consider:

- Activity type.
- Transaction context.
- Participant relationship.
- Relevant evidence.
- Policy requirements.
- Historical context where authorized.
- Signal reliability.
- Potential impact.
- Uncertainty.
- Applicable jurisdiction.

7.5 RISK OUTPUT

A risk assessment may contain:

- Assessment identifier.
- Subject.
- Activity or transaction reference.
- Risk category.
- Relevant policy.
- Assessment time.
- Assessment version.
- Findings.
- Confidence information.
- Evidence references.
- Known limitations.
- Recommended response.
- Review requirement.
- Expiration or reassessment condition.

7.6 RISK SCORE

A numerical score may be used only when its meaning, scale,
calibration, version, and permitted use are documented.

7.7 SCORE INTERPRETATION

A score must not be presented as a probability unless the model
is appropriately calibrated and the interpretation is justified.

7.8 MULTI-SIGNAL COMPOSITION

Combining signals must use documented rules and must account for
correlation, duplication, missing data, and conflicting evidence.

7.9 MISSING DATA

Missing data must not automatically be interpreted as evidence
of wrongdoing.

7.10 MODEL LIMITATIONS

Assessment outputs must expose relevant limitations to authorized
decision-makers.

7.11 MODEL DRIFT

Models must be monitored for drift, degradation, and changing
operational conditions.

7.12 FALSE-POSITIVE CONTROL

Detection quality must be evaluated alongside false-positive
rates and customer or participant impact.

7.13 FALSE-NEGATIVE CONTROL

Residual risk and undetected threats must be assessed using
appropriate validation methods.

7.14 NO UNBOUNDED AUTOMATION

A detection score alone must not authorize unlimited or permanent
adverse action.

# =============================================================================
# 8. RISK CLASSIFICATION AND RESPONSE POLICY
# =============================================================================

8.1 PURPOSE

Map assessed risk and evidence to governed response options.

8.2 RESPONSE DIMENSIONS

Response policy may consider:

- Threat category.
- Severity.
- Confidence.
- Evidence quality.
- Potential harm.
- Activity type.
- Scope of exposure.
- Reversibility.
- Legal requirements.
- Customer impact.
- Operational impact.
- Required approval.
- Review deadline.

8.3 RESPONSE CATEGORIES

Potential responses include:

- No action.
- Continue monitoring.
- Request additional evidence.
- Increase verification.
- Require step-up authentication.
- Apply a temporary rate limit.
- Hold an operation for review.
- Restrict a specific capability.
- Refer for manual investigation.
- Request an authorized transaction review.
- Request an authorized listing review.
- Suspend a defined relationship.
- Escalate to compliance or legal review.
- Apply a legally required control.
- Restore previously restricted capability after review.

8.4 RESPONSE POLICY CONTRACT

A response policy should define:

- Policy identifier.
- Policy owner.
- Scope.
- Applicable conditions.
- Required evidence.
- Permitted actions.
- Prohibited actions.
- Approval requirements.
- Maximum duration where applicable.
- Review deadline.
- Notification requirements.
- Appeal rights where applicable.
- Reassessment triggers.
- Version.
- Retirement rules.

8.5 PROPORTIONALITY

Choose the least restrictive action that adequately addresses
the established risk, unless applicable policy or law requires
a different response.

8.6 CONFIDENCE THRESHOLDS

Thresholds must be validated for the specific use case and
must not be generalized across unrelated threat categories.

8.7 HIGH-IMPACT ACTIONS

High-impact actions must receive the required human review or
other authorization.

8.8 LOW-CONFIDENCE SIGNALS

Low-confidence signals may justify monitoring or additional
verification but must not automatically establish misconduct.

8.9 EMERGENCY RESPONSE

Emergency response must have a defined trigger, scope, duration,
review process, and termination condition.

8.10 POLICY VERSIONING

Each material response must identify the policy version used.

# =============================================================================
# 9. INVESTIGATION AND CASE MANAGEMENT
# =============================================================================

9.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate investigations into suspected threats while preserving
evidence integrity, procedural fairness, and appropriate access.

9.2 CASE TYPES

Potential case types include:

- Account compromise.
- Transaction abuse.
- Suspected fraud.
- Seller misconduct.
- Counterfeit or unauthorized listing.
- Review manipulation.
- Promotion abuse.
- Security incident.
- Customer exploitation.
- Coordinated abuse.
- Compliance referral.
- Financial anomaly.
- Platform misuse.

9.3 CASE CONTRACT

A case should identify:

- Case identifier.
- Case type.
- Originating signal references.
- Subject references.
- Affected activities.
- Severity.
- Priority.
- Case owner.
- Status.
- Evidence references.
- Applicable policies.
- Investigation tasks.
- Findings.
- Decision references.
- Review requirements.
- Creation time.
- Last update.
- Resolution.
- Retention requirements.

9.4 CASE LIFECYCLE

Potential states include:

- Created.
- Awaiting triage.
- Assigned.
- Under investigation.
- Awaiting evidence.
- Awaiting external response.
- Awaiting specialist review.
- Decision pending.
- Resolved.
- Escalated.
- Reopened.
- Closed.
- Archived according to policy.

9.5 TRIAGE

Triage must consider potential harm, urgency, evidence quality,
operational exposure, and applicable response deadlines.

9.6 CASE ASSIGNMENT

Assignment must follow investigator authorization, specialization,
workload policy, and separation-of-duties requirements.

9.7 INVESTIGATION PLAN

A case may contain explicit hypotheses, required evidence, tasks,
responsible parties, and completion criteria.

9.8 EVIDENCE HANDLING

Evidence must retain provenance, access restrictions, integrity
information, and applicable retention requirements.

9.9 FINDINGS

Findings must distinguish verified facts, interpretations,
hypotheses, unresolved questions, and contradictory evidence.

9.10 CASE MERGING

Cases may be linked or merged only through governed rules that
preserve the identity and history of each original case.

9.11 CASE SPLITTING

Splitting a case must preserve evidence and relationship references.

9.12 CLOSURE

A case must not be closed merely because a target was restricted.
Required investigation, review, and documentation must be completed.

9.13 REOPENING

New evidence or changed circumstances may trigger an authorized
reopening process.

# =============================================================================
# 10. EVIDENCE MANAGEMENT AND CHAIN OF CUSTODY
# =============================================================================

10.1 AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical UCOS evidence, document, audit, and retention
capabilities.

10.2 EVIDENCE TYPES

Potential evidence includes:

- Canonical event references.
- Transaction records.
- Authentication outcomes.
- Access-control records.
- Participant documents.
- Customer reports.
- Seller submissions.
- Product or listing records.
- Communication records.
- Security telemetry.
- External verification results.
- Investigator observations.
- Relevant system logs.
- Approved model outputs.

10.3 EVIDENCE REFERENCE

An evidence reference should identify:

- Evidence identity.
- Canonical source.
- Source record.
- Subject.
- Relevant claim.
- Collection time.
- Source time.
- Provenance.
- Integrity metadata.
- Classification.
- Access policy.
- Retention policy.
- Verification status.
- Version.

10.4 EVIDENCE INTEGRITY

Use approved mechanisms to detect unauthorized alteration and
preserve required integrity information.

10.5 CHAIN OF CUSTODY

Where legally or operationally required, record evidence acquisition,
transfer, access, transformation, and disposition.

10.6 EVIDENCE ACCESS

Access must be restricted by case, role, purpose, jurisdiction,
and applicable policy.

10.7 EVIDENCE COPIES

Avoid unnecessary copies. Where a copy is legally or operationally
required, record its relationship to the canonical source.

10.8 EVIDENCE CORRECTION

Corrections must preserve required historical provenance.

10.9 RETENTION AND DISPOSAL

Apply canonical retention, legal hold, and disposal requirements.

10.10 EXTERNAL EVIDENCE

External evidence must be evaluated for source reliability,
authenticity, context, and permitted use.

10.11 CONFLICTING EVIDENCE

Conflicting evidence must be represented explicitly rather than
silently discarded.

10.12 EVIDENCE VS. CONCLUSION

A record's existence does not automatically establish the truth
of every interpretation made from it.

# =============================================================================
# 11. IDENTITY, ACCOUNT, AND ACCESS ABUSE
# =============================================================================

11.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate detection and response to unauthorized access,
identity misuse, account compromise, and abusive account creation.

11.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Credential compromise.
- Suspicious authentication sequences.
- Unauthorized account recovery.
- Impersonation.
- Account takeover indicators.
- Abusive account creation.
- Session misuse.
- Privilege escalation attempts.
- Unauthorized credential sharing.
- Suspicious administrative actions.

11.3 AUTHORITY

Authentication and authorization remain canonical domain
responsibilities.

11.4 RESPONSE OPTIONS

Depending on evidence and policy, responses may include:

- Additional verification.
- Step-up authentication.
- Session invalidation request.
- Credential reset request.
- Account recovery review.
- Scoped permission restriction.
- Security investigation.
- Account restriction.
- Customer notification through canonical communications.

11.5 ACCOUNT OWNERSHIP

Account ownership disputes must follow the canonical identity
and account-recovery processes.

11.6 DEVICE AND NETWORK SIGNALS

Device and network observations may be used only where lawful,
authorized, proportionate, and supported by approved policies.

11.7 SHARED ENVIRONMENTS

Shared devices, networks, workplaces, households, or public
access environments must not automatically imply collusion.

11.8 NO SOLE-SIGNAL PUNISHMENT

A single weak signal must not automatically establish account abuse.

11.9 RECOVERY

Legitimate customers must have a supported recovery process.

11.10 PRIVACY

Identity-risk monitoring must comply with applicable privacy
and data-minimization requirements.

# =============================================================================
# 12. TRANSACTION AND PAYMENT ABUSE
# =============================================================================

12.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate detection of suspicious transaction behavior while
preserving payment and order authorities.

12.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Unauthorized payment attempts.
- Suspicious transaction sequences.
- Duplicate transaction attempts.
- Payment instrument misuse indicators.
- Transaction velocity anomalies.
- Refund abuse indicators.
- Chargeback abuse indicators.
- Account-to-transaction inconsistencies.
- Suspected transaction manipulation.
- Unusual financial behavior requiring review.

12.3 AUTHORITY

Payment authorization, capture, reversal, refund execution,
financial accounting, and settlement remain with their canonical
authorities.

12.4 RISK INPUTS

Use only permitted and relevant inputs with appropriate provenance.

12.5 ACTION OPTIONS

Possible actions include:

- Additional verification.
- Transaction review.
- Temporary processing hold where authorized.
- Payment-domain risk review.
- Investigation case creation.
- Customer support referral.
- Authorized transaction restriction.

12.6 UNKNOWN OUTCOME

An unknown payment result must not be treated as either successful
or failed without authoritative reconciliation.

12.7 DUPLICATE PREVENTION

Retries must respect canonical idempotency and payment-processing
contracts.

12.8 CUSTOMER IMPACT

Controls must minimize unnecessary interruption to legitimate
transactions.

12.9 FINANCIAL RECORDS

Risk assessments must not directly alter canonical ledger entries.

12.10 DISPUTE INTEGRATION

Payment disputes and chargebacks must integrate with the
appropriate financial and dispute authorities.

# =============================================================================
# 13. SELLER, MERCHANT, AND PARTICIPANT ABUSE
# =============================================================================

13.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate detection and management of participant behavior that
may threaten marketplace integrity.

13.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Misrepresentation of business identity.
- Unauthorized product or brand claims.
- Counterfeit indicators.
- Repeated listing violations.
- Manipulated performance information.
- Fulfillment misrepresentation.
- Abusive customer interactions.
- Unauthorized account control.
- Collusive activity indicators.
- Attempts to evade an authorized restriction.
- Repeated creation of replacement accounts after enforcement.

13.3 AUTHORITY

Participant identity, commercial relationships, catalog, contracts,
compliance, and financial state remain with their canonical domains.

13.4 ASSESSMENT

Assess evidence, scope, severity, repeat behavior, uncertainty,
and possible alternative explanations.

13.5 ENFORCEMENT

Possible actions include:

- Request additional documentation.
- Request listing review.
- Restrict a defined category.
- Require corrective action.
- Suspend a specified capability.
- Refer for compliance review.
- Request relationship suspension through the authorized domain.

13.6 OPEN OBLIGATIONS

Participant restrictions must not automatically erase open orders,
returns, refunds, disputes, or other obligations.

13.7 SELLER APPEALS

Provide the review and appeal mechanisms required by applicable
policy and law.

13.8 REINSTATEMENT

Reinstatement must follow the canonical relationship and
authorization lifecycle.

13.9 NO AUTOMATIC GUILT BY ASSOCIATION

Relationships with a flagged participant must not automatically
establish misconduct by another participant.

13.10 FAIRNESS

Participant enforcement must be based on documented evidence and
approved policy.

# =============================================================================
# 14. PRODUCT, CATALOG, AND CONTENT ABUSE
# =============================================================================

14.1 PURPOSE

Coordinate identification and handling of unsafe, misleading,
prohibited, counterfeit, or otherwise unauthorized marketplace
content.

14.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Counterfeit indicators.
- Unauthorized brand use.
- Misleading claims.
- Prohibited products.
- Unsafe product claims.
- Misclassified listings.
- Duplicate or deceptive listings.
- Manipulated product attributes.
- Malicious links or embedded content.
- Repeated evasion of listing controls.

14.3 AUTHORITY

Product truth remains with the product master.

Listing publication and visibility remain with the canonical
catalog or listing authority.

Regulatory determinations remain with the appropriate compliance
authority.

14.4 DETECTION

Use authorized listing metadata, evidence, reports, approved
classification systems, and policy checks.

14.5 CONTENT REVIEW

Where automated evidence is uncertain, route the matter through
the applicable review process.

14.6 PROHIBITED CONTENT

Actions must follow the canonical prohibited-content taxonomy
and applicable legal requirements.

14.7 LISTING RESTRICTION

The trust-and-safety domain may request an authorized restriction
but must not silently overwrite canonical listing state.

14.8 COUNTERFEIT CLAIMS

A suspected counterfeit indicator must be distinguished from
a verified finding.

14.9 PRODUCT SAFETY

Potential safety hazards must be routed to the designated product
safety and compliance authorities.

14.10 RESTORATION

Restoration after removal or restriction must follow the applicable
review and authorization process.

# =============================================================================
# 15. REVIEW, REPUTATION, PROMOTION, AND LOYALTY ABUSE
# =============================================================================

15.1 PURPOSE

Protect the integrity of marketplace reviews, reputation systems,
promotions, and loyalty benefits.

15.2 REVIEW ABUSE

Potential patterns include:

- Coordinated rating manipulation.
- Fabricated review indicators.
- Incentivized review-policy violations.
- Repeated review submissions.
- Review coercion.
- Retaliatory review patterns.
- Manipulated reviewer relationships.

15.3 PROMOTION ABUSE

Potential patterns include:

- Repeated unauthorized benefit claims.
- Exploitation of eligibility rules.
- Automated coupon attempts.
- Coordinated promotional misuse.
- Unauthorized referral manipulation.

15.4 LOYALTY ABUSE

Potential patterns include:

- Duplicate benefit claims.
- Unauthorized reward redemption.
- Suspicious reward-transfer behavior.
- Repeated exploitation of reversal rules.
- Unauthorized manipulation of reward state.

15.5 AUTHORITY

Review moderation, promotion eligibility, and loyalty balances
remain with their canonical domains.

15.6 FALSE-POSITIVE PROTECTION

Similar behavior or common participation in a public promotion
does not independently prove collusion.

15.7 EVIDENCE

Decisions must identify the applicable policy and supporting
evidence.

15.8 REWARD REVERSAL

Reward reversals must use authorized loyalty operations.

15.9 CUSTOMER COMMUNICATION

Material adverse outcomes must be communicated according to
applicable policy and legal requirements.

15.10 APPEALS

Provide an appropriate correction or appeal route where required.

# =============================================================================
# 16. BOT, AUTOMATION, AND RESOURCE ABUSE
# =============================================================================

16.1 PURPOSE

Identify unapproved automation and abusive traffic without
unnecessarily excluding legitimate automated clients or assistive
technologies.

16.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential categories include:

- Credential stuffing indicators.
- Automated account creation.
- Excessive request rates.
- Automated transaction attempts.
- Unauthorized scraping.
- API resource exhaustion.
- Automated promotion exploitation.
- Malicious traffic patterns.
- Abusive retry behavior.

16.3 AUTHORITY

Network protection, API gateways, identity, and infrastructure
security remain with their canonical authorities.

16.4 CLASSIFICATION

Distinguish authorized integrations, accessibility tools, approved
automation, ordinary high-volume use, and malicious behavior.

16.5 RESPONSE OPTIONS

Possible responses include:

- Rate limiting.
- Additional verification.
- Temporary throttling.
- Request rejection.
- Integration review.
- Security investigation.
- Scoped credential revocation through the proper authority.

16.6 RATE-LIMIT POLICY

Limits must be configured according to operation, resource
capacity, client class, and approved policy.

16.7 ACCESSIBILITY

Detection controls must not unnecessarily block legitimate
assistive technologies.

16.8 RETRY STORMS

Use backpressure and bounded retry controls to prevent cascading
failures.

16.9 RESOURCE EXHAUSTION

Containment must follow approved infrastructure and security
procedures.

16.10 REVIEW

Material client or integration restrictions must have the
appropriate review mechanism.

# =============================================================================
# 17. COLLUSION AND RELATIONSHIP-BASED RISK
# =============================================================================

17.1 PURPOSE

Support authorized analysis of coordinated abuse involving
multiple accounts, participants, transactions, devices, or entities.

17.2 RELATIONSHIP TYPES

Potential relationships include:

- Shared ownership.
- Shared authorized administration.
- Transaction relationships.
- Fulfillment relationships.
- Common contractual relationships.
- Repeated interaction patterns.
- Known infrastructure relationships.
- Verified organizational connections.

17.3 GRAPH ANALYSIS

Graph analysis may identify patterns for review, but graph proximity
alone must not establish misconduct.

17.4 SHARED ATTRIBUTES

Shared addresses, devices, networks, contact points, or other
attributes may have legitimate explanations.

17.5 EVIDENCE WEIGHTING

The significance of a relationship must be evaluated according to
provenance, reliability, context, and alternative explanations.

17.6 ENTITY RESOLUTION

Use canonical entity-resolution capabilities where available.

17.7 PROHIBITED SHORTCUT

Do not automatically penalize every participant connected to a
suspected participant.

17.8 CASE LINKING

Related cases may be linked through governed relationships while
preserving their independent evidence and decision histories.

17.9 PRIVACY

Relationship analysis must follow purpose limitation, access
controls, and applicable retention policies.

17.10 REVIEW

High-impact decisions based on network or relationship analysis
must follow the applicable review requirements.

# =============================================================================
# 18. AI, MACHINE LEARNING, AND MODEL GOVERNANCE
# =============================================================================

18.1 PURPOSE

Enable approved analytical and AI-assisted detection while
maintaining accountable decisions and reproducible evidence.

18.2 PERMITTED USE CASES

Subject to approval, models may assist with:

- Anomaly detection.
- Signal classification.
- Evidence triage.
- Duplicate-pattern identification.
- Case prioritization.
- Relationship analysis.
- Threat trend analysis.
- Investigation summarization.
- Policy-relevant information extraction.
- False-positive analysis.

18.3 MODEL CONTRACT

A model must define:

- Model identity.
- Version.
- Owner.
- Intended use.
- Prohibited uses.
- Training-data governance.
- Input schema.
- Output schema.
- Validation evidence.
- Calibration where relevant.
- Known limitations.
- Monitoring.
- Drift criteria.
- Rollback strategy.
- Human-review requirements.

18.4 MODEL OUTPUT

Outputs must distinguish:

- Prediction.
- Confidence or uncertainty.
- Supporting features where permitted.
- Known limitations.
- Suggested action.
- Required review.

18.5 MODEL VS. DECISION

A model output is not automatically an authorized enforcement decision.

18.6 EXPLAINABILITY

Provide appropriate decision explanations to authorized reviewers.

18.7 HUMAN REVIEW

Require human review for decisions where policy, law, impact,
or uncertainty demands it.

18.8 TRAINING DATA

Training data must be lawfully obtained, purpose-appropriate,
governed, and protected.

18.9 FEEDBACK LOOPS

Do not use unreviewed enforcement outcomes as unquestioned ground
truth for subsequent training.

18.10 BIAS AND FAIRNESS

Evaluate relevant disparate impact, error distribution, and
potentially harmful proxy variables.

18.11 MODEL DRIFT

Monitor changes in model performance and underlying threat patterns.

18.12 PROVIDER NEUTRALITY

The architecture must not depend on one model provider.

18.13 PROMPT INJECTION

Retrieved evidence and user-submitted material must be treated
according to canonical AI security controls.

18.14 MODEL FAILURE

Fallback behavior must preserve required safety controls.

# 19. DECISION GOVERNANCE AND ENFORCEMENT

19.1 PURPOSE

- Case or assessment reference.

- Decision authority.

- Findings.
- Confidence and limitations where relevant.
- Scope.
- Effective time.
- Expiration or review time.
- Required notifications.
- Appeal eligibility.

- Decision status.

19.3 DECISION STATES

Potential states include:

- Proposed.
- Awaiting review.
- Approved.
- Rejected.
- Issued.
- Execution pending.
- Executed.
- Partially executed.
- Failed.
- Unknown outcome.
- Superseded.
- Revoked.
- Expired.

19.4 ENFORCEMENT CONTRACT

An enforcement request should specify:

- Request identifier.
- Decision reference.
- Target canonical authority.
- Requested action.
- Scope.
- Preconditions.
- Idempotency key where required.
- Effective period.
- Correlation identifier.
- Required confirmation.
- Failure behavior.

19.5 ENFORCEMENT EXECUTION

19.6 EXECUTION CONFIRMATION

19.7 PARTIAL EXECUTION

19.8 UNKNOWN OUTCOME

19.9 ACTION DURATION

19.10 NO PERMANENT ACTION BY DEFAULT

authority and legal or policy basis.

19.11 RESTORATION

When a restriction is reversed, restoration must be requested
through the canonical domain.

19.12 CUSTOMER OR PARTICIPANT NOTIFICATION

# 20. REVIEW, APPEALS, AND CORRECTION
# =============================================================================

20.1 PURPOSE

Provide governed mechanisms to challenge or correct material
risk assessments and enforcement decisions.

20.2 REVIEW TYPES

Potential review types include:

- Factual correction.
- Evidence reconsideration.
- Decision review.
- Enforcement-scope review.
- Account recovery.
- Participant appeal.
- Customer appeal.
- Specialist review.
- Independent review where required.

20.3 APPEAL RECORD

An appeal should identify:

- Appeal identifier.
- Original decision.
- Requester reference.
- Grounds.
- Submitted evidence.
- Applicable deadline.
- Assigned reviewer.
- Conflict-of-interest controls.
- Review status.
- Outcome.
- Rationale.
- Required corrective actions.

20.4 REVIEW INDEPENDENCE

Where required, the reviewer must not be the sole person responsible
for the original adverse decision.

20.5 CUSTOMER OR PARTICIPANT NOTICE

Provide the information required by applicable policy and law
without revealing protected detection methods or sensitive
third-party information.

20.6 CORRECTION

Verified errors must be corrected through the appropriate canonical
authority.

20.7 APPEAL OUTCOMES

Potential outcomes include:

- Decision upheld.
- Decision modified.
- Decision reversed.
- More evidence required.
- Matter remanded for reassessment.
- Appeal rejected under an applicable procedural rule.

20.8 RESTORATION

Reversal must trigger required restoration and reconciliation.

20.9 HISTORY

The original decision and its review history must remain traceable
where required.

20.10 ABUSE OF APPEAL PROCESS

Any restriction on repeated appeals must be governed, proportionate,
and consistent with applicable law.

# =============================================================================
# 21. CONTINUOUS MONITORING AND RISK REASSESSMENT
# =============================================================================

21.1 PURPOSE

Keep risk assessments and controls appropriate as evidence,
behavior, policies, and operating conditions change.

21.2 REASSESSMENT TRIGGERS

Potential triggers include:

- New material evidence.
- Revoked verification.
- Expired evidence.
- Changed participant relationship.
- New security incident.
- Changed transaction pattern.
- Changed compliance status.
- Policy update.
- Model drift.
- Appeal outcome.
- New authoritative domain event.
- Expiration of a temporary control.

21.3 REASSESSMENT CONTRACT

A reassessment should identify:

- Previous assessment.
- Trigger.
- New evidence.
- Policy version.
- Assessment method.
- Changed findings.
- Result.
- Required action.
- Review deadline.

21.4 FRESHNESS

Risk assessments must have explicit freshness requirements.

21.5 STALE RISK STATE

A stale assessment must not silently remain valid beyond its
authorized scope or validity period.

21.6 MONITORING FREQUENCY

Monitoring frequency must be determined by the applicable policy,
risk, operational cost, and legal constraints.

21.7 CHANGE PROPAGATION

Material reassessment outcomes must be routed to the appropriate
decision authority.

21.8 AUTOMATED REVERSAL

Automatic removal of a control is permitted only where explicitly
authorized and safe.

21.9 FALSE-POSITIVE LEARNING

Corrections and appeal outcomes may inform model improvement
through a governed process.

21.10 AUDIT

Reassessment history must remain traceable.

# =============================================================================
# 22. PRIVACY, DATA GOVERNANCE, AND RETENTION
# =============================================================================

22.1 PURPOSE LIMITATION

Risk data must be used only for authorized trust, safety,
security, compliance, or other approved purposes.

22.2 DATA MINIMIZATION

Collect only information necessary for the relevant assessment.

22.3 DATA CLASSIFICATION

Apply canonical classification to signals, evidence, cases,
assessments, decisions, and model outputs.

22.4 ACCESS CONTROL

Restrict access by role, purpose, case, resource, jurisdiction,
and legal authority.

22.5 RETENTION

Define retention according to applicable law, policy, contracts,
evidence requirements, and operational need.

22.6 LEGAL HOLD

Legal holds must follow canonical legal and evidence-management
procedures.

22.7 DATA CORRECTION

Incorrect data must be correctable through authorized processes.

22.8 DELETION

Deletion must respect lawful retention obligations and approved
data-governance rules.

22.9 CROSS-BORDER PROCESSING

Cross-border access and transfer must comply with applicable
legal and policy constraints.

22.10 THIRD-PARTY PROCESSORS

External processors must meet approved privacy, security,
retention, and contractual requirements.

22.11 DATA SHARING

Sharing with external parties must require an authorized purpose
and approved legal basis.

22.12 PRIVACY IMPACT

Material new monitoring or data-linkage capabilities must undergo
the required privacy assessment.

22.13 NO UNRESTRICTED SURVEILLANCE

The architecture must not enable unrestricted collection or
linkage of customer or participant information.

# =============================================================================
# 23. SECURITY OF THE TRUST-AND-SAFETY PLATFORM
# =============================================================================

23.1 PURPOSE

Protect the trust-and-safety capabilities themselves from
unauthorized access, manipulation, or compromise.

23.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential threats include:

- Investigator account compromise.
- Unauthorized case access.
- Evidence tampering.
- Privilege escalation.
- Unauthorized decision changes.
- Model manipulation.
- Policy tampering.
- Insider misuse.
- Unauthorized bulk export.
- Audit manipulation.
- Integration credential compromise.
- Enforcement command forgery.

23.3 ACCESS CONTROL

Apply least privilege, role separation, resource scoping, and
appropriate approval controls.

23.4 PRIVILEGED ACTIONS

High-impact actions must require the authorization and audit
specified by canonical policy.

23.5 SEPARATION OF DUTIES

Where required, separate signal review, evidence evaluation,
decision approval, and enforcement administration.

23.6 POLICY INTEGRITY

Policy modifications must follow approved governance, versioning,
and approval processes.

23.7 MODEL INTEGRITY

Model changes must follow approved model-release and validation
procedures.

23.8 EVIDENCE INTEGRITY

Use canonical evidence-integrity and audit controls.

23.9 SECRET MANAGEMENT

Integration credentials must use canonical secret-management
capabilities.

23.10 SECURITY MONITORING

Monitor unauthorized access, bulk retrieval, unusual administrative
actions, and suspicious configuration changes.

23.11 INCIDENT RESPONSE

Integrate platform incidents with canonical security incident
management.

23.12 RECOVERY

Recovery must preserve evidence integrity and decision history.

# =============================================================================

Reuse canonical UCOS event infrastructure, schemas, and governance.

ASSESSMENT EVENTS

CASE EVENTS

DECISION EVENTS

ENFORCEMENT EVENTS

- Event identity.

- Recording time.

- Causation reference.
- Data classification.
- Provenance.
- Policy version.

24.4 EVENT MINIMIZATION

Events must not contain unnecessary sensitive evidence or personal
data.

24.5 IDEMPOTENCY

Consumers must use canonical event identity and idempotency rules.

24.6 ORDERING

Out-of-order events must not silently overwrite newer authoritative
state.

24.7 REPLAY

Replay must not repeat adverse actions or other consequential
operations.

24.8 EVENT FAILURE

Failed processing must be observable, recoverable, and auditable.

# =============================================================================
# 25. API AND INTEGRATION CONTRACTS
# =============================================================================

25.1 API PRINCIPLES

Interfaces must be:

- Explicitly versioned.
- Authenticated.
- Authorized.
- Auditable where required.
- Idempotent where appropriate.
- Observable.
- Documented.
- Backward-compatible where required.
- Vendor-neutral.
- Governed by canonical UCOS API standards.

25.2 LOGICAL API GROUPS

A. SIGNAL INTAKE
   Accept authorized signal references and validate their contracts.

B. RISK ASSESSMENT
   Request or retrieve governed assessments.

C. CASE MANAGEMENT
   Create, assign, update, and retrieve authorized investigation cases.

D. EVIDENCE
   Reference evidence and retrieve permitted evidence metadata.

E. DECISION MANAGEMENT
   Propose, approve, issue, or retrieve authorized decisions.

F. ENFORCEMENT COORDINATION
   Request and track actions through canonical domain interfaces.

G. REVIEW AND APPEAL
   Submit and retrieve authorized review workflows.

H. REASSESSMENT
   Request and retrieve risk reassessments.

I. RECONCILIATION
   Detect and resolve discrepancies between decisions and domain state.

J. REPORTING
   Retrieve authorized aggregate risk and operational metrics.

These are logical API groups, not finalized endpoint definitions.

25.3 COMMAND VS. QUERY

Commands request state changes.

Queries retrieve authorized representations.

25.4 AUTHORIZATION

Every command must be validated by the target authority.

25.5 IDEMPOTENCY

Potentially duplicative commands must follow canonical idempotency
contracts.

25.6 ERROR MODEL

Errors must distinguish:

- Invalid input.
- Unauthorized request.
- Forbidden scope.
- Missing evidence.
- Policy rejection.
- Conflict.
- Stale version.
- External dependency failure.
- Timeout.
- Unknown outcome.
- Partial execution.
- Internal processing failure.

25.7 OUTCOME RECONCILIATION

A timeout must trigger authoritative status reconciliation before
a potentially duplicative retry.

25.8 VERSIONING

Breaking changes must follow canonical API governance.

25.9 EXTERNAL INTEGRATIONS

External services must be integrated through approved adapters or
canonical integration capabilities.

# =============================================================================
# 26. DATA MODEL AND RELATIONSHIP INTEGRITY
# =============================================================================

26.1 MODELING PRINCIPLE

The following are logical concepts requiring reconciliation with
the canonical UCOS data model.

They are not authorization to create duplicate tables, registries,
or entities.

26.2 LOGICAL CONCEPTS

- Threat Taxonomy Reference.
- Risk Signal.
- Risk Assessment.
- Assessment Evidence Reference.
- Detection Result.
- Investigation Case.
- Investigation Task.
- Evidence Reference.
- Investigation Finding.
- Decision Record.
- Enforcement Request.
- Enforcement Outcome.
- Restriction Reference.
- Appeal Record.
- Reassessment Record.
- Risk Control Reference.
- Reconciliation Exception.
- Model Evaluation Record.
- Policy Version Reference.
- Audit Reference.

26.3 IDENTIFIERS

All identifiers must follow canonical UCOS identifier governance.

26.4 RELATIONSHIP INTEGRITY

Every participant, customer, transaction, and case reference
must resolve to its canonical authority.

26.5 TEMPORAL INTEGRITY

Assessments, decisions, controls, and appeals must preserve
effective-time and historical semantics.

26.6 VERSIONING

Material state transitions and changes must be traceable.

26.7 PROJECTIONS

Operational dashboards and search indexes must remain derived
representations rather than independent authorities.

26.8 DUPLICATE DETECTION

Duplicate cases or signals must be handled through governed
deduplication rules.

26.9 HISTORICAL PRESERVATION

Required evidence, decisions, appeals, and corrections must retain
their authorized lineage.

26.10 SCHEMA EVOLUTION

All schema changes must follow canonical UCOS schema governance.

# =============================================================================
# 27. OBSERVABILITY AND OPERATIONAL CONTROL
# =============================================================================

27.1 PURPOSE

Provide visibility into threat detection, investigations,
enforcement, appeals, and residual risk.

27.2 OPERATIONAL METRICS

Potential measures include:

- Signal volume.
- Signal validation failure rate.
- Detection latency.
- Assessment latency.
- Case queue depth.
- Case resolution time.
- Evidence collection delay.
- False-positive rate.
- False-negative estimates.
- Appeal rate.
- Appeal reversal rate.
- Enforcement success rate.
- Enforcement reconciliation backlog.
- Control expiration backlog.
- Model drift.
- Policy evaluation failure.
- Customer-impact incidents.
- Participant-impact incidents.
- Repeat incident rate.
- Residual risk indicators.
- Privacy and access-control violations.

27.3 METRIC DEFINITIONS

Every metric must define its population, calculation, source,
time window, exclusions, freshness, owner, and limitations.

27.4 QUALITY GUARDRAILS

Detection throughput must not be optimized at the expense of
unacceptable false positives, procedural fairness, or privacy.

27.5 CORRELATION

Material workflows must carry canonical correlation identifiers.

27.6 LOGGING

Logs must not expose unnecessary sensitive data or protected
investigation details.

27.7 ALERTING

Alerts must include severity, affected authority, responsible
owner, and expected response.

27.8 CONTROL TOWER

The control tower must use governed data and must not become
an independent decision authority.

27.9 SERVICE LEVELS

Processing and response targets must be established through
approved business and operational requirements.

27.10 MONITORING FAILURE

Monitoring failure must not silently disable required security
or enforcement controls.

# =============================================================================
# 28. RECONCILIATION AND EXCEPTION MANAGEMENT
# =============================================================================

28.1 PURPOSE

Ensure that assessments, decisions, requested actions, and actual
canonical domain states remain consistent.

28.2 RECONCILIATION SCENARIOS

- An enforcement request is accepted but the target domain state
  remains unchanged.
- A restriction expires but remains active.
- A restriction is revoked but a downstream capability remains blocked.
- A risk decision is reversed but restoration is incomplete.
- A case is closed while required evidence remains unresolved.
- A payment-risk review is presented as a final payment decision.
- A listing restriction is applied without the expected decision record.
- A case contains duplicate or conflicting evidence references.
- An assessment uses a retired policy version.
- A model output is treated as an authorized decision.
- An appeal is upheld but affected systems are not corrected.
- A revoked verification result remains treated as valid.
- A duplicate event produces repeated enforcement.
- A control expires without reassessment.
- A portal projection contradicts the canonical enforcement state.
- A cross-domain operation times out with an unknown outcome.

28.3 EXCEPTION RECORD

An exception should identify:

- Exception identifier.
- Affected subject.
- Assessment or decision reference.
- Expected state.
- Observed state.
- Canonical authority.
- Severity.
- Detection time.
- Responsible owner.
- Remediation.
- Evidence.
- Resolution time.

28.4 SOURCE AUTHORITY

The designated canonical domain must resolve its authoritative state.

28.5 NO SILENT REPAIR

Material discrepancies must not be hidden by modifying only a
projection or local cache.

28.6 AUTOMATED RECONCILIATION

Automated correction is permitted only when explicitly governed,
safe, idempotent, and auditable.

28.7 HIGH-IMPACT EXCEPTIONS

High-impact unresolved exceptions must be escalated through
the approved governance and incident processes.

# =============================================================================
# 29. FAILURE SCENARIO CATALOG
# =============================================================================

FS-001 — MALFORMED SIGNAL

Expected control:
Reject or quarantine the signal and preserve appropriate provenance.

FS-002 — UNTRUSTED SOURCE

Expected control:
Apply source-validation policy and avoid treating the input as
authoritative evidence.

FS-003 — DUPLICATE SIGNAL

Expected control:
Deduplicate appropriately without losing material event history.

FS-004 — SIGNAL WITH STALE CONTEXT

Expected control:
Revalidate the relevant canonical state.

FS-005 — MODEL UNAVAILABLE

Expected control:
Use the approved fallback and preserve required safety controls.

FS-006 — MODEL DRIFT

Expected control:
Trigger evaluation, containment, rollback, or review according
to the approved model policy.

FS-007 — LOW-CONFIDENCE DETECTION

Expected control:
Apply proportionate review or verification rather than automatic
unsupported adverse action.

FS-008 — CONFLICTING EVIDENCE

Expected control:
Record the conflict and route it for authorized evaluation.

FS-009 — CASE ASSIGNMENT CONFLICT

Expected control:
Enforce assignment and separation-of-duties policy.

FS-010 — EVIDENCE INTEGRITY FAILURE

Expected control:
Quarantine affected evidence and initiate the appropriate review.

FS-011 — UNAUTHORIZED DECISION

Expected control:
Reject the action, preserve the audit record, and apply relevant
security monitoring.

FS-012 — POLICY CONFLICT

Expected control:
Escalate through canonical governance.

FS-013 — DUPLICATE ENFORCEMENT REQUEST

Expected control:
Use idempotency and reconcile the existing outcome.

FS-014 — ENFORCEMENT TIMEOUT

Expected control:
Mark the outcome unknown until authoritative reconciliation.

FS-015 — PARTIAL ENFORCEMENT

Expected control:
Track each affected domain and coordinate approved recovery.

FS-016 — APPEAL UPHELD

Expected control:
Trigger required correction and restoration through canonical
authorities.

FS-017 — EXPIRED RESTRICTION

Expected control:
Apply governed expiration and reassessment semantics.

FS-018 — FALSE POSITIVE

Expected control:
Provide an authorized correction and review process.

FS-019 — ACCOUNT COMPROMISE

Expected control:
Route protective actions through canonical identity and security
capabilities.

FS-020 — PAYMENT OUTCOME UNKNOWN

Expected control:
Reconcile with payment and order authorities.

FS-021 — COUNTERFEIT CLAIM UNVERIFIED

Expected control:
Preserve uncertainty and follow the approved review process.

FS-022 — SHARED DEVICE MISINTERPRETED

Expected control:
Avoid automatic adverse action based solely on shared-device evidence.

FS-023 — COORDINATED ABUSE HYPOTHESIS

Expected control:
Require evidence and authorized assessment before adverse action.

FS-024 — DATA ACCESS VIOLATION

Expected control:
Block access and initiate the appropriate security incident process.

FS-025 — PRIVACY RETENTION CONFLICT

Expected control:
Apply canonical retention and legal-hold rules.

FS-026 — MODEL EXPLANATION UNAVAILABLE

Expected control:
Follow the approved decision-review requirements; do not invent
an explanation.

FS-027 — CASE CLOSURE WITH OPEN TASKS

Expected control:
Prevent closure or record an explicitly authorized exception.

FS-028 — REASSESSMENT FAILURE

Expected control:
Track stale state, alert the responsible owner, and apply the
approved fallback policy.

FS-029 — AUDIT PIPELINE FAILURE

Expected control:
Follow the approved safe-processing behavior for material decisions.

FS-030 — CONTROL TOWER STALE DATA

Expected control:
Display freshness status and prevent stale projections from
authorizing decisions.

FS-031 — APPEAL DEADLINE MISSED BY SYSTEM

Expected control:
Escalate the processing failure and apply applicable procedural
protections.

FS-032 — EXTERNAL INTELLIGENCE REVOKED

Expected control:
Reassess decisions that materially depend on the affected source.

FS-033 — REPEATED ACCOUNT CREATION AFTER RESTRICTION

Expected control:
Use canonical identity resolution and approved review policy.

FS-034 — CROSS-DOMAIN POLICY VERSION MISMATCH

Expected control:
Detect the mismatch and follow the approved version-transition process.

FS-035 — RESTORATION FAILURE

Expected control:
Maintain explicit unresolved status and reconcile every affected
canonical authority.

# =============================================================================
# 30. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
# =============================================================================

AC-001
Every material trust-and-safety fact has a designated canonical owner.

AC-002
Existing UCOS risk, security, identity, compliance, and evidence
capabilities are reconciled before new components are proposed.

AC-003
Signals retain source provenance and freshness information.

AC-004
Signals are distinguished from verified evidence.

AC-005
Risk assessments identify their policies, methods, versions,
and material limitations.

AC-006
Risk scores cannot independently override canonical policy.

AC-007
Missing data is not automatically treated as proof of misconduct.

AC-008
Detection quality includes false-positive and customer-impact measures.

AC-009
High-impact decisions follow required approval and review controls.

AC-010
Every material decision has traceable authority and rationale.

AC-011
Enforcement requests are executed by the responsible canonical domain.

AC-012
Unknown enforcement outcomes trigger reconciliation.

AC-013
Duplicate requests do not produce duplicate adverse actions.

AC-014
Restrictions have explicit scope and effective-time semantics.

AC-015
Temporary controls have review or expiration requirements.

AC-016
Case evidence preserves required provenance and integrity.

AC-017
Conflicting evidence remains explicitly represented.

AC-018
Case access follows least privilege and separation-of-duties rules.

AC-019
Appeals and corrections are governed and traceable.

AC-020
Successful appeals trigger required correction and restoration.

AC-021
Identity-risk actions use canonical identity and security capabilities.

AC-022
Payment-risk actions preserve payment and financial authority.

AC-023
Catalog-risk actions preserve product and listing authority.

AC-024
Participant enforcement preserves unrelated open obligations.

AC-025
Graph relationships alone do not establish guilt by association.

AC-026
AI and model outputs are not treated as authorized decisions.

AC-027
Model versions, validation, drift, and limitations are governed.

AC-028
Sensitive information is protected by purpose and access controls.

AC-029
Retention and legal holds follow canonical governance.

AC-030
Risk events follow canonical event and idempotency contracts.

AC-031
Reconciliation detects divergence between decisions and domain state.

AC-032
Metrics have explicit definitions, owners, sources, and limitations.

AC-033
Operational failures are observable and recoverable.

AC-034
External intelligence retains provenance and permitted-use controls.

AC-035
The architecture does not introduce a duplicate identity,
financial, compliance, or transaction authority.

AC-036
Every approved requirement maps to implementation or reuse,
verification, and evidence.

AC-037
Certification claims are supported by reproducible evidence.

AC-038
Implementation is not initiated without explicit authorization.

These criteria are proposed. Their implementation and successful
verification have not been established by this document.

# 34. READINESS GATES
# =============================================================================

GATE G0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Review existing UCOS identity, security, authorization, fraud,
risk, compliance, payment, financial, catalog, participant,
evidence, case-management, audit, and governance artifacts.

EXIT:
Relevant canonical authorities and contracts are identified.

GATE G1 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

Classify every proposed capability as reusable, extensible,
duplicated, conflicting, missing, or unnecessary.

EXIT:
No unresolved authority duplication remains.

GATE G2 — THREAT AND SIGNAL MODEL

Reconcile taxonomy, signal semantics, evidence provenance,
and detection contracts.

EXIT:
Threat classifications and signal contracts are governed.

GATE G3 — RISK AND POLICY GOVERNANCE

Define assessment semantics, decision authority, policy precedence,
and permitted response actions.

EXIT:
Material risk decisions are traceable and appropriately authorized.

GATE G4 — INVESTIGATION AND EVIDENCE

Validate case lifecycle, evidence integrity, access control,
retention, and separation of duties.

EXIT:
Required investigation and evidence controls are approved.

GATE G5 — ENFORCEMENT AND RECOVERY

Validate canonical action interfaces, idempotency, unknown outcomes,
reversal, appeal, and reconciliation.

EXIT:
Material adverse actions have safe execution and recovery paths.

GATE G6 — PRIVACY AND SECURITY

Validate purpose limitation, least privilege, sensitive-data handling,
model governance, and platform security.

EXIT:
Required privacy and security approvals exist.

GATE G7 — OPERATIONAL READINESS

Validate metrics, alerting, failure handling, staffing, escalation,
and operational ownership.

EXIT:
Required operational controls are documented and tested.

GATE G8 — VERIFICATION

Execute approved tests and preserve reproducible evidence.

EXIT:
Required verification evidence exists.

GATE G9 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

Obtain required governance approvals and explicit implementation
authorization.

EXIT:
Only the approved scope may proceed to implementation.

# =============================================================================
# 35. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
# =============================================================================

1. Do not create a competing identity authority.
2. Do not create a second authentication or authorization system.
3. Do not create a duplicate payment, order, or financial authority.
4. Do not create a parallel compliance authority.
5. Do not create a shadow evidence repository when canonical
   evidence capabilities are available.
6. Do not treat a signal as verified evidence without appropriate
   validation.
7. Do not treat a model score as proof of misconduct.
8. Do not use an uncalibrated score as a probability.
9. Do not apply permanent adverse actions without the required
   authority and review.
10. Do not let a generalized risk score override canonical domain
    policy without explicit authorization.
11. Do not bypass separation-of-duties requirements.
12. Do not execute an enforcement action outside its authorized scope.
13. Do not retry an unknown consequential operation without
    appropriate reconciliation.
14. Do not assume a requested enforcement action succeeded.
15. Do not leave restrictions without required expiration or review
    semantics.
16. Do not treat missing data as proof of wrongdoing.
17. Do not infer collusion solely from shared devices, networks,
    addresses, or relationships.
18. Do not penalize unrelated participants merely because they are
    connected to a flagged participant.
19. Do not use sensitive personal information without an authorized
    purpose and applicable lawful basis.
20. Do not enable unrestricted surveillance or uncontrolled data linkage.
21. Do not expose protected investigation data to unauthorized users.
22. Do not allow investigators to bypass required audit controls.
23. Do not let AI or model outputs directly mutate canonical state
    without an authorized decision process.
24. Do not train models on unreviewed enforcement outcomes as
    unquestioned ground truth.
25. Do not conceal conflicting evidence.
26. Do not silently discard contradictory evidence.
27. Do not ignore appeal outcomes or verified corrections.
28. Do not restore capabilities by changing only a local projection.
29. Do not claim that a restriction is complete before authoritative
    confirmation.
30. Do not claim that a case is resolved while required work remains.
31. Do not claim that a detection system is effective without
    appropriate validation.
32. Do not claim that proposed APIs or events are already canonical.
33. Do not claim tests have passed without execution evidence.
34. Do not claim certification without reproducible evidence.
35. Do not claim a capability is missing before context assimilation.
36. Do not introduce vendor-specific coupling without approved
    architectural justification.
37. Do not modify the UCOS repository without explicit authorization.

# =============================================================================
# 37. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES
# =============================================================================

RULE 001 — CANONICAL AUTHORITY
Every material fact and state transition has a designated canonical
owner.

RULE 002 — KNOWLEDGE ONCE
Risk knowledge and evidence are reused through governed references.

RULE 003 — REUSE FIRST
Existing UCOS capabilities are evaluated before new capabilities
are introduced.

RULE 004 — SIGNALS ARE NOT FINDINGS
A signal initiates evaluation; it does not independently prove
misconduct.

RULE 005 — EVIDENCE IS PROVENANCE-BOUND
Evidence retains its source, integrity, context, and permitted use.

RULE 006 — RISK IS CONTEXTUAL
Risk assessments must identify their subject, activity, scope,
policy, and uncertainty.

RULE 007 — SCORES HAVE EXPLICIT SEMANTICS
A score is meaningful only within its documented and validated use.

RULE 008 — POLICIES GOVERN RESPONSES
Material actions must follow authorized response policies.

RULE 009 — PROPORTIONALITY IS REQUIRED
Use an appropriate action that addresses the established risk
without unnecessary restriction.

RULE 010 — DECISION AUTHORITY IS EXPLICIT
Every adverse decision identifies the authority permitted to make it.

RULE 011 — DOMAIN OWNERSHIP IS PRESERVED
Enforcement is executed through the affected canonical domain.

RULE 012 — UNKNOWN IS NOT SUCCESS
Unresolved outcomes remain explicitly unknown until reconciled.

RULE 013 — RETRIES MUST BE SAFE
Consequential commands must respect idempotency and authoritative
state reconciliation.

RULE 014 — RESTRICTIONS HAVE SCOPE
Every restriction identifies its affected activity and duration
or review conditions.

RULE 015 — HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY IS PRESERVED
High-impact decisions follow applicable human-review and
approval requirements.

RULE 016 — APPEALS ARE GOVERNED
Material decisions must support required review and correction.

RULE 017 — FALSE POSITIVES MATTER
Detection performance must account for erroneous adverse outcomes.

RULE 018 — RELATIONSHIPS DO NOT PROVE GUILT
Shared attributes and graph connections require contextual evaluation.

RULE 019 — AI IS NOT AN AUTHORITY
AI output must not bypass approved decision and enforcement processes.

RULE 020 — PRIVACY IS PURPOSE-BOUND
Risk data must be processed only for authorized purposes.

RULE 021 — RETENTION IS GOVERNED
Evidence and case data follow canonical retention and legal-hold rules.

RULE 022 — AUDIT IS REQUIRED
Material decisions and enforcement actions must be traceable.

RULE 023 — REASSESSMENT IS CONTROLLED
Changed evidence, policy, or circumstances trigger governed review.

RULE 024 — RESTORATION IS AUTHORITATIVE
Reversed restrictions must be removed through canonical domain
operations.

RULE 025 — OBSERVABILITY IS REQUIRED
Detection, investigation, enforcement, and appeals must be measurable.

RULE 026 — NO SHADOW LEDGER
Trust and safety must not create duplicate financial or transaction
records.

RULE 027 — NO SILENT POLICY CONFLICT
Conflicting policies are resolved through canonical governance.

RULE 028 — EXCEPTIONS ARE EXPLICIT
Unresolved discrepancies must have an owner and resolution path.

RULE 029 — CERTIFICATION REQUIRES EVIDENCE
Specification completeness does not prove operational effectiveness.

RULE 030 — IMPLEMENTATION REQUIRES AUTHORIZATION
This document alone does not authorize repository or production
changes.
