# =============================================================================
# 38. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
# =============================================================================

1. Do not create a second product master.
2. Do not create a competing product taxonomy.
3. Do not redefine canonical product attributes within search.
4. Do not invent product, variant, seller, or store identifiers.
5. Do not treat a search index as canonical business truth.
6. Do not create duplicate discovery engines without a documented
   reuse analysis.
7. Do not bypass canonical publication or eligibility rules.
8. Do not allow ranking or personalization to override mandatory
   constraints.
9. Do not disguise sponsored placements as organic relevance where
   disclosure is required.
10. Do not treat semantic similarity as proof of compatibility.
11. Do not present approximate availability as confirmed availability.
12. Do not treat indexed inventory as a reservation or guarantee.
13. Do not calculate authoritative prices outside the pricing authority.
14. Do not determine final offer redemption eligibility outside
    the canonical offer authority.
15. Do not expose restricted resources through autocomplete, facets,
    cached results, or alternate retrieval paths.
16. Do not leak cross-tenant or cross-user information through
    search, logs, caches, suggestions, or analytics.
17. Do not silently rewrite explicit user constraints.
18. Do not silently reinterpret exact identifiers as approximate terms.
19. Do not claim complete results when a material retrieval path failed.
20. Do not present estimated counts as exact counts.
21. Do not expose sensitive ranking features or personal data
    unnecessarily.
22. Do not create ungoverned synonyms or taxonomy relationships.
23. Do not hardcode industry-specific concepts into the universal core.
24. Do not hardcode a single language, currency, unit system,
    geographic model, or time zone.
25. Do not bind domain contracts to a specific search vendor.
26. Do not introduce unbounded semantic queries or aggregations.
27. Do not retry failed indexing indefinitely without controls.
28. Do not allow out-of-order updates to regress canonical projections.
29. Do not conceal index freshness or reconciliation failures.
30. Do not let search analytics become an unauthorized behavioral
    surveillance system.
31. Do not optimize ranking solely for clicks or conversion.
32. Do not use unreviewed interaction signals as unquestioned
    evidence of relevance.
33. Do not launch ranking experiments without approved guardrails.
34. Do not claim search quality without representative evaluation.
35. Do not claim accessibility compliance without appropriate testing.
36. Do not claim performance or scalability without measured evidence.
37. Do not mark proposed APIs, events, or registries as canonical
    before reconciliation.
38. Do not claim tests have passed without execution evidence.
39. Do not claim certification without reproducible evidence.
40. Do not modify the UCOS repository without explicit authorization.

# =============================================================================
# 39. MASTER TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS
# =============================================================================

39.1 TRACEABILITY CHAIN

Every approved discovery requirement must trace through:

CANONICAL SOURCE
    ->
BUSINESS REQUIREMENT
    ->
ARCHITECTURAL CAPABILITY
    ->
CANONICAL ARTIFACT OR APPROVED EXTENSION
    ->
API / EVENT / DATA CONTRACT
    ->
IMPLEMENTATION OR REUSE DECISION
    ->
TEST CASE
    ->
VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
    ->
GOVERNANCE APPROVAL
    ->
RELEASE AUTHORIZATION

39.2 REQUIREMENT IDENTIFIERS

Requirement identifiers must be allocated through canonical
UCOS identifier governance.

39.3 TRACEABILITY COMPLETENESS

No approved requirement may be considered complete when its
authoritative source, implementation or reuse decision, or
verification evidence is unknown.

39.4 BIDIRECTIONAL TRACEABILITY

Material implementation artifacts must trace back to an approved
requirement or an explicitly approved operational necessity.

39.5 CHANGE IMPACT

Changes to a canonical attribute, taxonomy, policy, resource
schema, or ranking contract must identify affected discovery
projections and tests.

39.6 ORPHAN PREVENTION

Unreferenced discovery artifacts must be detected through
canonical registry and dependency-governance mechanisms.

39.7 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Traceability must reference canonical facts instead of copying
their authoritative definitions into multiple documents.

# =============================================================================
# 40. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES
# =============================================================================

RULE 001 — CANONICAL SOURCE
Every business fact retains its canonical owner.

RULE 002 — KNOWLEDGE ONCE
Canonical knowledge is authored once and reused.

RULE 003 — REUSE FIRST
Existing discovery and search capabilities must be evaluated
before new capabilities are proposed.

RULE 004 — DERIVED INDEX
A search index is a retrieval projection, not the business
source of truth.

RULE 005 — EXPLICIT RESOURCE IDENTITY
Discoverable resources reference canonical identities.

RULE 006 — PRESERVE QUERY MEANING
Normalization must not silently alter material user intent.

RULE 007 — HARD CONSTRAINTS FIRST
Mandatory constraints are enforced before ranking.

RULE 008 — SEMANTIC MATCHING IS NOT AUTHORITY
Semantic similarity cannot override canonical facts or policies.

RULE 009 — ELIGIBILITY IS GOVERNED
Resource eligibility follows the appropriate canonical authority.

RULE 010 — RANKING IS VERSIONED
Ranking behavior has explicit policy, ownership, and evaluation.

RULE 011 — PERSONALIZATION IS CONTROLLED
Personalization respects consent, privacy, and explicit preferences.

RULE 012 — COMMERCIAL INFLUENCE IS TRANSPARENT
Sponsored placements follow approved disclosure requirements.

RULE 013 — EXACTNESS IS EXPLICIT
Exact matches, approximate matches, estimates, and unknowns
remain distinguishable.

RULE 014 — AVAILABILITY IS NOT GUARANTEED BY SEARCH
Authoritative confirmation comes from the appropriate domain.

RULE 015 — INDEX FRESHNESS IS MEASURED
Each material data class has explicit freshness requirements.

RULE 016 — SOURCE AUTHORITY WINS
Conflicts between canonical data and search projections are
resolved in favor of canonical authority.

RULE 017 — UPDATES ARE ORDER-SAFE
Out-of-order changes must not silently regress projections.

RULE 018 — DELETION PROPAGATES
Deleted, unpublished, or restricted resources follow explicit
invalidation semantics.

RULE 019 — PAGINATION IS CONTRACTUAL
Pagination, consistency, and continuation behavior are explicit.

RULE 020 — FACETS REUSE CANONICAL SCHEMAS
Search does not create duplicate attribute semantics.

RULE 021 — MULTILINGUAL SEMANTICS ARE GOVERNED
Language and locale handling preserve material meaning.

RULE 022 — PRIVACY IS PURPOSE-BOUND
Query, location, and personalization data are used only for
authorized purposes.

RULE 023 — SECURITY IS END-TO-END
Search, suggestions, facets, caches, logs, and analytics enforce
appropriate access boundaries.

RULE 024 — RESOURCE USAGE IS BOUNDED
Queries and retrieval operations have explicit resource budgets.

RULE 025 — PARTIAL RESULTS ARE TRANSPARENT
Material retrieval and eligibility failures are not concealed.

RULE 026 — QUALITY IS MEASURED
Discovery quality is evaluated using governed methods and
representative datasets.

RULE 027 — METRICS HAVE DEFINED SEMANTICS
Every metric has a documented source, population, and calculation.

RULE 028 — CHANGES ARE REVERSIBLE WHERE REQUIRED
Ranking, retrieval, and indexing changes have approved recovery
or rollback paths.

RULE 029 — PROJECTIONS ARE RECONCILABLE
Source-to-index discrepancies are detectable and resolvable.

RULE 030 — CERTIFICATION REQUIRES EVIDENCE
Specification completeness does not establish implementation
correctness or production readiness.

RULE 031 — VENDOR NEUTRALITY
Canonical contracts do not depend on one search or AI provider.

RULE 032 — ACCESSIBILITY IS PART OF DISCOVERY
Discovery interactions must meet applicable accessibility
requirements.

RULE 033 — NO FALSE COMPLETENESS
A partial or degraded response must not be represented as
exhaustive when it is not.

RULE 034 — NO SHADOW AUTHORITY
Discovery must not become the owner of the business facts it indexes.

RULE 035 — IMPLEMENTATION REQUIRES AUTHORIZATION
This specification alone does not authorize repository or
production changes.

# 0. PURPOSE, SCOPE, AND ARCHITECTURAL AUTHORITY
# =============================================================================

0.1 PURPOSE

Define a universal, reusable, extensible, auditable, and governed
pricing architecture for the Universal Marketplace.

The architecture must support the construction, evaluation,
quotation, presentation, validation, and controlled application
of prices across heterogeneous commercial domains.

It must support physical products, digital products, services,
subscriptions, rentals, appointments, usage-based offerings,
bundles, configurable offerings, marketplace services, and future
resource types without requiring a separate pricing engine for
each industry or channel.

The architecture must distinguish price determination from:

- Product identity.
- Product configuration.
- Seller identity.
- Cost accounting.
- Tax determination.
- Offer eligibility.
- Discount authorization.
- Inventory availability.
- Order calculation.
- Payment execution.
- Seller settlement.
- Accounting recognition.
- Financial reporting.
- Regulatory compliance.

These capabilities must integrate through canonical contracts
rather than duplicate their authorities.

0.2 PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Provide a canonical pricing capability that can answer:

1. What is the applicable price for a resource?
2. Which pricing policy applies?
3. Which price components contribute to the result?
4. Which currency and precision rules apply?
5. Which customer, seller, channel, jurisdiction, or context
   constraints affect the price?
6. Which effective-time rules apply?
7. Which discounts or offers may be considered?
8. Which tax or fee authorities must be consulted?
9. Which cost and margin constraints apply?
10. Is the result indicative, estimated, quoted, committed,
    accepted, expired, or invalidated?
11. What evidence explains how the price was determined?
12. Which canonical authorities must validate the result before
    a downstream transaction may proceed?

0.3 IN-SCOPE CAPABILITIES

A. Canonical price representation.
B. Price books and price schedules.
C. Base-price definition.
D. Context-aware price resolution.
E. Price-component composition.
F. Price calculation and rounding.
G. Price quotation.
H. Price validity and expiration.
I. Currency-aware pricing.
J. Quantity-based pricing.
K. Tiered pricing.
L. Volume pricing.
M. Usage-based pricing integration.
N. Subscription pricing integration.
O. Rental and duration-based pricing.
P. Configurable product pricing.
Q. Bundle pricing.
R. Geographic and jurisdictional price context.
S. Channel and seller-specific price policies.
T. Cost and margin guardrails.
U. Dynamic-pricing governance.
V. Price experimentation governance.
W. Tax and fee integration.
X. Discount and promotion integration.
Y. Price history and lineage.
Z. Price-change governance.
AA. Price validation and reconciliation.
AB. Price transparency and explanations.
AC. Pricing security and abuse controls.
AD. Pricing analytics and observability.
AE. Pricing quality verification.

0.4 OUT OF SCOPE AS A REPLACEMENT AUTHORITY

This specification does not establish a second canonical authority
for any of the following:

- Product or variant identity.
- Product attributes.
- Seller or merchant identity.
- Inventory.
- Customer identity.
- Consent and preferences.
- Currency definitions.
- Exchange-rate authority.
- Tax law interpretation.
- Tax calculation where owned by a canonical tax capability.
- Offer or coupon eligibility.
- Promotion eligibility.
- Contractual entitlement.
- Payment authorization.
- Order acceptance.
- Refund authorization.
- Settlement.
- Accounting.
- Revenue recognition.
- Financial ledgers.
- Regulatory decisions.

0.5 PRICING AUTHORITY BOUNDARY

Pricing determines or resolves a price under approved pricing
policies using authoritative inputs and explicitly defined rules.

Other domains remain authoritative for facts and decisions
assigned to them.

0.6 PRICING DOES NOT EQUAL PAYMENT

A calculated or quoted price does not authorize payment.

0.7 PRICING DOES NOT EQUAL TAX

A pricing result may incorporate a tax result obtained from
the canonical tax authority, but pricing must not create a
competing tax-law interpretation engine.

0.8 PRICING DOES NOT EQUAL PROMOTION ELIGIBILITY

Pricing may incorporate an authorized discount or promotion
decision. It must not independently grant a benefit controlled
by the canonical offer or promotion authority.

0.9 PRICING DOES NOT EQUAL SETTLEMENT

A customer-facing price must not be treated as the seller's
settlement amount or as an accounting entry.

0.10 CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

All proposed concepts, identifiers, events, APIs, registries,
and component boundaries must be reconciled with existing UCOS
artifacts before implementation is authorized.

# =============================================================================
# 1. ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
# =============================================================================

1.1 SINGLE CANONICAL SOURCE OF TRUTH

Every authoritative business fact must have one designated
canonical owner.

1.2 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

A canonical pricing rule or commercial fact must be authored
once and reused through governed references.

1.3 REUSE FIRST

Existing pricing, monetary, tax, offer, cost, accounting,
currency, contract, and configuration capabilities must be
identified before new components are proposed.

1.4 PRICE AS A GOVERNED RESULT

A price is not merely a numeric field. It is a result produced
under defined policies, inputs, effective-time rules, currency
semantics, and authority constraints.

1.5 EXPLICIT PRICE SEMANTICS

Every price representation must state what the amount means.

Examples of distinctions that may be relevant include:

- Unit price.
- Extended line price.
- Pre-discount price.
- Post-discount price.
- Tax-exclusive price.
- Tax-inclusive price.
- Indicative price.
- Quoted price.
- Contractual price.
- Amount payable.
- Seller proceeds.
- Internal cost.
- Accounting value.

These meanings must never be silently conflated.

1.6 EXPLICIT AUTHORITY

Pricing policies must identify the authority that owns each
input, decision, calculation, and approval.

1.7 DETERMINISTIC CALCULATION

Given the same authoritative inputs, policy versions,
effective-time context, calculation rules, and rounding
semantics, a calculation must produce a reproducible result.

If nondeterministic or probabilistic methods are used to propose
a price, the resulting decision must be governed and converted
into an explicitly recorded pricing decision before use.

1.8 FINANCIAL PRECISION

Monetary values must use suitable decimal or exact monetary
representations.

Binary floating-point arithmetic must not be used as the
uncontrolled source of truth for financial amounts.

1.9 EXPLICIT ROUNDING

Rounding mode, precision, sequence, and application boundary
must be specified by the relevant monetary and jurisdictional
rules.

1.10 TEMPORAL CORRECTNESS

Pricing rules must distinguish when a rule is recorded from
when it is intended to apply.

1.11 NO HIDDEN MUTATION

A price must not change without an identifiable rule, source,
version, effective time, and authorization where required.

1.12 EXPLAINABILITY

Material price components and calculation steps must be
traceable to their source rules and authoritative inputs.

1.13 CHANNEL CONSISTENCY

Channel-specific differences must be explicit and governed.

1.14 POLICY SEPARATION

Base pricing, discounts, tax, fees, and final payable amount
must remain logically distinguishable even when presented
as one customer-facing amount.

1.15 EXTENSIBILITY

New pricing methods must be added through governed contracts
without rewriting unrelated pricing capabilities.

1.16 DOMAIN AGNOSTICISM

The core pricing engine must not be limited to one industry,
product category, seller model, or commercial channel.

1.17 TECHNOLOGY NEUTRALITY

No specific programming language, database, cloud, search
engine, pricing vendor, tax provider, or model provider is
mandated.

1.18 NO FALSE PRECISION

Estimated or incomplete prices must not be presented as final
or contractually guaranteed prices.

1.19 FINANCIAL TRACEABILITY

Material pricing decisions must retain sufficient lineage
to reproduce and explain the result, subject to lawful retention
and privacy constraints.

1.20 GOVERNED EVOLUTION

Pricing rules and calculation changes must follow canonical
UCOS change-management and governance procedures.

# =============================================================================
# 2. LOGICAL ARCHITECTURE
# =============================================================================

2.1 PROPOSED LOGICAL COMPONENTS

A. PRICING REQUEST GATEWAY

Responsibilities:
- Validate pricing requests.
- Authenticate and authorize callers.
- Apply request limits.
- Establish correlation identifiers.
- Enforce tenant and domain boundaries.

B. PRICE CONTEXT RESOLVER

Responsibilities:
- Resolve the relevant product or service reference.
- Resolve the applicable seller or commercial context.
- Identify requested quantity, duration, usage, and configuration.
- Resolve permitted channel and jurisdiction context.
- Identify required authoritative inputs.

C. PRICE BOOK AND POLICY RESOLVER

Responsibilities:
- Identify candidate price books.
- Resolve policy applicability.
- Evaluate priority and precedence.
- Apply effective-time rules.
- Detect ambiguous or conflicting policies.

D. BASE PRICE RESOLVER

Responsibilities:
- Resolve the applicable base price or rate.
- Preserve source references.
- Validate the price representation.
- Identify the governing version.

E. PRICE COMPOSITION ENGINE

Responsibilities:
- Combine authorized price components.
- Apply defined calculation order.
- Maintain intermediate calculation lineage.
- Enforce arithmetic and rounding rules.

F. PRICING METHOD ADAPTERS

Responsibilities:
- Support governed pricing methods.
- Isolate method-specific logic.
- Preserve common price contracts.

G. DISCOUNT AND OFFER ADAPTER

Responsibilities:
- Request authoritative promotion and discount eligibility.
- Consume approved benefit decisions.
- Prevent duplicate or unauthorized discounts.

H. TAX AND FEE ADAPTER

Responsibilities:
- Request applicable tax or fee determinations.
- Preserve source authority and calculation metadata.
- Avoid independently implementing canonical tax logic.

I. COST AND MARGIN GUARDRAIL ADAPTER

Responsibilities:
- Consume authorized cost and margin inputs.
- Apply approved minimum or maximum commercial constraints.
- Escalate violations requiring approval.

J. PRICE QUOTATION SERVICE

Responsibilities:
- Produce quote representations.
- Record relevant policy versions.
- Define validity and expiration.
- Support downstream quote validation.

K. PRICE HISTORY AND LINEAGE SERVICE

Responsibilities:
- Preserve governed price history.
- Record material policy and price changes.
- Link calculation results to authoritative inputs.

L. PRICING VALIDATION SERVICE

Responsibilities:
- Verify arithmetic and policy consistency.
- Detect invalid or stale price components.
- Validate price-result invariants.

M. PRICING RECONCILIATION SERVICE

Responsibilities:
- Detect conflicts between derived price projections and
  canonical price authorities.
- Detect missing or duplicated price updates.
- Manage correction workflows.

N. PRICING ANALYTICS

Responsibilities:
- Measure price-resolution quality, performance, policy
  adherence, and approved business outcomes.

O. PRICING CONTROL TOWER

Responsibilities:
- Monitor latency, errors, stale rules, calculation failures,
  guardrail violations, and reconciliation backlogs.

2.3 ARCHITECTURAL INTERPRETATION

The diagram describes logical responsibilities, not mandatory
microservices or deployment units.

Components may be implemented together or separately where
approved architecture and workload evidence justify that choice.

No component boundary authorizes a duplicate canonical authority.

# =============================================================================
# 3. PRICING ONTOLOGY
# =============================================================================

3.1 PRICING REQUEST

A request to resolve, calculate, validate, or quote a price
for a defined resource and context.

3.2 PRICE

A monetary amount or governed rate with an explicit semantic
meaning, currency, precision, validity, and source.

3.3 BASE PRICE

The price or rate selected before applying additional price
components specified by the relevant policy.

3.4 PRICE COMPONENT

A separately identifiable element that contributes to the
result, such as a base amount, discount, fee, tax, surcharge,
or other authorized adjustment.

3.5 PRICE BOOK

A governed collection or projection of prices and associated
applicability rules.

3.6 PRICE POLICY

A governed set of rules determining price selection,
calculation, or application.

3.7 PRICE SCHEDULE

A price or rate associated with defined effective-time
or commercial applicability conditions.

3.8 PRICE QUOTE

A price result with explicit scope, inputs, validity,
calculation lineage, and acceptance conditions.

3.9 INDICATIVE PRICE

A nonbinding or preliminary amount whose assumptions and
limitations are explicitly identified.

3.10 CONTRACTUAL PRICE

A price determined by an applicable contractual authority.

3.11 PRICE VERSION

An identifiable version of a price definition or policy.

3.12 PRICE DECISION

A recorded outcome of resolving or calculating a price under
a defined context and policy version.

3.13 PRICE LINEAGE

The traceable relationship between a price result and the
inputs, rules, transformations, and authorities that produced it.

3.14 PRICE EFFECTIVE TIME

The time interval during which a price or pricing rule is
intended to apply.

3.15 PRICE RECORD TIME

The time when a price or rule was recorded by the system.

3.16 PRICE TIER

A governed price or rate applicable to a defined quantity,
usage, volume, or other threshold range.

3.17 PRICE COMPONENT ORDER

The explicitly governed sequence in which price components
are applied.

3.18 DISCOUNT

An authorized reduction or adjustment determined by the
canonical discount or offer authority.

3.19 FEE

A separately governed charge associated with a defined
commercial or operational condition.

3.20 TAX RESULT

A determination produced by the canonical tax authority
under applicable rules and facts.

3.21 PRICE GUARDRAIL

A policy constraint restricting permitted price decisions.

3.22 COST BASIS

A cost measure supplied by the canonical cost or financial
authority for an explicitly defined purpose.

3.23 MARGIN

A defined financial measure calculated from appropriately
classified revenue and cost values.

3.24 PRICE EXPERIMENT

An authorized experiment comparing alternative pricing
policies or outcomes under approved controls.

3.25 DYNAMIC PRICING

A governed process in which prices may change according to
approved inputs, constraints, and policy.

3.26 PRICE INTEGRITY

The property that a price is traceable, semantically correct,
authorized, temporally applicable, and consistent with the
relevant canonical authorities.

3.27 PRICE CONFIDENCE

A governed description of the completeness or reliability of
an estimated price, where such a measure is useful and justified.

3.28 PRICE EXPIRATION

The end of the period during which a price result may be used
under its defined validity conditions.

3.29 PRICE ACCEPTANCE

An explicit downstream or customer action accepting a quote
or contractual price under the applicable contract.

3.30 FINAL PAYABLE AMOUNT

The amount determined for a specific transaction after all
applicable pricing, discount, tax, fee, and adjustment rules
have been resolved by their appropriate authorities.

This amount must not be confused with the seller's settlement
amount or accounting revenue.

3.31 CANONICAL ONTOLOGY REQUIREMENT

These definitions must be reconciled with existing UCOS
monetary, pricing, product, offer, tax, accounting, and
commercial ontologies.

# =============================================================================
# 4. CANONICAL AUTHORITY MATRIX
# =============================================================================

4.1 PRODUCT AND SERVICE IDENTITY

Authority:
Canonical product, variant, service, or resource domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Consume canonical resource references and relevant attributes.

Prohibition:
Do not create pricing-owned product identity.

4.2 SELLER IDENTITY

Authority:
Canonical seller or participant domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Resolve seller context and applicable authorized commercial
policies.

Prohibition:
Do not independently establish seller eligibility.

4.3 BASE PRICE

Authority:
The canonical pricing authority established through UCOS
governance.

Pricing responsibility:
Resolve or calculate prices within the approved pricing boundary.

Prohibition:
Do not create a second price authority for the same resource
and commercial context.

4.4 COST

Authority:
Canonical cost, procurement, accounting, or financial domain
as applicable to the defined cost concept.

Pricing responsibility:
Consume permitted cost inputs for approved pricing guardrails.

Prohibition:
Do not redefine accounting cost or inventory valuation.

4.5 CURRENCY

Authority:
Canonical monetary and currency authority.

Pricing responsibility:
Use approved currency identity, precision, and representation.

Prohibition:
Do not hardcode currency precision assumptions into the
universal pricing core.

4.6 EXCHANGE RATES

Authority:
Canonical exchange-rate authority.

Pricing responsibility:
Use approved rates with source, timestamp, purpose, and
applicability semantics.

Prohibition:
Do not invent exchange rates or silently use a rate intended
for a different financial purpose.

4.7 TAX

Authority:
Canonical tax authority.

Pricing responsibility:
Supply relevant facts and consume authorized tax results.

Prohibition:
Do not create competing tax law or tax determination logic.

4.8 OFFERS AND DISCOUNTS

Authority:
Canonical offer and promotion domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Apply only approved benefit decisions under the relevant contract.

Prohibition:
Do not grant discounts solely because a pricing rule finds
them commercially desirable.

4.9 INVENTORY

Authority:
Canonical inventory domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Consume permitted availability or inventory context when
pricing rules explicitly require it.

Prohibition:
Do not reserve or allocate inventory.

4.10 CONTRACTS

Authority:
Canonical contract or agreement domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Honor applicable contractual price references.

Prohibition:
Do not override binding contractual conditions through
unapproved dynamic pricing.

4.11 CUSTOMER IDENTITY AND ENTITLEMENTS

Authority:
Canonical identity, account, entitlement, and consent domains.

Pricing responsibility:
Consume authorized context required to resolve an applicable price.

Prohibition:
Do not infer entitlement without an authorized decision.

4.12 ORDER

Authority:
Canonical order domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Provide price decisions or quotes for order calculation
and validation.

Prohibition:
Do not independently accept or mutate orders.

4.13 PAYMENT

Authority:
Canonical payment domain.

Pricing responsibility:
Provide validated monetary results for payment preparation.

Prohibition:
Do not authorize or execute payment.

4.14 SETTLEMENT

Authority:
Canonical settlement and financial ledger domains.

Pricing responsibility:
Provide relevant commercial price references and lineage.

Prohibition:
Do not treat a customer-facing price as seller proceeds.

4.15 ACCOUNTING

Authority:
Canonical accounting and financial reporting domains.

Pricing responsibility:
Supply approved pricing facts where required.

Prohibition:
Do not independently determine revenue recognition or
accounting treatment.

4.16 GEOGRAPHY AND JURISDICTION

Authority:
Canonical geographic and regulatory context domains.

Pricing responsibility:
Resolve the applicable context through approved contracts.

4.17 TEMPORAL AUTHORITY

Authority:
Canonical time and scheduling capabilities.

Pricing responsibility:
Apply effective-time semantics using canonical definitions.

4.18 PRICE PRESENTATION

Authority:
Canonical presentation, localization, and design-system
capabilities for display semantics.

Pricing responsibility:
Return appropriately typed price components and display metadata.

Prohibition:
Do not allow presentation formatting to alter authoritative amounts.

4.19 CONFLICT RESOLUTION

When a derived pricing representation conflicts with its
canonical source, the canonical source wins.

If multiple canonical authorities conflict, the issue must be
resolved through the approved governance process rather than
through arbitrary local precedence.

# =============================================================================
# 5. UNIVERSAL PRICE REPRESENTATION
# =============================================================================

5.1 PURPOSE

Define the minimum semantic information required to represent
a price without ambiguity.

5.2 LOGICAL PRICE CONTRACT

A price representation should include, where applicable:

- Canonical price identifier.
- Resource reference.
- Seller or commercial context reference.
- Price semantic type.
- Monetary amount or rate.
- Currency reference.
- Unit of measure.
- Quantity basis.
- Effective-time interval.
- Recording time.
- Version.
- Applicable price policy.
- Source authority.
- Tax-inclusion semantics.
- Discount-inclusion semantics.
- Fee-inclusion semantics.
- Applicable channel.
- Applicable jurisdiction.
- Applicable contract reference.
- Validity status.
- Approval status.
- Provenance.
- Data classification.
- Change reference.

5.3 PRICE TYPE

The price type must define what the amount represents.

A numeric amount without a semantic type is insufficient
for safe commercial calculation.

5.4 UNIT OF MEASURE

Unit-based pricing must identify the basis of the rate.

Examples include a unit of product, duration, usage quantity,
service instance, capacity unit, or another governed unit.

These examples do not constrain the universe of supported units.

5.5 TAX SEMANTICS

A price must identify whether tax is excluded, included,
separately represented, estimated, or not yet determined.

5.6 DISCOUNT SEMANTICS

A price must identify whether discounts have been considered,
applied, excluded, or not yet evaluated.

5.7 FINALITY

A price must distinguish indicative, calculated, quoted,
committed, accepted, expired, and invalidated states where
these states are applicable.

5.8 NULL AND UNKNOWN

Missing or unknown amounts must not be represented as zero.

5.9 ZERO PRICE

A zero price must be a valid explicit value when permitted,
not a substitute for missing data.

5.10 NEGATIVE AMOUNTS

Negative monetary values must be allowed only where the
applicable price-component or adjustment contract explicitly
permits them.

5.11 AMOUNT AND RATE

A monetary amount and a rate must remain distinct types.

5.12 CANONICAL IDENTIFIERS

All identifiers must follow UCOS identifier governance.

# =============================================================================
# 6. PRICE BOOKS AND PRICE POLICY GOVERNANCE
# =============================================================================

6.1 PURPOSE

Support governed price collections and applicability rules
without creating competing price authorities.

6.2 PRICE BOOK DIMENSIONS

A price book may be applicable to:

- A defined resource set.
- A seller.
- A customer segment where authorized.
- A commercial agreement.
- A channel.
- A geographic context.
- A jurisdiction.
- A currency.
- A quantity range.
- A usage profile.
- A temporal interval.
- A service or contract class.
- Other governed context dimensions.

6.3 PRICE BOOK CONTRACT

A price book should define:

- Canonical identifier.
- Name and description.
- Owner.
- Scope.
- Applicability conditions.
- Effective-time interval.
- Currency semantics.
- Version.
- Approval status.
- Precedence policy.
- Publication status.
- Change history.
- Applicable governance rules.

6.4 PRICE POLICY CONTRACT

A price policy should define:

- Policy identifier.
- Policy type.
- Applicability conditions.
- Inputs.
- Required authorities.
- Calculation method.
- Precedence.
- Effective time.
- Approval requirements.
- Constraints.
- Failure behavior.
- Output semantics.
- Version.
- Owner.
- Evaluation criteria.

6.5 PRICE BOOK SELECTION

Price book selection must follow explicit precedence rules.

6.6 AMBIGUOUS APPLICABILITY

If multiple price books match and no valid precedence rule
resolves the conflict, the result must be an explicit conflict
or governed escalation.

6.7 NO ARBITRARY LAST-WRITE-WINS

Update order must not silently determine commercial precedence.

6.8 INHERITANCE

If price-book inheritance is supported, inheritance rules must
define field-level override behavior and conflict detection.

6.9 OVERRIDE GOVERNANCE

Overrides must be authorized, scoped, versioned, time-bound
where appropriate, and auditable.

6.10 PUBLICATION

Draft prices must not become commercially active before
required approvals and publication conditions are satisfied.

6.11 RETIREMENT

Retiring a price book must preserve required history and define
the handling of active quotes or contractual references.

6.12 PRICE BOOK RECONCILIATION

Detect overlapping scopes, unresolved precedence, invalid
references, and incompatible price semantics.

# =============================================================================
# 7. PRICE RESOLUTION AND PRECEDENCE
# =============================================================================

7.1 PURPOSE

Resolve one applicable pricing policy or a governed combination
of policies for a given request.

7.2 RESOLUTION INPUTS

Potential inputs include:

- Canonical resource reference.
- Seller context.
- Requested quantity.
- Configuration.
- Contract reference.
- Customer entitlement reference.
- Channel.
- Geography.
- Jurisdiction.
- Currency.
- Effective time.
- Usage profile.
- Duration.
- Approved commercial segment.
- Requested price semantic type.

7.3 PRECEDENCE DIMENSIONS

Precedence may consider:

- Binding contract.
- Mandatory regulation.
- Explicit approved customer agreement.
- Approved seller policy.
- Channel-specific policy.
- General price book.
- Default pricing policy.

This list is illustrative. Actual precedence must be approved
for each applicable commercial context and cannot contradict
law, contract, or canonical governance.

7.4 NO UNIVERSAL PRECEDENCE ASSUMPTION

The architecture must not assume that one universal ordering
is correct for every domain or jurisdiction.

7.5 PRECEDENCE CONTRACT

A precedence contract must define:

- Applicable policy classes.
- Relative priority.
- Tie resolution.
- Conflict behavior.
- Override authority.
- Effective-time semantics.
- Audit requirements.
- Approval requirements.

7.6 DETERMINISTIC RESOLUTION

The same request, authoritative inputs, policy versions, and
effective-time context must resolve consistently.

7.7 EXPLICIT OVERRIDES

Overrides must identify the authorizing principal or system,
reason, scope, duration, and approval evidence where required.

7.8 POLICY CONFLICT

Unresolved policy conflict must not be silently converted
into an arbitrary price.

7.9 DEFAULT PRICE

A default price may be used only when the relevant policy
explicitly permits it.

7.10 NO PRICE AVAILABLE

If no valid price can be resolved, return a typed no-price
or unresolved-price outcome rather than inventing a value.

# =============================================================================
# 8. PRICING METHODS AND EXTENSIBILITY
# =============================================================================

8.1 PURPOSE

Support diverse pricing methods through a common contract.

8.2 BASE PRICING

Resolve a defined base amount or rate.

8.3 FIXED PRICING

Apply a fixed price for a defined resource and scope.

8.4 UNIT PRICING

Calculate a price from a rate and quantity under explicit
quantity and rounding rules.

8.5 TIERED PRICING

Apply rates or amounts according to governed threshold tiers.

8.6 VOLUME PRICING

Determine a price based on total quantity or volume.

8.7 PROGRESSIVE TIER PRICING

Apply different rates to portions of a quantity across tiers
where the approved pricing method defines progressive treatment.

8.8 ALL-UNITS TIER PRICING

Apply a selected tier's rate to the full qualifying quantity
where explicitly defined.

8.9 SUBSCRIPTION PRICING

Integrate with canonical subscription and billing capabilities
for recurring price terms and billing periods.

8.10 USAGE-BASED PRICING

Integrate with canonical metering and billing capabilities.

8.11 DURATION-BASED PRICING

Support rates based on defined duration units where appropriate.

8.12 RENTAL PRICING

Support authorized pricing for rental periods, deposits,
usage, and other defined components.

8.13 CONFIGURATION-BASED PRICING

Derive a price from canonical product configuration and
approved pricing rules.

8.14 BUNDLE PRICING

Support governed bundle prices while preserving component
references and applicable discount semantics.

8.15 CONTRACT PRICING

Resolve applicable contractual price terms through the
canonical contract authority.

8.16 NEGOTIATED PRICING

Support approved negotiation workflows without allowing
unauthorized users to bypass price guardrails.

8.17 USAGE COMMITMENTS

Support contractual or volume commitments through appropriate
commercial and billing integrations.

8.18 FREEMIUM AND ZERO-PRICE OFFERINGS

Represent zero-price and free-tier conditions explicitly,
including applicable usage and entitlement constraints.

8.19 DYNAMIC PRICING

Support controlled recalculation from approved input signals
and governed policy.

8.20 FORMULA-BASED PRICING

If formulas are supported, they must use a restricted,
typed, versioned, deterministic expression model.

8.21 PLUGGABLE PRICING METHOD CONTRACT

A pricing method extension should define:

- Method identifier.
- Version.
- Supported resource types.
- Required inputs.
- Optional inputs.
- Output semantics.
- Formula or algorithm definition.
- Monetary precision rules.
- Rounding behavior.
- Constraints.
- Failure behavior.
- Determinism properties.
- Security requirements.
- Evaluation requirements.
- Owner.
- Approval status.

8.22 NO ARBITRARY CODE EXECUTION

Pricing configuration must not permit uncontrolled executable
code or unbounded expressions.

8.23 METHOD REGISTRY

Pricing methods must be discovered through a governed canonical
registry where such a registry is approved and appropriate.

8.24 METHOD COMPATIBILITY

A method must not be applied to a resource or context outside
its declared scope.

# =============================================================================
# 9. PRICE COMPONENT COMPOSITION
# =============================================================================

9.1 PURPOSE

Combine price components without obscuring their semantics.

9.2 POTENTIAL COMPONENTS

- Base amount.
- Quantity extension.
- Configuration adjustment.
- Authorized discount.
- Authorized surcharge.
- Fee.
- Tax.
- Deposit.
- Rebate.
- Contractual adjustment.
- Other approved component.

9.3 COMPONENT CONTRACT

Each component should define:

- Component reference.
- Component type.
- Monetary amount or rate.
- Currency.
- Calculation basis.
- Application order.
- Sign semantics.
- Tax treatment.
- Discount interaction.
- Authority.
- Effective time.
- Version.
- Rounding rule.
- Inclusion status.
- Provenance.

9.4 ORDER OF OPERATIONS

The calculation sequence must be explicit.

9.5 DISCOUNT ORDER

The order in which discounts are applied must follow canonical
offer and pricing contracts.

9.6 TAX ORDER

Taxable basis, discount treatment, and tax calculation order
must be determined by the canonical tax authority and applicable
legal rules.

9.7 FEE ORDER

Fees must follow their defined calculation and tax treatment.

9.8 DEPOSITS

Deposits must remain distinguishable from earned revenue,
fees, taxes, and other price components.

9.9 NEGATIVE COMPONENTS

Negative components require explicit type and authorization.

9.10 COMPONENT DUPLICATION

A component must not be applied twice unless the canonical
policy explicitly requires distinct applications.

9.11 COMPONENT PROVENANCE

Every material component must trace to its originating
authority or approved calculation rule.

9.12 COMPOSITION FAILURE

If a required component cannot be resolved, the result must
follow the explicit failure policy rather than silently omitting it.

# =============================================================================
# 10. MONETARY ARITHMETIC AND ROUNDING
# =============================================================================

10.1 PURPOSE

Ensure monetary calculations are reproducible and semantically
correct.

10.2 MONETARY REPRESENTATION

Use a canonical exact monetary representation or suitable
decimal arithmetic under the approved monetary contract.

10.3 NO UNCONTROLLED FLOATING-POINT

Binary floating-point arithmetic must not serve as the
uncontrolled source of truth for financial calculations.

10.4 CURRENCY PRECISION

Precision and minor-unit semantics must come from the
canonical currency authority and applicable rules.

10.5 ROUNDING POLICY

A rounding policy must define:

- Rounding mode.
- Precision.
- Calculation stage.
- Aggregation stage.
- Unit or line-level application.
- Currency applicability.
- Jurisdiction applicability.
- Version.
- Owner.

10.6 INTERMEDIATE PRECISION

Intermediate calculations must preserve sufficient precision
until the approved rounding boundary.

10.7 LINE VS. TOTAL ROUNDING

The architecture must explicitly define whether rounding
occurs per component, unit, line, invoice, or another governed
boundary.

10.8 QUANTITY PRECISION

Quantity precision must follow the canonical unit and
measurement contract.

10.9 RATE PRECISION

Rates must preserve required precision until the defined
calculation boundary.

10.10 CONVERSION

Currency conversion must use an approved exchange-rate source,
rate purpose, effective time, and rounding policy.

10.11 NO IMPLICIT CURRENCY CONVERSION

A price must not silently change currency.

10.12 RECONCILIATION

Intermediate amounts and final totals must reconcile according
to the approved arithmetic model.

10.13 OVERFLOW AND RANGE

Amounts outside supported numeric bounds must produce an
explicit error or governed alternative.

10.14 NEGATIVE ZERO

Representations must normalize or distinguish negative zero
according to canonical monetary semantics.

10.15 VERIFICATION

Arithmetic correctness must be validated with boundary,
rounding, aggregation, and currency-specific test cases.

# =============================================================================
# 11. CURRENCY AND EXCHANGE-RATE INTEGRATION
# =============================================================================

11.1 PURPOSE

Support multiple currencies without duplicating monetary
or foreign-exchange authorities.

11.2 CURRENCY RESOLUTION

Currency must be explicit in the price contract.

11.3 CURRENCY SOURCE

Use canonical currency definitions and supported precision.

11.4 EXCHANGE-RATE PURPOSE

Different exchange-rate purposes must remain distinguishable.

Examples may include commercial quotation, accounting valuation,
settlement, or reporting.

These purposes must not be interchanged without authorization.

11.5 RATE PROVENANCE

A conversion result must retain the applicable rate reference,
source, effective time, and rate-purpose metadata.

11.6 RATE EXPIRATION

The policy must define when an exchange-rate result becomes
too stale for the requested purpose.

11.7 CONVERSION DIRECTION

Conversion direction and rate semantics must be explicit.

11.8 CONVERSION ROUNDING

Apply the approved currency-conversion rounding rule.

11.9 DISPLAY CURRENCY

Display currency must not be confused with the currency in
which a contractual obligation is denominated.

11.10 PRICE QUOTE CURRENCY

A quote must identify its denomination and any conversion
assumptions.

11.11 NO FABRICATED RATES

If a valid exchange rate is unavailable, return an explicit
unavailable or unresolved conversion outcome.

# =============================================================================
# 12. COST, MARGIN, AND COMMERCIAL GUARDRAILS
# =============================================================================

12.1 PURPOSE

Support approved commercial constraints while preserving
the authority of canonical cost and financial domains.

12.2 COST INPUTS

Potential cost inputs may include:

- Procurement cost.
- Manufacturing cost.
- Service-delivery cost.
- Fulfillment cost.
- Authorized variable cost.
- Other approved commercial cost basis.

These inputs must retain their canonical definitions.

12.3 COST SEMANTICS

A cost value must identify what it includes and excludes.

12.4 COST VERSION

Material cost inputs must identify their source and applicable version.

12.5 MARGIN DEFINITIONS

Margin metrics must explicitly define their numerator,
denominator, cost basis, and treatment of tax, discounts,
fees, and other adjustments.

12.6 MARGIN VS. MARKUP

Margin and markup must not be treated as interchangeable.

12.7 GUARDRAIL TYPES

Potential guardrails include:

- Minimum price.
- Maximum price.
- Minimum margin.
- Maximum discount.
- Maximum price movement.
- Approved price-change frequency.
- Contractual price boundary.
- Jurisdictional constraint.
- Seller-specific commercial constraint.
- Risk-based review threshold.

12.8 GUARDRAIL CONTRACT

A guardrail should define:

- Identifier.
- Owner.
- Applicable resource scope.
- Required inputs.
- Formula or evaluation method.
- Threshold.
- Effective time.
- Approval requirement.
- Failure behavior.
- Override permissions.
- Audit requirement.

12.9 GUARDRAIL VIOLATION

A violation must produce an explicit result, such as rejection,
review, approval escalation, or a permitted fallback.

12.10 NO SILENT OVERRIDE

A failed guardrail must not be ignored merely because a price
would otherwise improve conversion or revenue.

12.11 COST DATA UNAVAILABLE

Define whether pricing may proceed, requires review, or must
fail when a cost-dependent guardrail cannot be evaluated.

12.12 SENSITIVE COST DATA

Internal cost and margin data must not be exposed to unauthorized
customers, sellers, or other participants.

12.13 SELLER CONFIGURATION

Seller-defined pricing rules must remain within marketplace
policy and applicable legal constraints.

12.14 FINANCIAL AUTHORITY

Pricing guardrails do not replace canonical accounting,
procurement, or financial controls.

# =============================================================================
# 13. DYNAMIC PRICING GOVERNANCE
# =============================================================================

13.1 PURPOSE

Allow prices to respond to approved conditions without
uncontrolled or opaque commercial manipulation.

13.2 PERMITTED INPUT CATEGORIES

Subject to governance, inputs may include:

- Contractual rules.
- Approved cost changes.
- Supply and demand indicators.
- Time-based rules.
- Capacity constraints.
- Approved inventory context.
- Defined geographic context.
- Competitive information from authorized sources.
- Service-delivery conditions.
- Authorized business policy.
- Other explicitly approved inputs.

13.3 INPUT PROVENANCE

Every material input must have a source, permitted purpose,
freshness rule, and applicable authority.

13.4 DYNAMIC-PRICING POLICY

A policy must define:

- Scope.
- Eligible resources.
- Permitted inputs.
- Calculation method.
- Constraints.
- Minimum and maximum values where applicable.
- Maximum rate of change.
- Update frequency.
- Approval requirements.
- Effective time.
- Explanation requirements.
- Monitoring metrics.
- Rollback behavior.

13.5 PROHIBITED INPUTS

Inputs prohibited by law, regulation, contract, or canonical
ethical and marketplace policies must not be used.

13.6 CUSTOMER VULNERABILITY

Dynamic pricing must not exploit protected or sensitive
characteristics or prohibited vulnerability indicators.

13.7 PERSONALIZED PRICE GOVERNANCE

Personalized pricing requires explicit governance, lawful
purpose, transparency where required, and approved evaluation.

13.8 COMPETITIVE DATA

Competitive information must be obtained and used lawfully.
The system must not coordinate prices unlawfully or facilitate
prohibited collusive behavior.

13.9 PRICE STABILITY

Material price movement must follow defined thresholds,
cooldowns, or approval requirements where appropriate.

13.10 PRICE VOLATILITY

Unusual volatility must trigger monitoring and potentially
a controlled pause or review.

13.11 HUMAN REVIEW

High-impact or exceptional price changes may require approval
by an authorized role.

13.12 AUDITABILITY

A dynamic price decision must identify the relevant inputs,
policy version, calculation outcome, and authorization evidence.

13.13 ROLLBACK

The system must support reverting to an approved prior policy
or other governed fallback where safe.

13.14 NO UNCONTROLLED SELF-MODIFICATION

A pricing model or agent must not modify its own production
pricing policy without approved governance.

# =============================================================================
# 14. PRICE EXPERIMENTATION AND OPTIMIZATION
# =============================================================================

14.1 PURPOSE

Enable controlled evaluation of alternative pricing strategies.

14.2 EXPERIMENT TYPES

Potential experiments include:

- Price-point evaluation.
- Approved price elasticity analysis.
- Discount-policy comparison.
- Price-presentation evaluation.
- Contract-offer comparison.
- Pricing-method evaluation.
- Approved segmentation analysis.

14.3 EXPERIMENT CONTRACT

An experiment should define:

- Experiment identifier.
- Hypothesis.
- Scope.
- Eligibility rules.
- Candidate policies.
- Assignment method.
- Duration.
- Primary metric.
- Guardrail metrics.
- Statistical method.
- Sample-size requirements.
- Approval.
- Monitoring.
- Stop conditions.
- Rollback.
- Final decision record.

14.4 EXPERIMENT AUTHORITY

Reuse canonical experimentation and analytics capabilities.

14.5 ASSIGNMENT

Experiment assignment must be governed, reproducible where
required, and protected against unintended cross-group exposure.

14.6 LEGAL AND CONTRACTUAL GUARDRAILS

An experiment must not override legal, regulatory, contractual,
or mandatory commercial constraints.

14.7 FAIRNESS

Evaluate unintended differences in outcomes across relevant
groups under applicable policy and law.

14.8 CUSTOMER PROTECTION

Experiments must comply with applicable disclosure, consent,
and consumer-protection requirements.

14.9 PRICE EXPERIMENT INTEGRITY

Experimental results must not be misrepresented as established
facts without sufficient evidence.

14.10 ROLLBACK

Material harm, compliance violations, or guardrail breaches
must trigger the approved stop or rollback process.

14.11 EXPERIMENT COMPLETION

The final result must record the outcome, limitations, evidence,
and decision authority.

# =============================================================================
# 15. TAX AND FEE INTEGRATION
# =============================================================================

15.1 PURPOSE

Integrate tax and fee results without duplicating tax authority.

15.2 TAX INPUTS

Depending on the canonical tax contract, relevant facts may
include:

- Resource classification.
- Transaction type.
- Transaction location.
- Seller jurisdiction.
- Customer jurisdiction.
- Applicable tax context.
- Price components.
- Discount treatment.
- Tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive semantics.
- Effective time.
- Other legally relevant facts.

15.3 TAX AUTHORITY

Tax determination remains with the canonical tax capability.

15.4 TAX RESULT CONTRACT

A tax result should identify:

- Result reference.
- Tax authority.
- Applicable jurisdiction.
- Tax basis.
- Applicable rules or version.
- Tax components.
- Amount.
- Currency.
- Rounding semantics.
- Validity or calculation context.
- Source references.
- Error or uncertainty state.

15.5 TAX-INCLUSIVE PRICE

The contract must define whether and how included tax is
represented and reconciled.

15.6 TAX-EXCLUSIVE PRICE

The contract must define whether tax is added downstream or
included in the current result.

15.7 TAX UNAVAILABLE

If tax determination is required but unavailable, the system
must follow the approved legal and commercial failure policy.

15.8 FEES

Each fee must have a canonical owner and explicit calculation
semantics.

15.9 TAX ON FEES

Tax treatment of fees must be determined through the canonical
tax authority.

15.10 TAX RECONCILIATION

Price components and tax results must reconcile according to
the approved transaction calculation model.

15.11 NO HARDCODED TAX RULES

The universal pricing engine must not hardcode jurisdiction-
specific tax rates or legal interpretations.

# =============================================================================
# 16. DISCOUNT, OFFER, AND PROMOTION INTEGRATION
# =============================================================================

16.1 PURPOSE

Integrate authorized commercial benefits while preventing
duplicate or unauthorized reductions.

16.2 OFFER AUTHORITY

The canonical offer or promotion domain determines eligibility
for benefits it owns.

16.3 PRICING RESPONSIBILITY

Pricing consumes the authorized benefit decision and applies
its amount or rule under the agreed calculation contract.

16.4 DISCOUNT INPUTS

Potential inputs include:

- Benefit reference.
- Eligibility result.
- Applicable resource.
- Quantity.
- Customer entitlement.
- Effective time.
- Discount basis.
- Maximum benefit.
- Currency.
- Stacking constraints.
- Application order.
- Version.

16.5 DISCOUNT TYPES

The architecture may support fixed reductions, percentage
reductions, tiered benefits, bundle adjustments, loyalty
benefits, and other governed benefit types.

These types do not authorize the pricing domain to create
the underlying offer.

16.6 STACKING

Discount stacking must follow explicit canonical policy.

16.7 DUPLICATE BENEFIT

The same benefit must not be applied more than permitted.

16.8 DISCOUNT LIMITS

Maximum discounts and applicable guardrails must be enforced.

16.9 EXPIRED OFFER

Expired or revoked offers must not be treated as valid benefits.

16.10 PRICE PRESENTATION

The result must distinguish original price, discount amount,
and resulting amount where required.

16.11 BENEFIT REVALIDATION

Materially changed transaction context must trigger the
required revalidation.

16.12 FINAL TRANSACTION ELIGIBILITY

The canonical offer or order authority must validate benefits
at the appropriate transaction boundary.

# =============================================================================
# 17. PRICE QUOTATION AND COMMITMENT
# =============================================================================

17.1 PURPOSE

Represent a price result with explicit validity and acceptance
semantics.

17.2 QUOTE CONTRACT

A quote should include:

- Quote identifier.
- Request identifier.
- Resource references.
- Resource configuration.
- Quantity and units.
- Price components.
- Currency.
- Tax and fee semantics.
- Applicable policies.
- Effective time.
- Expiration.
- Validity conditions.
- Relevant source versions.
- Price lineage.
- Approval status.
- Quote status.
- Acceptance requirements.
- Revalidation requirements.

17.3 QUOTE STATUS

Possible states include:

- Draft.
- Calculated.
- Pending Approval.
- Issued.
- Accepted.
- Rejected.
- Expired.
- Superseded.
- Invalidated.
- Cancelled.

The canonical lifecycle must determine which states are required.

17.4 QUOTE VALIDITY

A quote must explicitly define what is held constant during
its validity period.

17.5 PRICE GUARANTEE

A quote is not a price guarantee unless the applicable contract
explicitly establishes that commitment.

17.6 RESOURCE AVAILABILITY

A price quote does not guarantee inventory, service availability,
or a reservation unless the relevant canonical domains confirm it.

17.7 QUOTE ACCEPTANCE

Acceptance must follow the applicable contractual and transaction
workflow.

17.8 QUOTE REVALIDATION

Revalidation may be required when material inputs change,
the quote expires, policy requires it, or the transaction context
differs from the quoted context.

17.9 QUOTE REPRODUCIBILITY

The system must retain enough permitted lineage to explain
the issued quote.

17.10 QUOTE IMMUTABILITY

An issued quote must not be silently overwritten.

Corrections must follow the canonical amendment, replacement,
or invalidation workflow.

17.11 EXPIRED QUOTE

An expired quote must not be treated as current without
authorized revalidation or reissuance.

17.12 NO PAYMENT AUTHORITY

Issuing or accepting a quote does not itself execute payment.

# =============================================================================
# 18. PRICE HISTORY, VERSIONING, AND LINEAGE
# =============================================================================

18.1 PURPOSE

Preserve sufficient evidence to explain material price changes
and reproduce historical decisions where permitted.

18.2 VERSIONED ARTIFACTS

Potential versioned artifacts include:

- Price definition.
- Price book.
- Pricing policy.
- Pricing method.
- Guardrail.
- Rounding policy.
- Quote.
- Dynamic-pricing configuration.
- Approved model reference.
- Tax result reference.
- Discount decision reference.

18.3 CHANGE RECORD

A material change record should include:

- Change identifier.
- Artifact reference.
- Previous version.
- New version.
- Change reason.
- Author or initiating authority.
- Approval evidence.
- Recording time.
- Effective time.
- Impact assessment.
- Related change request.

18.4 HISTORICAL PRICE

Historical price queries must define whether they return the
recorded historical decision, a recomputed result, or both.

18.5 RECOMPUTATION

A recomputed historical price must not be presented as the
original historical decision.

18.6 LINEAGE

Price lineage should reference:

- Resource identity.
- Source price.
- Policy versions.
- Calculation method.
- Quantity.
- Currency.
- Relevant exchange-rate reference.
- Discount decision.
- Tax result.
- Fee result.
- Guardrail outcomes.
- Effective-time context.
- Rounding rules.
- Output status.

18.7 RETENTION

Retention must follow canonical legal, financial, privacy,
and records-management policies.

18.8 IMMUTABILITY

Financially significant records must follow the approved
immutability and correction model.

18.9 NO HISTORY DELETION BY OVERWRITE

Material price history must not be erased by replacing
the current price value.

18.10 LINEAGE ACCESS

Price lineage must be accessible only to authorized users
and systems.

# =============================================================================
# 19. PRICE CHANGE MANAGEMENT
# =============================================================================

19.1 PURPOSE

Govern price changes from proposal through approval, publication,
activation, monitoring, and retirement.

19.2 LIFECYCLE

A proposed lifecycle may include:

1. Draft.
2. Validation.
3. Impact Analysis.
4. Approval.
5. Scheduled.
6. Published.
7. Active.
8. Superseded.
9. Retired.
10. Reconciled.

Actual states must follow canonical UCOS lifecycle conventions.

19.3 VALIDATION

Validate price semantics, currency, scope, effective time,
precedence, component compatibility, and guardrails.

19.4 IMPACT ANALYSIS

Assess affected resources, active quotes, price books, channels,
contracts, cached projections, and downstream consumers.

19.5 APPROVAL

Approval requirements must be based on authority, risk,
commercial scope, and applicable governance.

19.6 SCHEDULED CHANGES

Scheduled changes must activate according to canonical
temporal semantics.

19.7 CONFLICT DETECTION

Detect overlapping or incompatible price changes before activation.

19.8 PUBLICATION

Only approved prices may become active under the relevant policy.

19.9 ROLLBACK

Define whether a change may be rolled back, superseded, or
corrected through a compensating change.

19.10 ACTIVE QUOTES

A price change must not silently alter an issued quote whose
validity contract protects its terms.

19.11 CONTRACTUAL PRICES

Contractual commitments must follow the canonical contract
authority and amendment rules.

19.12 AUDIT

All material changes must have traceable change and approval evidence.

# =============================================================================
# 20. CUSTOMER-FACING PRICE TRANSPARENCY
# =============================================================================

20.1 PURPOSE

Ensure that customer-facing prices are understandable and
not materially misleading.

20.2 PRICE PRESENTATION

Presentation may include, where appropriate:

- Amount.
- Currency.
- Unit basis.
- Quantity.
- Tax inclusion.
- Discount.
- Fees.
- Deposit.
- Recurrence.
- Duration.
- Validity.
- Eligibility conditions.
- Mandatory charges.
- Relevant limitations.

20.3 PRESENTATION VS. AUTHORITY

Formatting and display components must not alter the underlying
authoritative amount.

20.4 PRELIMINARY PRICE

Estimated or indicative amounts must be clearly distinguished
from finalized quotes.

20.5 RECURRING PRICE

Recurring charges must identify the relevant billing period
and material recurring conditions.

20.6 USAGE-BASED PRICE

Usage-based pricing must explain the applicable unit and rate
where required.

20.7 TAX DISCLOSURE

Tax information must follow canonical tax and disclosure policies.

20.8 FEES

Mandatory fees must be represented according to applicable
consumer-protection and commercial rules.

20.9 DISCOUNT PRESENTATION

Discount claims must be supported by the canonical offer and
price-history authorities.

20.10 REFERENCE PRICES

Reference, original, crossed-out, or comparative prices must
follow applicable law and canonical policy.

20.11 FALSE URGENCY

Price expiration and scarcity messages must not be fabricated
or manipulated.

20.12 PRICE DIFFERENCES

Where materially different prices are displayed across
contexts, the system must follow applicable disclosure,
contractual, and marketplace policies.

20.13 ACCESSIBILITY

Price components and changes must be presented accessibly.

20.14 LOCALIZATION

Formatting must use canonical locale and currency rules.

# =============================================================================
# 21. SELLER AND MARKETPLACE COMMERCIAL GOVERNANCE
# =============================================================================

21.1 PURPOSE

Support seller autonomy within explicit marketplace rules.

21.2 SELLER PRICE AUTHORITY

Seller-defined prices must follow the canonical seller,
catalog, contract, and marketplace policy boundaries.

21.3 MARKETPLACE RULES

Marketplace policies may define permitted pricing methods,
disclosure requirements, fee handling, or review thresholds.

21.4 SELLER-SPECIFIC PRICE BOOKS

Seller-specific price books must have explicit scope and
authorization.

21.5 PRICE OWNERSHIP

The system must distinguish marketplace-defined prices,
seller-defined prices, negotiated prices, and contractually
determined prices.

21.6 NO UNAUTHORIZED OVERWRITE

The marketplace must not silently overwrite seller-owned
prices unless an authorized policy or contract permits it.

21.7 PRICE VALIDATION

Seller price changes must be validated against applicable
policy and mandatory constraints.

21.8 COMMERCIAL INTERVENTION

Marketplace intervention must be traceable and supported by
the applicable policy and authority.

21.9 PRICE DISPUTES

Disputed prices must follow the canonical dispute and case
management process.

21.10 SELLER VISIBILITY

Seller-facing explanations must not disclose unauthorized
competitor data or internal security mechanisms.

21.11 SELLER ANALYTICS

Seller pricing analytics must respect data-access, aggregation,
competition, and privacy policies.

21.12 COMPETITION COMPLIANCE

Pricing controls must not facilitate prohibited collusion,
price fixing, or unlawful exchange of competitively sensitive data.

# =============================================================================
# 22. PRICING SECURITY AND ABUSE PREVENTION
# =============================================================================

22.1 PURPOSE

Protect pricing decisions, configurations, and commercial
information from unauthorized access or manipulation.

22.2 THREAT CATEGORIES

Potential threats include:

- Unauthorized price modification.
- Unauthorized price-book publication.
- Guardrail bypass.
- Quote tampering.
- Price-history alteration.
- Currency manipulation.
- Exchange-rate substitution.
- Discount duplication.
- Tax-result substitution.
- Unauthorized cost-data exposure.
- Tenant boundary violations.
- Price enumeration.
- Automated quote abuse.
- Resource-exhaustion attacks.
- Configuration injection.
- Unauthorized formula execution.
- Experiment manipulation.
- Dynamic-pricing manipulation.
- Insider misuse.
- Audit-log tampering.

22.3 AUTHENTICATION

Use canonical identity and authentication services.

22.4 AUTHORIZATION

Enforce role, resource, tenant, operation, and approval boundaries.

22.5 SEPARATION OF DUTIES

Where required, separate price authoring, approval, publication,
and override permissions.

22.6 PRIVILEGED OPERATIONS

Price overrides and policy publication require explicit
authorization and auditability.

22.7 CONFIGURATION SECURITY

Pricing expressions and configurations must be validated,
bounded, versioned, and protected from injection.

22.8 QUOTE INTEGRITY

Quotes and continuation or reference tokens must be protected
against unauthorized modification.

22.9 SENSITIVE DATA

Cost, margin, contractual terms, and pricing strategy must
not be exposed beyond authorized purposes.

22.10 AUDIT PROTECTION

Material pricing audit records must follow canonical
integrity and access controls.

22.11 ABUSE DETECTION

Integrate with canonical security and trust-and-safety capabilities.

22.12 INCIDENT RESPONSE

Suspected price manipulation or material disclosure must
trigger the appropriate incident workflow.

# =============================================================================
# 23. PRIVACY, FAIRNESS, AND ETHICAL PRICING
# =============================================================================

23.1 PURPOSE

Ensure that pricing inputs and decisions comply with applicable
privacy, fairness, consumer-protection, and marketplace policies.

23.2 PURPOSE LIMITATION

Personal information may be used only for authorized purposes.

23.3 DATA MINIMIZATION

Use only the personal or contextual information required by
the approved pricing policy.

23.4 SENSITIVE ATTRIBUTES

Sensitive or protected characteristics must not be used in
prohibited pricing decisions.

23.5 INFERRED VULNERABILITY

Inferred vulnerability must not be used to exploit customers.

23.6 PERSONALIZED PRICING

Personalized pricing must have explicit governance and
appropriate legal and transparency review.

23.7 FAIRNESS EVALUATION

Evaluate materially different outcomes across relevant
groups where required and lawful.

23.8 EXPLANATION

Material pricing decisions must be explainable to authorized
reviewers and, where required, affected participants.

23.9 AUTOMATED DECISIONS

Automated pricing must have defined oversight, monitoring,
and intervention mechanisms.

23.10 RETENTION

Pricing-related personal data must follow approved retention
and deletion policies.

23.11 CONSENT

Consent and preference requirements must be enforced by
their canonical authorities.

23.12 ETHICAL GUARDRAILS

Revenue optimization must not override legal obligations,
contractual commitments, or approved ethical constraints.

# =============================================================================
# 24. PRICING ANALYTICS AND OBSERVABILITY
# =============================================================================

24.1 PURPOSE

Provide operational and commercial visibility without
creating an unauthorized financial source of truth.

24.2 OPERATIONAL METRICS

Potential metrics include:

- Pricing request volume.
- Pricing latency.
- Error rate.
- Timeout rate.
- Policy-resolution failure rate.
- Quote-generation latency.
- Currency-conversion failure rate.
- Tax-adapter failure rate.
- Discount-adapter failure rate.
- Guardrail violation rate.
- Price-change activation failures.
- Stale price rate.
- Reconciliation backlog.
- Calculation mismatch rate.
- Resource consumption.
- Cost per pricing request.

24.3 QUALITY METRICS

Potential metrics include:

- Price-resolution correctness.
- Policy applicability correctness.
- Arithmetic correctness.
- Rounding consistency.
- Quote reproducibility.
- Price freshness.
- Conflict-detection coverage.
- Price explanation completeness.
- Downstream price validation failures.

24.4 COMMERCIAL METRICS

Where authorized, metrics may include:

- Price realization.
- Gross margin.
- Discount utilization.
- Conversion outcomes.
- Revenue impact.
- Price elasticity estimates.
- Refund and cancellation correlations.
- Seller adoption.
- Quote acceptance rate.

24.5 METRIC DEFINITIONS

Each metric must define its formula, source, population,
currency semantics, time window, and limitations.

24.6 CURRENCY NORMALIZATION

Aggregated monetary metrics must use an approved currency
normalization policy.

24.7 ESTIMATED VS. ACTUAL

Forecasts and estimates must remain distinguishable from
realized financial outcomes.

24.8 ANALYTICS AUTHORITY

Pricing analytics must not replace accounting, financial
ledgers, or canonical transaction records.

24.9 PRIVACY

Behavioral and customer-level analytics must follow approved
privacy and access controls.

24.10 OBSERVABILITY

Material calculation stages must be traceable through
appropriate correlation and lineage identifiers.

24.11 ALERTING

Alerts must define severity, ownership, thresholds, and
approved response procedures.

24.12 CONTROL TOWER

The pricing control tower is a derived operational view,
not a canonical financial authority.

# =============================================================================
# 25. PERFORMANCE, SCALABILITY, AND COST GOVERNANCE
# =============================================================================

25.1 DESIGN OBJECTIVE

Support growth in resources, sellers, price books, pricing
methods, currencies, policy complexity, and pricing request
volume without requiring fundamental redesign.

25.2 NO INFINITE-THROUGHPUT CLAIM

Physical infrastructure is finite. Scalability must be
engineered and measured against explicit workload targets.

25.3 SCALABILITY DIMENSIONS

Consider:

- Number of resources.
- Number of variants.
- Number of sellers.
- Number of price books.
- Number of pricing policies.
- Number of concurrent requests.
- Pricing method complexity.
- Quote volume.
- Currency conversion volume.
- Tax and offer integration latency.
- Policy publication frequency.
- Historical lineage volume.
- Reconciliation workload.
- Geographic distribution.
- Tenant isolation.
- Audit retention.

25.4 RESOURCE BUDGETS

Each pricing operation must have defined processing and
dependency budgets.

25.5 DEPENDENCY ISOLATION

A slow tax or offer authority must not create unbounded
resource consumption across all pricing requests.

25.6 CACHING

Caching is permitted only where price validity, context,
authorization, and freshness semantics remain correct.

25.7 CACHE KEYS

Cache identity must include every context dimension material
to price resolution.

25.8 CACHE INVALIDATION

Material price, policy, tax-context, offer, or other relevant
changes must trigger the required invalidation or revalidation.

25.9 GRACEFUL DEGRADATION

A degraded response must remain semantically honest.

The system must not silently convert a failed authoritative
calculation into a final price.

25.10 CAPACITY TESTING

Use representative load, stress, endurance, and failure testing.

25.11 COST OBSERVABILITY

Measure computational and dependency costs where feasible.

25.12 PERFORMANCE TARGETS

Latency, throughput, availability, and freshness targets must
be established from approved workload and business requirements.

# =============================================================================
# 26. FAILURE HANDLING AND RECOVERY
# =============================================================================

26.1 FAILURE CLASSIFICATION

Potential failures include:

- Invalid pricing request.
- No applicable price.
- Conflicting price books.
- Invalid currency.
- Missing exchange rate.
- Unsupported pricing method.
- Invalid formula.
- Guardrail violation.
- Cost source unavailable.
- Tax authority unavailable.
- Offer authority unavailable.
- Contract authority unavailable.
- Stale price.
- Expired quote.
- Invalid policy version.
- Rounding mismatch.
- Unauthorized override.
- Price-history inconsistency.
- Duplicate component.
- Currency mismatch.
- Invalid quantity.
- Quote tampering.
- Reconciliation failure.
- Policy publication failure.

26.2 EXPLICIT OUTCOMES

Failures must produce a typed result rather than a fabricated amount.

26.3 REQUIRED DEPENDENCY FAILURE

When a required authority is unavailable, follow the defined
failure policy for that authority and use case.

26.4 OPTIONAL DEPENDENCY FAILURE

An optional component may be omitted only when its omission
is permitted and the resulting price semantics remain correct.

26.5 RETRIES

Retries must be bounded, observable, and safe.

26.6 TIMEOUTS

Every external dependency must have explicit timeout behavior.

26.7 CIRCUIT BREAKERS

Dependency protection must prevent cascading failure.

26.8 FALLBACK PRICE

Fallback pricing is allowed only when explicitly governed,
authorized, and valid for the context.

26.9 STALE PRICE

A stale price must be rejected, revalidated, or presented
with permitted limitations according to policy.

26.10 QUOTE EXPIRATION

An expired quote must not be silently treated as current.

26.11 RECOVERY

Recovery must preserve price lineage and prevent duplicate
financial effects in downstream systems.

26.12 NO FALSE SUCCESS

A successful transport response must not conceal a failed
mandatory price calculation.

# =============================================================================

27.5 EVENT ORDERING

27.6 REPLAY

27.7 EVENT SECURITY

through unauthorized event subscriptions.

27.8 FAILED EVENTS

through governed procedures.

# =============================================================================
# 28. API AND INTEGRATION CONTRACTS
# =============================================================================

28.1 API PRINCIPLES

Interfaces must be:

- Versioned.
- Authenticated.
- Authorized.
- Observable.
- Bounded.
- Explicit about monetary semantics.
- Explicit about currency.
- Explicit about validity.
- Explicit about failure.
- Compatible with canonical UCOS contracts.
- Vendor-neutral.

28.2 LOGICAL API GROUPS

A. PRICE RESOLUTION
   Resolve a price for a defined resource and context.

B. PRICE CALCULATION
   Calculate a price under an approved pricing method.

C. PRICE VALIDATION
   Validate a price result, quote, or calculation.

D. PRICE BOOK LOOKUP
   Resolve applicable price-book references.

E. QUOTE MANAGEMENT
   Create, issue, validate, accept, expire, or invalidate quotes
   through the approved lifecycle.

F. PRICE HISTORY
   Retrieve authorized historical price decisions and lineage.

G. PRICE POLICY MANAGEMENT
   Access or update pricing policies through approved governance.

H. PRICE CHANGE MANAGEMENT
   Submit, validate, approve, schedule, and publish price changes.

I. PRICE RECONCILIATION
   Identify and manage price inconsistencies.

J. PRICING ANALYTICS
   Retrieve authorized aggregate pricing metrics.

These are logical API groups, not finalized endpoint definitions.

28.3 COMMAND-QUERY SEPARATION

Read operations and state-changing operations must remain
distinguishable.

28.4 AUTHORIZATION

Callers must be authorized for the relevant resources,
commercial context, fields, and operations.

28.5 MONEY CONTRACTS

Monetary values must have explicit amount, currency, semantic
type, and applicable precision.

28.6 IDEMPOTENCY

State-changing requests must follow canonical idempotency
requirements.

28.7 ERROR MODEL

Errors should distinguish:

- Invalid request.
- No applicable price.
- Conflicting policies.
- Unsupported pricing method.
- Currency mismatch.
- Missing exchange rate.
- Guardrail violation.
- Required dependency unavailable.
- Expired quote.
- Unauthorized operation.
- Approval required.
- Policy conflict.
- Stale result.
- Invalid version.
- Resource budget exceeded.
- Internal processing failure.

28.8 VERSIONING

Breaking changes must follow canonical UCOS API governance.

28.9 EXTERNAL PROVIDERS

External pricing, tax, exchange-rate, or analytical services
must be integrated through approved adapters.

28.10 NO PROVIDER LOCK-IN

Canonical pricing contracts must remain independent of
a particular external provider.
