# =============================================================================
# 30. RECONCILIATION AND EXCEPTION MANAGEMENT
# =============================================================================

30.1 PURPOSE

Detect and resolve inconsistencies among price definitions,
pricing policies, derived results, and canonical financial
or commercial authorities.

30.2 RECONCILIATION SCENARIOS

- Two active price books match the same context without a
  valid precedence rule.
- A price definition references a nonexistent resource.
- A price definition uses an unsupported currency.
- A price component uses incompatible monetary semantics.
- A pricing policy refers to a retired method.
- A policy is activated before approval.
- A price change fails to propagate to a derived projection.
- A stale price is presented as current.
- An issued quote is overwritten.
- An expired quote is accepted without required revalidation.
- A discount is applied twice.
- A tax result is associated with an incompatible context.
- A conversion uses an invalid exchange-rate purpose.
- A calculation uses incorrect rounding.
- A cost input is stale for a cost-sensitive guardrail.
- A margin rule uses an ambiguous cost basis.
- A contractual price is overridden without authorization.
- A seller-owned price is modified without authority.
- A dynamic-pricing policy exceeds an approved movement threshold.
- A price experiment violates a guardrail.
- A price component lacks source provenance.
- A zero amount is confused with a missing amount.
- A price is displayed in the wrong currency.
- A required fee is omitted from a finalized price.
- A tax-inclusive amount is presented as tax-exclusive.
- A price projection conflicts with the canonical price authority.
- A price event is replayed and creates duplicate changes.
- A quote references an obsolete policy version.
- A final payable amount does not reconcile with its components.
- An unauthorized user changes a pricing guardrail.
- An aggregation combines currencies without an approved conversion.

30.3 EXCEPTION RECORD

An exception should identify:

- Exception identifier.
- Affected price or policy reference.
- Canonical source authority.
- Expected state.
- Observed state.
- Applicable version.
- Severity.
- Detection time.
- Business impact.
- Responsible owner.
- Remediation status.
- Resolution evidence.

30.4 SOURCE AUTHORITY

The relevant canonical domain resolves business truth.

The pricing capability resolves price construction and pricing-
specific policy problems within its authorized boundary.

30.5 HIGH-IMPACT EXCEPTIONS

Unauthorized price changes, invalid contractual prices,
material financial inconsistencies, and prohibited price
disclosures must follow the appropriate incident workflow.

30.6 AUTOMATED CORRECTION

Automated repair is permitted only when explicitly governed,
safe, reproducible, and auditable.

30.7 NO SILENT REPAIR

Material discrepancies must not be concealed through display-only
changes or untraceable recalculation.

# =============================================================================
# 31. FAILURE SCENARIO CATALOG
# =============================================================================

FS-001 — NO APPLICABLE PRICE
Expected: Return an explicit unresolved-price outcome.

FS-002 — MULTIPLE CONFLICTING PRICE BOOKS
Expected: Apply approved precedence or return a conflict.

FS-003 — INVALID CURRENCY
Expected: Reject the invalid currency reference.

FS-004 — EXCHANGE RATE UNAVAILABLE
Expected: Return an explicit conversion failure unless an
approved fallback is valid for the context.

FS-005 — UNSUPPORTED PRICING METHOD
Expected: Reject or route through an approved alternative.

FS-006 — INVALID QUANTITY
Expected: Enforce canonical quantity and unit semantics.

FS-007 — ROUNDING MISMATCH
Expected: Identify the violated rounding contract and prevent
an inconsistent final result.

FS-008 — CURRENCY MISMATCH
Expected: Reject incompatible component composition or apply
an explicitly authorized conversion.

FS-009 — DUPLICATE DISCOUNT
Expected: Prevent duplicate application unless expressly permitted.

FS-010 — OFFER AUTHORITY UNAVAILABLE
Expected: Follow the defined failure policy without inventing
benefit eligibility.

FS-011 — TAX AUTHORITY UNAVAILABLE
Expected: Follow the applicable tax and commercial failure policy.

FS-012 — GUARDRAIL BREACH
Expected: Reject, escalate, or request authorized approval.

FS-013 — STALE PRICE
Expected: Revalidate, reject, or identify the permitted stale status.

FS-014 — EXPIRED QUOTE
Expected: Prevent use as a current quote without authorization.

FS-015 — ISSUED QUOTE OVERWRITTEN
Expected: Preserve the issued record and use the canonical
amendment or invalidation workflow.

FS-016 — CONTRACTUAL PRICE OVERRIDDEN
Expected: Enforce contract authority and trigger the required
review or incident process.

FS-017 — UNAUTHORIZED PRICE CHANGE
Expected: Reject the operation and audit the attempt.

FS-018 — PRICE BOOK ACTIVATED WITHOUT APPROVAL
Expected: Prevent activation and raise a governance exception.

FS-019 — COST INPUT UNAVAILABLE
Expected: Apply the approved cost-sensitive guardrail policy.

FS-020 — MARGIN FORMULA AMBIGUOUS
Expected: Reject the formula until its financial semantics
are explicitly defined.

FS-021 — DYNAMIC PRICE VOLATILITY
Expected: Trigger the approved monitoring, pause, or review behavior.

FS-022 — PROHIBITED PERSONALIZED PRICING INPUT
Expected: Reject the input and record the appropriate policy outcome.

FS-023 — PRICE COMPONENT OMITTED
Expected: Fail validation if the component is mandatory.

FS-024 — TAX-INCLUSION SEMANTICS CONFLICT
Expected: Reject the ambiguous result and resolve the tax contract.

FS-025 — ZERO PRICE CONFUSED WITH MISSING PRICE
Expected: Preserve explicit zero and unknown as distinct states.

FS-026 — EVENT REPLAY DUPLICATES CHANGE
Expected: Enforce idempotent processing.

FS-027 — OUT-OF-ORDER POLICY UPDATE
Expected: Prevent regression to an older active policy version.

FS-028 — PRICE HISTORY TAMPERING
Expected: Block unauthorized mutation and initiate the
appropriate security response.

FS-029 — COST DATA LEAK
Expected: Block unauthorized disclosure and investigate.

FS-030 — TENANT BOUNDARY VIOLATION
Expected: Prevent access and trigger the security workflow.

FS-031 — QUOTE CONTEXT CHANGED
Expected: Revalidate according to the quote's validity contract.

FS-032 — FINAL TOTAL DOES NOT RECONCILE
Expected: Block finalization or escalate under approved policy.

FS-033 — CURRENCY AGGREGATION INVALID
Expected: Require approved currency normalization.

FS-034 — PRICE CHANGE FAILS TO PROPAGATE
Expected: Identify stale projections and initiate reconciliation.

FS-035 — EXPERIMENT GUARDRAIL BREACH
Expected: Stop or mitigate the experiment according to policy.

FS-036 — UNAUTHORIZED FORMULA EXECUTION
Expected: Reject execution and trigger security monitoring.

FS-037 — PRICE PRESENTATION MISLEADING
Expected: Correct the presentation and apply required review.

FS-038 — TAX OR FEE RESULT HAS WRONG CONTEXT
Expected: Reject the incompatible component.

FS-039 — STALE CONTRACT REFERENCE
Expected: Revalidate the applicable contract authority.

FS-040 — PRICING SUCCESS MASKS REQUIRED FAILURE
Expected: Return an explicit failure or unresolved result.

FS-041 — SELLER PRICE MUTATED WITHOUT AUTHORITY
Expected: Block the change and preserve audit evidence.

FS-042 — EXCHANGE-RATE PURPOSE MISUSED
Expected: Reject the conversion.

FS-043 — PRICE POLICY VERSION MISMATCH
Expected: Resolve version compatibility before producing
a final result.

FS-044 — HISTORICAL RECOMPUTATION MISREPRESENTED
Expected: Distinguish the original decision from a recomputed result.

FS-045 — DUPLICATE PRICE COMPONENT
Expected: Detect and reject unauthorized duplicate composition.

# 32. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
# =============================================================================

AC-001
Every pricing fact has an identified canonical authority.

AC-002
Existing UCOS pricing and financial capabilities are reconciled
before new capabilities are proposed.

AC-003
Price representations have explicit semantic types.

AC-004
Every monetary amount identifies its currency.

AC-005
Currency precision comes from canonical monetary semantics.

AC-006
Financial calculations use appropriate exact or decimal
arithmetic under the approved contract.

AC-007
Rounding rules are explicit, versioned, and reproducible.

AC-008
Price books have explicit scope, ownership, applicability,
and effective-time semantics.

AC-009
Conflicting price policies cannot silently produce an arbitrary
commercial result.

AC-010
Pricing-method extensions implement the approved common contract.

AC-011
Price components have explicit calculation and provenance semantics.

AC-012
Tax determination remains with the canonical tax authority.

AC-013
Discount and offer eligibility remains with the canonical
offer authority.

AC-014
Cost and margin guardrails use correctly defined financial inputs.

AC-015
Margin and markup are not conflated.

AC-016
Contractual prices cannot be overridden without authorized
governance.

AC-017
Dynamic pricing has approved inputs, constraints, monitoring,
and rollback behavior.

AC-018
Pricing experiments have explicit guardrails and approval.

AC-019
Personalized pricing follows applicable legal, privacy, and
ethical requirements.

AC-020
Issued quotes have explicit validity and expiration semantics.

AC-021
Issued quotes cannot be silently overwritten.

AC-022
Historical price decisions preserve required lineage.

AC-023
A recomputed historical price is distinguishable from the
original recorded decision.

AC-024
Price changes follow governed approval and publication workflows.

AC-025
Stale prices are handled according to explicit freshness policy.

AC-026
Price calculations reconcile with their component amounts.

AC-027
Currency conversions use approved exchange-rate sources and purposes.

AC-028
Mandatory tax and fee components cannot be silently omitted.

AC-029
Pricing APIs distinguish unresolved prices, invalid inputs,
policy conflicts, and dependency failures.

AC-030
Pricing configurations cannot execute unbounded or unauthorized code.

AC-031
Cost and margin data are protected from unauthorized disclosure.

AC-032
Tenant and authorization boundaries are preserved.

AC-033
Price history and material decisions are auditable.

AC-034
Pricing changes and projections are reconcilable.

AC-035
Pricing metrics distinguish estimates from realized financial outcomes.

AC-036
Price explanations identify material calculation sources and rules.

AC-037
All proposed contracts and registries are reconciled with
canonical UCOS governance.

AC-038
Every approved requirement traces to a canonical artifact,
implementation or reuse decision, and verification evidence.

AC-039
Required arithmetic, rounding, currency, and component tests
are defined and executed before certification.

AC-040
Implementation requires context assimilation, canonical
reconciliation, required approvals, and explicit authorization.

These acceptance criteria are proposed. No successful verification
is claimed by this document.

# 36. READINESS GATES
# =============================================================================

GATE G0 — CONTEXT ASSIMILATION

Review existing UCOS monetary, pricing, product, variant,
catalog, offer, promotion, tax, currency, exchange-rate,
cost, accounting, contract, quote, order, and settlement artifacts.

EXIT CRITERION:
Relevant canonical capabilities and authorities are identified.

GATE G1 — CANONICAL RECONCILIATION

Classify each proposed capability as reusable, extensible,
duplicated, conflicting, missing, or unnecessary.

EXIT CRITERION:
No unresolved authority duplication remains.

GATE G2 — PRICE ONTOLOGY

Reconcile price semantics, components, monetary representation,
currency, quantity, and validity.

EXIT CRITERION:
Price values are semantically unambiguous.

GATE G3 — POLICY AND PRECEDENCE

Validate policy applicability, priority, conflict behavior,
effective-time semantics, and override authorization.

EXIT CRITERION:
No unresolved policy conflict can silently produce a price.

GATE G4 — CALCULATION CORRECTNESS

Validate pricing methods, component composition, precision,
rounding, currency conversion, and reconciliation.

EXIT CRITERION:
Calculation contracts are deterministic and testable.

GATE G5 — FINANCIAL AND COMMERCIAL GUARDRAILS

Validate cost and margin semantics, contractual constraints,
tax integration, offers, fees, and seller authority.

EXIT CRITERION:
No unauthorized commercial or financial authority is introduced.

GATE G6 — QUOTES AND PRICE CHANGES

Validate quote validity, expiration, history, approval,
publication, and rollback.

EXIT CRITERION:
Price commitments and material changes have explicit lifecycles.

GATE G7 — SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND ETHICS

Validate authorization, separation of duties, cost-data
protection, privacy, fairness, and dynamic-pricing controls.

EXIT CRITERION:
Required controls and approvals are documented.

GATE G8 — VERIFICATION

Execute approved arithmetic, rounding, currency, policy,
security, performance, failure, and reconciliation tests.

EXIT CRITERION:
Required verification evidence is reproducible.

GATE G9 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION

Obtain the required governance approvals and explicit
implementation authorization.

EXIT CRITERION:
Only the approved scope may proceed.

# =============================================================================
# 37. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
# =============================================================================

1. Do not create a competing canonical pricing authority.
2. Do not create a second monetary or currency authority.
3. Do not redefine canonical product, variant, or seller identity.
4. Do not duplicate tax determination.
5. Do not duplicate offer eligibility.
6. Do not duplicate accounting, payment, settlement, or ledger truth.
7. Do not conflate price, cost, revenue, settlement, and payable amount.
8. Do not represent a monetary amount without explicit currency semantics.
9. Do not represent a missing price as zero.
10. Do not silently convert currencies.
11. Do not invent exchange rates.
12. Do not use an exchange rate for an incompatible financial purpose.
13. Do not use uncontrolled binary floating-point as the financial
    source of truth.
14. Do not leave rounding behavior implicit.
15. Do not apply duplicate price components without authorization.
16. Do not silently omit a required tax, fee, or discount component.
17. Do not invent offer eligibility.
18. Do not override contractual pricing without authorization.
19. Do not bypass price guardrails.
20. Do not permit unauthorized price-book publication.
21. Do not allow ambiguous policy precedence to produce arbitrary prices.
22. Do not execute unbounded or unauthorized pricing formulas.
23. Do not allow dynamic pricing to use prohibited inputs.
24. Do not allow automated models to modify production pricing
    policy without governance.
25. Do not use sensitive or protected characteristics in prohibited
    pricing decisions.
26. Do not expose internal cost or margin data to unauthorized parties.
27. Do not silently overwrite issued quotes.
28. Do not treat expired quotes as current without authorization.
29. Do not misrepresent recomputed historical prices as original decisions.
30. Do not let presentation formatting alter authoritative amounts.
31. Do not represent estimated prices as final or guaranteed.
32. Do not aggregate currencies without an approved normalization policy.
33. Do not treat customer price as seller settlement.
34. Do not treat a price quote as a payment authorization.
35. Do not silently change contractual price commitments.
36. Do not conceal price calculation or reconciliation failures.
37. Do not create duplicate pricing APIs, registries, or events without
    a documented reuse analysis.
38. Do not claim financial correctness without executed verification.
39. Do not claim certification without reproducible evidence.
40. Do not modify the UCOS repository without explicit authorization.

# =============================================================================
# 38. MASTER TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS
# =============================================================================

38.1 TRACEABILITY CHAIN

Every approved pricing requirement must trace through:

CANONICAL AUTHORITY
    ->
BUSINESS REQUIREMENT
    ->
PRICING POLICY OR METHOD
    ->
CANONICAL ARTIFACT OR APPROVED EXTENSION
    ->
MONETARY / API / EVENT CONTRACT
    ->
IMPLEMENTATION OR REUSE DECISION
    ->
TEST CASE
    ->
VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
    ->
GOVERNANCE APPROVAL
    ->
RELEASE AUTHORIZATION

38.2 REQUIREMENT IDENTIFIERS

Requirement identifiers must be allocated through canonical
UCOS identifier governance.

38.3 BIDIRECTIONAL TRACEABILITY

Material implementation artifacts must trace back to an
approved requirement or an explicitly approved operational need.

38.4 FINANCIAL LINEAGE

Every financially significant price decision must preserve
the required input, policy, calculation, and output lineage.

38.5 CHANGE IMPACT

Changes to currency semantics, rounding policies, price methods,
tax contracts, offer contracts, or precedence rules must identify
affected consumers and verification requirements.

38.6 ORPHAN PREVENTION

Unreferenced pricing artifacts must be detected through
canonical registry and dependency-governance mechanisms.

38.7 KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Traceability must reference canonical financial and commercial
definitions instead of duplicating their authoritative content.

# =============================================================================
# 39. FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULES
# =============================================================================

RULE 001 — CANONICAL AUTHORITY
Every pricing fact has one designated canonical owner.

RULE 002 — KNOWLEDGE ONCE
Canonical pricing knowledge is authored once and reused.

RULE 003 — REUSE FIRST
Existing UCOS pricing and monetary capabilities must be
evaluated before new capabilities are proposed.

RULE 004 — EXPLICIT SEMANTICS
Every price amount has a defined meaning.

RULE 005 — EXPLICIT CURRENCY
Every monetary result has an explicit currency reference.

RULE 006 — EXACT FINANCIAL ARITHMETIC
Monetary calculations follow approved precision and arithmetic rules.

RULE 007 — EXPLICIT ROUNDING
Rounding behavior is governed, versioned, and reproducible.

RULE 008 — DETERMINISTIC RESOLUTION
The same authoritative inputs and policies produce the same
result under the same defined calculation context.

RULE 009 — GOVERNED PRECEDENCE
Conflicting pricing policies cannot silently produce arbitrary prices.

RULE 010 — PLUGGABLE METHODS
Pricing methods use an explicit, governed extension contract.

RULE 011 — COMPONENT LINEAGE
Material price components retain their source and calculation lineage.

RULE 012 — TAX AUTHORITY
Tax determination remains with the canonical tax capability.

RULE 013 — OFFER AUTHORITY
Offer eligibility remains with the canonical offer capability.

RULE 014 — FINANCIAL BOUNDARIES
Pricing does not replace accounting, payment, settlement, or ledgers.

RULE 015 — COST SEMANTICS
Cost and margin calculations use explicitly defined financial inputs.

RULE 016 — GUARDRAIL ENFORCEMENT
Mandatory commercial constraints cannot be silently bypassed.

RULE 017 — DYNAMIC-PRICING GOVERNANCE
Automated price changes use approved inputs, constraints, and oversight.

RULE 018 — QUOTE INTEGRITY
Issued quotes have explicit validity and cannot be silently overwritten.

RULE 019 — HISTORICAL DISTINCTION
Original historical decisions remain distinguishable from recomputations.

RULE 020 — TEMPORAL CORRECTNESS
Effective time and recording time remain distinct.

RULE 021 — PRICE CHANGE GOVERNANCE
Material price changes follow approval and publication rules.

RULE 022 — CONTRACTUAL INTEGRITY
Contractual pricing cannot be overridden by unapproved optimization.

RULE 023 — SELLER AUTHORITY
Seller-owned pricing follows explicit ownership and marketplace boundaries.

RULE 024 — PRICE TRANSPARENCY
Customer-facing representations must not be materially misleading.

RULE 025 — PRIVACY AND FAIRNESS
Pricing inputs and outcomes follow applicable privacy and fairness rules.

RULE 026 — SECURITY
Price definitions, policies, quotes, and history are protected against
unauthorized access or modification.

RULE 027 — RECONCILIATION
Price results and their components must reconcile under the approved model.

RULE 028 — OBSERVABILITY
Material pricing failures, stale inputs, and policy violations are visible.

RULE 029 — EXPLICIT FAILURE
A failed mandatory calculation must not produce a fabricated final price.

RULE 030 — NO SHADOW AUTHORITY
Pricing must not become the canonical owner of external-domain facts.

RULE 031 — VENDOR NEUTRALITY
Canonical pricing contracts remain independent of specific vendors.

RULE 032 — EVIDENCE-BASED QUALITY
Pricing correctness requires appropriate verification evidence.

RULE 033 — NO FALSE CERTIFICATION
A complete specification does not establish implementation correctness.

RULE 034 — CONTROLLED EVOLUTION
Material pricing changes follow canonical UCOS governance.

RULE 035 — IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORIZATION
This specification alone does not authorize repository or production changes.

Document 016 will define the Universal Marketplace Payment and Payment Orchestration Specification. Its scope is payment processing and payment-state authority, including authorization, capture, voids, refunds integration, payment routing, provider abstraction, idempotency, failure recovery, reconciliation, and security.
The specification will preserve the boundaries established in the proposed master index:
- Document 015 — Pricing: authoritative commercial price construction and price quotation.
- Document 016 — Payments: authoritative payment processing and payment transaction state.
- Document 008 — Marketplace Operations: order orchestration, operational exception handling, settlement, and related reconciliation responsibilities, subject to canonical scope reconciliation.
- Document 018 — Cart and Checkout: purchase-journey coordination, to be specified later and integrated through explicit contracts.
The document below is a proposed architecture specification, not evidence that existing UCOS artifacts have been inspected, implementation has begun, or payment capabilities have been certified.

## DOCUMENT STATUS DECLARATION

This specification defines the proposed architecture, capabilities, requirements, contracts, invariants, security boundaries, failure-handling principles, and acceptance criteria for the Universal Marketplace Payment and Payment Orchestration domain.

It is a proposed canonical candidate until reconciled against the authoritative UCOS architecture, existing marketplace specifications, registries, constitutions, and implementation contracts.

No claim is made that this document has been merged into the UCOS repository, that the proposed identifiers are registered, or that any implementation, automated test, security assessment, or certification has been completed.

The specification must not override an existing canonical UCOS authority.

Where an existing canonical authority already defines a concept, its authority must be reused. Any conflict must be resolved through formal architectural reconciliation before implementation.

---

# PART I — EXECUTIVE ARCHITECTURE

## 1. PURPOSE

The purpose of this specification is to define a universal, extensible, secure, auditable, provider-neutral payment capability for UCOS Ω∞.

The payment domain must support payment processing across multiple marketplace models, industries, transaction types, participant structures, geographical jurisdictions, currencies, channels, and execution environments.

The architecture must support simple transactions as well as complex commercial arrangements without embedding assumptions about a particular payment provider, bank, payment method, currency, country, industry, database, cloud, programming language, or deployment model.

The payment capability must coordinate payment operations while preserving the authority of the systems responsible for:

- Commercial pricing.
- Purchase intent and checkout.
- Order lifecycle.
- Inventory and fulfillment.
- Customer and participant identity.
- Fraud and risk decisions.
- Financial accounting.
- Seller settlement.
- Tax determination.
- Refund eligibility.
- Regulatory compliance.
- Audit and governance.

The payment domain is responsible for payment execution semantics and payment transaction truth, not for independently redefining every business concept that participates in a transaction.

## 2. ARCHITECTURAL VISION

Establish a universal payment orchestration capability that:

1. Accepts a validated payment intent.
2. Verifies authorization to initiate the requested operation.
3. Validates the commercial and operational context required for processing.
4. Selects an eligible payment execution route.
5. Invokes a suitable payment instrument, processor, acquirer, bank, wallet, or other authorized payment mechanism.
6. Tracks asynchronous and synchronous outcomes.
7. Preserves transaction identity and idempotency.
8. Prevents unauthorized duplicate execution.
9. Maintains an auditable history of payment state transitions.
10. Supports authorization, capture, void, reversal, refund coordination, and applicable payment-specific operations.
11. Reconciles internal records with external payment evidence.
12. Exposes canonical payment state to authorized consumers.
13. Supports recovery from timeouts, partial failures, delayed notifications, and external-system outages.
14. Enables new payment methods and providers through governed extensions.
15. Supports continuous verification of financial and security invariants.

The architecture must favor correctness and recoverability over optimistic assumptions about external-system behavior.

## 3. DESIGN PRINCIPLES

### 3.1 Canonical authority

Every business fact has one authoritative owner.

Payment records must not become an alternative authority for order totals, tax determination, product prices, inventory, seller settlement, or accounting balances.

### 3.2 Knowledge Once

Canonical payment semantics, payment states, identifiers, and shared definitions must be authored once and reused.

Multiple representations are allowed when they are derived, explicitly mapped, and traceable to their canonical source.

### 3.3 Provider neutrality

Provider-specific behavior must be isolated behind governed integration contracts.

Provider-neutrality does not imply that every provider supports every capability or that provider differences can be eliminated.

Unsupported capabilities must be explicitly declared and validated.

### 3.4 Technology neutrality

The architecture must not mandate a particular:

- Programming language.
- Database.
- Message broker.
- Cloud platform.
- Operating system.
- API framework.
- Container runtime.
- Workflow engine.
- Deployment topology.
- Observability vendor.

Concrete implementation choices must be recorded through approved architecture decisions.

### 3.5 Explicit state

Payment states must be modeled explicitly.

A timeout must never be interpreted automatically as proof that a payment failed.

An HTTP success response must not automatically be interpreted as proof of financial completion.

### 3.6 Idempotent execution

Every externally consequential operation must have an idempotency strategy.

The strategy must account for internal retries, concurrent requests, delayed callbacks, external-provider semantics, and ambiguous outcomes.

### 3.7 Evidence-based financial truth

Financial state must be supported by authoritative transaction evidence.

The system must distinguish:

- A requested operation.
- An operation accepted for processing.
- A provider-reported result.
- A verified financial outcome.
- A reconciled financial record.

### 3.8 Fail closed where necessary

Security violations, unauthorized operations, invalid currency representations, contradictory financial instructions, and prohibited state transitions must not proceed.

When external uncertainty prevents a definitive result, the system must preserve uncertainty explicitly rather than manufacture a success or failure.

### 3.9 Append-only audit history

Material payment state transitions and financial evidence must be recorded in an auditable history.

Corrections must be represented through compensating or superseding records rather than destructive rewriting of historical financial evidence.

### 3.10 Context Assimilation Gate

No implementation may begin until relevant canonical context has been discovered, read, reconciled, and accepted.

# PART II — SCOPE AND BOUNDARIES

## 4. IN-SCOPE CAPABILITIES

The payment domain includes:

1. Payment intent management.
2. Payment operation lifecycle.
3. Payment attempt management.
4. Payment instrument references.
5. Payment method capability declarations.
6. Payment provider integration.
7. Payment routing and failover policy.
8. Authorization processing.
9. Capture processing.
10. Authorization cancellation and void operations.
11. Reversal processing where supported.
12. Refund execution coordination.
13. Payment status inquiry.
14. Asynchronous result processing.
15. Provider notification processing.
16. Idempotency and duplicate suppression.
17. Transaction correlation.
18. Provider capability discovery.
19. Payment operation policy enforcement.
20. Payment execution risk controls.
21. Payment-specific fraud and risk integration.
22. Payment-specific authentication integration.
23. Payment token references.
24. Payment operation limits and constraints.
25. Currency and amount validation.
26. Payment operation concurrency control.
27. Financial evidence ingestion.
28. Payment reconciliation.
29. Payment exception management.
30. Payment audit history.
31. Payment operational monitoring.
32. Payment failure recovery.
33. Provider contract validation.
34. Payment integration certification.
35. Payment capability registration.
36. Payment lifecycle event publication.
37. Payment data lineage.
38. Payment security controls.
39. Payment configuration governance.
40. Payment capability extensibility.

## 5. EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE

Unless a separately approved architecture decision assigns a narrowly defined responsibility to this domain, the following remain outside its canonical authority.

### 5.1 Commercial price construction

Owned by the authoritative pricing domain, proposed as Document 015.

Payment processing consumes a validated payable amount and its associated commercial context.

Payment processing must not independently recalculate the authoritative product price, discount, or commercial total.

### 5.2 Cart and checkout orchestration

Planned for Document 018.

Checkout coordinates the purchase journey and requests payment operations through explicit contracts.

Payment processing must not own the entire checkout workflow.

### 5.3 Order lifecycle

Owned by the authoritative order domain, with operational scope described in Document 008 pending reconciliation.

Payment processing must not independently create competing order-state truth.

### 5.4 Inventory and fulfillment

Owned by the relevant inventory, order, fulfillment, and operational authorities.

Payment processing may consume reservation or fulfillment references when required by policy.

### 5.5 Tax determination

Owned by the authoritative tax capability.

Payment processing may consume a validated payable total and tax-related references, but it must not silently become the tax calculation authority.

### 5.6 Seller settlement

The marketplace settlement authority remains within the reconciled financial and operational architecture, including Document 008 where applicable.

A payment capture is not automatically equivalent to seller settlement.

### 5.7 General ledger and accounting

The accounting authority determines ledger posting semantics and financial account balances.

Payment processing must provide traceable transaction facts and accounting integration evidence without creating a competing general ledger.

### 5.8 Canonical identity

Customer, seller, merchant, administrator, and service identities must be resolved through the existing canonical identity authority.

### 5.9 General fraud intelligence

Document 013 is the proposed marketplace trust, safety, and fraud authority.

This document defines payment-specific enforcement interfaces, not a competing fraud intelligence universe.

### 5.10 General security and compliance

Existing UCOS security, privacy, identity, governance, and compliance authorities remain authoritative.

This specification defines payment-specific applications of those controls.

# PART III — CANONICAL PAYMENT ONTOLOGY

## 6. CANONICAL TERMS

The following definitions are proposed for reconciliation.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Payment Intent | A request to perform a defined payment-related financial operation in a specific commercial context. |
| Payment | The canonical payment aggregate representing the payment lifecycle and its related operations. |
| Payment Attempt | One execution attempt associated with a payment operation. |
| Payment Operation | A requested action such as authorization, capture, void, reversal, or refund. |
| Payment Instrument Reference | A governed reference to a payment mechanism, token, wallet, account instrument, or equivalent authorized payment source. |
| Payment Method | A classification of how payment is initiated or executed. |
| Payment Provider | An external or internal participant capable of performing a declared payment capability. |
| Payment Route | A governed execution path through one or more authorized payment components. |
| Payment Authorization | A provider-confirmed approval to reserve or approve an amount under a defined payment arrangement. |
| Payment Capture | An instruction to complete or initiate the financial collection associated with a supported authorization or payment arrangement. |
| Payment Void | An instruction to cancel an eligible operation before its relevant financial completion boundary. |
| Payment Reversal | A payment-system operation intended to negate or unwind a prior transaction according to the supported payment protocol. |
| Refund | A payment-related operation intended to return funds or value under an authorized refund instruction. |
| Payment Attempt Outcome | The observed or verified outcome of one execution attempt. |
| Provider Reference | An identifier assigned by a payment provider to a payment or operation. |
| Idempotency Key | A stable key used to recognize repeated requests representing the same logical operation. |
| Payment Evidence | A record or observation supporting a payment-state assertion. |
| Payment Reconciliation | Comparison of internal payment records against external payment evidence and other authoritative financial records. |
| Payment Exception | A condition requiring controlled recovery, investigation, or human intervention. |
| Payment Capability Declaration | A machine-readable statement of the capabilities and constraints supported by a payment method, provider, route, or instrument. |
| Payment Execution Policy | A governed rule set determining whether and how a payment operation may execute. |
| Financial Operation | A state-changing payment operation with a defined amount, currency, identity, and business purpose. |
| External Financial Side Effect | A consequential action outside the internal system, such as a provider instruction that may cause a financial transaction. |
| Uncertain Outcome | A state in which the system cannot yet establish whether the requested external operation succeeded. |

## 7. ONTOLOGY INVARIANTS

### 7.1 Distinct identities

The following identifiers must remain distinct:

- Payment ID.
- Payment intent ID.
- Payment operation ID.
- Payment attempt ID.
- Order ID.
- Checkout ID.
- Refund request ID.
- Refund operation ID.
- Provider transaction reference.
- Provider operation reference.
- Idempotency key.
- Reconciliation record ID.
- Settlement reference.
- Accounting reference.

An identifier may reference another identifier, but one identifier must not be reused as the canonical identity of a different entity type.

### 7.2 Distinct financial concepts

The architecture must distinguish:

- Requested amount.
- Authorized amount.
- Captured amount.
- Refunded amount.
- Reversed amount.
- Remaining capturable amount.
- Remaining refundable amount.
- Provider-reported amount.
- Reconciled amount.
- Settled amount.
- Accounted amount.

These amounts must not be treated as interchangeable.

### 7.3 Amount and currency integrity

Every monetary amount must have an explicit currency or other formally defined unit where the underlying payment system supports it.

The representation must use exact decimal or integer-minor-unit semantics as appropriate to the currency and instrument.

Binary floating-point arithmetic must not be used as the authoritative representation for financial amounts.

Currency precision and permitted rounding must be defined by canonical currency rules and applicable payment contracts.

### 7.4 Immutable operation identity

Once a financial operation has been submitted for external execution, its identity, intended amount, currency, and business purpose must not be silently mutated.

A correction requires a governed new operation or compensating action.

### 7.5 Evidence-based state

Every material state transition must be supported by:

- The operation that initiated the transition.
- The observed evidence.
- The authority that accepted the evidence.
- The relevant timestamp information.
- The transition rule.
- The resulting state.

Responsible for:
- Provider responses.

- Transaction reports.
- External financial evidence.
- Evidence provenance.
- Conflict detection.
9.4 Reconciliation plane
Responsible for:
- Matching internal and external records.
- Detecting discrepancies.

PART V — PAYMENT LIFECYCLE
10. PAYMENT INTENT LIFECYCLE
A proposed payment intent lifecycle is:
CREATED
   |
   v
VALIDATING
   |
   +------> REJECTED
   |
   v
VALIDATED
   |
   v
READY_FOR_EXECUTION
   |
   v
EXECUTING
   |
   +------> REQUIRES_CUSTOMER_ACTION
   |
   +------> PENDING_EXTERNAL_RESULT
   |
   +------> OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN
   |
   +------> FAILED
   |
   v
RESOLVED

This is a conceptual lifecycle. It must not be implemented as one universal enum if it combines independent concepts that require separate state machines.
The implementation must distinguish intent lifecycle, payment lifecycle, operation lifecycle, attempt lifecycle, and reconciliation lifecycle.
10.1 Intent states
Proposed intent states:
- CREATED
- VALIDATING
- REJECTED
- VALIDATED
- READY_FOR_EXECUTION
- EXECUTION_REQUESTED
- EXPIRED
- CANCELLED
A validated intent is not proof of successful payment.
10.2 Payment aggregate states
Proposed high-level states:
- CREATED
- PENDING
- REQUIRES_ACTION
- AUTHORIZED
- PARTIALLY_CAPTURED
- CAPTURED
- PARTIALLY_REFUNDED
- REFUNDED
- CANCELLED
- FAILED
- OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN
- CLOSED
These states must be derived from the underlying operation history and permitted business rules.
A payment may require more expressive projections when multiple authorizations, captures, refunds, currencies, or payment instruments are supported.
10.3 Operation states
Each financial operation must have its own lifecycle.
Proposed operation states:
- CREATED
- VALIDATING
- READY
- SUBMITTED
- PROVIDER_ACCEPTED
- PENDING
- REQUIRES_ACTION
- SUCCEEDED
- FAILED
- DECLINED
- CANCEL_REQUESTED
- CANCELLED
- OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN
- RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED
- COMPENSATED
Not every operation supports every state.
The permitted state transitions must be defined by the operation type, provider capability, payment method, and applicable policy.
10.4 Attempt states
Proposed attempt states:
- CREATED
- DISPATCHED
- PROVIDER_ACKNOWLEDGED
- PENDING
- SUCCEEDED
- FAILED
- TIMED_OUT
- OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN
- ABANDONED
- RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED
An attempt timing out does not establish that the external provider failed to execute it.
10.5 Refund states
Refund requests and refund operations must have separate identities.
Proposed refund operation states:
- REQUESTED
- VALIDATING
- APPROVED
- SUBMITTED
- PENDING
- SUCCEEDED
- FAILED
- OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN
- RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED
- CANCELLED
A refund request is not itself proof that funds have been returned.
The refund authority must establish whether a refund is permitted. The payment domain executes and verifies the payment-side operation.
PART VI — FINANCIAL INVARIANTS
11. AMOUNT AND STATE INVARIANTS
The following invariants are mandatory design requirements, subject to validation against the applicable payment method and provider semantics.
11.1 Currency consistency
For each operation, the amount, currency, payment context, and provider request must be consistent.
Currency conversion must not occur implicitly.
When currency conversion is supported, the applicable conversion authority, rate, timestamp, fees, rounding rules, and resulting amounts must be explicit.
11.2 Capture constraints
For a conventional authorization-and-capture flow:
- Captures must reference an eligible authorization or supported payment arrangement.
- Capture amounts must be positive where the operation requires a positive amount.
- A capture must not exceed the remaining capturable amount.
- Concurrent captures must be coordinated to prevent over-capture.
- Partial capture must be explicitly supported by the relevant capability declaration.
- Multiple captures must follow the provider's supported semantics.
- A failed capture must not automatically be interpreted as a successful financial reversal.
Some payment methods use immediate debit or other flows without a separate authorization stage. Their lifecycle must be represented through explicit method-specific contracts rather than forced into an incompatible card-oriented model.
11.3 Refund constraints
For a conventional refundable payment:
REFUNDABLE_AMOUNT
    = VERIFIED_ELIGIBLE_CAPTURED_AMOUNT
    - VERIFIED_SUCCESSFUL_REFUNDS
    - OTHER_APPLICABLE_REFUND_RESERVATIONS
    - OTHER_POLICY_DEFINED_EXCLUSIONS

This is a conceptual formula, not a universal rule for every payment method.
The implementation must account for the relevant provider semantics, pending refund operations, chargebacks, reversals, prior partial refunds, and other applicable constraints.
A refund must not exceed the amount that is legally and operationally eligible for refund under the applicable contract.
11.4 Operation uniqueness
Each logical operation must have a stable operation identifier.
Retries of the same logical operation must not create additional financial effects.
A genuinely new financial action must receive a new operation identity.
11.5 No silent mutation
An operation submitted externally must not have its amount, currency, destination, or business purpose silently changed.
A changed instruction requires an authorized new operation or a formally supported amendment mechanism.
11.6 Evidence consistency
A provider notification must not be accepted as authoritative merely because it contains a familiar transaction identifier.
Evidence must pass authentication, correlation, validation, and state-transition checks.
11.7 State monotonicity
State progression must not erase historical financial facts.
A later correction may supersede a previous interpretation, but it must preserve the original evidence and record the correction.
11.8 Uncertainty preservation
An unresolved external outcome must remain explicitly uncertain until sufficient evidence establishes the correct result.
The system must not initiate an independent financial retry merely because the previous request timed out.
11.9 Independent operations
Authorization, capture, void, reversal, refund, and settlement are distinct operations.
They must not be collapsed into one generic "payment completed" flag.
11.10 No false settlement
A successful payment operation does not, by itself, establish that funds have settled into the marketplace's or seller's bank account.
PART VII — PAYMENT INTENT CONTRACT
12. CANONICAL PAYMENT INTENT
A proposed logical payment intent contract is:
{
  "payment_intent_id": "opaque-stable-identifier",
  "tenant_id": "canonical-tenant-reference",
  "commercial_context": {
    "order_id": "canonical-order-reference",
    "checkout_id": "optional-checkout-reference",
    "purchase_reference": "stable-purchase-reference"
  },
  "payer": {
    "identity_reference": "canonical-identity-reference"
  },
  "payee_context": {
    "merchant_reference": "canonical-merchant-reference"
  },
  "amount": {
    "value": "1250.00",
    "currency": "ISO-4217-code-when-applicable"
  },
  "operation_intent": {
    "operation_type": "AUTHORIZE",
    "capture_policy": "EXPLICIT_POLICY_REFERENCE"
  },
  "payment_method_selection": {
    "selection_policy_reference": "canonical-policy-reference",
    "instrument_reference": null
  },
  "commercial_evidence": {
    "price_quote_reference": "canonical-price-quote-reference",
    "quote_version": "canonical-version-reference"
  },
  "risk_context": {
    "risk_decision_reference": "optional-authoritative-reference"
  },
  "execution_constraints": {
    "expiry": "explicit-time-bound",
    "permitted_methods": [],
    "required_capabilities": []
  },
  "idempotency_key": "opaque-operation-scoped-key",
  "correlation_id": "opaque-correlation-reference",
  "metadata": {},
  "created_at": "UTC-timestamp",
  "schema_version": "canonical-contract-version"
}

This is an illustrative logical contract, not an approved production schema.
12.1 Contract rules
1. Identifiers must follow the relevant canonical identifier authority.
2. Monetary values must use exact financial representations.
3. The currency code must be validated against the authoritative currency registry.
4. The commercial reference must resolve to an authorized source of truth.
5. The payer and merchant references must resolve through canonical identity and participant authorities.
6. The operation type must be explicitly declared.
7. The idempotency key must be scoped according to the operation contract.
8. Expiry must be validated before a new external financial effect is initiated.
9. A quote reference must be validated when the operation depends on a commercial quotation.
10. Risk context must reference the authoritative risk decision when required.
11. Unknown fields must be handled according to the contract's compatibility policy.
12. Untrusted metadata must not override canonical fields.
13. Sensitive authentication material must not be placed in general-purpose metadata.
14. A schema version must not be used as a substitute for semantic compatibility validation.
PART VIII — PAYMENT OPERATION CONTRACT
13. OPERATION REQUEST
A proposed operation request is:
{
  "operation_id": "opaque-stable-operation-id",
  "payment_id": "canonical-payment-reference",
  "operation_type": "CAPTURE",
  "amount": {
    "value": "1250.00",
    "currency": "ISO-4217-code-when-applicable"
  },
  "references": {
    "authorization_operation_id": "required-when-applicable",
    "provider_transaction_reference": "optional-provider-reference",
    "business_operation_reference": "canonical-business-reference"
  },
  "execution_policy_reference": "canonical-policy-reference",
  "idempotency_key": "operation-scoped-key",
  "expected_state_version": 4,
  "reason_code": "canonical-reason-code",
  "correlation_id": "opaque-correlation-reference",
  "requested_at": "UTC-timestamp",
  "schema_version": "canonical-contract-version"
}

13.1 Operation validation
Before execution, the payment domain must validate:
- Caller identity.
- Caller authorization.
- Tenant and merchant boundaries.
- Payment existence and state.
- Operation type.
- Amount and currency.
- Idempotency.
- Applicable business authorization.
- Applicable risk and compliance decisions.
- Provider capability.
- Operation expiry.
- Concurrency constraints.
- Required references.
- Provider-specific limitations.
- Applicable payment policy.
13.2 State-version protection
Where concurrent operations could create conflicting financial outcomes, the implementation must use a concurrency-control strategy such as conditional state transitions, optimistic concurrency, or an equivalent proven mechanism.
A stale state version must not silently authorize an operation against outdated financial state.
PART IX — PAYMENT METHOD AND PROVIDER ABSTRACTION
14. PAYMENT METHOD MODEL
The architecture must support extensible payment method categories without embedding a fixed exhaustive list into its ontology.
Possible categories include:
- Card-based methods.
- Bank-account-based methods.
- Bank transfer.
- Wallet-based methods.
- Account-to-account payments.
- Real-time payment systems.
- Deferred payment methods.
- Buy-now-pay-later arrangements.
- Cash-based payment references.
- Stored-value instruments.
- Tokenized payment credentials.
- Approved alternative payment methods.
- Future payment mechanisms.
These are examples, not a mandatory catalog or a claim that all methods are legally available in all jurisdictions.
Each method must be registered through the applicable canonical capability registry.
15. PAYMENT CAPABILITY DECLARATION
Each method or provider must declare its supported capabilities and constraints.
A proposed capability declaration includes:
{
  "capability_declaration_id": "stable-capability-id",
  "provider_reference": "canonical-provider-reference",
  "method_reference": "canonical-method-reference",
  "version": "capability-version",
  "supported_operations": [
    "AUTHORIZE",
    "CAPTURE",
    "VOID",
    "REFUND",
    "STATUS_INQUIRY"
  ],
  "features": {
    "supports_partial_capture": true,
    "supports_multiple_captures": false,
    "supports_partial_refund": true,
    "supports_idempotency": true,
    "supports_async_result": true,
    "supports_status_inquiry": true,
    "supports_authorization_expiry": true
  },
  "constraints": {
    "supported_currencies": [],
    "supported_regions": [],
    "supported_channels": [],
    "minimum_amount_policy": "policy-reference",
    "maximum_amount_policy": "policy-reference"
  },
  "security": {
    "authentication_profile": "approved-profile-reference",
    "webhook_verification_profile": "approved-profile-reference",
    "credential_reference": "secret-manager-reference"
  },
  "operational": {
    "health_status": "UNKNOWN",
    "configuration_version": "version-reference",
    "effective_from": "timestamp",
    "effective_until": null
  }
}

The example is illustrative. A real declaration must use canonical schemas and must not expose secrets.
15.1 Capability truth
The registry must distinguish:
- Declared capability.
- Verified capability.
- Temporarily available capability.
- Suspended capability.
- Deprecated capability.
- Prohibited capability.
A provider's advertised feature must not automatically be treated as verified.
15.2 Capability discovery
Consumers must discover supported payment capabilities through the canonical registry or governed interface.
The system must not require source-code changes merely to recognize a newly registered payment method, provided the method fits existing contracts and approved extension points.
A new method that introduces fundamentally new semantics may require a formal architecture decision and contract evolution.
16. PROVIDER ADAPTER CONTRACT
Each provider connector must implement the applicable portions of a provider-neutral contract.
Conceptual operations:
initializePaymentIntent()
validateOperation()
authorizePayment()
capturePayment()
voidPayment()
reversePayment()
refundPayment()
queryPaymentStatus()
queryOperationStatus()
retrieveTransactionEvidence()
normalizeProviderResult()
verifyProviderNotification()
validateProviderCapabilities()
performProviderHealthCheck()

Unsupported operations must return an explicit unsupported-capability result.
They must not be simulated using unsafe or semantically different operations.
16.1 Adapter responsibilities
The adapter must:
- Translate canonical requests into provider-specific requests.
- Validate provider-specific constraints.
- Preserve canonical operation identity.
- Apply supported provider idempotency semantics.
- Normalize responses without losing material information.
- Preserve provider references.
- Map provider error categories.
- Support status inquiry where available.
- Verify provider notifications through an approved mechanism.
- Record connector and contract versions.
- Protect credentials.
- Enforce timeouts and bounded resource consumption.
- Prevent leakage of sensitive information.
- Preserve evidence needed for reconciliation.
16.2 Adapter prohibitions
A connector must not:
- Invent financial success.
- Convert an uncertain result into a definitive failure without evidence.
- Retry an uncertain financial operation without a safe recovery strategy.
- Silently change amount or currency.
- Bypass policy enforcement.
- expose secrets through logs.
- Modify canonical payment history destructively.
- Claim a provider supports an operation that has not been verified.
- Create duplicate financial operations during recovery.
PART X — PAYMENT ROUTING
17. ROUTING OBJECTIVE
The routing engine selects an eligible execution route based on governed policy, verified capability, transaction constraints, risk controls, and current operational evidence.
Routing must not be driven solely by cost or availability.
18. ROUTING CONSTRAINTS
Before selecting a route, evaluate:
1. Payment method compatibility.
2. Currency support.
3. Merchant and tenant eligibility.
4. Jurisdictional constraints.
5. Transaction amount limits.
6. Channel compatibility.
7. Authentication requirements.
8. Risk and compliance restrictions.
9. Provider capability.
10. Provider health.
11. Idempotency support.
12. Transaction deadline.
13. Applicable fee policy.
14. Availability and resilience policy.
15. Data residency and security requirements where applicable.
16. Contract version compatibility.
17. Provider-specific transaction restrictions.
18. Prior attempt state.
19. Whether a prior attempt remains uncertain.
20. Whether a retry or alternate route could create duplicate financial effects.
19. ROUTING DECISION
The routing engine must produce an explainable routing decision.
The decision record should contain:
- Routing decision ID.
- Payment and operation references.
- Candidate routes considered.
- Eligibility outcomes.
- Rejection reasons.
- Selected route.
- Applicable policy version.
- Capability declaration version.
- Relevant operational signals.
- Decision timestamp.
- Correlation ID.
Sensitive risk information must be access-controlled and minimized.
19.1 Routing precedence
Routing policy must separate hard eligibility constraints from optimization preferences.
A conceptual sequence is:
Request validation
    |
    v
Authorization and policy checks
    |
    v
Hard eligibility constraints
    |
    v
Verified capability filtering
    |
    v
Operational health assessment
    |
    v
Permitted routing policy
    |
    v
Eligible route selection
    |
    v
Durable operation registration
    |
    v
External execution

No optimization preference may override a hard security, legal, or financial constraint.
19.2 Failover safety
Provider failover is permitted only when the system can establish that the next attempt will not create an unauthorized duplicate financial effect.
Where the previous provider outcome is uncertain, the system must first use an appropriate recovery procedure, such as:
- Querying operation status.
- Reusing the same provider-supported idempotency identity.
- Waiting for authenticated asynchronous evidence.
- Reconciliation against provider transaction evidence.
- Escalating to a controlled investigation process.
An alternate provider must not automatically receive a new charge request simply because the original provider timed out.
PART XI — IDEMPOTENCY AND CONCURRENCY
20. IDEMPOTENCY REQUIREMENTS
Every state-changing payment operation must have an explicit idempotency policy.
The policy must define:
- Key scope.
- Key uniqueness.
- Retention period.
- Payload equivalence.
- Duplicate response behavior.
- Concurrent request handling.
- Operation recovery.
- Provider propagation.
- Expiry behavior.
- Audit evidence.
- Conflict resolution.
20.1 Same key, same logical request
When a request is repeated with the same idempotency key and equivalent canonical payload, the system must return the established operation result or its current authoritative status.
It must not create a second logical financial operation.
20.2 Same key, different request
When a key is reused with a materially different operation payload, the system must reject the request as an idempotency conflict.
It must not silently reinterpret the original operation.
20.3 Concurrent duplicates
Concurrent duplicate requests must be serialized, coordinated, or otherwise controlled so that they cannot create multiple independent logical operations.
20.4 External provider behavior
Internal idempotency does not automatically guarantee external idempotency.
The adapter must account for the provider's actual idempotency guarantees, key scope, retention, and response behavior.
If the provider does not provide adequate idempotency, the system must apply an explicit risk-controlled execution and recovery policy.
20.5 Durable operation registration
Before initiating a consequential external operation, the implementation must durably register enough operation identity and intent information to recover safely from process failure.
The architecture must not depend on an in-memory record as the only evidence that a payment operation was initiated.
PART XII — AUTHORIZATION, CAPTURE, VOID AND REVERSAL
21. AUTHORIZATION
Authorization processing must:
- Validate the payment intent.
- Verify applicable authorization and risk decisions.
- Verify method and provider capability.
- Validate amount and currency.
- Establish operation identity.
- Apply idempotency.
- Execute the provider operation.
- Preserve provider evidence.
- Record the authoritative operation state.
- Publish the appropriate canonical event.
- Expose the result through an authorized contract.
An authorization is not necessarily a completed capture or a settled financial transaction.
22. CAPTURE
Capture processing must:
- Verify that capture is permitted.
- Validate the relevant authorization or payment arrangement.
- Check the remaining capturable amount.
- Enforce concurrency controls.
- Validate currency consistency.
- Apply idempotency.
- Confirm provider support for partial or multiple captures where applicable.
- Preserve the operation and provider references.
- Process asynchronous outcomes.
- Reconcile ambiguous outcomes.
A capture operation must not silently capture more than the authorized remaining amount under the applicable payment contract.
23. VOID
A void operation must validate whether the relevant payment operation remains eligible for cancellation.
The system must not assume that every provider supports voiding every operation.
Where a void cannot be executed because the operation has crossed the relevant financial boundary, the system must follow the applicable recovery, reversal, refund, or exception process.
24. REVERSAL
Reversal semantics vary by payment method and provider.
The architecture must define reversal eligibility and effect for each supported payment capability.
A reversal must reference the operation it affects and must preserve its original evidence.
A reversal request is not proof that the reversal succeeded.
25. OPERATIONAL RULE
Every financial operation must preserve the relationship among:
Payment
  └── Payment Operation
        ├── Idempotency Identity
        ├── Payment Attempt(s)
        ├── Provider Reference(s)
        ├── Evidence Record(s)
        ├── State Transition(s)
        └── Reconciliation Reference(s)

The exact cardinalities must be defined by the canonical data model and the supported payment semantics.
PART XIII — REFUND COORDINATION
26. REFUND AUTHORITY
The payment domain executes payment-side refund operations.
The authoritative business domain determines whether the refund is permitted.
The request must reference the approved refund decision or another authorized business instruction.
The payment domain must not independently invent refund eligibility based solely on a customer request.
27. REFUND VALIDATION
Before executing a refund, validate:
- The referenced payment.
- The referenced captured or otherwise refundable transaction.
- The refund authorization.
- The refundable balance.
- The currency.
- The operation identity.
- The payment method's refund capabilities.
- Provider limitations.
- Applicable risk and compliance constraints.
- Duplicate refund requests.
- Concurrent refund operations.
- Any existing unresolved refund outcome.
28. PARTIAL AND MULTIPLE REFUNDS
The architecture must support partial refunds where permitted.
Multiple refunds must be coordinated against the verified refundable amount.
The implementation must account for pending refund operations that reserve part of the refundable amount.
The exact reservation model must be defined so that concurrent requests cannot exceed the permissible refund balance.
29. REFUND FAILURE
If a refund operation fails definitively, the system must record the failure and preserve the evidence.
If the outcome is uncertain, the system must not immediately create an independent refund attempt that could cause a duplicate refund.
It must first apply the defined recovery strategy.
30. REFUND COMPLETION
Refund completion must be based on the applicable payment method's authoritative success semantics.
A provider acknowledgement that merely accepts a refund request is insufficient when the provider's contract distinguishes request acceptance from completed refund execution.
The system must expose the actual state and any outstanding uncertainty to authorized consumers.
PART XIV — PAYMENT AUTHENTICATION AND CUSTOMER ACTION
31. CUSTOMER ACTION
Some payment methods require additional customer interaction or authentication.
The payment domain must support a governed action-required flow without exposing unrestricted internal execution capabilities to the client.
A customer-action contract may contain:
- Action reference.
- Payment reference.
- Required action type.
- Approved continuation mechanism.
- Expiry.
- Current action status.
- Permitted return path.
- Correlation reference.
Sensitive authentication data must not be placed in ordinary application logs, general event payloads, or unprotected metadata.
32. TRUST BOUNDARY
The client must not be allowed to declare a payment successful merely by returning to a success URL or sending a client-side confirmation.
The authoritative payment result must come from validated payment evidence and the applicable provider contract.
33. AUTHENTICATION OUTCOMES
The architecture must distinguish:
- Authentication requested.
- Authentication in progress.
- Customer action required.
- Authentication completed.
- Authentication failed.
- Authentication outcome uncertain.
- Authentication result accepted by the payment method.
- Payment authorization outcome.
Successful authentication does not, by itself, prove successful payment.
PART XV — PAYMENT SECURITY
34. SECURITY OBJECTIVES
Payment security must protect:
- Financial integrity.
- Confidentiality of sensitive payment information.
- Authentication and authorization.
- Integrity of provider requests and responses.
- Payment operation uniqueness.
- Transaction evidence.
- Audit history.
- Credential confidentiality.
- Administrative controls.
- Availability of critical payment operations.
35. SENSITIVE DATA CLASSIFICATION
Payment data must be classified according to the canonical UCOS data-classification authority.
At minimum, distinguish:
1. Public payment capability metadata.
2. Internal payment identifiers and operational metadata.
3. Confidential commercial and transaction records.
4. Restricted personal and financial data.
5. Highly restricted payment credentials and authentication data.
The precise classifications must be reconciled with the existing UCOS security and data-governance authorities.
36. CARD DATA AND TOKENIZATION
Where card payments are supported, the implementation must minimize exposure to cardholder data and sensitive authentication data.
Prefer approved tokenization and appropriately scoped payment-provider-hosted collection mechanisms where compatible with the business and regulatory requirements.
Do not assume that tokenization, encryption, or the use of an external payment provider automatically removes every component from the applicable compliance scope.
Applicable PCI Security Standards Council requirements must be assessed against the actual data flows, components, service-provider relationships, and operating model. The PCI SSC identifies PCI DSS as a baseline for protecting payment account data and publishes separate standards for related payment technologies and environments.
Official reference:
https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/Standards/
37. SECRET MANAGEMENT
Provider credentials, signing keys, certificates, and other secrets must:
- Be stored in an approved secret-management mechanism.
- Never be embedded in source code.
- Never be committed to repositories.
- Never be returned in ordinary API responses.
- Never be emitted into ordinary logs.
- Be restricted by least privilege.
- Support rotation and revocation.
- Have explicit ownership and lifecycle.
- Be monitored for unauthorized access.
- Be separated by environment and security boundary.
38. PROVIDER NOTIFICATION SECURITY
Provider notifications must be validated according to the provider's supported security protocol.
Controls may include:
- Signature verification.
- Mutual authentication where supported.
- Authenticated transport.
- Timestamp validation.
- Replay detection.
- Event identity validation.
- Provider-account binding.
- Payload validation.
- Transaction-reference correlation.
- Event deduplication.
- Rate limiting.
- Audit logging.
The architecture must not assume that every provider supports the same notification-security mechanism.
Unsupported or invalid notifications must not change authoritative payment state.
39. ACCESS CONTROL
Access must be governed through canonical UCOS identity and authorization authorities.
Permissions must be scoped by the applicable tenant, merchant, payment, operation, and administrative boundary.
Privileged actions must be separately authorized.
Examples include:
- Initiating a payment.
- Capturing a payment.
- Initiating a refund.
- Changing provider configuration.
- Changing routing policy.
- Suspending a provider.
- Resolving a financial exception.
- Replaying an event.
- Changing reconciliation rules.
- Accessing restricted payment evidence.
40. AUDIT
Audit records must capture, as applicable:
- Actor or service identity.
- Action.
- Target entity.
- Authorization decision.
- Reason.
- Relevant configuration version.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Evidence references.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Result.
- Failure classification.
Audit history must be protected against unauthorized modification and deletion.
Retention and deletion policies must comply with the applicable legal, privacy, and canonical governance requirements.
41. SECURITY INCIDENTS
The architecture must support:
- Credential compromise detection.
- Provider compromise response.
- Suspicious transaction escalation.
- Unauthorized configuration-change detection.
- Replay and duplicate-operation detection.
- Restricted-data exposure response.
- Provider isolation.
- Controlled suspension of affected payment routes.
- Evidence preservation.
- Incident correlation.
- Recovery and reactivation approval.
A provider may be suspended when a verified security or operational condition requires it, but the suspension must not silently discard unresolved financial operations.
PART XVI — FRAUD AND RISK INTEGRATION
42. AUTHORITY BOUNDARY
Document 013 is the proposed canonical authority for marketplace trust, safety, fraud prevention, and risk intelligence.
Document 016 consumes and enforces applicable payment-specific decisions.
It must not create an independent competing fraud scoring authority.
43. PAYMENT RISK CONTEXT
Depending on policy, the payment domain may submit or reference:
- Transaction amount.
- Currency.
- Payment method.
- Merchant reference.
- Customer identity reference.
- Device or session references.
- Transaction history references.
- Payment velocity indicators.
- Geographic context.
- Provider risk signals.
- Authentication outcome.
- Existing risk decision.
- Applicable policy version.
Data must be minimized according to the applicable privacy and security rules.
44. RISK DECISION OUTCOMES
A risk authority may return policy-defined outcomes such as:
- ALLOW.
- DENY.
- REQUIRE_ADDITIONAL_AUTHENTICATION.
- REQUIRE_REVIEW.
- RESTRICT_PAYMENT_METHOD.
- RESTRICT_AMOUNT.
- REQUIRE_ADDITIONAL_EVIDENCE.
- DEFER_DECISION.
These are proposed examples and must be reconciled with the canonical risk ontology.
The payment domain must honor the authoritative decision and its permitted scope.
45. RISK SERVICE FAILURE
If a mandatory risk decision cannot be obtained, the payment domain must apply the approved failure policy.
It must not silently bypass a mandatory risk control merely because a dependency is unavailable.
A policy may permit bounded degraded operation for specifically approved low-risk cases, but that exception must be explicit, auditable, and governed.
PART XVII — PAYMENT EVENTS
46. EVENT MODEL
Payment events communicate material facts about payment state.
They must be distinct from commands requesting actions.
A command expresses an intention.
An event expresses an accepted fact or observation with an explicit evidence status.
47. PROPOSED CANONICAL EVENTS
The following names are proposed and must be registered through the canonical UCOS event authority.
Event	Meaning
PaymentIntentCreated	A payment intent was created.
PaymentIntentValidated	A payment intent passed the defined validation rules.
PaymentIntentRejected	A payment intent was rejected.
PaymentCreated	A canonical payment aggregate was established.
PaymentAuthorizationRequested	An authorization operation was requested.
PaymentAuthorizationPending	Authorization remains unresolved.
PaymentAuthorized	Authorization success was established under the applicable contract.
PaymentCaptureRequested	A capture operation was requested.
PaymentCapturePending	Capture remains unresolved.
PaymentCaptured	Capture success was established under the applicable contract.
PaymentVoidRequested	A void operation was requested.
PaymentVoided	Void success was established.
PaymentReversalRequested	A reversal operation was requested.
PaymentReversed	Reversal success was established.
PaymentRefundRequested	A refund operation was requested.
PaymentRefundPending	Refund outcome remains unresolved.
PaymentRefunded	Refund success was established under the applicable contract.
PaymentActionRequired	Additional action is required.
PaymentOperationFailed	An operation failed definitively under the applicable contract.
PaymentOutcomeUncertain	The result cannot yet be established.
PaymentReconciliationRequired	Reconciliation is required.
PaymentReconciled	A reconciliation result was recorded.
PaymentExceptionRaised	A governed exception was created.
PaymentProviderStatusChanged	Provider capability or operational status changed.
PaymentRouteSuspended	A route was suspended.

48. EVENT ENVELOPE
A proposed logical event envelope is:
{
  "event_id": "globally-unique-event-identifier",
  "event_type": "PaymentAuthorized",

  "schema_version": "canonical-schema-version"

The envelope is illustrative.
Actual field definitions, mandatory attributes, data classification, schema evolution, and event registration must be established by the canonical event authority.
49. EVENT DELIVERY RULES
1. Events must have stable identifiers.
2. Duplicate delivery must be expected.
3. Consumers must be idempotent.
4. Event ordering must not be assumed globally.
5. Relevant ordering constraints must be explicitly defined.
6. Consumers must validate event identity and schema.
7. Sensitive payment data must be minimized.
8. Events must not expose credentials or authentication secrets.
9. Event publication must not claim a state transition that has not been accepted.
10. Material events must remain traceable to their originating operation and evidence.
11. Delivery failures must be observable and recoverable.
12. Event replay must not trigger a new financial side effect merely because an event is replayed.
PART XVIII — API CONTRACTS
50. API DESIGN PRINCIPLES
Payment APIs must be:
- Explicit.
- Versioned.
- Authorized.
- Idempotent where required.
- Auditable.
- Provider-neutral.
- Consistent with canonical domain contracts.
- Safe under retries.
- Clear about uncertainty.
- Compatible with asynchronous processing.
- Documented with machine-readable schemas.
51. PROPOSED API CATALOG
These are logical operations, not final approved routes.
API ID	Operation	Purpose
MPS-016-API-001	Create Payment Intent	Register a proposed payment intent.
MPS-016-API-002	Validate Payment Intent	Validate intent and commercial references.
MPS-016-API-003	Retrieve Payment	Retrieve an authorized payment projection.
MPS-016-API-004	Request Authorization	Request a payment authorization.
MPS-016-API-005	Request Capture	Request an eligible capture.
MPS-016-API-006	Request Void	Request an eligible void.
MPS-016-API-007	Request Reversal	Request a supported reversal.
MPS-016-API-008	Request Refund Execution	Execute an authorized refund instruction.

MPS-016-API-011	Query Operation Status	Resolve a specific operation's status.
MPS-016-API-012	Submit Provider Notification	Receive provider event evidence.
MPS-016-API-013	Register Payment Capability	Register a governed capability declaration.
MPS-016-API-014	Retrieve Payment Capability	Retrieve a capability declaration.
MPS-016-API-015	Retrieve Payment Methods	Discover eligible payment methods.
MPS-016-API-016	Request Reconciliation	Request an authorized reconciliation operation.
MPS-016-API-017	Retrieve Reconciliation Result	Retrieve a reconciliation result.
MPS-016-API-018	Resolve Payment Exception	Submit an authorized exception-resolution instruction.
MPS-016-API-019	Suspend Payment Route	Request an authorized route suspension.
MPS-016-API-020	Restore Payment Route	Request an authorized route restoration.


52. API RESPONSE SEMANTICS
An API response must distinguish:
- Request rejected before operation creation.
- Operation created and accepted for processing.
- Operation still pending.
- Additional action required.
- Operation succeeded.
- Operation failed definitively.
- Outcome uncertain.
- Operation requires reconciliation.
The exact response codes and schemas must be defined in the final API contracts.
An API timeout must not be interpreted as proof that the underlying payment operation failed.

A proposed canonical error taxonomy includes:
- INVALID_REQUEST.
- SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED.
- UNAUTHORIZED.
- FORBIDDEN.
- PAYMENT_NOT_FOUND.
- OPERATION_NOT_FOUND.
- INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION.
- CURRENCY_NOT_SUPPORTED.
- AMOUNT_OUT_OF_RANGE.
- CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE.
- PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE.
- PROVIDER_REJECTED.
- AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED.
- RISK_POLICY_REJECTED.
- IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT.
- CONCURRENT_OPERATION_CONFLICT.
- QUOTE_INVALID_OR_EXPIRED.
- PAYMENT_OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN.
- RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED.
- POLICY_CONFIGURATION_ERROR.
- COMPLIANCE_RESTRICTION.
- RATE_LIMITED.
- TEMPORARY_DEPENDENCY_FAILURE.
- INTERNAL_PROCESSING_ERROR.
These codes must be reconciled with the canonical UCOS error ontology.
External provider messages must be normalized without exposing sensitive information or falsely collapsing materially different outcomes.
PART XIX — DATA MODEL
54. CANONICAL ENTITY CANDIDATES
The following entities are proposed for reconciliation with the existing UCOS ontology and registry authorities.
54.1 Payment

Proposed attributes:

- Payment lifecycle projection.

- Closure status.
- Relevant policy reference.

- Requested amount.
- Currency.
- Intended operation.
- Expiry.
- Validation status.
- Policy references.

- Payment ID.
- Operation type.
- Requested amount.

- Operation state.
- Idempotency identity.

- Provider reference.
- Creation timestamp.
- Submission timestamp.
- Resolution timestamp.
- State version.
54.4 Payment Attempt
Represents an execution attempt.
Proposed attributes:
- Attempt ID.
- Operation ID.
- Provider reference.
- Route reference.
- Attempt sequence.
- Dispatch timestamp.
- Outcome classification.
- Timeout classification.
- Provider response reference.

- Provider reference.

Represents a material observation supporting a payment assertion.
