55. DATA OWNERSHIP
The payment domain owns its canonical payment records and operation history, subject to existing UCOS canonical authority.
It references rather than duplicates authoritative records for:
- Customer identity.
- Merchant identity.
- Orders.
- Product and service catalog.
- Price quotations.
- Tax determinations.
- Refund eligibility decisions.
- Settlement instructions.
- Accounting postings.
- Fraud decisions.
- Regulatory policies.
Derived projections are permitted when their lineage, freshness, ownership, and invalidation behavior are explicit.
56. RETENTION AND DELETION
Payment records must follow approved retention and privacy policies.
Financial evidence may be subject to legal or regulatory retention obligations.
Sensitive personal data must not be retained indefinitely merely because it is associated with a payment.
Where deletion is required, the implementation must apply the canonical retention and privacy rules while preserving any legally required financial records and audit evidence.
PART XX — DURABLE PROCESSING AND RECOVERY
57. DURABLE OPERATION PROCESSING
The implementation must persist the logical operation and its recovery information before initiating a consequential external action.
The architecture must define how it recovers when:
- The application fails before dispatch.
- The application fails during dispatch.
- The provider executes but the response is lost.
- The provider responds but local persistence fails.
- A callback arrives before the synchronous response.
- A callback is delivered more than once.
- The provider reports contradictory results.
- An operation is accepted but remains unresolved.
- The event publisher fails.
- The reconciliation process detects a discrepancy.
58. INTERNAL TRANSACTION BOUNDARY
Internal state changes and event publication must use a reliable consistency pattern.
A transactional outbox or an equivalent verified mechanism may be used where appropriate.
The implementation must not claim that a local database transaction and an external provider transaction are one atomic transaction unless a real, supported protocol establishes that guarantee.
59. RETRY CLASSIFICATION
Retries must be classified by operation semantics and evidence.
Safe retry candidates
An operation may be retried when:
- It is known not to have been dispatched.
- The provider definitively rejected it before execution.
- The provider contract guarantees idempotent execution for the same operation identity.
- A verified status inquiry establishes that retrying is safe.
- An approved recovery protocol explicitly permits the retry.
Unsafe retry candidates
A new financial attempt must not be initiated automatically when:
- The previous operation may have executed.
- The provider's outcome is unknown.
- The idempotency guarantee has expired or is unavailable.
- The provider cannot establish operation status.
- Conflicting evidence exists.
- The operation could cause a duplicate charge, capture, or refund.
In these cases, the system must preserve uncertainty and initiate the appropriate recovery or reconciliation process.
60. RECOVERY WORKFLOW


flowchart TD
    START["Payment Operation Submitted"]
    RESPONSE{"Definitive Result Received?"}
    SUCCESS{"Verified Success?"}
    FAIL["Record Definitive Failure"]
    UNCERTAIN["Mark Outcome Uncertain"]
    QUERY["Query Provider Status"]
    EVIDENCE{"Sufficient Evidence?"}
    RESOLVE["Resolve Operation State"]
    RECON["Create Reconciliation Case"]
    REVIEW["Controlled Investigation"]
    COMPLETE["Publish Accepted State Change"]

    START --> RESPONSE
    RESPONSE -->|Yes| SUCCESS
    RESPONSE -->|No or Timeout| UNCERTAIN
    SUCCESS -->|Yes| RESOLVE
    SUCCESS -->|No| FAIL
    UNCERTAIN --> QUERY
    QUERY --> EVIDENCE
    EVIDENCE -->|Yes| RESOLVE
    EVIDENCE -->|No| RECON
    RECON --> REVIEW
    REVIEW -->|Evidence established| RESOLVE
    REVIEW -->|Still unresolved| RECON
    RESOLVE --> COMPLETE



The recovery workflow must be bounded and observable.
Repeated inability to resolve an outcome must escalate according to the approved exception policy rather than generate an endless automatic retry loop.
PART XXI — RECONCILIATION
61. RECONCILIATION OBJECTIVE
Reconciliation determines whether internal payment records agree with relevant external payment evidence and other authoritative financial records.
It is a financial correctness control, not merely a reporting feature.
62. RECONCILIATION SOURCES
Depending on the payment method, the architecture may reconcile against:
- Provider transaction records.
- Provider status inquiries.
- Provider-generated transaction reports.
- Acquirer records.
- Bank transaction evidence.
- Refund reports.
- Reversal records.
- Settlement records.
- Accounting integration evidence.
- Internal payment operation history.
Each source must have an explicit authority classification.
63. RECONCILIATION MATCHING
Matching may use:
- Provider transaction reference.
- Provider operation reference.
- Payment operation ID.
- Merchant reference.
- Amount.
- Currency.
- Transaction type.
- Relevant timestamps.
- Approved external reference mappings.
Matching by amount and timestamp alone must not be treated as definitive where multiple transactions could legitimately share those values.
64. RECONCILIATION OUTCOMES
Proposed outcomes include:
- MATCHED.
- MATCHED_WITH_TIMING_DIFFERENCE.
- INTERNAL_RECORD_MISSING.
- EXTERNAL_RECORD_MISSING.
- AMOUNT_MISMATCH.
- CURRENCY_MISMATCH.
- DUPLICATE_EXTERNAL_RECORD.
- DUPLICATE_INTERNAL_OPERATION.
- UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION.
- STATUS_CONFLICT.
- REFUND_MISMATCH.
- REVERSAL_MISMATCH.
- PROVIDER_REFERENCE_MISMATCH.
- REQUIRES_INVESTIGATION.
- RESOLVED_WITH_EVIDENCE.
These outcomes must be reconciled with the canonical financial exception taxonomy.
65. RECONCILIATION SAFEGUARDS
1. Reconciliation must not silently rewrite payment history.
2. Corrections must retain source evidence.
3. Financial discrepancies must remain traceable.
4. Unmatched transactions must be assigned a governed disposition.
5. Reconciliation rules must be versioned.
6. Reprocessing must be idempotent.
7. Duplicate reports must not duplicate financial effects.
8. Manual adjustments must require authorization.
9. Material discrepancies must trigger appropriate escalation.
10. Accounting and settlement systems must retain their own canonical responsibilities.
66. RECONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT BOUNDARY
Payment reconciliation verifies payment-operation evidence.
Settlement reconciliation verifies the relevant movement or allocation of funds under the settlement authority.
Accounting reconciliation verifies the corresponding accounting treatment.
These processes may share evidence, but their meanings and authorities must not be conflated.
PART XXII — CONFIGURATION AND GOVERNANCE
67. PAYMENT CONFIGURATION
Governed configuration may include:
- Provider capability declarations.
- Route definitions.
- Method eligibility.
- Amount limits.
- Currency restrictions.
- Risk-policy references.
- Timeout policies.
- Retry policies.
- Provider-specific operation constraints.
- Reconciliation rules.
- Notification verification settings.
- Operational suspension controls.
68. CONFIGURATION VERSIONING
Material configuration changes must be versioned and auditable.
Each relevant decision or operation must be traceable to the configuration version applicable at the time of the decision.
A configuration change must not silently reinterpret a previously submitted operation.
69. CONFIGURATION APPROVAL
High-impact changes must require the approvals specified by the applicable UCOS governance authority.
Examples include:
- Adding a payment provider.
- Enabling a new payment method.
- Changing routing precedence.
- Changing payment limits.
- Altering retry behavior.
- Changing refund policy integration.
- Modifying notification authentication.
- Changing reconciliation matching rules.
- Restoring a suspended payment route.
70. PROVIDER LIFECYCLE
A provider may have states such as:
- DISCOVERED.
- REGISTERED.
- UNDER_REVIEW.
- CAPABILITY_VALIDATION.
- SECURITY_VALIDATION.
- APPROVED.
- ACTIVE.
- DEGRADED.
- SUSPENDED.
- DEPRECATED.
- RETIRED.
These states describe the proposed provider lifecycle and must be reconciled with the canonical registry and governance model.
A provider must not become active merely because its credentials have been entered.
PART XXIII — NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
71. RELIABILITY
The implementation must define reliability objectives for:
- Payment intent creation.
- Operation registration.
- Provider dispatch.
- Result processing.
- Status inquiry.
- Notification intake.
- Event publication.
- Reconciliation.
- Exception handling.
The exact objectives must be derived from approved business criticality, payment-provider guarantees, regulatory requirements, and operational constraints.
72. PERFORMANCE
Performance requirements must be specified separately for:
- Internal validation.
- Payment routing.
- Provider invocation.
- Synchronous response handling.
- Asynchronous result processing.
- Status inquiry.
- Reconciliation.
- Administrative queries.
External provider latency must be measured separately from internal processing latency.
A system must not conceal provider delays by reporting an operation as successful before its outcome is established.
73. SCALABILITY
The architecture must support independently scalable workloads where justified, including:
- Payment request processing.
- Provider callback processing.
- Status polling.
- Reconciliation.
- Exception processing.
- Audit and evidence processing.
- Event publication.
Scaling must not compromise idempotency, concurrency control, tenant isolation, or financial invariants.
74. AVAILABILITY
The system must distinguish availability of the payment orchestration capability from availability of each external provider.
Provider unavailability must be represented explicitly.
The architecture must not promise end-to-end payment availability greater than the actual supported execution paths and dependencies permit.
75. RESILIENCE
Required resilience controls include:
- Bounded timeouts.
- Controlled retries.
- Circuit breaking where appropriate.
- Provider isolation.
- Backpressure.
- Durable queues or equivalent recovery mechanisms.
- Dead-letter or quarantine handling.
- Dependency health monitoring.
- Controlled degradation.
- Recovery procedures.
- Reconciliation of unresolved financial operations.
76. MULTI-TENANCY
Tenant isolation must apply to:
- Payment operations.
- Provider configurations.
- Instrument references.
- Access controls.
- Routing policies.
- Payment evidence.
- Operational reporting.
- Reconciliation records.
- Administrative functions.
Cross-tenant access must be explicitly authorized and auditable.
77. ACCESSIBILITY AND INTERNATIONALIZATION
Customer-facing payment flows must follow applicable accessibility requirements.
Localized presentation must not change canonical financial amounts, operation identity, or underlying payment semantics.
Language, locale, formatting, and customer-facing text must remain separate from canonical monetary representation.
PART XXIV — OBSERVABILITY
78. REQUIRED OBSERVABILITY
The implementation must expose governed operational measures for:
- Payment intent volume.
- Authorization outcomes.
- Capture outcomes.
- Refund outcomes.
- Provider latency.
- Provider error rates.
- Uncertain outcomes.
- Duplicate-operation suppression.
- Idempotency conflicts.
- Notification verification failures.
- Delayed operation resolution.
- Reconciliation discrepancies.
- Unresolved exceptions.
- Provider capability availability.
- Route suspension.
- Retry volume.
- Financial mismatch severity.
79. CORRELATION
The system must support end-to-end correlation across:
- Commercial purchase context.
- Payment intent.
- Payment.
- Operation.
- Attempt.
- Provider transaction.
- Notification.
- Reconciliation record.
- Accounting integration reference.
- Settlement integration reference.
Correlation identifiers must not be treated as authorization credentials.
80. ALERTING
Alerts must be triggered by governed thresholds and conditions.
High-priority conditions include:
- Suspected duplicate financial execution.
- A material increase in uncertain outcomes.
- Payment evidence conflicts.
- Unexplained amount mismatches.
- Provider authentication failures.
- Unauthorized configuration changes.
- Abnormal operation failure rates.
- Reconciliation backlog beyond approved limits.
- Cross-tenant access violations.
- Suspected credential compromise.
Alert thresholds and response procedures must be defined through the operational governance process.
PART XXV — FORMAL FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
81. REQUIREMENT CONVENTION
The following requirements use the prefix MPS-016-FR.
The term MUST expresses a mandatory architectural requirement for an implementation claiming conformance to this specification.
The requirements remain proposed until reconciled with the canonical UCOS authorities.
81.1 Payment intent and validation
MPS-016-FR-001 — Canonical Intent
The system MUST represent payment intent through an explicitly identified, versioned contract.
MPS-016-FR-002 — Commercial Reference
The system MUST validate required commercial references against their authoritative sources.
MPS-016-FR-003 — Amount Validation
The system MUST validate the amount and currency according to the applicable canonical financial rules.
MPS-016-FR-004 — Intent Expiry
The system MUST enforce applicable intent-expiry rules before initiating a new external financial effect.
MPS-016-FR-005 — Intent Authorization
The system MUST validate caller authorization before accepting a payment intent.
81.2 Payment operation lifecycle
MPS-016-FR-006 — Stable Operation Identity
Every logical financial operation MUST have a stable operation identifier.
MPS-016-FR-007 — Operation State Machine
Every supported operation type MUST have explicitly defined permitted state transitions.
MPS-016-FR-008 — Separate Operation Semantics
Authorization, capture, void, reversal, refund, and settlement MUST remain semantically distinct.
MPS-016-FR-009 — Durable Operation Registration
The system MUST durably register the operation and its recovery identity before initiating a consequential external action.
MPS-016-FR-010 — State Versioning
State-changing operations MUST use an approved concurrency-control mechanism.
81.3 Idempotency
MPS-016-FR-011 — Idempotent Operation Submission
State-changing operations MUST have a defined idempotency strategy.
MPS-016-FR-012 — Duplicate Request Handling
Equivalent duplicate requests MUST NOT create additional logical financial operations.
MPS-016-FR-013 — Idempotency Conflict
Reusing an idempotency key with a materially different request MUST be rejected.
MPS-016-FR-014 — External Idempotency
The provider adapter MUST account for actual provider idempotency guarantees and limitations.
MPS-016-FR-015 — Retry Safety
The system MUST NOT automatically create a new financial attempt when a prior attempt may have executed and its outcome remains uncertain.
81.4 Provider abstraction and routing
MPS-016-FR-016 — Provider Contract
Every supported provider connector MUST implement the applicable canonical adapter contract.
MPS-016-FR-017 — Capability Declaration
Every active provider and method MUST have a governed capability declaration.
MPS-016-FR-018 — Capability Verification
The system MUST distinguish advertised capabilities from verified capabilities.
MPS-016-FR-019 — Route Eligibility
Every routing decision MUST enforce mandatory eligibility and security constraints.
MPS-016-FR-020 — Route Traceability
Every routing decision MUST be traceable to its applicable policy and capability versions.
81.5 Authorization and capture
MPS-016-FR-021 — Authorization Evidence
The system MUST preserve evidence supporting an authorization result.
MPS-016-FR-022 — Capture Eligibility
A capture MUST reference an eligible authorization or supported payment arrangement.
MPS-016-FR-023 — Capture Limit
The system MUST prevent capture beyond the applicable remaining capturable amount.
MPS-016-FR-024 — Void Eligibility
A void MUST be validated against the applicable operation and provider semantics.
MPS-016-FR-025 — Reversal Integrity
A reversal MUST reference the operation it affects and preserve its original evidence.
81.6 Refunds
MPS-016-FR-026 — Refund Authorization
A refund operation MUST reference an authorized business instruction.
MPS-016-FR-027 — Refund Balance
The system MUST validate the applicable refundable balance before execution.
MPS-016-FR-028 — Concurrent Refund Protection
Concurrent refund operations MUST be coordinated to prevent unauthorized excess refunds.
MPS-016-FR-029 — Refund Uncertainty
An uncertain refund outcome MUST NOT trigger an unsafe independent refund attempt.
MPS-016-FR-030 — Refund Evidence
The system MUST preserve evidence supporting the refund outcome.
81.7 Asynchronous processing
MPS-016-FR-031 — Notification Authentication
Provider notifications MUST be authenticated and validated according to the applicable provider contract.
MPS-016-FR-032 — Notification Deduplication
Duplicate notifications MUST NOT cause duplicate financial operations.
MPS-016-FR-033 — Notification Correlation
Notifications MUST be correlated to an authorized payment or operation reference.
MPS-016-FR-034 — Contradictory Evidence
Contradictory payment evidence MUST be preserved and escalated under the applicable resolution policy.
MPS-016-FR-035 — Outcome Uncertainty
The system MUST represent unresolved external outcomes explicitly.
81.8 Financial evidence and reconciliation
MPS-016-FR-036 — Evidence Provenance
Material payment evidence MUST retain source and provenance information.
MPS-016-FR-037 — Reconciliation Capability
The system MUST support reconciliation of internal payment records against applicable external evidence.
MPS-016-FR-038 — Discrepancy Recording
Material discrepancies MUST be recorded through governed reconciliation records or exceptions.
MPS-016-FR-039 — Historical Integrity
Reconciliation MUST NOT destructively erase original payment evidence.
MPS-016-FR-040 — Settlement Boundary
The system MUST distinguish payment operation outcomes from settlement and accounting outcomes.
81.9 Security and governance
MPS-016-FR-041 — Canonical Authorization
Payment operations MUST use the applicable canonical identity and authorization authorities.
MPS-016-FR-042 — Secret Protection
Provider credentials and sensitive authentication material MUST be protected through approved controls.
MPS-016-FR-043 — Restricted Data
Payment data MUST be classified, handled, and retained according to applicable canonical security and privacy rules.
MPS-016-FR-044 — Auditability
Material payment state transitions and privileged operations MUST be auditable.
MPS-016-FR-045 — Provider Suspension
The system MUST support governed suspension of an unsafe or unavailable payment route without discarding unresolved operations.
81.10 Reliability and integration
MPS-016-FR-046 — Durable Recovery
The system MUST support recovery of unresolved operations after process or infrastructure failure.
MPS-016-FR-047 — Event Traceability
Canonical payment events MUST be traceable to the relevant operation and accepted evidence.
MPS-016-FR-048 — Event Deduplication
Consumers MUST be able to handle duplicate delivery without creating duplicate financial effects.
MPS-016-FR-049 — Operational Monitoring
The implementation MUST expose the required payment reliability, failure, uncertainty, and reconciliation measures.
MPS-016-FR-050 — Controlled Extensibility
New providers and payment methods MUST be integrated through governed extension points and capability declarations.
PART XXVI — ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
82. ACCEPTANCE CRITERION CONVENTION
The following criteria use the prefix MPS-016-AC.
Passing these criteria requires evidence from implementation-level tests or equivalent approved verification.
They have not been executed by producing this document.
AC-001 — Intent Validation
Given a payment intent with a valid commercial reference, authorized caller, valid amount, and supported currency, the system accepts the intent for further processing.
AC-002 — Invalid Amount Rejection
Given an invalid or prohibited amount, the system rejects the request without initiating an external financial effect.
AC-003 — Currency Mismatch
Given inconsistent payment and provider currency requirements, the system rejects or explicitly resolves the mismatch according to policy without implicit conversion.
AC-004 — Duplicate Authorization Request
Given two equivalent requests with the same idempotency identity, the system creates no more than one logical authorization operation.
AC-005 — Idempotency Conflict
Given the same idempotency key with a materially different amount, currency, or operation type, the system rejects the conflicting request.
AC-006 — Concurrent Capture
Given concurrent capture requests competing for the same remaining authorization amount, the system prevents unauthorized excess capture.
AC-007 — Partial Capture
Given a provider that supports partial capture, the system correctly validates and records the supported partial-capture operation.
AC-008 — Unsupported Capture
Given a payment method that does not support the requested capture operation, the system rejects the operation without simulating unsupported behavior.
AC-009 — Provider Timeout
Given a provider timeout after a request may have executed, the system records an uncertain outcome and follows the approved recovery procedure.
AC-010 — Safe Retry
Given evidence that an operation was not executed, the system permits a retry under the approved idempotency and retry policy.
AC-011 — Unsafe Retry Prevention
Given an unresolved prior charge attempt, the system does not automatically create an independent charge through another provider.
AC-012 — Duplicate Notification
Given repeated delivery of the same authenticated provider notification, the system does not create duplicate financial effects.
AC-013 — Invalid Notification
Given an unauthenticated or invalid provider notification, the system does not accept it as authoritative payment evidence.
AC-014 — Out-of-Order Notification
Given valid notifications delivered out of order, the system applies permitted transitions without erasing established financial history.
AC-015 — Contradictory Provider Evidence
Given contradictory evidence for the same operation, the system preserves the conflict and creates the required reconciliation or investigation record.
AC-016 — Refund Authorization
Given a refund request without the required business authorization, the system rejects execution.
AC-017 — Refund Balance
Given a refund exceeding the applicable refundable amount, the system rejects or constrains the request according to the approved policy.
AC-018 — Concurrent Refunds
Given concurrent refund requests, the system prevents the total authorized refundable amount from being exceeded.
AC-019 — Refund Timeout
Given an uncertain refund outcome, the system does not create an unsafe duplicate refund operation.
AC-020 — Void Eligibility
Given an operation that is no longer eligible for voiding, the system rejects the void or follows the approved alternative process.
AC-021 — Reversal Traceability
Given a reversal operation, the system preserves its link to the original operation and records the outcome independently.
AC-022 — Provider Capability
Given a provider without a required capability, the routing engine excludes that provider from the corresponding route.
AC-023 — Provider Suspension
Given an authorized route suspension, new operations cannot use the suspended route except under an explicitly approved exception policy.
AC-024 — Route Recovery
Given restoration of a suspended route, the system requires the configured recovery conditions and approvals before reactivation.
AC-025 — Provider Isolation
Given a provider outage, unaffected eligible routes remain isolated from unnecessary failure propagation.
AC-026 — State Concurrency
Given concurrent state-changing requests, the system rejects or safely coordinates stale transitions.
AC-027 — Durable Recovery
Given process failure after operation registration, the system can recover the operation without inventing success or initiating an unsafe duplicate.
AC-028 — Event Publication
Given a committed internal state transition, the corresponding event is published or remains durably pending publication under the approved delivery mechanism.
AC-029 — Event Replay
Given replay of a historical event, consumers do not repeat the underlying financial operation.
AC-030 — Reconciliation Match
Given matching internal and external transaction evidence, the reconciliation engine records the appropriate matching result.
AC-031 — Reconciliation Mismatch
Given a material amount or currency discrepancy, the engine records the discrepancy and initiates the required handling process.
AC-032 — Settlement Boundary
Given a successful payment capture without settlement evidence, the system does not claim that settlement has completed.
AC-033 — Audit Evidence
Given a material payment state transition, the system records the required actor, operation, evidence, and state history.
AC-034 — Secret Protection
Given ordinary logs, API responses, and events, restricted provider credentials and sensitive authentication material are not exposed.
AC-035 — Tenant Isolation
Given a caller operating in one tenant, the system denies unauthorized access to another tenant's payment operations and evidence.
AC-036 — Risk Policy Enforcement
Given a mandatory risk denial, the system does not execute the prohibited payment operation.
AC-037 — Risk Dependency Failure
Given failure of a mandatory risk dependency, the system applies the approved fail-closed or explicitly governed degraded-mode policy.
AC-038 — Provider Contract Change
Given an incompatible provider contract change, the system detects the incompatibility before activating the affected configuration.
AC-039 — Configuration Traceability
Given a payment operation, the system can identify the relevant routing and policy configuration versions.
AC-040 — Canonical Ownership
Given a request that requires an order, price, identity, or refund eligibility fact, the payment domain resolves it through the authoritative source rather than creating competing canonical truth.
AC-041 — Uncertain Outcome Visibility
Given an unresolved payment outcome, authorized consumers receive a status that accurately communicates uncertainty.
AC-042 — Callback Before Response
Given a valid provider callback arriving before the synchronous response is processed, the system safely correlates both observations without duplicating the operation.
AC-043 — Provider Idempotency Expiry
Given an expired provider idempotency window and an uncertain previous operation, the system follows a safe recovery or investigation process rather than assuming retry safety.
AC-044 — Configuration Rollback
Given a defective routing configuration, authorized operators can restore an approved configuration version without rewriting historical operation evidence.
AC-045 — Reconciliation Reprocessing
Given repeated processing of the same external transaction report, the system does not create duplicate financial effects or duplicate logical reconciliation outcomes.
AC-046 — Multi-Currency Isolation
Given operations in different currencies, the system maintains independent currency-consistent amounts and does not aggregate them as if they shared a currency.
AC-047 — Evidence Preservation
Given a correction to a prior state interpretation, the original evidence remains available and the correction is recorded with provenance.
AC-048 — Bounded Recovery
Given a persistently unavailable provider, automated recovery remains bounded and escalates unresolved operations according to policy.
AC-049 — Access Revocation
Given revocation of a provider credential or operator permission, subsequent operations are denied according to the applicable revocation and in-flight-operation policies.
AC-050 — Cross-Domain Consistency
Given a change to a relevant upstream contract, the implementation detects affected payment dependencies and requires the appropriate compatibility verification before rollout.
PART XXVII — VERIFICATION STRATEGY
83. REQUIRED VERIFICATION CLASSES
The implementation must define and execute the applicable verification classes.
83.1 Unit verification
Verify:
- Amount validation.
- Currency validation.
- State transitions.
- Idempotency.
- Operation eligibility.
- Capability matching.
- Error classification.
- Routing constraints.
- Reconciliation matching.
- Policy enforcement.
83.2 Contract verification
Verify:
- Provider adapter contracts.
- API schemas.
- Event schemas.
- Error contracts.
- Provider capability declarations.
- Version compatibility.
- Notification contracts.
83.3 Integration verification
Verify:
- Provider request and response handling.
- Asynchronous notification processing.
- Durable operation registration.
- Event publication.
- Reconciliation ingestion.
- Risk and authorization integration.
- Refund authorization integration.
- Accounting and settlement interfaces.
83.4 Property-based verification
Test financial invariants across generated valid and invalid operation sequences.
Examples include:
- Captured amounts never exceed applicable capture constraints.
- Refund amounts never exceed the applicable refundable balance.
- Duplicate requests do not create additional logical operations.
- Currency values remain consistent.
- Unauthorized state transitions never succeed.
- An uncertain outcome is never silently converted to success or failure.
- Historical evidence is preserved across corrections.
83.5 Concurrency verification
Test:
- Simultaneous authorization requests.
- Concurrent capture operations.
- Concurrent refunds.
- Duplicate callbacks.
- Out-of-order events.
- Concurrent configuration changes.
- Stale state versions.
- Concurrent reconciliation processing.
83.6 Fault injection
Simulate:
- Provider timeout.
- Network interruption.
- Provider response loss.
- Process crash.
- Database failure.
- Event publication failure.
- Duplicate notification.
- Delayed notification.
- Invalid signature.
- Provider outage.
- Conflicting provider records.
- Recovery after credential rotation.
83.7 Security verification
Test:
- Authentication and authorization.
- Tenant isolation.
- Secret leakage.
- Notification forgery.
- Replay attacks.
- Input validation.
- Access-control bypass.
- Configuration tampering.
- Audit integrity.
- Restricted-data exposure.
83.8 End-to-end verification
Verify the complete payment journey across the relevant canonical domains without allowing one domain to become an alternative source of truth for another.

87. IMPLEMENTATION PROHIBITIONS
Before the relevant gates are satisfied, implementation must not:
- Create competing payment identifiers.
- Duplicate canonical monetary or currency models.
- Introduce a provider-specific business model as the canonical payment ontology.
- Bypass canonical identity or authorization.
- Initiate financial execution before durable operation registration.
- Retry uncertain financial operations unsafely.
- Treat callback receipt as proof of payment.
- Treat a client redirect as proof of payment.
- Treat capture as settlement.
- Treat settlement as accounting completion.
- Create independent refund eligibility rules that conflict with the refund authority.
- Hardcode provider selection into unrelated domain logic.
- Persist secrets in source code or general metadata.
- Suppress material reconciliation discrepancies.
- Rewrite financial history destructively.
- Introduce undocumented cross-domain dependencies.
- Claim security or regulatory certification without evidence.

UCOS-MKT-MASTER-SPECIFICATION-016 defines the proposed Universal Marketplace Payment and Payment Orchestration architecture.
Its central architectural commitment is that payment processing must be:
- Explicitly modeled.
- Canonically governed.
- Financially consistent.
- Idempotent where required.
- Safe under concurrency.
- Recoverable under uncertainty.
- Provider-neutral.
- Technology-neutral.
- Auditable.
- Secure by design.
- Reconciliation-capable.
- Extensible through governed contracts.
- Integrated with existing UCOS authorities.
- Verified through measurable acceptance criteria.
The payment domain must not invent financial truth when external evidence is unavailable.
It must not create duplicate financial effects because an operation timed out.
It must not confuse authorization, capture, refund, settlement, and accounting.
It must not replace existing canonical UCOS authorities with local copies.
It must preserve the provenance of material financial evidence and make unresolved outcomes visible to authorized operators and consuming domains.

UCOS-MKT-MASTER-SPECIFICATION-017 will define the Universal Marketplace Offers, Promotions, Coupons and Incentives Specification.
Its primary architectural objective is to provide one extensible commercial-incentive system for the UCOS marketplace—covering simple discounts, complex promotion combinations, personalized offers, campaigns, eligibility rules, budgets, redemption limits, geographic and temporal conditions, and future incentive mechanisms.
The critical authority boundaries are:
- Document 015 — Pricing: owns canonical price construction, price quotations, monetary arithmetic, and commercial price authority.
- Document 017 — Offers and Incentives: owns promotion definitions, eligibility, incentive evaluation, stacking rules, redemption authorization, budget constraints, and promotion lifecycle.
- Document 018 — Cart, Checkout and Purchase Commitment: will coordinate the purchase journey and consume validated pricing and promotion results.
- Document 008 — Marketplace Operations: retains its reconciled authority over orders, refunds, operational workflows, and related financial operations.
An offer must never independently rewrite the canonical price or create a competing source of truth for the purchase total. The specification below defines the proposed architecture and requirements; canonical reconciliation, implementation, testing, and certification remain separate approval gates.

## DOCUMENT STATUS DECLARATION

This document defines the proposed architecture for universal commercial offers, promotions, coupons, incentives, eligibility, redemption, stacking, campaign integration, budgets, and incentive governance within UCOS Ω∞.

It is a proposed domain specification and must be reconciled with existing UCOS constitutions, canonical registries, commercial architecture, pricing contracts, identity authorities, campaign architecture, loyalty architecture, and marketplace implementation artifacts before approval.

No claim is made that the proposed identifiers have been registered, that this specification has been committed to a repository, or that implementation, testing, or certification has occurred.

If an existing UCOS canonical authority already owns a concept described here, that authority takes precedence.

This specification must not create duplicate product, pricing, customer identity, campaign, payment, tax, accounting, or governance authorities.

---

# PART I — EXECUTIVE ARCHITECTURE

## 1. PURPOSE

The purpose of this specification is to establish a universal, reusable, extensible, policy-governed commercial incentive capability for the UCOS marketplace.

The capability must support the complete lifecycle of commercial incentives, from creation and eligibility definition through evaluation, reservation, application, redemption, financial allocation, cancellation, expiration, reversal, measurement, and audit.

It must support diverse commercial models without hardcoding a particular industry, product category, payment method, country, currency, customer type, or business model.

The architecture must support:

- Percentage discounts.
- Fixed-value discounts.
- Product-specific discounts.
- Category-specific discounts.
- Order-level discounts.
- Quantity-based incentives.
- Volume discounts.
- Tiered discounts.
- Bundle offers.
- Buy-X-get-Y offers.
- Free gifts.
- Free or discounted fulfillment.
- Conditional promotions.
- Coupon-based promotions.
- Automatically applied promotions.
- Personalized offers.
- Audience-specific incentives.
- Loyalty-related benefits.
- Referral incentives.
- Membership benefits.
- Subscription incentives.
- Partner-funded offers.
- Merchant-funded offers.
- Marketplace-funded offers.
- Jointly funded incentives.
- Time-bound campaigns.
- Budget-constrained promotions.
- Location-constrained promotions.
- Contractual commercial incentives.
- Future incentive mechanisms that do not yet exist.

These are capability examples, not a fixed exhaustive list.

New incentive types must be introduced through governed capability definitions and extension contracts rather than modifications scattered across unrelated domains.

## 2. ARCHITECTURAL VISION

Establish a universal incentive system in which an authorized business actor can define an incentive, specify its eligibility and constraints, publish it through a governed lifecycle, evaluate it against an eligible commercial context, calculate its permitted incentive effect through the canonical pricing authority, reserve limited resources, authorize redemption, and preserve a complete audit trail.

The system must provide:

1. Canonical incentive definitions.
2. Reusable eligibility conditions.
3. Explicit incentive-effect definitions.
4. A deterministic evaluation model.
5. Governed promotion combination rules.
6. Controlled coupon issuance and redemption.
7. Budget and quota enforcement.
8. Audience and participant targeting.
9. Temporal and geographic eligibility.
10. Product and service eligibility.
11. Channel and transaction-context eligibility.
12. Campaign and journey integration.
13. Fraud and abuse prevention.
14. Transparent customer-facing outcomes.
15. Safe concurrent redemption.
16. Reversible and compensating operations.
17. Financial allocation and attribution.
18. Provider- and technology-neutral integration.
19. Versioned configuration and reproducible evaluation.
20. Complete traceability from offer definition to realized commercial effect.

## 3. CORE ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLE

**An incentive is a governed commercial rule that may propose an economic benefit; it is not an independent pricing authority.**

The incentive domain determines:

- Which incentive is eligible.
- Why it is eligible.
- Which conditions must hold.
- Which incentive effect is permitted.
- Whether the incentive may be combined with others.
- Whether a code, quota, budget, or reservation is required.
- Whether redemption may proceed.
- Which funding policy applies.
- Which evidence must be retained.

The pricing domain determines the canonical monetary calculation and price quotation according to the approved pricing contract.

The purchase domain coordinates the commercial journey and consumes the resulting validated price and incentive information.

The order, payment, settlement, and accounting authorities retain their respective responsibilities.

---

# PART II — ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES

## 4. KNOWLEDGE ONCE

Each canonical concept must have one authoritative definition.

An offer, promotion, coupon, incentive, campaign, funding agreement, eligibility rule, and redemption must not be represented as interchangeable copies of the same object.

Multiple domains may reference a canonical object, but each must preserve its ownership and semantic meaning.

## 5. CANONICAL AUTHORITY

Every material commercial fact must have an authoritative owner.

| Concept | Proposed authority |
|---|---|
| Product and service identity | Existing canonical Product/Service authority |
| Product taxonomy | Existing canonical Taxonomy authority |
| Customer identity | Existing canonical Identity authority |
| Merchant and seller identity | Existing canonical Participant authority |
| Commercial price | Document 015 or the reconciled canonical Pricing authority |
| Incentive definition | Document 017, subject to reconciliation |
| Eligibility evaluation | Incentive domain using authoritative facts |
| Final monetary calculation | Canonical Pricing authority |
| Cart and purchase coordination | Planned Document 018 |
| Order lifecycle | Existing canonical Order authority |
| Payment operation | Document 016 or the reconciled Payment authority |
| Refund eligibility | Authoritative business domain |
| Refund execution | Payment and operational authorities |
| Seller settlement | Canonical Settlement/Financial authority |
| Tax determination | Canonical Tax authority |
| Fraud and trust decisions | Document 013 or existing canonical Trust and Safety authority |
| Customer communication | Existing customer experience and communications authorities |
| Campaign orchestration | Existing canonical Campaign authority, if present |
| Loyalty balance and points ledger | Existing canonical Loyalty authority, if present |
| Accounting ledger | Canonical Accounting authority |
| Analytics metrics | Canonical Analytics authority |
| Registry and artifact identity | Existing UCOS registry authority |

This matrix is provisional until existing UCOS artifacts are reconciled.

## 6. DOMAIN AND TECHNOLOGY AGNOSTICISM

The architecture must not require:

- A specific commerce platform.
- A particular promotion engine.
- A specific programming language.
- A specific database.
- A specific cloud.
- A specific campaign product.
- A specific payment provider.
- A specific message broker.
- A specific search engine.
- A specific identity provider.
- A specific rules engine.
- A specific AI model.
- A specific deployment architecture.

Implementations may select technologies through approved architecture decisions, but business semantics must remain independent of those choices.

## 7. ZERO DUPLICATION

The architecture must prevent:

- Duplicate incentive definitions.
- Duplicate eligibility rules.
- Duplicate coupon identities.
- Duplicate redemption records.
- Competing price calculations.
- Multiple authoritative campaign records.
- Duplicate funding balances.
- Duplicate loyalty balances.
- Competing redemption counters.
- Multiple definitions of the same stacking policy.
- Untraceable copies of canonical configuration.

Derived projections and caches are permitted only when their source, ownership, freshness, and invalidation behavior are explicit.

## 8. DETERMINISM

Given equivalent canonical inputs, equivalent configuration versions, equivalent policy context, and equivalent authoritative facts, the evaluation engine must produce equivalent evaluation results.

Any permitted nondeterminism must be explicit, governed, recorded, and reproducible to the extent required by the business and regulatory context.

## 9. FAIL-SAFE INCENTIVE EXECUTION

When the system cannot verify an essential eligibility condition, budget reservation, coupon state, or redemption constraint, it must apply the relevant approved failure policy.

The architecture must distinguish:

- A condition that is false.
- A condition that is unknown.
- A condition that could not be evaluated.
- A condition that is temporarily unavailable.
- A condition that requires additional evidence.

An unavailable dependency must not silently become an affirmative eligibility decision.

## 10. CONTEXT ASSIMILATION GATE

No implementation may begin until existing UCOS canonical context has been discovered, read, reconciled, and accepted.

# PART III — SCOPE AND BOUNDARIES

## 11. IN-SCOPE CAPABILITIES

The domain includes:

1. Incentive ontology.
2. Offer lifecycle.
3. Promotion lifecycle.
4. Coupon lifecycle.
5. Incentive-effect catalog.
6. Eligibility-rule definitions.
7. Eligibility evaluation.
8. Promotion composition.
9. Promotion stacking.
10. Promotion exclusion.
11. Promotion precedence.
12. Incentive application decisions.
13. Coupon-code generation and registration.
14. Coupon redemption control.
15. Customer and audience targeting.
16. Product and service targeting.
17. Category and assortment targeting.
18. Merchant and seller targeting.
19. Channel targeting.
20. Geographic eligibility.
21. Temporal eligibility.
22. Quantity and spend thresholds.
23. Usage limits.
24. Budget and quota constraints.
25. Funding attribution.
26. Reservation management.
27. Redemption finalization.
28. Redemption cancellation.
29. Incentive reversal and compensation.
30. Incentive allocation contracts.
31. Promotion transparency.
32. Eligibility explanations.
33. Campaign integration.
34. Loyalty integration.
35. Referral integration.
36. Payment-benefit integration.
37. Partner-benefit integration.
38. Fraud and abuse controls.
39. Promotion analytics integration.
40. Audit and lineage.
41. Versioned policy configuration.
42. Capability registration.
43. Controlled extension.
44. Testing and certification contracts.

## 12. OUT-OF-SCOPE AUTHORITIES

### 12.1 Price construction

The incentive domain must not independently define the authoritative price of a product, service, order, or commercial transaction.

It may define an incentive effect such as:

- A percentage reduction.
- A fixed reduction.
- A maximum permitted reduction.
- A free item.
- A fulfillment benefit.
- A reward entitlement.
- A conditional commercial benefit.

The pricing authority determines how the effect is translated into the canonical commercial calculation.

### 12.2 Tax calculation

The incentive domain must not independently decide tax jurisdiction, tax classification, tax rates, or statutory tax treatment.

Whether a particular discount affects the taxable base depends on the applicable legal and tax rules.

The canonical tax authority must determine or validate the relevant tax treatment.

### 12.3 Payment execution

The incentive domain does not authorize, capture, void, reverse, or refund payment transactions.

Payment-related incentives must use explicit contracts with Document 016 or the reconciled canonical payment authority.

### 12.4 Order management

The incentive domain does not own order lifecycle, fulfillment, shipment, delivery, or order cancellation.

It provides incentive decisions and associated evidence to the authoritative purchasing and order domains.

### 12.5 Loyalty ledger

The incentive domain must not create a competing loyalty-points balance or reward ledger.

It may define an incentive that grants a loyalty benefit, subject to the authoritative loyalty rules and ledger.

### 12.6 Campaign orchestration

A campaign is not necessarily an offer.

A campaign may contain, activate, distribute, or coordinate one or more offers, but campaign identity and orchestration must remain with the canonical campaign authority.

### 12.7 Customer identity

Customer targeting must reference canonical identity and audience authorities.

The incentive domain must not create independent customer identities.

### 12.8 Fraud intelligence

The incentive domain applies the relevant risk and abuse decisions but does not replace the canonical trust and safety authority.

---

# PART IV — CANONICAL ONTOLOGY

## 13. CANONICAL TERMS

| Term | Proposed definition |
|---|---|
| Commercial Incentive | A governed benefit or advantage offered under explicit commercial conditions. |
| Offer | A business-facing or customer-facing representation of a commercial proposition. |
| Promotion | A governed rule configuration that determines when an incentive may be offered or applied. |
| Incentive Definition | The canonical configuration describing the benefit, constraints, and lifecycle of an incentive. |
| Incentive Effect | The abstract commercial effect permitted by an incentive. |
| Coupon | A governed redemption instrument or code associated with an incentive or promotion. |
| Coupon Code | A human- or machine-presentable code used to request a coupon-related benefit. |
| Redemption | A governed operation that consumes or finalizes an eligible incentive entitlement. |
| Redemption Attempt | An attempt to redeem a coupon or incentive. |
| Eligibility Rule | A reusable rule that evaluates whether a defined condition is satisfied. |
| Eligibility Evaluation | A recorded evaluation of relevant conditions against a defined context. |
| Eligibility Decision | The accepted outcome of an eligibility evaluation. |
| Incentive Reservation | A temporary or governed allocation of limited incentive resources. |
| Promotion Combination | A defined relationship describing whether and how incentives may be combined. |
| Stacking Policy | A governed rule defining permitted combinations and their calculation order. |
| Promotion Exclusion | A rule prohibiting specified incentives from being combined. |
| Promotion Priority | A governed ordering attribute used where ordering is semantically required. |
| Campaign | A coordinated business initiative that may reference offers and incentives. |
| Audience | A canonical group, segment, or population defined by an authoritative audience mechanism. |
| Funding Source | The authoritative party or account responsible for an incentive's economic cost. |
| Funding Allocation | A governed allocation of an incentive's cost among authorized funding participants. |
| Promotion Budget | A governed limit on permitted incentive expenditure or commitment. |
| Redemption Limit | A constraint on permitted redemption counts or quantities. |
| Redemption Quota | A governed quantity or capacity available for redemption. |
| Incentive Allocation | A record of how an incentive's monetary or nonmonetary effect is attributed to eligible targets. |
| Provisional Incentive | An incentive whose application depends on verification or another unresolved condition. |
| Incentive Evaluation Snapshot | A reproducible record of the inputs, rules, and policy versions used for an evaluation. |
| Incentive Liability | A governed financial or contractual obligation associated with an incentive. |
| Incentive Reversal | A compensating operation that corrects or reverses a prior incentive effect where permitted. |
| Incentive Expiration | The end of an incentive's eligibility or validity under its defined lifecycle. |
| Incentive Revocation | A governed withdrawal of an incentive or entitlement. |
| Promotion Version | An immutable or explicitly versioned representation of promotion configuration. |
| Redemption Evidence | Evidence supporting a redemption decision or outcome. |

These definitions are proposed canonical candidates and must be reconciled with existing UCOS terminology.

## 14. DISTINCT CONCEPTS

The following must not be conflated:

- Offer versus promotion.
- Promotion versus campaign.
- Coupon versus coupon code.
- Incentive definition versus incentive effect.
- Eligibility evaluation versus eligibility decision.
- Evaluation versus reservation.
- Reservation versus redemption.
- Redemption versus order completion.
- Discount versus price.
- Discount amount versus final payable amount.
- Promotion budget versus funding balance.
- Funding allocation versus seller settlement.
- Reward entitlement versus loyalty ledger entry.
- Provisional incentive versus finalized incentive.
- Promotion expiration versus coupon expiration.
- Revocation versus reversal.
- Redemption cancellation versus financial refund.
- Promotion attribution versus financial accounting.
- Customer-facing explanation versus authoritative eligibility evidence.

## 15. CANONICAL IDENTITY MODEL

Every canonical object must have a stable identifier under the applicable UCOS identifier authority.

The following identities must remain distinct:

- Incentive ID.
- Offer ID.
- Promotion ID.
- Promotion version ID.
- Campaign ID.
- Coupon ID.
- Coupon code identity.
- Eligibility rule ID.
- Eligibility evaluation ID.
- Eligibility decision ID.
- Reservation ID.
- Redemption ID.
- Redemption attempt ID.
- Incentive allocation ID.
- Funding agreement ID.
- Budget ID.
- Quota ID.
- Customer identity reference.
- Merchant identity reference.
- Product identity reference.
- Cart reference.
- Order reference.
- Price quotation reference.
- Payment reference.
- Reversal reference.

An implementation may use opaque identifiers, natural identifiers, or composite identifiers where permitted by the canonical identity authority.

A coupon code is not automatically the canonical identity of the coupon object.

PART V — UNIVERSAL INCENTIVE MODEL
17. INCENTIVE DEFINITION
A canonical incentive definition must describe the intended benefit without embedding the entire purchasing, pricing, payment, or fulfillment implementation.
A proposed logical contract is:
{
  "incentive_id": "canonical-incentive-reference",
  "incentive_type": "REGISTERED-INCENTIVE-TYPE",
  "name": "Customer-facing-name-reference",
  "description": "Localized-description-reference",
  "status": "DRAFT",
  "version": "immutable-version-reference",
  "owner_reference": "canonical-owner-reference",
  "promotion_reference": "canonical-promotion-reference",
  "effect": {
    "effect_type": "REGISTERED-EFFECT-TYPE",
    "effect_definition_reference": "canonical-effect-reference"
  },
  "eligibility": {
    "rule_set_reference": "canonical-rule-set-reference"
  },
  "combination_policy_reference": "canonical-stacking-policy-reference",
  "funding_policy_reference": "canonical-funding-policy-reference",
  "validity": {
    "start": "explicit-time-bound",
    "end": "explicit-time-bound-or-null",
    "timezone_policy_reference": "canonical-time-policy"
  },
  "limits": {
    "budget_reference": "optional-budget-reference",
    "quota_reference": "optional-quota-reference",
    "redemption_policy_reference": "canonical-redemption-policy"
  },
  "governance": {
    "approval_policy_reference": "canonical-approval-policy",
    "publication_policy_reference": "canonical-publication-policy"
  },
  "schema_version": "canonical-schema-version"
}

This is an illustrative logical model, not an approved production schema.
18. INCENTIVE DEFINITION RULES
An incentive definition must:
1. Have a stable identity.
2. Reference a governed effect type.
3. Reference its eligibility rules.
4. Declare its effective period.
5. Declare the owner and applicable governance policy.
6. Declare the applicable combination policy.
7. Declare funding responsibilities where relevant.
8. Declare applicable redemption constraints.
9. Declare whether explicit coupon interaction is required.
10. Declare whether reservation is required.
11. Identify whether the benefit is monetary or nonmonetary.
12. Reference canonical product, customer, merchant, and geographic authorities as needed.
13. Identify relevant external dependencies.
14. Declare whether the benefit is provisional.
15. Be versioned and auditable.
16. Have a defined lifecycle.
17. Be discoverable through the applicable registry.
18. Be subject to validation before publication.
19. INCENTIVE EFFECT CATALOG
The effect catalog must be extensible and governed.
Proposed effect categories include:
19.1 Monetary reduction
- Percentage reduction.
- Fixed-value reduction.
- Maximum-capped reduction.
- Minimum-guaranteed reduction, where contractually valid.
- Tiered reduction.
- Quantity-based reduction.
- Unit-price incentive.
- Line-level incentive.
- Order-level incentive.
- Conditional reduction.
- Bundle-related reduction.
19.2 Commercial entitlement
- Free eligible item.
- Discounted eligible item.
- Complimentary service.
- Complimentary fulfillment.
- Fulfillment fee reduction.
- Access to a special commercial price.
- Upgrade entitlement.
- Additional service entitlement.
- Bonus quantity.
- Commercial benefit with a defined eligibility condition.
19.3 Loyalty and engagement benefits
- Bonus points.
- Reward entitlement.
- Membership benefit.
- Referral benefit.
- Loyalty multiplier.
- Future benefit entitlement.
These effects must be executed through their authoritative domains.
For example, the offer domain may request a bonus-points benefit, but the canonical loyalty authority determines the actual ledger effect.
19.4 Funding-related incentives
- Merchant-funded incentive.
- Marketplace-funded incentive.
- Partner-funded incentive.
- Co-funded incentive.
- Contractually sponsored incentive.
The effect definition must identify the applicable funding policy without pretending that a funding allocation is itself a completed financial settlement.
19.5 Future effects
New effect types may be registered when their semantics can be represented through governed contracts.
A new effect type must not silently introduce a new canonical price, payment, identity, inventory, or accounting authority.
PART VI — PROMOTION MODEL
20. PROMOTION DEFINITION
A promotion defines the conditions under which a governed incentive may be offered, evaluated, reserved, or redeemed.
A promotion must not be treated as an arbitrary script with unrestricted access to marketplace data and financial operations.
A proposed promotion contract includes:
- Promotion identity.
- Promotion version.
- Incentive reference.
- Eligibility rule-set reference.
- Effective period.
- Geographic constraints.
- Audience constraints.
- Product and service constraints.
- Channel constraints.
- Quantity and spend constraints.
- Coupon requirements.
- Stacking policy.
- Exclusion policy.
- Budget and quota references.
- Funding policy.
- Approval status.
- Publication status.
- Audit references.
21. PROMOTION LIFECYCLE
Proposed lifecycle:
DRAFT
  |
  v
VALIDATING
  |
  +------> REJECTED
  |
  v
APPROVED
  |
  v
SCHEDULED
  |
  v
ACTIVE
  |
  +------> PAUSED
  |          |
  |          v
  |        ACTIVE
  |
  +------> EXPIRED
  |
  +------> REVOKED
  |
  v
ARCHIVED

Not every transition is permitted from every state.
The lifecycle must distinguish configuration approval, publication, activation, suspension, expiration, and archival.
21.1 Draft
The promotion is being defined and must not be available for ordinary redemption.
21.2 Validating
The promotion is undergoing schema, rule, dependency, security, funding, and policy validation.
21.3 Approved
Required approvals have been granted.
Approval does not automatically mean the promotion is active.
21.4 Scheduled
The promotion has been approved and configured for future activation.
21.5 Active
The promotion is eligible for evaluation, subject to its effective period, dependencies, and constraints.
21.6 Paused
New evaluations or redemptions are restricted according to the approved suspension policy.
Already finalized redemptions must not be silently erased.
21.7 Expired
The promotion is outside its permitted effective period.
21.8 Revoked
The promotion has been withdrawn under an authorized governance decision.
21.9 Archived
The promotion is retained for audit, analytics, and historical interpretation but is not available for new ordinary redemption.
22. VERSION IMMUTABILITY
A published promotion version must have stable semantics.
A material change to eligibility, effect, funding, stacking, or redemption behavior must produce a governed new version unless the canonical versioning authority explicitly supports an alternative mechanism.
Historical evaluations and redemptions must retain the exact promotion version that governed their decisions.
23. PUBLICATION VALIDATION
Before publication, the system must validate:
- Schema completeness.
- Eligibility-rule validity.
- Effect-type registration.
- Rule dependency availability.
- Temporal consistency.
- Geographic constraints.
- Audience references.
- Product and service references.
- Coupon requirements.
- Stacking and exclusion consistency.
- Budget and quota configuration.
- Funding authorization.
- Applicable approval requirements.
- Security policy.
- Conflicting promotions.
- Required explanatory content.
- Evaluation determinism.
- Required acceptance tests.
Invalid or contradictory configurations must not become active.
PART VII — ELIGIBILITY ENGINE
24. ELIGIBILITY OBJECTIVE
The eligibility engine evaluates whether an incentive may be offered or applied in a defined context.
It must use canonical facts and registered rules rather than duplicating business data.
25. ELIGIBILITY DIMENSIONS
Eligibility may depend on:
25.1 Participant context
- Customer identity reference.
- Customer status.
- Customer segment.
- Membership reference.
- Seller or merchant.
- Authorized business account.
- Partner relationship.
- Participant eligibility.
25.2 Product and service context
- Product identity.
- Service identity.
- Product category.
- Taxonomy reference.
- Brand reference.
- Variant or configuration.
- Assortment membership.
- Product lifecycle state.
- Merchant assortment.
- Service eligibility.
25.3 Commercial context
- Quantity.
- Eligible subtotal.
- Basket composition.
- Purchase type.
- Commercial agreement.
- Price quotation reference.
- Previous purchase conditions.
- New-customer condition.
- Order or transaction context.
25.4 Temporal context
- Effective start.
- Effective end.
- Time of evaluation.
- Time of redemption.
- Recurring time window.
- Day or date conditions.
- Business calendar.
- Timezone policy.
- Applicable cutoff rules.
25.5 Geographic context
- Authorized location reference.
- Country or jurisdiction.
- Region.
- Administrative area.
- Service area.
- Delivery destination.
- Store location.
- Geographic containment.
- Geographic eligibility policy.
The architecture must not hardcode a fixed hierarchy of geographic entities. It must use the canonical Geography authority.
25.6 Channel context
- Web.
- Mobile application.
- Physical store.
- Assisted commerce.
- Partner channel.
- Marketplace API.
- Subscription channel.
- Other registered channels.
These are examples, not a fixed list.
25.7 Payment context
- Payment method eligibility.
- Authorized instrument category.
- Payment-provider capability.
- Payment-related commercial agreement.
- Approved payment-benefit reference.
Payment conditions must use Document 016 or the canonical payment authority.
Sensitive payment credentials must not be required as general eligibility data.
25.8 Risk and compliance context
- Risk decision reference.
- Trust and safety restriction.
- Eligibility restriction.
- Applicable policy.
- Compliance condition.
- Fraud-related eligibility constraint.
The canonical risk authority determines the relevant risk decision.
25.9 Resource context
- Remaining promotion budget.
- Remaining coupon quota.
- Per-customer redemption limit.
- Per-order redemption limit.
- Merchant funding allocation.
- Partner funding allocation.
- Reserved incentive capacity.
These facts must be validated against their authoritative sources.
26. ELIGIBILITY RULE MODEL
Eligibility rules must be composable and machine-readable.
A rule may express:
- Equality.
- Inequality.
- Membership.
- Exclusion.
- Numeric comparison.
- Quantity threshold.
- Monetary threshold.
- Temporal interval.
- Geographic containment.
- Existence.
- Nonexistence.
- Count.
- Aggregate condition.
- Relationship traversal through an authorized canonical contract.
- Explicit reference to an approved external decision.
A rule engine must not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary databases, source code execution, shell commands, or unauthorized external services.
27. RULE COMPOSITION
A rule set may combine conditions using governed operators such as:
- ALL.
- ANY.
- NONE.
- AT_LEAST.
- EXACTLY.
- NOT.
- THRESHOLD.
- POLICY_REFERENCE.
The semantics of each operator must be defined by the canonical rule authority.
A proposed logical rule is:
{
  "rule_set_id": "canonical-rule-set-reference",
  "version": "immutable-version-reference",
  "composition": "ALL",
  "conditions": [
    {
      "condition_id": "condition-001",
      "subject_reference": "canonical-subject-reference",
      "operator": "GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL",
      "value_reference": "canonical-value-reference"
    },
    {
      "condition_id": "condition-002",
      "subject_reference": "canonical-subject-reference",
      "operator": "IN_SET",
      "value_reference": "canonical-set-reference"
    }
  ],
  "unknown_policy_reference": "canonical-unknown-handling-policy",
  "schema_version": "canonical-schema-version"
}

The example is illustrative and not a final production schema.
28. THREE-VALUED ELIGIBILITY LOGIC
Eligibility evaluation must distinguish at least:
- TRUE.
- FALSE.
- UNKNOWN.
An evaluation may also return a technical error classification separate from the logical result.
TRUE
The condition has been established as satisfied.
FALSE
The condition has been established as not satisfied.
UNKNOWN
The system lacks sufficient authoritative evidence to determine the result.
ERROR
The evaluation could not be completed due to a technical or contract failure.
The policy must specify how UNKNOWN and ERROR are handled for each decision type.
For ordinary financial redemption, unknown mandatory conditions must not be silently treated as true.
29. ELIGIBILITY DECISION
An eligibility decision must record:
- Decision ID.
- Evaluation ID.
- Incentive reference.
- Promotion version.
- Context reference.
- Condition outcomes.
- Authoritative fact references.
- Decision result.
- Rejection or qualification reasons.
- Policy version.
- Evaluation timestamp.
- Expiry or revalidation requirement.
- Correlation ID.
A decision is valid only for its defined context and validity conditions.
A prior eligible result must not automatically authorize a later redemption if the relevant conditions may have changed.
30. ELIGIBILITY EXPLANATIONS
The system must provide safe, understandable reason codes for ineligible promotions.
Possible reasons include:
- PROMOTION_NOT_ACTIVE.
- PROMOTION_NOT_YET_ACTIVE.
- PROMOTION_EXPIRED.
- CUSTOMER_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- CUSTOMER_AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED.
- PRODUCT_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- CATEGORY_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- MINIMUM_SPEND_NOT_MET.
- MINIMUM_QUANTITY_NOT_MET.
- MAXIMUM_QUANTITY_EXCEEDED.
- LOCATION_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- CHANNEL_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- PAYMENT_METHOD_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
- COUPON_REQUIRED.
- COUPON_INVALID.
- COUPON_EXPIRED.
- COUPON_ALREADY_REDEEMED.
- REDEMPTION_LIMIT_REACHED.
- BUDGET_EXHAUSTED.
- FUNDING_NOT_AVAILABLE.
- STACKING_NOT_PERMITTED.
- EXCLUDED_BY_HIGHER_PRECEDENCE_RULE.
- RISK_RESTRICTION.
- COMPLIANCE_RESTRICTION.
- ELIGIBILITY_UNVERIFIABLE.
- REQUIRED_DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE.
Reason codes must be canonicalized and must not expose sensitive fraud or security signals to unauthorized consumers.
PART VIII — PROMOTION EVALUATION AND APPLICATION
31. EVALUATION PIPELINE



The proposed evaluation pipeline is:

flowchart TD
    REQUEST["Evaluation Request"]
    CONTEXT["Resolve Canonical Context"]
    VERSION["Resolve Applicable Promotion Versions"]
    VALIDATE["Validate Input and Authorization"]
    ELIGIBILITY["Evaluate Eligibility"]
    FILTER["Filter Ineligible Promotions"]
    RISK["Apply Required Risk and Policy Decisions"]
    STACK["Resolve Stacking and Exclusions"]
    RESOURCE["Check Budgets, Quotas and Limits"]
    EFFECT["Produce Eligible Incentive Effects"]
    PRICING["Request Canonical Pricing Evaluation"]
    RESULT["Return Evaluation Result"]
    RESERVE["Reserve Required Resources"]
    REVALIDATE["Revalidate Before Final Redemption"]
    FINALIZE["Finalize Redemption"]
    AUDIT["Record Evidence and Publish Events"]

    REQUEST --> VALIDATE
    VALIDATE --> CONTEXT
    CONTEXT --> VERSION
    VERSION --> ELIGIBILITY
    ELIGIBILITY --> FILTER
    FILTER --> RISK
    RISK --> STACK
    STACK --> RESOURCE
    RESOURCE --> EFFECT
    EFFECT --> PRICING
    PRICING --> RESULT
    RESULT --> RESERVE
    RESERVE --> REVALIDATE
    REVALIDATE --> FINALIZE
    FINALIZE --> AUDIT
