130. CONTRACT COMPATIBILITY
Every contract must have a compatibility policy.
The policy must define:
- Compatible additions.
- Breaking changes.
- Deprecation.
- Migration.
- Version negotiation where required.
- Consumer discovery.
- Schema validation.
- Historical event interpretation.
A contract must not be changed incompatibly merely because all consumers are assumed to be updated simultaneously.
PART XXXVI — NONFUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
131. RELIABILITY
The system must preserve durable purchase state and safely recover from dependency failures.
Reliability objectives must be measurable and approved.
132. AVAILABILITY
Availability objectives must be established for:
- Cart reads.
- Cart writes.
- Checkout initialization.
- Checkout validation.
- Purchase commitment.
- Purchase status retrieval.
- Reconciliation.
The system must distinguish the availability of the checkout coordinator from the availability of required purchase dependencies.
133. DURABILITY
Durable records must meet the approved recovery and persistence requirements.
The system must not acknowledge a durable business transition before the required durability condition is satisfied.
134. CORRECTNESS
The system must preserve:
- Cart version integrity.
- Quote validity.
- Purchase authorization.
- Reservation integrity.
- Payment-operation integrity.
- Idempotency.
- Order handoff integrity.
- Commitment uniqueness.
- Historical traceability.
135. SECURITY
Security requirements include:
- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Tenant isolation.
- Least privilege.
- Secret management.
- Encryption as required.
- Audit.
- Privacy.
- Secure event handling.
- Dependency security.
- Administrative controls.
136. MAINTAINABILITY
The system must support:
- Modular domain boundaries.
- Explicit contracts.
- Automated contract verification.
- Architecture decision records.
- Traceability.
- Dependency visibility.
- Governed extension.
- Controlled deprecation.
- Operational diagnostics.
137. PORTABILITY
The architecture must not require a specific:
- Cloud provider.
- Database.
- Message broker.
- API gateway.
- Workflow engine.
- Payment provider.
- Container platform.
- Programming language.
- Deployment topology.
A concrete implementation may select technologies through approved architecture decisions.
138. OBSERVABILITY
Every material business transition must be observable through approved operational and audit mechanisms.
Observability must not require exposing sensitive information.
PART XXXVII — PROPOSED FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
139. REQUIREMENT REGISTER
The following 50 requirements are proposed identifiers pending canonical registry reconciliation.
Cart Requirements
MPS-018-FR-001 — Cart Creation
The system shall create a uniquely identified cart under an authorized ownership context.
MPS-018-FR-002 — Cart Persistence
The system shall persist cart state according to the approved durability and retention policies.
MPS-018-FR-003 — Cart Versioning
The system shall provide a reliable versioning or equivalent concurrency-control mechanism for cart mutations.
MPS-018-FR-004 — Cart Item Validation
The system shall validate product, configuration, quantity, and applicable commercial references through their authoritative domains.
MPS-018-FR-005 — Cart Mutation Idempotency
The system shall prevent duplicate business effects for repeated cart mutation requests under the same valid idempotency contract.
MPS-018-FR-006 — Cart Merge Governance
The system shall merge carts only when ownership, commercial, configuration, and lifecycle rules permit the merge.
MPS-018-FR-007 — Cart Expiration
The system shall apply governed cart expiration without inventing unrelated payment, reservation, or order transitions.
MPS-018-FR-008 — Cart History
The system shall preserve the mutation and lineage evidence required by applicable audit and recovery policies.
MPS-018-FR-009 — Cart Price Projection
The system shall distinguish estimated cart pricing from an authoritative valid commercial quote.
MPS-018-FR-010 — Cart Ownership
The system shall enforce authorized access to cart state and mutation operations.
Checkout Requirements
MPS-018-FR-011 — Checkout Initialization
The system shall initialize a checkout session against a valid purchase intent and purchase profile.
MPS-018-FR-012 — Checkout Durability
The system shall persist sufficient checkout state to recover from process and network interruptions.
MPS-018-FR-013 — Checkout State Machine
The system shall enforce a governed checkout state machine and reject illegal transitions.
MPS-018-FR-014 — Context Resolution
The system shall resolve required canonical references before allowing commitment.
MPS-018-FR-015 — Purchase Profile Resolution
The system shall resolve and enforce the applicable purchase profile and policy versions.
MPS-018-FR-016 — Material Change Detection
The system shall detect material changes to purchase inputs and invalidate or revalidate dependent decisions.
MPS-018-FR-017 — Checkout Validation
The system shall return structured validation outcomes with authoritative decision references and actionable reason codes.
MPS-018-FR-018 — Checkout Expiration
The system shall apply governed checkout expiration and reconcile dependent operations where required.
MPS-018-FR-019 — Checkout Recovery
The system shall support authorized recovery from interrupted checkout sessions without assuming prior decisions remain valid.
MPS-018-FR-020 — Checkout Status
The system shall expose an authorized, durable status query for checkout operations.
Commercial Requirements
MPS-018-FR-021 — Authoritative Pricing
The system shall obtain authoritative commercial quotations from the canonical Pricing authority.
MPS-018-FR-022 — Quote Validity
The system shall validate quote validity before purchase commitment.
MPS-018-FR-023 — Offer Evaluation
The system shall obtain offer eligibility and stacking decisions from the canonical Offers authority.
MPS-018-FR-024 — Offer Redemption
The system shall coordinate offer reservation and finalization according to the authoritative offer lifecycle.
MPS-018-FR-025 — Tax Determination
The system shall obtain applicable tax decisions from the canonical Tax authority.
MPS-018-FR-026 — Fee Determination
The system shall use governed fee definitions and applicable authoritative calculations.
MPS-018-FR-027 — Monetary Integrity
The system shall preserve canonical currency, precision, rounding, allocation, and total-composition rules.
MPS-018-FR-028 — Customer Confirmation
The system shall require customer reconfirmation when material changes trigger an applicable confirmation requirement.
MPS-018-FR-029 — Commercial Snapshot
The system shall preserve references to the material commercial decisions used for commitment.
MPS-018-FR-030 — Commercial Disclosure
The system shall provide the required purchase disclosures before the applicable commitment boundary.
Resource and Payment Requirements
MPS-018-FR-031 — Resource Coordination
The system shall coordinate required inventory, capacity, reservation, and other resource authorities.
MPS-018-FR-032 — Reservation Integrity
The system shall prevent commitment based on an invalid, expired, or unconfirmed required reservation.
MPS-018-FR-033 — Reservation Idempotency
The system shall use the authoritative resource-reservation idempotency contract.
MPS-018-FR-034 — Payment Coordination
The system shall coordinate payment operations through the canonical Payment authority.
MPS-018-FR-035 — Payment Uncertainty
The system shall preserve and reconcile uncertain payment outcomes before initiating potentially duplicative payment operations.
MPS-018-FR-036 — Payment Security
The system shall minimize payment-sensitive data and prohibit unauthorized storage or logging of protected payment credentials.
MPS-018-FR-037 — Risk Enforcement
The system shall enforce required authoritative risk decisions and approved failure policies.
MPS-018-FR-038 — Multi-Resource Recovery
The system shall provide a governed recovery strategy for purchases requiring multiple independent resources.
MPS-018-FR-039 — Compensation Tracking
The system shall track authorized compensating operations until their outcomes are resolved or escalated.
MPS-018-FR-040 — Dependency Failure Handling
The system shall classify dependency failures and apply explicit retry, recovery, and escalation policies.
Commitment and Operational Requirements
MPS-018-FR-041 — Commitment Preconditions
The system shall validate all required purchase commitment preconditions before initiating commitment.
MPS-018-FR-042 — Commitment Idempotency
The system shall prevent duplicate purchase commitments for repeated requests representing the same logical commitment.
MPS-018-FR-043 — Canonical Order Handoff
The system shall hand off committed purchases through the canonical Order Management contract.
MPS-018-FR-044 — Unknown Commitment Outcome
The system shall support authoritative status resolution when order creation or commitment outcomes are uncertain.
MPS-018-FR-045 — Commitment Receipt
The system shall return a durable, authorized commitment receipt when the commitment outcome is established.
MPS-018-FR-046 — Event Integrity
The system shall publish or consume business events according to canonical ownership, durability, and deduplication contracts.
MPS-018-FR-047 — Reconciliation
The system shall reconcile checkout state with authoritative payment, resource, and order states.
MPS-018-FR-048 — Audit and Lineage
The system shall preserve required decision, operation, transition, and commitment lineage.
MPS-018-FR-049 — Security and Privacy
The system shall enforce applicable authorization, tenant isolation, data minimization, retention, and audit requirements.
MPS-018-FR-050 — Verification and Traceability
The system shall maintain traceability from approved requirements to architecture contracts, implementation artifacts, automated tests, verification evidence, and certification decisions.
PART XXXVIII — PROPOSED ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
140. ACCEPTANCE REGISTER
The following 50 criteria are proposed and must be mapped to the canonical UCOS verification framework.
MPS-018-AC-001 — Unique Cart Identity
Given an authorized cart creation request, when the operation succeeds, then the cart has a unique canonical identifier and an auditable creation record.
MPS-018-AC-002 — Durable Cart State
Given a successful cart mutation, when the serving process restarts, then the committed cart state remains recoverable according to the approved durability policy.
MPS-018-AC-003 — Concurrent Mutation
Given two conflicting mutations against the same cart version, when both are submitted concurrently, then the system prevents silent lost updates.
MPS-018-AC-004 — Invalid Product Reference
Given an invalid product reference, when cart validation occurs, then the system rejects or flags the item according to policy without fabricating product validity.
MPS-018-AC-005 — Duplicate Mutation
Given the same mutation request and idempotency key, when the request is replayed, then the operation does not create a duplicate business effect.
MPS-018-AC-006 — Incompatible Cart Merge
Given carts with incompatible commercial or configuration contexts, when a merge is requested, then the system rejects the merge or invokes an explicitly approved resolution process.
MPS-018-AC-007 — Cart Expiration
Given an expired cart, when a purchase action is requested, then the system follows the governed expiration and recovery policy.
MPS-018-AC-008 — Mutation Traceability
Given a material cart mutation, when audit evidence is queried by an authorized actor, then the relevant mutation and version lineage can be reconstructed.
MPS-018-AC-009 — Estimated Price
Given an estimated cart price, when the quote validity is absent or expired, then the interface does not present that estimate as a guaranteed current purchase amount.
MPS-018-AC-010 — Unauthorized Cart Access
Given an actor without permission, when the actor requests another party's cart, then access is denied without unauthorized data disclosure.
MPS-018-AC-011 — Checkout Initialization
Given a valid purchase intent, when checkout initialization succeeds, then a durable checkout session is created with the correct intent reference.
MPS-018-AC-012 — Checkout Recovery
Given an interrupted checkout, when an authorized recovery request is made, then the system restores the durable state and revalidates decisions that may have become stale.
MPS-018-AC-013 — Illegal State Transition
Given a checkout state that does not permit a requested transition, when the transition is attempted, then the system rejects it and preserves state integrity.
MPS-018-AC-014 — Context Failure
Given a required canonical context cannot be resolved, when checkout validation occurs, then the system does not fabricate the missing authoritative context.
MPS-018-AC-015 — Policy Versioning
Given a checkout session bound to a policy version, when the policy changes, then historical evidence retains the version used and the active workflow follows the approved policy-update rules.
MPS-018-AC-016 — Material Change
Given a material change to purchase inputs, when the change is detected, then affected decisions are invalidated or revalidated according to the dependency contract.
MPS-018-AC-017 — Structured Validation
Given a failed validation, when the result is returned, then it includes an appropriate reason category, recovery guidance, and required authoritative references without exposing prohibited data.
MPS-018-AC-018 — Checkout Expiration
Given an expired checkout, when cleanup executes, then external payment and resource effects are resolved through their respective authorities.
MPS-018-AC-019 — Checkout Resumption
Given a resumable checkout, when it is resumed, then stale quotes, expired reservations, and uncertain operations are checked before commitment continues.
MPS-018-AC-020 — Status Query
Given an authorized checkout status request, when the operation completes, then the result reflects durable checkout evidence and clearly identifies unresolved outcomes.
MPS-018-AC-021 — Authoritative Price
Given a purchase request, when a commercial quote is obtained, then the final amount originates from the canonical Pricing authority.
MPS-018-AC-022 — Expired Quote
Given an expired quote, when commitment is requested, then the system obtains a permitted replacement or rejects commitment until the quote is valid.
MPS-018-AC-023 — Offer Eligibility
Given an ineligible offer, when checkout evaluates the offer, then the system does not apply the discount based solely on client input.
MPS-018-AC-024 — Offer Redemption Recovery
Given an uncertain offer redemption outcome, when a retry is initiated, then the system resolves the original operation before creating a potentially duplicative redemption.
MPS-018-AC-025 — Tax Authority
Given a transaction requiring tax determination, when checkout calculates the purchase total, then the applicable result is obtained through the canonical Tax authority.
MPS-018-AC-026 — Fee Governance
Given a requested fee without an authorized definition, when checkout evaluates the purchase, then the fee is rejected or withheld according to policy.
MPS-018-AC-027 — Monetary Consistency
Given a purchase with discounts, taxes, and fees, when the total is established, then the amount conforms to the authoritative monetary representation and rounding rules.
MPS-018-AC-028 — Price Reconfirmation
Given a material price change requiring consent, when the quote changes, then commitment is blocked until the required confirmation is recorded.
MPS-018-AC-029 — Historical Commercial Evidence
Given a committed purchase, when its commercial lineage is queried by an authorized actor, then the system identifies the quote and material commercial decision references used.
MPS-018-AC-030 — Purchase Disclosure
Given a purchase requiring customer disclosure, when commitment is requested, then the required disclosure and confirmation conditions are satisfied.
MPS-018-AC-031 — Reservation Authority
Given a required resource reservation, when checkout proceeds, then the reservation state is established by the authoritative resource domain.
MPS-018-AC-032 — Expired Reservation
Given an expired required reservation, when commitment is requested, then the system does not treat the reservation as valid without authorized renewal or reacquisition.
MPS-018-AC-033 — Duplicate Reservation
Given a reservation request replayed under the same logical idempotency key, when processed, then no unintended duplicate resource allocation occurs.
MPS-018-AC-034 — Payment Authority
Given a purchase requiring payment, when checkout evaluates payment readiness, then the payment condition is determined from authoritative Payment-domain evidence.
MPS-018-AC-035 — Payment Timeout
Given a payment request times out after possible execution, when checkout recovers, then it resolves the original operation before initiating a potentially duplicative payment.
MPS-018-AC-036 — Payment Credential Protection
Given sensitive payment data, when logs, traces, and operational records are generated, then prohibited payment credentials are not exposed.
MPS-018-AC-037 — Risk Denial
Given an authoritative risk denial, when checkout attempts commitment, then the purchase is blocked in accordance with policy.
MPS-018-AC-038 — Multi-Resource Failure
Given a purchase requiring multiple resource reservations, when one reservation fails after another succeeds, then the system follows the approved compensation or partial-commitment strategy.
MPS-018-AC-039 — Compensation Failure
Given a compensation operation fails, when its outcome is recorded, then the system retains the unresolved operation and raises the required operational signal.
MPS-018-AC-040 — Dependency Timeout
Given a required dependency timeout, when checkout evaluates the result, then the system distinguishes failure from an unknown external outcome.
MPS-018-AC-041 — Commitment Preconditions
Given a purchase missing a required precondition, when commitment is requested, then the system does not establish a successful commitment.
MPS-018-AC-042 — Duplicate Commitment
Given the same logical commitment is submitted repeatedly, when requests are processed concurrently or sequentially, then no unintended duplicate purchase is created.
MPS-018-AC-043 — Canonical Order Ownership
Given a purchase requiring an order, when order creation is requested, then the order is established through the canonical Order Management contract.
MPS-018-AC-044 — Unknown Order Outcome
Given an order creation timeout, when checkout recovers, then it resolves whether the canonical order exists before retrying a potentially duplicative creation.
MPS-018-AC-045 — Commitment Receipt
Given a confirmed commitment, when the receipt is retrieved by an authorized actor, then it references the authoritative commitment and canonical order result.
MPS-018-AC-046 — Duplicate Event
Given an event is delivered more than once, when the consumer processes it, then duplicate delivery does not create unintended duplicate business effects.
MPS-018-AC-047 — Cross-Domain Reconciliation
Given inconsistent checkout and authoritative domain states, when reconciliation runs, then the mismatch is classified and assigned to an authorized recovery path.
MPS-018-AC-048 — Decision Lineage
Given a committed purchase, when its decision history is reconstructed, then the required policy, quote, reservation, payment, risk, and order references are available.
MPS-018-AC-049 — Tenant Isolation
Given a cross-tenant request without authorization, when the request is processed, then access is denied and no unauthorized purchase data is exposed.
MPS-018-AC-050 — End-to-End Traceability
Given an approved functional requirement, when verification evidence is reviewed, then the requirement maps to its governing contract, implementation artifact, test, and applicable certification result.
PART XXXIX — VERIFICATION STRATEGY
141. VERIFICATION LAYERS
Verification must occur at multiple levels.
141.1 Static Verification
Validate:
- Identifier uniqueness.
- Schema validity.
- Contract consistency.
- Dependency direction.
- Namespace ownership.
- Prohibited dependency detection.
- Requirement traceability.
- Policy completeness.
- State-machine transition completeness.
- Event schema compatibility.
141.2 Unit Verification
Validate:
- Cart mutation rules.
- Quantity constraints.
- State transitions.
- Idempotency logic.
- Version checks.
- Validation result construction.
- Error mapping.
- Policy selection.
- Snapshot construction.
- Recovery decisions.
141.3 Contract Verification
Validate:
- Pricing integration.
- Offers integration.
- Tax integration.
- Inventory integration.
- Capacity integration.
- Payment integration.
- Risk integration.
- Order Management integration.
- Event producer and consumer contracts.
141.4 Property-Based Verification
Test invariants over generated inputs and operation sequences.
Examples:
- Duplicate commitment requests do not create duplicate purchases.
- Invalid state transitions never produce a committed state.
- A stale quote cannot bypass quote-validity rules.
- Unauthorized actors cannot access protected carts.
- Conflicting cart updates are detected or resolved by explicit policy.
- A failed resource reservation cannot be reported as confirmed.
- An uncertain payment outcome cannot be treated as a definitive decline without authoritative evidence.
- A committed purchase retains its original decision lineage.
- Replaying an eligible operation preserves the defined idempotency semantics.
141.5 Concurrency Verification
Test:
- Simultaneous cart mutation.
- Simultaneous checkout submission.
- Duplicate idempotency keys.
- Concurrent resource reservations.
- Concurrent quote refresh and commitment.
- Event reordering.
- Concurrent compensation.
- Duplicate order handoff.
141.6 Fault Injection
Inject:
- Network interruption.
- Process crash.
- Dependency timeout.
- Delayed response.
- Duplicate response.
- Duplicate event.
- Lost acknowledgment.
- Partial write failure.
- Event publication failure.
- Payment uncertainty.
- Order creation uncertainty.
- Reservation expiration during checkout.
- Reconciliation backlog.
141.7 Security Verification
Test:
- Authorization boundaries.
- Tenant isolation.
- Replay protection.
- Idempotency-key abuse.
- Sensitive-data leakage.
- Forged events.
- Privilege escalation.
- Malicious client input.
- Rate-limit enforcement.
- Administrative controls.
141.8 End-to-End Verification
Test complete purchase journeys across the actual authoritative dependencies.
At minimum, cover:
- Successful purchase.
- Invalid product.
- Stale quote.
- Price change requiring reconfirmation.
- Offer ineligibility.
- Tax dependency failure.
- Inventory contention.
- Reservation expiration.
- Payment decline.
- Payment timeout.
- Risk denial.
- Order handoff timeout.
- Duplicate submission.
- Partial multi-merchant failure.
- Compensation failure.
- Interrupted checkout recovery.
- Cross-tenant access attempt.
141.9 Recovery Verification
Demonstrate that unresolved operations can be identified, queried, retried safely, compensated where permitted, and escalated when automatic recovery cannot establish a valid result.
142. VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
Each test result must identify:
- Test identifier.
- Requirement identifier.
- Test environment.
- Software or artifact version.
- Relevant configuration version.
- Input data reference.
- Expected result.
- Actual result.
- Execution timestamp.
- Pass/fail status.
- Evidence location.
- Failure details where applicable.
Certification must be based on actual evidence, not on the presence of a test plan.

PART XLI — PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE GAP REGISTER
144. GAP REGISTER
The following gaps require evidence-based resolution during context assimilation.
MPS-018-GAP-001 — Canonical Namespace Verification
Confirm that the proposed UCOS-MKT-CHK namespace is valid and unique.
MPS-018-GAP-002 — Master Index Reconciliation
Confirm the official specification sequence and all existing document identifiers.

Discover and assess any existing canonical Cart implementation or specification.

PART XLV — ABSOLUTE PROHIBITIONS
157. ARCHITECTURAL PROHIBITIONS
The implementation must not:
1. Create a competing product authority.
2. Create a competing pricing authority.
3. Create a competing tax authority.
4. Create a competing payment authority.
5. Create a competing inventory authority.
6. Create a competing order authority.
7. Create a competing financial ledger.
8. Bypass canonical identity or authorization.
9. Trust client-supplied authoritative commercial values.
10. Treat an expired quote as valid without authorization.
11. Treat an expired reservation as confirmed.
12. Treat a timeout as proof of failure.
13. Treat a timeout as proof of success.
14. Blindly retry an uncertain payment operation.
15. Create duplicate purchases on repeated submission.
16. Fabricate canonical order identifiers.
17. Silently discard unresolved compensation.
18. Hide partial commitment.
19. Publish untrue business events.
20. Allow stale events to overwrite newer authoritative state.
21. Introduce ungoverned business identifiers.
22. Create circular dependencies.
23. Access another domain's private database as an integration shortcut.
24. Embed secrets in source code.
25. Expose payment credentials in logs or traces.
26. Bypass required customer consent.
27. Let AI override canonical commercial decisions.
28. Use analytics projections as transaction authorities.
29. Create unregistered extensions that alter purchase semantics.
30. Introduce silent fallback behavior that changes material commercial terms.
31. Claim end-to-end exactly-once processing without a defined and verified guarantee.
32. Claim zero downtime, zero data loss, or infinite scale without evidence.
33. Mark tests passed without execution evidence.
34. Claim certification without authorized certification evidence.
35. Begin implementation solely because this specification has been drafted.

PART XLVII — FINAL ARCHITECTURAL SUMMARY
161. CANONICAL RESPONSIBILITY MODEL
The final responsibility model is:
Cart
- Maintains canonical cart state.
- Maintains item composition.
- Controls cart mutations and versioning.
- Records purchase intent references.
Purchase Intent
- Represents the governed intent to buy.
- Supports cart-based and non-cart-based commerce.
- Preserves source and commercial context.
Checkout
- Coordinates purchase preparation.
- Resolves applicable purchase policy.
- Obtains authoritative commercial decisions.
- Coordinates resource, payment, and risk requirements.
- Validates readiness for commitment.
- Maintains checkout state and recovery evidence.
Purchase Commitment
- Coordinates the governed transition to durable purchase commitment.
- Enforces commitment preconditions.
- Maintains idempotency and commitment evidence.
- Resolves uncertain commitment outcomes.
- Coordinates canonical order handoff.
Pricing
- Owns authoritative price calculations and quote semantics.
Offers
- Owns offer definitions, eligibility, stacking, and redemption semantics.
Tax
- Owns authoritative tax decisions.
Inventory and Capacity
- Own resource availability, reservations, and reservation lifecycle.
Payment
- Owns authoritative payment operations and payment state.
Trust, Safety and Risk
- Owns risk assessments and enforcement decisions.
Order Management
- Owns canonical order identity, order records, and order lifecycle.
Fulfillment
- Owns the execution of applicable fulfillment obligations.
Settlement and Accounting
- Own their respective financial records and financial lifecycle.
Governance, Registries, Audit and Lineage
- Govern identifiers, artifacts, contracts, evidence, dependencies, and certification.

### Document Status Rule

This document defines a proposed architectural baseline.

The presence of a requirement, API, event, entity, identifier, state, or acceptance criterion in this specification does not establish that the corresponding artifact exists in the UCOS repository.

All proposed identifiers, state models, interfaces, and contracts must pass the applicable canonical registry, dependency, ontology, taxonomy, governance, and verification checks before being treated as approved implementation contracts.

No implementation authorization is implied.

---

# 1. EXECUTIVE ARCHITECTURAL STATEMENT

## 1.1 Purpose

Universal Marketplace Order Lifecycle and Order Management establishes the canonical capability responsible for creating, identifying, governing, versioning, tracking, and maintaining marketplace orders throughout their authorized commercial lifecycle.

The domain provides a reliable and auditable representation of the commercial order established through an authorized purchase-commitment process.

It must support heterogeneous commerce models, including physical goods, digital goods, services, bookings, subscriptions, rentals, bundled offerings, multi-merchant purchases, split fulfillment, regulated transactions, and future commerce models without requiring the order architecture to be redesigned for each new business category.

The architecture must not depend on a particular industry, merchant model, geographic jurisdiction, fulfillment provider, payment provider, programming language, database, cloud platform, or communication protocol.

## 1.2 Core Architectural Separation

The system must preserve the following authority boundaries:

1. Cart owns the canonical representation of purchase intent.
2. Checkout owns checkout-session orchestration and purchase preparation.
3. Purchase Commitment owns the governed establishment of the commercial commitment before order creation, subject to the approved commerce contract.
4. Order Management owns the canonical order record and its lifecycle.
5. Product Management owns product and service definitions.
6. Pricing owns authoritative price calculations and price quotations.
7. Offers and Promotions own offer eligibility, promotion evaluation, and redemption rules.
8. Tax owns authoritative tax determinations and tax calculations.
9. Inventory owns stock and inventory-state authority.
10. Capacity Management owns applicable capacity availability and allocation authority.
11. Payment owns payment instruments, payment attempts, authorizations, captures, and payment-state authority.
12. Fulfillment owns fulfillment planning, fulfillment execution, and delivery-state authority.
13. Returns owns return eligibility and return-process authority.
14. Refunds owns refund authorization and refund-execution authority.
15. Disputes owns dispute-process authority where that capability is separately established.
16. Settlement and Accounting own their respective financial settlement, ledger, and accounting records.
17. Identity owns identity records and authentication authority.
18. Access Governance owns authorization policy and access-decision authority.
19. Trust and Safety owns its canonical risk, abuse, and enforcement processes.
20. Compliance Governance owns applicable policy interpretation and compliance-control authority.

These boundaries are architectural contracts, not optional implementation conventions.

## 1.3 Fundamental Principle

An order is not a cart, payment, shipment, invoice, reservation, refund, or accounting entry.

An order is a canonical commercial record containing the governed purchase structure, the applicable commercial evidence, the parties and obligations relevant to that order, its lifecycle state, and references to independently governed processes.

The order must preserve enough information to reconstruct what was commercially committed, what was subsequently changed through authorized procedures, what obligations were created, and what lifecycle outcomes occurred.

## 1.4 Required Outcomes

The architecture must enable:

- Globally unambiguous order identity within the governed identifier system.
- Deterministic order creation.
- Exactly-once business effects under at-least-once or repeated message delivery.
- Safe handling of concurrent requests.
- Immutable historical evidence with governed amendments.
- Independent payment and fulfillment lifecycles.
- Multi-merchant and multi-obligation order structures.
- Partial fulfillment and partial cancellation.
- Versioned order snapshots.
- Explicit customer and merchant visibility.
- Traceable cancellation, return, refund, and dispute references.
- Recoverable processing after timeouts, failures, or uncertain outcomes.
- Automated reconciliation.
- Domain-agnostic extension.
- Policy-based configuration.
- Auditability and regulatory adaptability.
- Complete requirement-to-contract-to-test traceability.

---

# 2. CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES

The following principles govern the design.

## 2.1 Single Canonical Authority

Every business concept must have one canonical authority.

An implementation may maintain local caches, projections, replicas, indexes, and derived views, but these must not become competing sources of truth.

The canonical Order Management domain is the authority for the order record, order version history, order lifecycle decisions, order-level amendments, and order-level audit lineage.

It is not the authority for independently owned payment, inventory, fulfillment, return, refund, tax, or accounting state.

## 2.2 Knowledge Once Principle

Every canonical definition must be authored once and reused through governed references.

The architecture must not independently redefine:

- Identity.
- Product.
- Merchant.
- Customer.
- Price.
- Currency.
- Tax.
- Offer.
- Payment.
- Inventory.
- Capacity.
- Fulfillment.
- Return.
- Refund.
- Dispute.
- Settlement.
- Jurisdiction.
- Consent.
- Security policy.
- Audit evidence.
- Time.
- Address.
- Communication channel.
- Regulatory obligation.

Where an external domain provides a canonical contract, Order Management must consume that contract rather than create a competing definition.

## 2.3 Explicit Authority

Every field, state, decision, transition, and side effect must have a declared owner.

No component may silently acquire authority over a neighboring domain.

## 2.4 Append-Only Historical Evidence

Historical commercial evidence must not be silently overwritten.

Authorized amendments create new versions or explicit amendment records.

Audit events must preserve historical truth even when the current order representation changes.

## 2.5 Deterministic State Transitions

A lifecycle transition must be governed by:

- The current canonical state.
- The requested command.
- Applicable authorization.
- Applicable policy version.
- Relevant domain evidence.
- Concurrency conditions.
- Explicit transition rules.
- Defined side effects.
- Defined failure behavior.

Unrecognized or unauthorized transitions must not be applied.

## 2.6 No False Atomicity

The architecture must not assume that multiple independently governed services share a distributed database transaction.

Cross-domain coordination must explicitly handle partial completion, timeouts, uncertain outcomes, retries, compensation, and reconciliation.

## 2.7 Idempotent Business Effects

Repeated delivery of the same authorized command must not create unintended duplicate orders, duplicate order lines, duplicate commitments, or duplicate lifecycle effects.

## 2.8 Fail Safely

When an operation cannot establish the truth of a critical precondition, the system must not silently assume success.

Depending on the operation, it must reject, defer, isolate, mark the outcome as uncertain, or enter an explicitly governed exception state.

## 2.9 Domain-Agnostic Design

Commerce-specific variation must be expressed through governed capabilities, schemas, policies, and profiles rather than hard-coded industry branches.

## 2.10 Technology Neutrality

No business rule may require a specific:

- Programming language.
- Runtime.
- Database.
- Message broker.
- Cloud provider.
- Container platform.
- Search engine.
- API gateway.
- Workflow engine.
- Identity vendor.
- Payment provider.
- Fulfillment provider.

## 2.11 Automatic Discovery

Discoverable capabilities, schemas, policies, event types, transition definitions, and plugins must be registered through governed registries.

Discovery must be deterministic, permission-aware, version-aware, and auditable.

## 2.12 Zero Silent Data Loss

Every accepted order command must produce a durable, traceable outcome or an explicit recoverable failure.

## 2.13 Explicit Temporal Semantics

Every timestamp must have defined temporal meaning, precision, and serialization rules.

The architecture must distinguish event occurrence time, event recording time, effective time, expiration time, and processing time where relevant.

## 2.14 Security by Construction

Authorization, tenant isolation, data minimization, evidence protection, and auditability must be built into domain contracts rather than added as optional middleware.

## 2.15 Compatibility Before Change

Schema evolution, event evolution, and API evolution must preserve declared compatibility guarantees or require an explicitly governed breaking change.

## 2.16 No Orphan Capabilities

Every capability must have:

- An owner.
- A purpose.
- A canonical identifier.
- A contract.
- A dependency declaration.
- A lifecycle.
- A verification strategy.
- A retirement policy.

---

# 3. SCOPE AND BOUNDARIES

## 3.1 Included Capabilities

Order Management includes the following canonical responsibilities.

### A. Order Identity and Creation

- Order identity assignment.
- Order creation authorization.
- Purchase-commitment validation.
- Idempotent creation.
- Duplicate detection.
- Order provenance.
- Initial order version.
- Initial lifecycle state.

### B. Order Structure

- Order header.
- Order lines.
- Merchant or provider grouping.
- Commercial line snapshots.
- Obligation references.
- Relationships between parent and derived orders.
- Bundle and package relationships.
- Partial fulfillment relationships.
- Order-level and line-level attributes.

### C. Order Lifecycle

- Lifecycle state evaluation.
- Transition validation.
- Acceptance and confirmation.
- Processing readiness.
- Partial completion.
- Completion.
- Cancellation coordination.
- Closure.
- Exception handling.
- Reopening only where explicitly permitted.
- Terminal-state governance.

### D. Order Versioning

- Immutable version history.
- Authorized amendments.
- Before-and-after evidence.
- Change reason.
- Actor identity.
- Policy version.
- Effective time.
- Version lineage.

### E. Cross-Domain Coordination

- Payment references.
- Inventory reservation references.
- Capacity reservation references.
- Fulfillment obligation references.
- Delivery references.
- Return references.
- Refund references.
- Dispute references.
- Tax evidence references.
- Settlement references.
- Risk-decision references.

### F. Operational Control

- Order search and retrieval.
- Customer-facing order projections.
- Merchant-facing order projections.
- Operational exception queues.
- Reconciliation.
- Audit.
- Notifications through separately governed communication capabilities.
- Lifecycle analytics.
- Administrative controls.
- Retention and archival governance.

## 3.2 Explicitly Excluded Authority

The following responsibilities must not be absorbed into Order Management.

| Capability | Canonical Owner | Order Management Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Product definition | Product Domain | Reference product identity and commercial snapshot |
| Product taxonomy | Product Taxonomy Domain | Reference canonical taxonomy where required |
| Merchant identity | Merchant Domain | Reference merchant identity and applicable version |
| Customer identity | Identity/Customer Domain | Reference authorized subject identity |
| Cart contents | Cart Domain | Consume authorized purchase-intent references |
| Checkout session | Checkout Domain | Consume the resulting authorized commitment |
| Commercial commitment | Purchase Commitment Domain | Validate provenance and establish the order record |
| Price calculation | Pricing Domain | Consume quote and preserve applicable evidence |
| Promotion eligibility | Offers Domain | Consume offer evaluation and redemption references |
| Tax calculation | Tax Domain | Preserve tax determination evidence |
| Stock availability | Inventory Domain | Consume inventory decisions and reservation references |
| Resource capacity | Capacity Domain | Consume capacity decisions and reservation references |
| Payment execution | Payment Domain | Reference payment obligations and payment outcomes |
| Fulfillment execution | Fulfillment Domain | Coordinate order obligations and track references |
| Shipment execution | Delivery/Logistics Domain | Consume delivery-state evidence |
| Return authorization | Returns Domain | Reference return cases and outcomes |
| Refund execution | Refunds Domain | Reference refund cases and outcomes |
| Dispute adjudication | Disputes Domain | Reference dispute cases and outcomes |
| Financial settlement | Settlement Domain | Provide order references and reconcile relationships |
| Accounting ledger | Accounting Domain | Provide traceable order references |
| Risk decision | Trust and Safety Domain | Consume governed decisions and evidence |
| Access decision | Access Governance | Enforce declared authorization policies |
| Notification delivery | Communication Domain | Emit notification-worthy domain events |
| Customer support case | Customer Service Domain | Expose order context through authorized interfaces |

This table establishes proposed boundaries. Existing canonical UCOS artifacts take precedence after reconciliation.

## 3.3 Boundary Rule

Order Management may maintain a local reference, projection, or historical snapshot of information owned by another domain when required for correctness, auditability, performance, or commercial evidence.

Such a snapshot must declare:

- Source authority.
- Source identifier.
- Source version.
- Capture time.
- Effective time, where relevant.
- Integrity metadata.
- Applicable retention policy.
- Whether the snapshot is immutable evidence or a refreshable projection.

A snapshot must never be represented as the current authoritative state of the source domain unless that authority has explicitly been delegated.

# 4. CANONICAL ORDER ONTOLOGY

## 4.1 Ontological Model

The canonical model must distinguish an order from the objects related to it.

### Core Concepts

1. Order.
2. Order Identity.
3. Order Version.
4. Order Line.
5. Order Line Version.
6. Order Group.
7. Order Relationship.
8. Order Obligation.
9. Order Acceptance.
10. Order Confirmation.
11. Order Amendment.
12. Order Cancellation Request.
13. Order Cancellation Outcome.
14. Order Snapshot.
15. Order Lifecycle Transition.
16. Order Lifecycle Event.
17. Order Exception.
18. Order Evidence Reference.
19. Order Policy Evaluation.
20. Order Actor.
21. Order Provenance.
22. Order Closure.
23. Order Reconciliation Record.
24. Order Projection.
25. Order Retention Record.

These concepts are proposed canonical terms. They must be reconciled with the UCOS glossary and ontology registries before approval.

## 4.2 Order

An Order is a governed commercial record representing an accepted or otherwise validly established purchase relationship under a specific commercial context.

An order must contain or reference:

- Canonical order identity.
- Tenant or organizational scope, where applicable.
- Originating purchase commitment.
- Relevant commercial parties.
- Order lines.
- Order-level commercial evidence.
- Applicable currency and monetary representation.
- Relevant policy and terms versions.
- Lifecycle state.
- Current order version.
- Creation provenance.
- Relevant obligations.
- Related domain references.
- Audit lineage.
- Applicable retention classification.

Not every field must be physically stored in the order record. Canonical references and governed snapshots may be used where the authority boundary and retention requirements permit.

## 4.3 Order Line

An Order Line represents a separately identifiable commercial component of an order.

An order line may represent a product, service, bundle component, subscription obligation, booking, rental, digital entitlement, or another governed commerce item.

An order line must have a stable identity within its order and must preserve the commercial meaning established at commitment time.

An order line must not be identified solely by a mutable product name, display title, array position, or SKU text.

## 4.4 Order Group

An Order Group represents a governed grouping of order lines or obligations.

Possible grouping dimensions include:

- Merchant.
- Provider.
- Fulfillment destination.
- Delivery obligation.
- Commercial agreement.
- Service provider.
- Scheduling context.
- Regulatory jurisdiction.
- Payment arrangement.
- Operational processing requirement.

Grouping must be policy-driven and extensible.

A group is not automatically a separate legal order. Its commercial and legal meaning must be explicitly declared.

## 4.5 Order Version

An Order Version represents a specific governed representation of an order at a point in its version history.

It must contain:

- Order identifier.
- Version identifier.
- Version sequence or equivalent ordering token.
- Change classification.
- Change reason.
- Change actor.
- Effective timestamp, where applicable.
- Recorded timestamp.
- Previous-version reference.
- Integrity evidence.
- Changed-field or changed-entity references.
- Applicable policy version.
- Resulting lifecycle state.

The implementation may use sequence numbers, immutable version identifiers, event-derived versioning, or another approved mechanism.

The externally observable behavior must remain unambiguous.

## 4.6 Order Amendment

An Order Amendment is an authorized change to the order's governed representation or obligations after initial creation.

An amendment must not silently rewrite historical commercial evidence.

Each amendment must specify:

- Amendment identity.
- Target order and version.
- Requested changes.
- Initiating actor.
- Reason.
- Authorization evidence.
- Applicable policy.
- Preconditions.
- Impact assessment.
- Required domain approvals.
- Resulting version.
- Related compensation or follow-up operations.
- Final outcome.

## 4.7 Order Obligation

An Order Obligation represents a commitment-related responsibility that must be fulfilled, satisfied, discharged, cancelled, or otherwise resolved.

Examples of obligation categories may include:

- Delivery.
- Digital entitlement.
- Service performance.
- Appointment delivery.
- Subscription activation.
- Rental availability.
- Merchant performance.
- Customer payment.
- Regulatory disclosure.

Obligations must be extensible through canonical obligation types and schemas.

An obligation may be fulfilled by another domain. Order Management tracks the relationship and relevant lifecycle evidence without taking over the executing domain's authority.

## 4.8 Order Snapshot

An Order Snapshot is an immutable or explicitly versioned representation of selected order data and referenced commercial evidence.

Snapshots may be used for:

- Customer order history.
- Merchant processing.
- Invoice preparation.
- Dispute evidence.
- Compliance review.
- Audit.
- Reconciliation.
- Historical commercial interpretation.

A snapshot must identify its capture boundary and the sources from which its content was derived.

## 4.9 Order Relationship

An Order Relationship connects orders or order-related entities through a typed, governed relationship.

Supported relationship categories may include:

- Parent and child.
- Original and replacement.
- Original and split.
- Related order.
- Superseding order.
- Consolidated order.
- Cross-order dependency.
- Exchange order.
- Rebooking order.

The relationship registry must define each relationship's semantics, cardinality, allowed lifecycle states, and authorization requirements.

## 4.10 Separation of State Concepts

The architecture must never collapse the following into a single unqualified status:

- Order lifecycle state.
- Payment state.
- Inventory state.
- Fulfillment state.
- Delivery state.
- Return state.
- Refund state.
- Dispute state.
- Settlement state.
- Compliance state.

A customer-facing aggregate status may be computed from these states, but it must be a derived projection with an explicit derivation rule.

# 5. CANONICAL IDENTIFIERS AND NAMING

## 5.1 Proposed Identifier Namespace

Proposed domain prefix:

`UCOS-MKT-ORD`

Proposed document prefix:

`MPS-019`

Proposed requirement prefix:

`MPS-019-FR`

Proposed acceptance-criterion prefix:

`MPS-019-AC`

Proposed architecture decision prefix:

`MPS-019-ADR`

Proposed gap prefix:

`MPS-019-GAP`

Proposed event namespace:

`ucos.marketplace.order.*`

Proposed API namespace:

`/marketplace/orders`

These identifiers are provisional until checked against canonical UCOS naming and registry rules.

## 5.2 Order Identity Requirements

An order identifier must:

- Be unique within its declared identity scope.
- Remain stable throughout the order's lifetime.
- Avoid encoding mutable business attributes.
- Avoid exposing sensitive personal information.
- Support distributed creation.
- Support authorized external references.
- Be collision-resistant under the declared operating model.
- Be traceable to its canonical issuer or identity namespace.
- Remain independent of physical database keys.

## 5.3 Identity Separation

The architecture must distinguish:

- Canonical Order ID.
- External Order Reference.
- Order Line ID.
- Order Group ID.
- Order Version ID.
- Purchase Commitment ID.
- Merchant Order Reference.
- Fulfillment Obligation ID.
- Payment Reference.
- Return Reference.
- Refund Reference.
- Dispute Reference.
- Idempotency Key.
- Correlation ID.
- Causation ID.
- Trace ID.

No identifier may be reused for a different semantic purpose merely because its representation is technically compatible.

## 5.4 Identifier Registry Requirements

The canonical identifier registry must define:

- Namespace ownership.
- Uniqueness scope.
- Issuance rules.
- Format constraints.
- Validation rules.
- Collision handling.
- Retirement policy.
- External alias policy.
- Privacy constraints.
- Migration policy.

# 6. ORDER AUTHORITY MODEL

## 6.1 Authority Declaration

Order Management is the proposed canonical authority for:

1. Order record identity and canonical existence.
2. Order-level lifecycle state.
3. Order-version lineage.
4. Order-line membership within an order.
5. Authorized order amendments.
6. Order-level acceptance evidence.
7. Order relationships.
8. Order-level exception records.
9. Order lifecycle audit lineage.
10. Order closure decisions.
11. Order-level derived operational status.
12. Order-to-domain reference relationships.

These authorities are bounded by applicable commercial agreements and governance rules.

## 6.2 External Authority Dependencies

Order Management must not fabricate authoritative evidence for:

- Price calculation.
- Tax determination.
- Payment success.
- Stock availability.
- Reservation validity.
- Shipment dispatch.
- Delivery completion.
- Return eligibility.
- Refund execution.
- Settlement completion.
- Risk approval.
- Regulatory authorization.

The order may record the evidence needed to explain a decision, but the source domain remains authoritative for its own decision.

## 6.3 Authority Matrix

| Data or Decision | Owner | Consumer Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Order ID | Order Management | Reference |
| Order lifecycle | Order Management | Query or subscribe |
| Order version | Order Management | Query or reference |
| Order-line membership | Order Management | Query or reference |
| Product identity | Product Domain | Reference |
| Product commercial snapshot | Source domain plus governed order snapshot | Preserve captured evidence |
| Price quote | Pricing | Validate freshness and reference |
| Promotion evaluation | Offers | Validate and reference |
| Tax calculation | Tax | Validate and reference |
| Payment authorization | Payment | Reference payment outcome |
| Inventory reservation | Inventory | Reference reservation outcome |
| Fulfillment task | Fulfillment | Reference task and outcome |
| Return case | Returns | Reference case and outcome |
| Refund execution | Refunds | Reference execution outcome |
| Settlement record | Settlement | Reference settlement outcome |
| Customer identity | Identity/Customer Domain | Reference authorized subject |
| Merchant identity | Merchant Domain | Reference authorized party |
| Access decision | Access Governance | Enforce decision |
| Order projection | Order Management or authorized projection service | Derive from canonical data |
| Customer notification | Communication Domain | Consume authorized events |

# 7. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE

## 7.1 Logical Components

The proposed Order Management domain consists of the following logical components.

### 7.1.1 Order Command Interface

Receives authorized commands to create, amend, cancel, accept, close, or otherwise change an order.

Responsibilities:

- Schema validation.
- Authentication context validation.
- Authorization enforcement.
- Idempotency.
- Request correlation.
- Command normalization.
- Policy selection.
- Contract-version validation.

### 7.1.2 Order Lifecycle Engine

Evaluates and executes permitted lifecycle transitions.

Responsibilities:

- Current-state evaluation.
- Transition eligibility.
- Preconditions.
- Policy evaluation.
- Concurrency checks.
- State-transition recording.
- Transition-result production.

### 7.1.3 Order Creation Coordinator

Coordinates order creation from an authorized purchase commitment.

Responsibilities:

- Source-commitment validation.
- Commitment uniqueness.
- Commercial evidence validation.
- Order identity assignment.
- Initial order structure creation.
- Initial version creation.
- Durable creation outcome.
- Downstream event publication.

### 7.1.4 Order Versioning Engine

Manages version lineage and authorized amendments.

Responsibilities:

- Version sequence.
- Change validation.
- Historical preservation.
- Before-and-after evidence.
- Amendment records.
- Optimistic concurrency.
- Version integrity.

### 7.1.5 Order Composition Engine

Manages order headers, lines, groups, and relationships.

Responsibilities:

- Canonical order structure.
- Line identity.
- Grouping.
- Parent-child relationships.
- Multi-merchant composition.
- Partial obligation representation.

### 7.1.6 Domain Integration Coordinator

Coordinates interactions with independent domains.

Responsibilities:

- Contract-based invocation.
- Reference validation.
- Event correlation.
- Timeout handling.
- Retry classification.
- Compensation coordination.
- Reconciliation scheduling.

It must not become a universal owner of neighboring domain state.

### 7.1.7 Order Query and Projection Engine

Provides authorized read models.

Responsibilities:

- Customer order views.
- Merchant order views.
- Operational views.
- Administrative views.
- Search integration.
- Projection freshness metadata.
- Access-aware field filtering.

### 7.1.8 Order Evidence and Audit Service

Maintains order-related audit evidence and provenance references.

Responsibilities:

- Change attribution.
- Evidence linkage.
- Integrity metadata.
- Audit event correlation.
- Retention policy enforcement.
- Authorized evidence retrieval.

### 7.1.9 Exception and Reconciliation Engine

Identifies and resolves inconsistent or incomplete cross-domain workflows.

Responsibilities:

- Uncertain-outcome detection.
- Missing-event detection.
- Duplicate-event detection.
- Reference reconciliation.
- Stuck-process detection.
- Repair workflow initiation.
- Exception escalation.
- Resolution evidence.

### 7.1.10 Policy and Configuration Interface

Loads approved order policies and transition definitions.

Responsibilities:

- Policy version resolution.
- Effective-time evaluation.
- Scope evaluation.
- Policy provenance.
- Change validation.
- Rollback to a previously approved policy where permitted.

### 7.1.11 Order Event Publisher

Publishes durable lifecycle events.

Responsibilities:

- Event schema validation.
- Event identity.
- Transactional consistency between state changes and event publication.
- Publication retry.
- Duplicate-safe delivery.
- Event lineage.

### 7.1.12 Order Administration Interface

Provides controlled operational actions.

Responsibilities:

- Authorized investigation.
- Exception resolution.
- Evidence inspection.
- Policy-governed correction.
- Reconciliation management.
- Administrative audit.

Administrative access must not bypass canonical transition rules.
