# 33. PERFORMANCE AND SCALABILITY

## 33.1 Scalability Principles

The architecture must support growth in:

- Order volume.
- Order-line count.
- Merchant count.
- Tenant count.
- Concurrent commands.
- Event volume.
- Query volume.
- Historical retention.
- Regional distribution.
- Commerce-profile diversity.
- Integration count.

No single database, process, queue, or global lock should be assumed to handle all future scale.

## 33.2 Performance Targets

Final targets must be derived from workload analysis, business criticality, service-level objectives, and deployment constraints.

The following are proposed initial targets, not measured results or certified commitments.

| Operation | Proposed Target |
|---|---|
| Order retrieval, standard projection | p95 ≤ 250 ms |
| Order retrieval, standard projection | p99 ≤ 750 ms |
| Order creation, synchronous admission | p95 ≤ 500 ms when required dependencies are responsive |
| Simple local lifecycle transition | p95 ≤ 300 ms |
| Order command authorization | p95 ≤ 100 ms, excluding external human approval |
| Standard projection freshness | ≤ 5 seconds under healthy operating conditions |
| Event publication delay | p95 ≤ 2 seconds under healthy operating conditions |
| Order search | p95 ≤ 1 second for standard indexed queries |
| Idempotent retry resolution | p95 ≤ 250 ms when the prior result is available locally |

These targets require validation through representative benchmarks.

They must not encourage weakening transactional integrity or security controls.

## 33.3 Load Profiles

The implementation must test:

- Normal load.
- Peak load.
- Burst load.
- Sustained overload.
- High-concurrency creation.
- High-concurrency amendment.
- Event replay.
- Projection rebuild.
- Dependency outage.
- Recovery after outage.
- Large order structures.
- Large historical order datasets.

## 33.4 Capacity Planning

Capacity planning must include:

- Orders per second.
- Order lines per order.
- Events per order.
- Version growth.
- Audit growth.
- Projection storage.
- Search indexing.
- Retention tiers.
- Backup volume.
- Recovery workload.
- Reconciliation backlog.

## 33.5 Backpressure

The system must implement governed backpressure where required.

Backpressure must not silently drop accepted order commands or required lifecycle events.

---

# 34. RELIABILITY, AVAILABILITY, AND DISASTER RECOVERY

## 34.1 Reliability Requirements

The system must tolerate:

- Process failure.
- Node failure.
- Network partition.
- Database failover.
- Message-broker failure.
- Dependency outage.
- Delayed events.
- Duplicate events.
- Out-of-order events.
- Regional disruption.
- Corrupted projection.
- Interrupted workflows.

## 34.2 Proposed Service Objectives

The following are candidate targets requiring business and operational approval.

| Objective | Proposed Initial Target |
|---|---|
| Order command service availability | ≥ 99.95% monthly |
| Canonical order durability | No acknowledged committed order lost within the approved durability model |
| Order creation duplicate prevention | 100% for the defined uniqueness invariant |
| Unauthorized lifecycle transitions | Zero accepted unauthorized transitions |
| Historical version preservation | 100% for retained canonical order history |
| Required event recovery | 100% recoverability under the approved event-durability contract |
| Projection recoverability | Rebuildable from canonical data and retained event/source evidence |
| Reconciliation coverage | All defined cross-domain invariants covered by registered controls |

These targets are not proof of implementation or achieved service levels.

## 34.3 Durability

The implementation must define what an acknowledged order creation means in terms of durable persistence.

The response must not indicate durable success before the declared persistence guarantee has been met.

## 34.4 Disaster Recovery

The architecture must define:

- Recovery Time Objective.
- Recovery Point Objective.
- Backup strategy.
- Replication strategy.
- Failover rules.
- Regional recovery.
- Restore validation.
- Event replay.
- Idempotency restoration.
- Audit preservation.
- Post-recovery reconciliation.

Final RTO and RPO values must be established through business impact analysis.

## 34.5 Disaster Recovery Testing

Recovery procedures must be tested under controlled conditions.

A backup is not considered validated solely because a backup job reports success.

Restoration must verify canonical order integrity, version lineage, identifier uniqueness, and required event consistency.

---

# 35. GOVERNANCE AND POLICY MANAGEMENT

## 35.1 Governance Requirements

Every order policy must have:

- Canonical identifier.
- Owner.
- Purpose.
- Version.
- Effective interval.
- Scope.
- Approval status.
- Dependencies.
- Conflict-resolution rules.
- Audit history.
- Retirement conditions.

## 35.2 Policy Types

Policy categories may include:

- Order acceptance.
- Order composition.
- Merchant participation.
- Amendment eligibility.
- Cancellation eligibility.
- Closure eligibility.
- Retention.
- Evidence requirements.
- Data access.
- Commerce profile.
- Obligation completion.
- Cross-domain coordination.
- Exception handling.
- Reconciliation.
- Automation.
- Regulatory controls.

## 35.3 Policy Precedence

The policy engine must define deterministic precedence.

Potential precedence dimensions include:

- Mandatory legal controls.
- Canonical platform constraints.
- Tenant policy.
- Commercial agreement.
- Merchant policy.
- Commerce profile.
- Channel-specific configuration.
- Individual transaction constraints.

The exact precedence must be approved by canonical governance.

Lower-priority policies must not override mandatory controls.

## 35.4 Effective-Time Policy Resolution

The system must distinguish policy effective time from policy publication time.

Historical order interpretation must preserve the policy version applicable to the relevant decision.

## 35.5 Policy Changes

Policy changes must be versioned and auditable.

Changes must not retroactively modify historical order evidence unless an authorized legal or compliance process explicitly requires a correction.

## 35.6 Configuration Validation

Configuration must be validated before activation.

Invalid configurations must not silently fall back to unsafe defaults.

---

# 36. IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACTS AND BOUNDARIES

## 36.1 Required Contracts

The implementation must establish canonical contracts for:

1. Order identity.
2. Order creation.
3. Order retrieval.
4. Order versioning.
5. Order composition.
6. Order lifecycle transitions.
7. Order amendment.
8. Order cancellation.
9. Order closure.
10. Order obligations.
11. Commercial snapshots.
12. Payment references.
13. Inventory references.
14. Capacity references.
15. Fulfillment references.
16. Return references.
17. Refund references.
18. Dispute references.
19. Order events.
20. Idempotency.
21. Error taxonomy.
22. Reconciliation.
23. Audit.
24. Authorization.
25. Retention.
26. Extension registration.
27. Observability.
28. Compatibility.
29. Migration.
30. Certification.

## 36.2 Contract-First Rule

No implementation component may independently invent a contract that duplicates a canonical UCOS contract.

Before creating a new interface, the implementation must:

1. Discover the existing canonical artifact.
2. Verify its ownership and status.
3. Check compatibility with the requirement.
4. Reuse it if sufficient.
5. Extend it through the governed evolution mechanism if necessary.
6. Create a new canonical artifact only if the existing model cannot satisfy the requirement without semantic corruption.

## 36.3 Domain Boundary Rule

A component must not bypass the public or approved internal contract of another canonical domain merely because direct database access is technically possible.

## 36.4 Persistence Boundary

Only authorized Order Management components may write canonical order state.

Projections, reporting services, plugins, analytics consumers, and integration adapters must not independently modify the canonical order record.

## 36.5 Integration Adapter

An integration adapter may translate between external and canonical contracts.

It must not redefine the meaning of order states, identifiers, or commercial evidence.

## 36.6 Error Contract

Every integration contract must define:

- Error classification.
- Retryability.
- Timeout behavior.
- Unknown-outcome handling.
- Idempotency.
- Compensation.
- Reconciliation.
- Observability.
- Security requirements.

---

# 37. NONFUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

The following requirements apply across the architecture.

## 37.1 Correctness

Order identity, state transitions, versioning, and source-commitment uniqueness must be enforced at the canonical authority boundary.

## 37.2 Durability

Acknowledged canonical order changes must satisfy the declared durability contract.

## 37.3 Availability

The service must meet approved availability objectives without weakening critical consistency or authorization invariants.

## 37.4 Scalability

The architecture must scale through approved partitioning, horizontal expansion, workload isolation, and asynchronous processing.

## 37.5 Security

All protected operations must enforce authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, and data classification.

## 37.6 Maintainability

Every capability must have explicit ownership, dependencies, contracts, tests, documentation, and retirement procedures.

## 37.7 Extensibility

New commerce profiles must be introduced through governed extensions rather than mandatory core rewrites.

## 37.8 Interoperability

The system must expose versioned contracts that can be consumed by heterogeneous systems.

## 37.9 Observability

Every meaningful order transition and cross-domain workflow must be traceable.

## 37.10 Auditability

Every material order change must have a traceable actor, reason, policy, and outcome.

## 37.11 Recoverability

Canonical records and required event histories must support validated restoration and reconciliation.

## 37.12 Portability

Business semantics must not depend on a specific cloud, database, runtime, or vendor.

## 37.13 Accessibility

User-facing order experiences must conform to applicable accessibility requirements.

## 37.14 Privacy

Personal and commercial data must be processed according to authorized purpose, retention, and access policies.

## 37.15 Compatibility

Schema and contract evolution must be governed and verifiable.

## 37.16 Determinism

Equivalent valid inputs under equivalent policy and evidence conditions must produce equivalent business decisions, except where explicitly declared nondeterministic external decisions are involved.

## 37.17 Reproducibility

The system must preserve sufficient evidence to reconstruct why a material order decision was made.

## 37.18 Operational Simplicity

The architecture must avoid unnecessary service boundaries, duplicate workflows, overlapping ownership, and uncontrolled plugin proliferation.

---

# 38. FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

The following 50 requirements form the proposed functional baseline.

Identifiers are provisional.

## FR-001 — Canonical Order Identity

The system shall assign a stable canonical identifier to every successfully created order.

## FR-002 — Source Commitment Validation

The system shall validate the source purchase commitment through its authoritative contract before creating an order where such a commitment is required.

## FR-003 — Duplicate Creation Prevention

The system shall prevent duplicate order creation for source commitments whose declared cardinality permits only one order.

## FR-004 — Idempotent Creation

The system shall support safe repetition of order-creation commands.

## FR-005 — Initial Version Creation

The system shall create an initial version record for every successfully created order.

## FR-006 — Canonical Order Retrieval

The system shall provide authorized retrieval of canonical order information.

## FR-007 — Order Search

The system shall support authorized order search within declared access and data-governance boundaries.

## FR-008 — Order-Line Management

The system shall maintain canonical order-line identities and membership.

## FR-009 — Order Grouping

The system shall support governed grouping of order lines and obligations.

## FR-010 — Multi-Merchant Structure

The system shall support orders containing multiple merchant or provider groups where permitted by the applicable profile.

## FR-011 — Order Relationship Management

The system shall maintain typed and auditable relationships between orders.

## FR-012 — Lifecycle Validation

The system shall reject lifecycle transitions that violate the registered transition contract.

## FR-013 — Transition Audit

The system shall record an audit entry for every material lifecycle transition.

## FR-014 — Order Acceptance

The system shall support governed order acceptance where required.

## FR-015 — Order Confirmation

The system shall support governed order confirmation where the commerce profile defines a distinct confirmation stage.

## FR-016 — Order Rejection

The system shall support authorized rejection with an explicit reason and evidence.

## FR-017 — Versioned Amendments

The system shall record authorized amendments as new versions or equivalent governed immutable change records.

## FR-018 — Amendment Concurrency

The system shall detect stale-version amendment attempts and prevent silent overwrites.

## FR-019 — Amendment Impact Evaluation

The system shall support evaluation of amendment impact before committing changes where the operation requires pre-evaluation.

## FR-020 — Commercial Evidence Preservation

The system shall preserve or reference the applicable commercial evidence established at order commitment.

## FR-021 — Price Evidence Integration

The system shall reference authoritative pricing evidence without becoming the pricing authority.

## FR-022 — Tax Evidence Integration

The system shall reference authoritative tax evidence without becoming the tax authority.

## FR-023 — Payment Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and payment operations.

## FR-024 — Inventory Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and inventory reservations where applicable.

## FR-025 — Capacity Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and capacity reservations where applicable.

## FR-026 — Fulfillment Obligation Management

The system shall maintain order obligations and references to authoritative fulfillment records.

## FR-027 — Partial Fulfillment

The system shall represent partial fulfillment without incorrectly marking outstanding obligations as fulfilled.

## FR-028 — Cancellation Requests

The system shall accept and evaluate authorized cancellation requests.

## FR-029 — Partial Cancellation

The system shall support partial cancellation where the applicable profile and obligations permit it.

## FR-030 — Cancellation Compensation Tracking

The system shall track required cancellation-related operations and unresolved compensation.

## FR-031 — Return Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and return cases.

## FR-032 — Refund Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and refund cases.

## FR-033 — Dispute Reference Management

The system shall maintain authorized relationships between orders and dispute cases.

## FR-034 — Closure Governance

The system shall evaluate order closure against the applicable closure policy.

## FR-035 — Immutable History

The system shall preserve historical order versions and material lifecycle evidence according to retention policy.

## FR-036 — Order Event Publication

The system shall publish registered lifecycle events through the approved event contract.

## FR-037 — Event Duplication Tolerance

The system shall support duplicate-safe processing of order events.

## FR-038 — Event Publication Recovery

The system shall support recovery of required event publication after transient failure.

## FR-039 — Cross-Domain Reconciliation

The system shall identify and track defined inconsistencies between order records and referenced domain records.

## FR-040 — Exception Management

The system shall provide controlled exception creation, investigation, resolution, and audit.

## FR-041 — Customer Projection

The system shall provide an authorized customer-facing order projection.

## FR-042 — Merchant Projection

The system shall provide an authorized merchant-facing order projection.

## FR-043 — Projection Freshness

The system shall expose sufficient metadata to evaluate projection freshness where freshness matters.

## FR-044 — Authorization Enforcement

The system shall enforce object-level authorization for protected order operations.

## FR-045 — Tenant Isolation

The system shall prevent unauthorized cross-tenant access and modification.

## FR-046 — Retention Enforcement

The system shall apply the relevant canonical retention and legal-hold policies.

## FR-047 — Extension Registration

The system shall support governed registration and validation of order-related extensions.

## FR-048 — Operational Observability

The system shall expose metrics, logs, traces, and lifecycle evidence necessary for operational management.

## FR-049 — Disaster Recovery

The system shall support validated recovery of canonical order records and required historical evidence.

## FR-050 — Traceability

The system shall maintain traceability from requirements and contracts to verification evidence and certification decisions.

# 39. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

The following 50 acceptance criteria are proposed. Passing them must be demonstrated through actual tests and evidence; listing them does not establish that they have passed.

## AC-001 — Unique Order Identity

Given two independent valid order-creation operations, when both succeed, each order has a distinct canonical identifier within the declared uniqueness scope.

## AC-002 — Commitment Validation

Given an invalid or unauthorized source commitment, when creation is requested, the system rejects the request without creating an unauthorized order.

## AC-003 — Concurrent Duplicate Prevention

Given concurrent requests for the same single-order commitment, when both execute, no more than one canonical order is created.

## AC-004 — Idempotent Replay

Given a successfully processed creation request, when the identical request is repeated with the same valid idempotency scope, the system returns the original outcome or an equivalent canonical result without creating another order.

## AC-005 — Idempotency Conflict

Given an existing idempotency key associated with a materially different request, when the key is reused, the system rejects the conflicting request.

## AC-006 — Initial Version

Given a successfully created order, when its canonical record is retrieved, the initial version and its provenance are available.

## AC-007 — Authorized Retrieval

Given a caller without permission to access an order, when retrieval is attempted, the system does not disclose the protected order data.

## AC-008 — Search Isolation

Given multiple tenants, when a tenant searches for orders, the results contain only records permitted by the applicable access policy.

## AC-009 — Stable Line Identity

Given an existing order line, when the order is amended, the line's identity remains stable unless a governed replacement or split operation explicitly changes the relationship.

## AC-010 — Multi-Merchant Composition

Given a permitted multi-merchant order, when one merchant group progresses independently, the system preserves the distinct states and obligations of each group.

## AC-011 — Typed Order Relationship

Given a parent-child or replacement relationship, when retrieved, its type, endpoints, and required lineage are available.

## AC-012 — Invalid Transition Rejection

Given a transition that is not permitted from the current state, when requested, the system rejects it without applying the prohibited state change.

## AC-013 — Transition Audit

Given a successful material lifecycle transition, when audit history is retrieved, the transition's actor, reason where applicable, prior state, resulting state, and policy context are available.

## AC-014 — Acceptance Evidence

Given a profile requiring explicit acceptance, when acceptance evidence is missing or invalid, the system does not report the order as accepted.

## AC-015 — Profile-Specific Confirmation

Given a profile that distinguishes acceptance from confirmation, when confirmation conditions remain unsatisfied, the system does not incorrectly enter the confirmed state.

## AC-016 — Rejection Evidence

Given an authorized rejection, when the rejection is completed, the order retains its rejection reason and applicable decision evidence.

## AC-017 — Amendment Versioning

Given an authorized amendment, when it succeeds, a new version or approved immutable change record is created and the previous historical evidence remains available.

## AC-018 — Stale Amendment

Given a stale expected version, when an amendment is submitted, the system rejects or defers the operation according to contract and does not silently overwrite the newer version.

## AC-019 — Amendment Preview

Given an amendment requiring impact evaluation, when previewed, the system returns the applicable identified impacts or an explicit unresolved outcome without committing the amendment.

## AC-020 — Commercial Snapshot

Given an order created from a commercial commitment, when the relevant historical order evidence is retrieved, the system can identify the commercial source versions used at commitment time.

## AC-021 — Pricing Authority

Given a price reference, when pricing evidence is invalid or stale under the applicable policy, the system does not independently treat the reference as a valid authoritative quote.

## AC-022 — Tax Authority

Given a required tax determination, when authoritative tax evidence is missing, the system follows the profile's defined failure behavior rather than inventing a tax result.

## AC-023 — Payment Uncertainty

Given a payment operation with an unknown outcome, when the order workflow evaluates its status, the system does not incorrectly represent the payment as definitively failed or successful.

## AC-024 — Inventory Reference Integrity

Given an order requiring a reservation, when the reservation reference is invalid, the system follows the approved order policy and records the inconsistency.

## AC-025 — Capacity Reference Integrity

Given an order requiring capacity, when capacity evidence is unavailable, the system does not fabricate an allocation.

## AC-026 — Fulfillment Obligation Integrity

Given a newly authorized fulfillment obligation, when its reference is recorded, the relationship to the canonical order and relevant line or obligation is preserved.

## AC-027 — Partial Fulfillment

Given an order with multiple fulfillment obligations, when only some obligations are completed, the order is not incorrectly marked as fully fulfilled.

## AC-028 — Cancellation Authorization

Given an unauthorized cancellation request, when submitted, the system rejects the request and preserves the existing order state.

## AC-029 — Partial Cancellation Accounting

Given a line with partially cancellable quantity, when cancellation succeeds, the system preserves the cancelled and outstanding quantities or equivalent obligation units without duplication.

## AC-030 — Cancellation Compensation

Given a cancelled order with an unresolved external compensation, when the cancellation result is retrieved, the unresolved compensation remains explicitly identifiable.

## AC-031 — Return Reference

Given a valid return case, when it is associated with an order, the relationship remains traceable without transferring return authority to Order Management.

## AC-032 — Refund Reference

Given a refund case, when its execution is pending, the order does not falsely represent the refund as executed.

## AC-033 — Dispute Reference

Given an authorized dispute relationship, when order evidence is retrieved by an authorized actor, the applicable dispute reference and order provenance are available.

## AC-034 — Closure Preconditions

Given an order that does not satisfy its closure policy, when closure is requested, the system rejects or defers closure with an explicit reason.

## AC-035 — Historical Immutability

Given a material order amendment, when earlier versions are retrieved, their historical content remains unchanged under the approved retention model.

## AC-036 — Event Publication

Given a committed state transition that requires an event, when the operation succeeds, the event publication obligation is durably recorded.

## AC-037 — Duplicate Event Processing

Given the same event is delivered repeatedly, when the consumer processes it, the duplicate deliveries do not create duplicate business effects.

## AC-038 — Event Recovery

Given a transient publication failure, when recovery runs, the required event can be published or the failure becomes an explicitly recorded unrecoverable exception.

## AC-039 — Reconciliation Detection

Given a deliberately introduced mismatch between an order reference and its authoritative source, when reconciliation runs, the mismatch is detected and recorded.

## AC-040 — Exception Resolution

Given an order exception, when an authorized resolution is completed, the system records the resolution evidence and applies only a permitted resulting transition.

## AC-041 — Customer Projection Authorization

Given a customer request, when the customer retrieves an order projection, the system exposes only the data and operations authorized for that customer.

## AC-042 — Merchant Projection Authorization

Given a merchant request, when the merchant retrieves order information, the system excludes unauthorized data and unrelated merchant obligations.

## AC-043 — Projection Freshness

Given an asynchronously maintained projection, when it is stale, the system exposes sufficient freshness metadata or follows the approved fallback policy.

## AC-044 — Object-Level Authorization

Given an authenticated actor without permission for a particular order operation, when the operation is attempted, authentication alone does not authorize it.

## AC-045 — Tenant Boundary

Given a cross-tenant request without explicit authorized delegation, when it is submitted, the system prevents access and records the applicable security event.

## AC-046 — Retention Policy

Given an order subject to a retention or legal-hold policy, when a deletion or archival operation is requested, the system applies the governing policy and records the result.

## AC-047 — Plugin Contract Validation

Given a plugin with an incompatible or unauthorized contract, when activation is attempted, the system rejects or isolates it without corrupting canonical order state.

## AC-048 — Operational Traceability

Given an order creation followed by multiple transitions, when the authorized trace is retrieved, the relevant commands, events, domain references, and outcomes can be correlated.

## AC-049 — Recovery Integrity

Given a tested restoration scenario, when recovery completes, the system validates order identity uniqueness, required version history, and required event consistency.

## AC-050 — Certification Traceability

Given a required functional capability, when certification evidence is assembled, the capability can be traced to its approved requirement, contract, test result, and certification decision.

---

# 40. PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS

The following architecture decision records are proposed for formal review.

No decision is considered approved solely because it appears in this specification.

## ADR-001 — Order Management Is the Canonical Order Authority

**Decision proposal:** Establish Order Management as the sole canonical authority for order identity, order lifecycle, order version history, and order-level relationships.

**Rationale:** Prevent competing order records and inconsistent lifecycle decisions.

**Consequences:** Other domains must consume order contracts rather than independently redefine the order.

## ADR-002 — Purchase Commitment Is the Authorized Creation Boundary

**Decision proposal:** Create orders from an authorized purchase commitment or another explicitly registered creation source.

**Rationale:** Preserve the distinction between purchase intent, commercial commitment, and order lifecycle.

**Consequence:** Direct creation sources require explicit governance.

## ADR-003 — Order Identity Is Independent of Database Identity

**Decision proposal:** Use a canonical identifier independent of physical storage keys.

**Rationale:** Support migration, distribution, integration, and long-lived references.

## ADR-004 — Order History Is Versioned and Auditable

**Decision proposal:** Preserve immutable historical commercial evidence and represent amendments explicitly.

**Rationale:** Support reproducibility, dispute resolution, and commercial integrity.

## ADR-005 — State Transitions Are Governed Commands

**Decision proposal:** Prohibit arbitrary direct state mutation.

**Rationale:** Ensure consistent preconditions, authorization, audit, and side effects.

## ADR-006 — Payment State Remains Independently Owned

**Decision proposal:** Reference payment outcomes without making payment state part of the canonical order state machine.

**Rationale:** Prevent conflicting authority and misleading financial status.

## ADR-007 — Fulfillment State Remains Independently Owned

**Decision proposal:** Represent fulfillment obligations and authoritative fulfillment references separately from order lifecycle.

**Rationale:** Support partial fulfillment and independent operational progress.

## ADR-008 — Cross-Domain Workflows Explicitly Handle Uncertainty

**Decision proposal:** Require defined unknown-outcome and reconciliation behavior.

**Rationale:** Prevent false success or false failure after distributed-system timeouts.

## ADR-009 — Business Idempotency Is Mandatory for Critical Commands

**Decision proposal:** Require idempotency and relevant business uniqueness controls.

**Rationale:** Prevent duplicate orders and duplicate side effects.

## ADR-010 — Order Composition Is Profile-Driven

**Decision proposal:** Represent commerce variation through registered schemas and profiles.

**Rationale:** Avoid hard-coded assumptions about products, merchants, and fulfillment.

## ADR-011 — Multi-Merchant Orders Preserve Independent Obligations

**Decision proposal:** Permit merchant groups and their obligations to progress independently.

**Rationale:** Avoid forcing all order components into a single operational lifecycle.

## ADR-012 — Read Models Are Noncanonical

**Decision proposal:** Treat search indexes and customer or merchant projections as derived views.

**Rationale:** Preserve canonical ownership and permit independent read optimization.

## ADR-013 — Events Carry Explicit Identity and Version Metadata

**Decision proposal:** Use the canonical UCOS event envelope and registered schemas.

**Rationale:** Support correlation, replay, compatibility, and audit.

## ADR-014 — Event Publication Must Be Recoverable

**Decision proposal:** Use an approved durable event-publication consistency mechanism.

**Rationale:** Prevent lost events after committed order changes.

## ADR-015 — Plugins Cannot Bypass Canonical Contracts

**Decision proposal:** Restrict plugins to governed extension points.

**Rationale:** Prevent unauthorized mutation and hidden dependencies.

## ADR-016 — AI Does Not Own Canonical Order Decisions

**Decision proposal:** Require AI-proposed actions to pass through deterministic controls.

**Rationale:** Preserve authority, authorization, and auditability.

## ADR-017 — Policy Versions Are Preserved with Decisions

**Decision proposal:** Store references to the policies applicable to material order decisions.

**Rationale:** Enable historical reconstruction and explainability.

## ADR-018 — Monetary Values Use Canonical Exact-Money Semantics

**Decision proposal:** Use canonical money and currency definitions and suitable exact representations.

**Rationale:** Prevent rounding and precision defects.

## ADR-019 — Temporal Semantics Are Explicit

**Decision proposal:** Use the canonical temporal model for timestamps, effective intervals, and deadlines.

**Rationale:** Prevent time-zone and deadline ambiguity.

## ADR-020 — Reconciliation Is a First-Class Capability

**Decision proposal:** Register reconciliation rules for cross-domain invariants.

**Rationale:** Detect and recover from inconsistencies that cannot be eliminated through local transactions alone.

## ADR-021 — Authorization Is Object- and Operation-Aware

**Decision proposal:** Evaluate access against the requested operation and the target order.

**Rationale:** Prevent identifier-based unauthorized access.

## ADR-022 — Retention Is Policy-Driven

**Decision proposal:** Apply canonical retention, deletion, and legal-hold rules.

**Rationale:** Avoid universal retention assumptions that conflict with legal obligations.

## ADR-023 — Service Boundaries Are Logical Before Physical

**Decision proposal:** Define domain contracts independently of deployment topology.

**Rationale:** Avoid premature microservice fragmentation and preserve portability.

## ADR-024 — Performance Targets Require Evidence

**Decision proposal:** Treat proposed latency and availability targets as hypotheses until approved and measured.

**Rationale:** Prevent unsupported operational guarantees.

## ADR-025 — Canonical Reconciliation Precedes Implementation

**Decision proposal:** Reconcile this specification with existing UCOS artifacts, registries, and dependencies before implementation.

**Rationale:** Enforce reuse, eliminate duplication, and prevent conflicting canonical definitions.

---

# 41. PROPOSED ARCHITECTURAL GAPS AND RESOLUTIONS

The following gaps must be closed before the specification is considered implementation-ready.

## GAP-001 — Master Index Reconciliation

**Gap:** The complete authoritative marketplace specification index has not been verified in this document.

**Required resolution:** Retrieve the canonical master index, reconcile numbering and scope, and establish the approved dependency map.

## GAP-002 — Existing Order Artifacts

**Gap:** Existing UCOS order entities, schemas, and capabilities have not been inventoried here.

**Required resolution:** Discover and classify existing artifacts before creating replacements.

## GAP-003 — Canonical Order Ontology

**Gap:** Proposed order concepts may overlap with existing canonical concepts.

**Required resolution:** Reconcile definitions, synonyms, ownership, and relationships against the canonical ontology.

## GAP-004 — Identifier Namespace

**Gap:** The proposed `UCOS-MKT-ORD` prefix has not been verified.

**Required resolution:** Validate against the identifier registry.

## GAP-005 — State-Machine Canonicalization

**Gap:** The proposed lifecycle states may overlap with existing state vocabularies.

**Required resolution:** Establish the canonical lifecycle model and transition registry.

## GAP-006 — Purchase Commitment Contract

**Gap:** The exact canonical Purchase Commitment contract and its permitted creation cardinalities are not established here.

**Required resolution:** Define the authoritative source contract and duplicate-prevention invariant.

## GAP-007 — Merchant Acceptance Semantics

**Gap:** Merchant acceptance requirements vary by commercial model.

**Required resolution:** Define profile-specific acceptance rules and evidence.

## GAP-008 — Commercial Snapshot Schema

**Gap:** The complete snapshot schema and canonical source-version rules require confirmation.

**Required resolution:** Reuse canonical evidence and versioning contracts.

## GAP-009 — Order-Line Quantity Semantics

**Gap:** Non-quantity-based commerce may require richer obligation models.

**Required resolution:** Establish canonical quantity and obligation-unit semantics.

## GAP-010 — Multi-Order Relationships

**Gap:** Parent, child, split, replacement, and consolidated order semantics require formal cardinality and lifecycle rules.

**Required resolution:** Define the canonical order relationship registry.

## GAP-011 — Payment Contract

**Gap:** Payment reference semantics and authoritative events must be reconciled.

**Required resolution:** Validate the canonical Payment contract and state mapping.

## GAP-012 — Inventory and Capacity Contracts

**Gap:** Reservation semantics and expiration behavior are not established here.

**Required resolution:** Reconcile Inventory and Capacity contracts.

## GAP-013 — Fulfillment Completion

**Gap:** Fulfillment completion conditions vary by commerce profile.

**Required resolution:** Establish the canonical Fulfillment contract and completion semantics.

## GAP-014 — Cancellation Coordination

**Gap:** Cross-domain cancellation compensation rules require detailed contracts.

**Required resolution:** Define operation ownership, compensation, timeout, and reconciliation rules.

## GAP-015 — Return and Refund Boundaries

**Gap:** Return and refund integration contracts have not been verified.

**Required resolution:** Reconcile Returns and Refunds capabilities and event schemas.

## GAP-016 — Dispute Evidence

**Gap:** Evidence retention and access requirements vary by dispute type and jurisdiction.

**Required resolution:** Establish canonical dispute-evidence contracts and retention rules.

## GAP-017 — Closure Policy

**Gap:** The universal closure conditions have not been approved.

**Required resolution:** Define profile-specific closure semantics and terminal-state rules.

## GAP-018 — Event Envelope

**Gap:** The proposed event fields require reconciliation with the canonical UCOS event standard.

**Required resolution:** Reuse the canonical envelope and registry.

## GAP-019 — Event Ordering

**Gap:** The exact ordering guarantee required for each aggregate is not established.

**Required resolution:** Define ordering scopes, version checks, and out-of-order handling.

## GAP-020 — Event Retention and Replay

**Gap:** Replay, archival, and retention requirements require confirmation.

**Required resolution:** Define the event-retention and recovery contract.

## GAP-021 — Physical Persistence Design

**Gap:** No physical persistence model has been validated against workload or consistency requirements.

**Required resolution:** Conduct data and workload architecture analysis.

## GAP-022 — Global Identity Strategy

**Gap:** Distributed identifier issuance and migration semantics require canonical confirmation.

**Required resolution:** Reconcile the identity and identifier infrastructure.

## GAP-023 — Data Classification

**Gap:** Order fields require explicit classification under the canonical data-governance model.

**Required resolution:** Map every field to its data classification and access policy.

## GAP-024 — Privacy and Retention

**Gap:** Retention, deletion, legal hold, and jurisdiction-specific processing require formal mapping.

**Required resolution:** Reconcile privacy and retention policies.

## GAP-025 — Certification Baseline

**Gap:** Required certification evidence and pass thresholds have not been established.

**Required resolution:** Approve the certification matrix and verification strategy.

# 42. DEPENDENCY AND TRACEABILITY MODEL

## 42.1 Dependency Categories

Dependencies must be classified as:

- Mandatory.
- Conditional.
- Optional.
- Advisory.
- Asynchronous.
- Derived.
- External.
- Prohibited.

## 42.2 Proposed Dependency Map

| Dependency | Relationship | Required Control |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Authentication and subject references | Canonical identity contracts |
| Access Governance | Authorization | Operation-level enforcement |
| Purchase Commitment | Authorized order source | Source validation and uniqueness |
| Product | Product/service identity | Canonical references and snapshots |
| Merchant | Merchant identity and relationship | Authorization and provenance |
| Pricing | Price determination | Quote validation |
| Offers | Offer evaluation | Promotion evidence |
| Tax | Tax determination | Tax evidence validation |
| Inventory | Stock reservation | Reservation validation |
| Capacity | Resource reservation | Capacity evidence |
| Payment | Payment execution | Reference and outcome reconciliation |
| Fulfillment | Obligation execution | Obligation coordination |
| Delivery | Delivery outcome | Authoritative event consumption |
| Returns | Return lifecycle | Return reference validation |
| Refunds | Refund execution | Refund reference validation |
| Disputes | Dispute lifecycle | Evidence and access controls |
| Settlement | Financial settlement | Reconciliation |
| Accounting | Accounting records | Canonical financial references |
| Trust and Safety | Risk decisions | Authorized decision consumption |
| Communication | Notifications | Event-based integration |
| Temporal | Time semantics | Canonical temporal contract |
| Geography | Address and jurisdiction context | Canonical geographic references |
| Governance | Policies and approvals | Versioned policy resolution |
| Knowledge Registry | Artifact discovery | Reuse-first discovery |
| Event Infrastructure | Durable event distribution | Delivery and recovery guarantees |
| Observability | Operational telemetry | Traceability and alerting |

## 42.3 Dependency Direction

Order Management may consume the contracts of canonical neighboring domains.

Neighboring domains must not acquire authority over the order record merely because they initiate a related operation.

## 42.4 Circular Dependency Prevention

The dependency registry must detect and reject prohibited circular dependencies.

Where asynchronous relationships create apparent graph cycles, the architecture must distinguish runtime message relationships from compile-time or ownership dependencies.

## 42.5 Traceability Chain

Every material requirement must be traceable through:

    Requirement
        ↓
    Canonical Capability
        ↓
    Ontology / Contract
        ↓
    Architecture Component
        ↓
    Implementation Artifact
        ↓
    Verification Case
        ↓
    Execution Evidence
        ↓
    Certification Decision

A missing link must be reported as a traceability gap.

---

# 43. VERIFICATION STRATEGY

## 43.1 Verification Objectives

Verification must demonstrate that the implementation satisfies the approved architecture, contracts, functional requirements, nonfunctional requirements, security constraints, and lifecycle invariants.

## 43.2 Required Verification Layers

### A. Static Verification

Verify:

- Schema validity.
- Contract validity.
- Identifier uniqueness.
- Registry consistency.
- Dependency direction.
- Circular dependency constraints.
- Policy schema validity.
- Event schema compatibility.
- Documentation and reference integrity.

### B. Unit Verification

Verify:

- Order creation rules.
- Lifecycle transitions.
- Version creation.
- Amendment eligibility.
- Idempotency behavior.
- State aggregation.
- Error classification.
- Policy resolution.
- Quantity and obligation invariants.

### C. Contract Verification

Verify compatibility with:

- Purchase Commitment.
- Pricing.
- Offers.
- Tax.
- Payment.
- Inventory.
- Capacity.
- Fulfillment.
- Returns.
- Refunds.
- Disputes.
- Settlement.
- Identity.
- Access Governance.
- Event infrastructure.

### D. Integration Verification

Verify:

- Order creation from commitment.
- Payment reference lifecycle.
- Reservation coordination.
- Fulfillment obligation creation.
- Cancellation coordination.
- Return and refund references.
- Event publication and consumption.
- Cross-domain reconciliation.

### E. Concurrency Verification

Test:

- Concurrent creation.
- Duplicate commitments.
- Concurrent amendments.
- Concurrent cancellation and fulfillment.
- Version conflicts.
- Event races.
- Duplicate message delivery.
- Projection rebuild under load.

### F. Failure-Injection Verification

Test:

- Database failure.
- Network partition.
- Dependency timeout.
- Event publication failure.
- Duplicate event delivery.
- Out-of-order events.
- Unknown payment outcome.
- Interrupted cancellation.
- Interrupted amendment.
- Partial compensation.
- Regional failover.

### G. Security Verification

Test:

- Unauthorized order retrieval.
- Cross-tenant access.
- Privileged-operation controls.
- Malicious event payloads.
- Replay attacks.
- Plugin isolation.
- Sensitive-data exposure.
- Administrative misuse.
- Authorization race conditions.

### H. Data Integrity Verification

Test:

- Identifier uniqueness.
- Version sequence integrity.
- Order-line relationships.
- Order relationship integrity.
- Evidence lineage.
- Event-to-order consistency.
- Retention enforcement.
- Recovery correctness.

### I. Performance Verification

Test:

- Latency.
- Throughput.
- Resource utilization.
- Peak concurrency.
- Sustained load.
- Burst load.
- Projection freshness.
- Reconciliation throughput.
- Recovery under backlog.

### J. Disaster Recovery Verification

Test:

- Backup restoration.
- Identifier preservation.
- Historical version preservation.
- Event replay.
- Idempotency restoration.
- Cross-domain reconciliation after recovery.

## 43.3 Property-Based Testing

The implementation should test general invariants across generated valid and invalid inputs.

Examples include:

- An order ID is never assigned to two distinct canonical orders.
- An unauthorized transition never succeeds.
- A stale amendment never silently overwrites a newer version.
- A repeated idempotent command never produces duplicate business effects.
- A completed order cannot have an unexplained loss of required historical evidence.
- A derived fulfillment status never exceeds the authoritative evidence available under its derivation rules.

## 43.4 Model-Based Testing

The approved lifecycle state machine should be used to generate transition sequences and verify that implementation behavior matches the model.

## 43.5 Verification Evidence

Every executed test must produce evidence containing:

- Test identifier.
- Requirement reference.
- Environment.
- Software or artifact version.
- Test inputs.
- Expected result.
- Actual result.
- Execution timestamp.
- Pass/fail status.
- Relevant logs or trace references.
- Defect references.
- Reviewer or automated verifier identity.

## 43.6 Verification Integrity

A test must not be reported as passed unless it was executed successfully under the declared conditions.

A mock or simulated dependency must be identified as such.

Passing unit tests does not establish production readiness.

Certification must be based on recorded evidence.

A gate must have:

- Gate identifier.
- Scope.
- Required controls.
- Evidence requirements.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Responsible authority.
- Actual result.
- Defect references.
- Approval record.
- Decision timestamp.

A gate must not be marked PASS solely because its documentation exists.

# 46. ABSOLUTE ARCHITECTURAL PROHIBITIONS

The implementation must not:

1. Create competing canonical order authorities.
2. Duplicate an existing canonical order ontology without approval.
3. Treat Cart as the canonical order record.
4. Treat a checkout session as an order.
5. Create orders from unverified purchase commitments where commitment verification is required.
6. Allow duplicate canonical orders for a single-order source commitment.
7. Mutate lifecycle state without transition validation.
8. Silently overwrite historical commercial evidence.
9. Assume every commerce model requires physical inventory.
10. Assume every order contains physical products.
11. Assume every order has one merchant.
12. Assume every order has one payment.
13. Assume every order has one fulfillment.
14. Assume every order has one delivery.
15. Assume every cancellation automatically reverses all side effects.
16. Treat a refund request as a completed refund.
17. Treat a payment timeout as definitive payment failure.
18. Treat a payment reference as proof of payment success.
19. Treat an order projection as canonical authority.
20. Trust client-supplied tenant scope without authorization.
21. Permit direct database mutation that bypasses canonical contracts.
22. Permit plugins to bypass lifecycle validation.
23. Let AI independently override canonical authority.
24. Use hard-coded business rules where registered policies are required.
25. Hard-code one country, currency, calendar, language, or tax model.
26. Use floating-point arithmetic as the authoritative representation of monetary amounts.
27. Assume global event ordering.
28. Assume distributed transactions without a verified guarantee.
29. Blindly replay irreversible operations.
30. Silently drop required events.
31. Delete historical evidence without applicable authorization.
32. Bypass legal holds.
33. Expose sensitive data through logs or events without a valid requirement.
34. Claim unverified service levels as achieved.
35. Claim tests passed without execution evidence.
36. Claim implementation is complete because the architecture is documented.
37. Create unregistered APIs, events, identifiers, or policies without the applicable governance process.
38. Implement before resolving material canonical ownership conflicts.
39. Introduce circular dependencies without an approved and validated architectural rationale.
40. Declare certification without passing the required gates.

This specification is ready to enter canonical reconciliation when its scope and dependencies can be compared against the actual UCOS Marketplace architecture.

It is ready for implementation planning only when the required architecture decisions, contracts, and unresolved gaps have been approved or explicitly dispositioned.

It is ready for implementation only when the required canonical baselines and implementation authorization exist.

It is ready for certification only when the implementation and its evidence have been verified against approved requirements.

| Dimension | Required Condition |
|---|---|
| Domain completeness | All order lifecycle responsibilities are explicitly scoped |
| Ontology completeness | Canonical concepts, relationships, and ownership are defined |
| Authority completeness | Cross-domain ownership boundaries are explicit |
| Lifecycle completeness | Permitted transitions and terminality rules are governed |
| Contract completeness | APIs, events, errors, and versioning are specified |
| Data completeness | Data ownership, lineage, retention, and consistency are specified |
| Security completeness | Authentication, authorization, isolation, and evidence controls are defined |
| Privacy completeness | Data minimization, retention, deletion, and legal holds are governed |
| Failure completeness | Unknown outcomes, retries, compensation, and reconciliation are addressed |
| Extensibility completeness | New commerce models can be added through governed contracts |
| Verification completeness | Requirements map to executable acceptance criteria |
| Operational completeness | Monitoring, recovery, incident handling, and ownership are defined |
| Governance completeness | Policies, identifiers, approvals, and change processes are explicit |
| Registry completeness | All artifacts and dependencies are registered |
| Certification completeness | Gates and evidence requirements are defined |

No numerical completeness percentage should be claimed until the dimensions are evaluated against the actual canonical registry and implementation evidence.

# 1. EXECUTIVE ARCHITECTURAL STATEMENT

## 1.1 Purpose

Universal Marketplace Order Financial Reconciliation and Commercial Accountability establishes a governed capability for identifying, explaining, tracking, and resolving discrepancies between marketplace commercial obligations and independently authoritative financial records.

A marketplace order can generate numerous financially relevant records across independently governed domains.

Examples include:

- Commercial order commitments.
- Price quotations.
- Discounts and promotions.
- Tax determinations.
- Payment obligations.
- Payment authorizations.
- Payment captures.
- Payment reversals.
- Refund obligations.
- Refund executions.
- Merchant receivables.
- Marketplace commissions.
- Merchant payables.
- Settlement instructions.
- Settlement confirmations.
- Accounting entries.
- External processor reports.
- Bank statements.
- Chargebacks.
- Financial adjustments.
- Currency conversions.
- Fees.
- Withholding obligations.
- Financial corrections.

These records do not necessarily share a single identifier, transaction boundary, processing schedule, data model, or authoritative system.

The architecture must establish reliable reconciliation across these records without creating a competing financial authority.

## 1.2 Core Responsibility

The proposed capability owns:

1. Reconciliation case identity.
2. Reconciliation rule execution.
3. Matching and comparison decisions within its approved scope.
4. Discrepancy classification.
5. Reconciliation evidence.
6. Exception tracking.
7. Reconciliation workflow state.
8. Resolution coordination.
9. Reconciliation lineage.
10. Reconciliation reporting.
11. Reconciliation control evidence.
12. Reconciliation certification evidence.

It does not become the canonical authority for payment execution, refunds, settlement, accounting, tax, pricing, or the order itself.

## 1.3 Fundamental Distinction

**Commercial truth, payment truth, settlement truth, and accounting truth are related but not interchangeable.**

For example:

- An order can be commercially valid while payment is pending.
- A payment can be captured while merchant settlement remains pending.
- A refund can be authorized while its execution remains unresolved.
- A settlement instruction can be generated without confirmation that funds reached the intended destination.
- A processor report can disagree with a payment service's recorded outcome.
- An accounting entry can exist while the corresponding external financial movement remains under investigation.

The reconciliation capability must preserve these distinctions.

## 1.4 Intended Outcomes

The architecture must provide:

- Deterministic financial matching.
- Explicit reconciliation scopes.
- Versioned reconciliation rules.
- Complete source provenance.
- Duplicate-resistant ingestion.
- Exact monetary comparison.
- Currency-aware reconciliation.
- Partial and many-to-many matching.
- Time-aware reconciliation.
- Automated discrepancy detection.
- Safe and auditable resolution.
- Cross-domain consistency controls.
- Financial evidence preservation.
- Governed manual intervention.
- Reproducible reconciliation results.
- Separation between detection and financial mutation.
- Comprehensive operational visibility.
- Domain-agnostic extension.

## 1.5 Architectural Boundary

The reconciliation capability answers:

- Do these records correspond?
- Are their values consistent under the applicable rules?
- What evidence supports the comparison?
- What discrepancy exists?
- Which domain owns the discrepancy?
- What action is authorized?
- Has the discrepancy been resolved?
- Can the result be independently reproduced?

It must not independently answer authoritative questions such as:

- Was a payment actually executed?
- Is a refund legally due?
- Has a merchant been paid?
- Is a tax amount legally correct?
- Is an accounting entry valid?
- Has a bank transfer definitively settled?

Those questions remain with the respective authoritative domains.

---

# 2. CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES

## 2.1 Single Canonical Authority

Every financial concept must have one declared canonical owner.

Reconciliation may compare and reference data from multiple owners, but it must not silently replace them.

## 2.2 Knowledge Once Principle

Canonical financial concepts must be authored once and reused.

The architecture must reuse existing definitions for:

- Money.
- Currency.
- Exchange rates.
- Financial instruments.
- Payment operations.
- Refund operations.
- Settlement.
- Accounting entries.
- Tax determinations.
- Commercial commitments.
- Merchant obligations.
- Financial adjustments.
- Financial evidence.
- Temporal semantics.
- Identity.
- Jurisdiction.
- Data classification.
- Audit.
- Policy.

New concepts may be introduced only where an actual semantic gap has been established.

## 2.3 Reconciliation Is Not Execution

Detecting a discrepancy does not authorize changing financial records.

Every corrective action must be routed through the canonical authority responsible for that action.

## 2.4 Evidence Before Resolution

A discrepancy must not be marked resolved merely because an operator has acknowledged it.

Resolution requires evidence that satisfies the applicable reconciliation policy.

## 2.5 Exact Monetary Semantics

Financial comparisons must use canonical monetary types, currency definitions, precision rules, and rounding policies.

Binary floating-point arithmetic must not be used as the authoritative representation of monetary amounts.

## 2.6 Deterministic Matching

Equivalent records under equivalent rules and evidence must produce reproducible matching results.

Where probabilistic or heuristic matching is permitted, the system must preserve its evidence, confidence, decision policy, and required approval.

## 2.7 Temporal Correctness

The system must distinguish transaction time, business-effective time, recording time, settlement time, and reconciliation time.

It must not treat records as inconsistent merely because their legitimate processing times differ.

## 2.8 Append-Only Evidence

Material reconciliation decisions, source snapshots, adjustments, and resolution evidence must be preserved under the applicable retention policy.

Corrections must not silently erase previous decisions.

## 2.9 Idempotent Processing

Repeated ingestion, matching, or event delivery must not create duplicate financial effects or duplicate reconciliation cases for the same defined discrepancy.

## 2.10 Explicit Uncertainty

If the system cannot establish whether a financial operation succeeded, it must represent uncertainty explicitly.

It must not manufacture a successful or failed outcome.

## 2.11 Separation of Detection and Remediation

Discrepancy detection and financial remediation must be distinct operations with distinct authorization requirements.

## 2.12 Technology Neutrality

The business model must not depend on a particular database, programming language, payment processor, bank, cloud platform, accounting package, or messaging system.

## 2.13 Automatic Discovery

Reconciliation rules, source adapters, evidence schemas, matching strategies, and policy definitions must be discoverable through canonical registries.

## 2.14 Least Privilege

Access to financial evidence and corrective operations must be restricted according to role, purpose, tenant, merchant, jurisdiction, data classification, and operation.

## 2.15 No Silent Financial Mutation

No discrepancy-resolution process may directly mutate another domain's authoritative financial records without invoking the approved contract.

## 2.16 Reproducibility

A reconciliation result must be reproducible from the retained source evidence, rule version, policy version, matching inputs, and execution context, subject to the applicable retention and privacy constraints.

---

# 3. SCOPE AND AUTHORITY BOUNDARIES

## 3.1 Included Capabilities

The proposed domain includes:

- Financial source registration.
- Reconciliation-source configuration.
- Source-data ingestion.
- Source-record normalization.
- Source-record identity.
- Duplicate ingestion prevention.
- Reconciliation batch management.
- Reconciliation-run management.
- Record matching.
- Aggregate matching.
- Many-to-many matching.
- Monetary comparison.
- Currency comparison.
- Timing-window evaluation.
- Fee reconciliation.
- Tax reconciliation.
- Payment reconciliation.
- Refund reconciliation.
- Settlement reconciliation.
- Accounting reconciliation.
- Merchant-balance reconciliation.
- External processor reconciliation.
- Bank or financial-institution statement reconciliation.
- Discrepancy classification.
- Exception management.
- Resolution coordination.
- Evidence management.
- Financial-control reporting.
- Reconciliation analytics.
- Audit and certification evidence.

The final scope must be reconciled against existing UCOS finance, payment, settlement, accounting, and marketplace operations capabilities.

## 3.2 Excluded Authorities

| Capability | Canonical Authority | Reconciliation Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Order Management | Consume order and order-version evidence |
| Purchase Commitment | Purchase Commitment Domain | Consume commercial commitment evidence |
| Pricing | Pricing Domain | Compare authoritative price determinations |
| Offers | Offers Domain | Compare promotion and discount evidence |
| Tax | Tax Domain | Compare authoritative tax determinations |
| Payment | Payment Domain | Compare payment operations and outcomes |
| Refunds | Refunds Domain | Compare refund obligations and execution outcomes |
| Settlement | Settlement Domain | Compare settlement instructions and outcomes |
| Accounting | Accounting Domain | Compare ledger entries and accounting balances |
| Banking integration | Banking/Financial Integration Domain | Consume statement and transaction evidence |
| Merchant | Merchant Domain | Resolve merchant identity and relationship |
| Identity | Identity Domain | Resolve authorized actor identity |
| Access Governance | Access Governance | Authorize protected operations |
| Risk | Trust and Safety / Risk Domain | Provide authoritative risk decisions |
| Currency | Canonical Currency Domain | Define currency identity and properties |
| Exchange Rates | Canonical FX Domain | Provide approved rate evidence |
| Temporal | Canonical Temporal Domain | Define temporal interpretation |
| Jurisdiction | Canonical Geography and Regulatory Domains | Provide jurisdictional context |
| Audit | Canonical Audit Capability | Preserve governed audit records |
| Order lifecycle | Order Management | Provide canonical order state |
| Financial Reconciliation | Proposed UCOS-MKT-FRC | Own reconciliation cases, matching outcomes, discrepancies, and resolution workflows |

## 3.3 Boundary Enforcement

The reconciliation capability may maintain a versioned evidence snapshot from an authoritative domain.

Such a snapshot must declare:

- Source capability.
- Source entity.
- Source identifier.
- Source version.
- Capture time.
- Effective time where applicable.
- Schema version.
- Integrity metadata.
- Data classification.
- Retention policy.

A snapshot is not automatically a live authoritative record.

## 3.4 Authority of Reconciliation Results

A reconciliation result may establish that two or more records:

- Match under a defined rule.
- Differ under a defined rule.
- Remain unmatched.
- Cannot yet be conclusively compared.
- Require manual review.
- Require an authoritative source-domain decision.

It cannot independently establish that the underlying financial transaction was legally or operationally correct.

---

# 4. CANONICAL FINANCIAL RECONCILIATION ONTOLOGY

All definitions in this section are proposed and must be reconciled against the UCOS ontology registry.

## 4.1 Reconciliation

A governed process that compares two or more independently sourced records, balances, events, or aggregates against a declared set of rules and produces an auditable result.

## 4.2 Reconciliation Source

A registered authoritative or evidentiary source from which financial records are obtained.

A source may be an internal domain, external processor, financial institution, merchant system, accounting system, or approved file-based integration.

## 4.3 Source Record

A uniquely identifiable record received from a registered source.

The source record must preserve the original source identity and relevant provenance.

## 4.4 Normalized Financial Record

A governed representation of a source record transformed into a canonical comparison format.

Normalization must not silently change the financial meaning of the source record.

## 4.5 Reconciliation Scope

A declared set of records and rules to be reconciled together.

A scope may be defined by:

- Source pair.
- Source group.
- Merchant.
- Tenant.
- Financial account.
- Currency.
- Time interval.
- Settlement period.
- Transaction category.
- Jurisdiction.
- Reconciliation purpose.
- Other registered dimensions.

## 4.6 Reconciliation Run

A uniquely identifiable execution of a reconciliation scope against a particular source-data and policy snapshot.

## 4.7 Reconciliation Batch

A logical group of source records processed under a common ingestion or reconciliation boundary.

A batch is not necessarily a single accounting period or settlement cycle.

## 4.8 Matching Candidate

A potential relationship between two or more source records that may correspond to the same underlying business or financial activity.

## 4.9 Match Group

A governed grouping of source records that have been matched under an approved reconciliation rule.

## 4.10 Discrepancy

A detected difference, missing relationship, unexpected record, or unresolved condition that violates or cannot yet satisfy a reconciliation rule.

## 4.11 Reconciliation Case

A canonical record representing the lifecycle of a reconciliation result, including its evidence, discrepancy classification, assigned ownership, investigation, and resolution.

## 4.12 Resolution Action

An authorized action intended to resolve a discrepancy.

Examples may include:

- Request authoritative status verification.
- Request a corrected source record.
- Initiate an approved adjustment.
- Request a refund review.
- Request a settlement investigation.
- Correct a mapping.
- Re-run reconciliation.
- Close a false-positive case with evidence.

## 4.13 Resolution Evidence

The evidence establishing the outcome of a resolution action.

## 4.14 Reconciliation Snapshot

An immutable or explicitly versioned representation of the source data and rules used in a reconciliation run.

## 4.15 Reconciliation Rule

A versioned, governed definition of which records should be compared, how they should be matched, which differences are acceptable, and what outcomes should be produced.

## 4.16 Reconciliation Control

A registered invariant or control used to detect or prevent an unacceptable financial inconsistency.

## 4.17 Financial Provenance

The traceable lineage connecting a reconciled record to its source, transformations, matching decisions, and resulting evidence.

## 4.18 Reconciliation Confidence

A declared measure of the strength of a match where the matching strategy is not purely deterministic.

Confidence is not a substitute for mandatory evidence or approval.

## 4.19 Reconciliation Coverage

The proportion or scope of expected records, balances, and relationships for which the required reconciliation has been performed and its outcome established.

## 4.20 Reconciliation Closure

The governed conclusion that a reconciliation case or run has reached its permitted final outcome.

Closure does not imply that the underlying financial transaction has been changed.

## 5.1 Namespace

Proposed domain prefix:

`UCOS-MKT-FRC`

`MPS-020-GAP`

`ucos.marketplace.financial-reconciliation.*`

These identifiers remain provisional.

## 5.2 Core Identifiers

The model must distinguish:

- Reconciliation Source ID.
- Source Record ID.
- Source Record Version.
- Reconciliation Scope ID.
- Reconciliation Batch ID.
- Reconciliation Run ID.
- Reconciliation Case ID.
- Matching Candidate ID.
- Match Group ID.
- Discrepancy ID.
- Resolution Action ID.
- Resolution Evidence ID.
- Reconciliation Rule ID.
- Reconciliation Rule Version.
- Financial Account Reference.
- Payment Reference.
- Refund Reference.
- Settlement Reference.
- Accounting Entry Reference.
- Order Reference.
- Merchant Reference.
- Currency Reference.
- External Transaction Reference.
- Idempotency Key.
- Correlation ID.
- Causation ID.

No identifier may be reused across distinct semantic concepts.

## 5.3 Identity Requirements

Identifiers must:

- Be unique within their declared scope.
- Remain stable throughout their governed lifecycle.
- Avoid encoding sensitive personal or financial data.
- Support distributed processing.
- Preserve external source identity.
- Support migration and historical references.
- Be discoverable through canonical registries where applicable.

# 6. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE

## 6.1 Logical Components

### 6.1.1 Source Registry

Maintains approved source definitions and integration contracts.

### 6.1.2 Source Ingestion Gateway

Receives source records through authorized interfaces.

It must support APIs, events, files, streams, or other registered transport mechanisms.

### 6.1.3 Source Evidence Store

Preserves original source evidence under the applicable integrity, privacy, and retention policies.

### 6.1.4 Normalization Engine

Maps source-specific representations into canonical comparison structures.

### 6.1.5 Reconciliation Scope Manager

Determines which records and rules belong to each reconciliation run.

### 6.1.6 Matching Engine

Identifies deterministic and approved probabilistic relationships between records.

### 6.1.7 Comparison Engine

Evaluates matched records against declared monetary, temporal, identity, status, and relationship rules.

### 6.1.8 Discrepancy Engine

Classifies differences and creates reconciliation cases.

### 6.1.9 Reconciliation Orchestrator

Coordinates multi-source reconciliation runs and their progress.

### 6.1.10 Resolution Coordinator

Initiates authorized resolution requests through canonical domain contracts.

### 6.1.11 Evidence and Lineage Service

Preserves source references, rule versions, matching decisions, and resolution evidence.

### 6.1.12 Reconciliation Query Service

Provides authorized operational and analytical views.

### 6.1.13 Reconciliation Policy Registry

Maintains approved matching rules, tolerances, escalation rules, and closure conditions.

### 6.1.14 Reconciliation Control Tower

Provides operational visibility into coverage, discrepancies, backlogs, unresolved outcomes, and control health.

This is a proposed logical capability. It must be reconciled against any existing UCOS Control Tower or monitoring architecture to prevent duplication.

### 6.1.15 Audit Integration

Records required reconciliation decisions and protected financial actions through the canonical audit capability.
